A domain expert drafts each task from a workflow in their own professional practice. The draft is audited by the review agent and cross-reviewed by two randomly assigned human reviewers, and it enters
CLE
only after clearing both gates. A rejection at either gate returns the task to its author for revision.
For each level, the task designer defines the occupational role and working context, provides the input artefacts, specifies the expected deliverable, and writes a checklist of criteria that a passing submission must satisfy. A task-review agent then audits the draft using a review skill authored and refined by human experts over multiple iterations. Following the skill’s predefined review criteria, the agent checks whether each task meets the benchmark’s design requirements. The review includes checks on format compliance, the authenticity of input files, answer leakage, rubric verifiability, and continual-learning design. The review agent also switches to an actor role and runs the task end to end through the same interface available to an evaluated agent. This real execution verifies that the task functions as intended, poses a realistic and non-trivial challenge, and exhibits a clear progression in difficulty across levels. These checks help keep the benchmark challenging for current agents, leaving room to measure gains from continued learning. Each review returns one of five conference-style verdicts, Strong Accept, Accept, Borderline, Major Revision, or Reject, together with itemised findings and concrete revision suggestions. Task designers revise and resubmit their drafts until they meet the acceptance standard. We provide further details in Appendix
C
.
Tasks receiving Accept or higher proceed to final human review. Each task is assigned two randomly selected reviewers, who independently conduct a full manual review. A task is admitted only if both reviewers accept it; otherwise, it returns to the task designer for revision. The 120 tasks that clear both the automated and human review stages constitute the released benchmark.

Even the best-performing configuration, Claude Code with Opus 5, completes only 42.17% of levels in Trial 1 and 47.67% in Trial 2 (

9

Feedback and revision.
Higher completion in Trial 1 does not necessarily imply larger absolute gains in Trial 2. Of the 17 configurations, 16 achieve higher overall completion in Trial 2, with a median increase of 5.33 percentage points (pp). Although Claude Code with Opus 5 leads in Trial 1 completion, Sonnet 5 shows a larger increase, at 13.17 pp compared with 5.50 pp (
Figure
9
A–B). These results motivate evaluating gains from the additional feedback and revision opportunity alongside performance under a single submission.
Improvements in overall completion do not always extend to later levels of the task ladder. With Sonnet 5, the number of fully completed tasks increases from 8 in Trial 1 to 23 in Trial 2. By contrast, both Qwen3.8-Max configurations show higher cumulative pass rates at L1–L3 but unchanged rates at L4–L5 (
Table
1
). These results motivate examining both how agents improve with feedback and revision and whether those gains extend to later assignments that build on earlier experience.

Resource costs.
Resource comparisons depend on both the completion metric and the resource considered. In Trial 2, Codex with Terra and Sol both achieve 33.17% overall completion, but Terra costs $83.16 and takes 20.20 hours, compared with $210.83 and 28.20 hours for Sol. However, Sol completes 21 full tasks compared with Terra’s 15 (
Table
1
). Equal overall completion thus masks differences in full-task completion, which matter when interpreting total resource use.
Monetary cost and runtime also yield different trade-offs. Hermes-Agent with Hy3 lies on the observed cost–completion frontier but not the runtime–completion frontier, achieving 27.33% completion for $16.18 while requiring 80.30 hours (
Figure
10
A–B). These totals cover complete evaluation runs, whose workloads vary with the levels reached and revisions performed. Together, these results motivate assessing resource use alongside both overall and full-task completion, while treating monetary cost and runtime as separate constraints.

5.1
General Agent Capability Benchmarks
General agent benchmarks evaluate capabilities such as reasoning, information gathering and synthesis, planning, and tool use. These capabilities are assessed through tasks ranging from question answering and software engineering to everyday workflows, with performance measured by answer correctness or successful task completion

Professional workflows bring additional demands on task duration, environment continuity, and outcome verification. Agents’ Last Exam covers expert-developed, long-horizon tasks with verifiable outcomes across multiple industries

[

. WildClawBench runs tasks inside deployed command-line agent harnesses using real tools, combining rule-based checks, environment-state auditing, and model-based judgement to verify outcomes

5.2
Memory and Context Learning Benchmarks
Memory benchmarks assess the retention and use of information from interaction histories. LoCoMo evaluates long-term conversational memory through question answering, event summarisation, and multimodal dialogue generation

. LongMemEval studies reasoning across sessions, tracking changing knowledge, and abstaining when historical evidence is insufficient

[

. CL-bench evaluates the acquisition and application of knowledge supplied in context through expert-authored tasks requiring new domain knowledge, rules, procedures, and patterns inferred from empirical data
[

. These evaluations address both access to prior information and the application of newly acquired knowledge. CLE evaluates knowledge reuse through professional task outcomes, while allowing each harness to determine what to retain and how to use it.
5.3
Experience Accumulation and Reuse Benchmarks
Recent work has introduced benchmarks that evaluate knowledge transfer, memory use, skill evolution, and adaptation over sequences of tasks. LifelongAgentBench constructs skill-grounded, interdependent tasks in database, operating-system, and knowledge-graph environments, with verifiable outcomes and sequential evaluation of knowledge transfer

[

[

Task design.
Human-authored / verified
: every task is human-authored or individually human-verified;
marks mixed provenance such as generated tasks with only sampled human review.
Stateful env.
: the agent interacts with a mutable web, app, API, OS, database, or service environment, rather than only local static files or final-answer strings;
marks environments available for only part of the tasks.
Multi-Modal
: at least one task includes a non-text input the agent must process, such as images, screenshots, audio, video, or visually grounded documents.
Learning protocol.
Tiered tasks
: tasks unlock in an ordered curriculum;
marks a fixed order without gating, or gating present only in a subset of tasks.
Cross-level reuse
: later levels require artefacts, facts, or strategies produced in earlier levels;
marks settings where earlier work only helps, or where the dependence appears only in a subset of tasks.
Config. attempts
: the protocol grants a configurable per-level submission budget in which a failed attempt returns feedback the agent can act on before resubmitting.
Feedback and grading.
Milestone feedback
reports progress through task stages without disclosing failures on individual evaluation criteria.
Agentic judge
denotes grading by an evaluation agent with tools;
indicates LLM-based grading without tool use.
Audit trail
provides access to judgements on individual criteria, supporting evidence, or evaluator logs;
indicates task-level pass/fail results with execution logs only.
6
Conclusion
We introduced the Continual Learning Exam (
CLE
), a benchmark for evaluating continual learning in realistic human–AI cowork settings.
CLE
comprises 120 human-authored and human-verified tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder that connects successive assignments through reusable information and artefacts. Stateful environments and human-defined rubrics support task execution and verification throughout each ladder. Across 17 agent configurations with fixed model parameters, the best-performing system completes only 47.67% of levels, even with diagnostic feedback and an opportunity for revision. Feedback and revision improve most configurations, but these gains do not consistently extend to completing entire task ladders.
CLE
remains challenging for current models and agent harnesses, providing a setting for developing and evaluating methods that acquire, retain, and reuse experience to improve performance across successive assignments.

Appendix C
Agent Auto Review with Feedback
We use a task-review agent to conduct the initial review of each task draft and provide feedback to its author for revision before final review by two human reviewers.
Human expertise as a review skill.
The auto-review process follows criteria derived from human expertise in task design. We consolidate review criteria developed and iteratively refined by the benchmark development team into a reusable review skill. The skill specifies what the review agent should inspect, how to apply the review criteria, and how to organise its findings into actionable feedback for the task contributor.
Feedback-driven human–agent iteration.
As illustrated in

7
and
11

It returns evidence-grounded findings that identify the affected component, explain why it violates a design criterion, and suggest a concrete direction for revision. Task authors use the feedback to revise their drafts and submit them for another round of review. This cycle can repeat throughout task construction.
Figure 11:
Review-Agent Interface Used during Task Construction.
A task contributor uploads a complete five-level task together with its supporting files and receives a conference-style verdict, review comments, and revision suggestions after the review agent completes its execution and design checks.
Final human review.
Tasks receiving an automated verdict of Accept or Strong Accept proceed to independent review by two human reviewers. A task is admitted to the benchmark only if both reviewers accept it; otherwise, it returns to the author for revision. This separation of roles combines the coverage and consistency of agent-assisted review with the contextual judgement and accountability of human experts. The development team can refine the review skill based on recurring issues identified during task construction, allowing lessons from earlier review rounds to improve feedback for later task authors.

article.headline: 持续学习基准CLE：最强系统仅通过47.7%关卡
article.lede: 50余位专家做出120个五级任务阶梯，17套前沿智能体配置中最好的一套也只通过47.67%的关卡。
article.problem: 现有智能体基准大多把任务彼此独立地出题和打分，衡量的是单题解题能力，而不是智能体能否靠积累的经验变得更强。记忆类基准（如 LoCoMo、LongMemEval）考察历史信息的检索与问答，不检验记住的东西是否改善了后续任务执行。带持久状态的工作流基准能模拟跨应用连续操作，但状态延续本身并不等于能力随经验增长，要测「越做越好」就需要一条受控反馈下的任务序列。
article.method: 作者提出 Continual Learning Exam（CLE）：120 个人工撰写并人工审核的任务，每个任务是一个五级阶梯，共 600 关，覆盖 12 个职业领域的 89 种岗位；关卡之间通过工具与技能、数据依赖、策略、用户偏好、领域知识五类可迁移知识相连，后一关建立在前一关的产物与经验之上。环境包含 23,981 个真实输入文件（77 种扩展名）、19 个有状态模拟应用共 1,024 个 API，评分依据 16,125 条人工撰写的细则，由一个多轮评估智能体在隔离容器中取证核验。实验对比两种协议：K=1 每关只能提交一次且无反馈；K=2 首次失败后返回基于细则类别的诊断反馈，并允许修改后重交一次。
article.results: 在 17 套 harness–模型配置上，最好的 Claude Code + Opus 5 在 K=1 下通过 42.17% 的关卡，K=2 下升至 47.67%，完整通关五级的任务仅占 23.33%（28/120）。17 套配置中 16 套在加入诊断反馈与重交后提升，中位增益 5.33 个百分点；Claude Sonnet 5 提升最大，为 13.17 个百分点（完整通关任务从 8 个增至 23 个）。整体上半程与后半程落差明显：K=2 下各配置的关卡通过率中位数在 L1 为 62.50%，到 L5 仅 8.33%；在六个共用基座模型上，Hermes-Agent 相对 OpenClaw 的平均优势从 K=1 的 9.56 个百分点扩大到 K=2 的 11.42 个百分点。评估智能体与人工标注在细则条目级别的一致率为 96.86%，重复三次评分的一致率为 99.46%（553/556）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「经验复用」从抽象口号变成了可打分的任务阶梯，为后训练和 harness 设计提供了明确的靶子：目前前沿智能体在单关尚可，跨关卡累积经验几乎失效。数据集也可直接用于后训练，以强化模型的持续学习能力。
article.limitations: 实验中模型参数全程冻结，测的只是 harness 层面的非参数学习，标题里的「RSI」对应的是论文自设能力分级中的 T4/T5，本次评测并未覆盖。K=1 与 K=2 的对比把诊断反馈和额外重交混在一起，论文自己也指出，仍缺少一个把 harness 重置到初始状态、其余条件固定的对照来分离跨任务知识保留的贡献；此外后期关卡的统计样本很小（K=2 下 L4→L5 的中位分母仅 14 个任务，17 套配置中有 7 套不足 10 个），成本也不低（Opus 5 在 K=2 下单次评测耗资 720.56 美元、58.90 小时）。
article.figure_caption_zh: CLE 概览：每个任务由五个前后衔接、靠可迁移知识串联的关卡组成，智能体通过 API 操作有状态应用，评估智能体依据人工撰写的评分细则核验提交结果；K=1 时每关仅一次提交且无诊断反馈，K=2 时首次失败后给出反馈并允许再提交一次。

email_papers.title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model
email_papers.abstract: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.
email_papers.content: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.

article.headline: 用坑点预判世界模型引导黑盒智能体
article.lede: PAWM在有限多步未来内预判失败，仅在可能踩坑时介入，以引导黑盒LLM智能体。
article.problem: 黑盒大语言模型智能体擅长长程推理与精确动作生成，但对特定任务环境如何演化缺乏内化知识。已有世界模型通常逐步预测下一观测，成本高且信息有限，因为单步观测提供的任务指导有限，而且并非每一步都需要预见。论文因此追问：面向智能体任务，世界模型应当预测什么、又该在何时被调用。
article.method: 作者提出坑点预判世界模型PAWM，在有限多步未来内预判潜在坑点，并选择性地在坑点出现时介入，预测即将发生的失败以引导智能体避开。PAWM分两阶段训练：先在带智能体坑点标签的合成数据上做监督微调，再与黑盒LLM进行GRPO协同训练，以在目标环境中进一步优化。
article.results: 以Claude Sonnet 4.5为黑盒智能体时，PAWM在ScienceWorld上提升24.3%，在WebArena-Lite上提升7.7%，并优于多种基线；论文未给出其他基准或绝对分数。
article.why_it_matters: 它把世界模型的用途从逐步预测观测转向选择性预判失败，为黑盒LLM智能体提供了一种更聚焦的环境特定引导方式。若能在更多环境复现，这类介入机制可能降低长程任务中的试错成本。
article.limitations: 论文仅在ScienceWorld和WebArena-Lite两个基准上报告结果，跨模型、跨环境的泛化能力仍待验证。选择性介入若漏判坑点可能失效，原文未给出漏判率或额外调用成本。

email_papers.title: Build, Don't Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players
email_papers.abstract: Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback, their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days AutoTavern built TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of TavernAgent, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games. TavernAgent plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard's measure, its last 20 records average a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server's ten highest-rated players on every statistic (2.34, 59%). TavernBench, 960 tasks in 40 scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player: TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern.

Build, Don’t Play:
Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a
Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players
Changlian Ma

Abstract
Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own
against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and
battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present
AutoTavern
, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed
research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback,
their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days
AutoTavern

TavernGym
, the

TavernAgent
, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games.

placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server’s ten highest-rated players on
every statistic (2.34, 59%).
TavernBench

scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player:
TavernAgent

91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in
0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no

https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern

1
Introduction
Figure 1:
TavernBench
at a glance.
(a) Accuracy (%) per capability, with the play score
counting only answers within the second a live turn allows per decision; numbers:
TavernAgent
. (b) Play score against seconds per

Table
4
.
Games have long served as milestones for artificial intelligence, from Go and chess
(
Silver et al., 2016
;
Silver et al., 2018
)
to StarCraft II, Dota 2, poker, Mahjong and
Stratego
(
Vinyals et al., 2019
;
Berner et al., 2019
;
Brown and Sandholm, 2019
;
Li et al., 2020
;
Perolat et al., 2022
)
.
Each of these systems was the product of a large team of human experts who built the
environment, designed the learning algorithm and debugged the countless ways in which a
simulated training world differs from the real game. Today, LLM agents write and run much of
the code behind such systems, and a growing line of work asks whether they can automate the
research itself
(
Lu et al., 2024
;
Yamada et al., 2026
;
Wijk et al., 2025
;
Srikanth et al., 2026
)
.
Existing evidence, however, comes from benchmark tasks or paper reviews; it remains open whether
agents can carry a hard, real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against
people, where performance is ultimately measured in the real game.
We study this question in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, Blizzard’s eight-player auto-battler, played by millions. Each
turn a player spends gold in a randomly stocked tavern to buy, sell and position minions, then
fights an automatic battle against one opponent; players are eliminated in turn until one
remains. The game combines stochastic shops and battles, hidden information about seven
opponents, a shared card pool, a horizon of hundreds of decisions with a reward only at the end,
and a content base of nearly one thousand interacting cards, heroes and trinkets that changes
with every patch. No faithful simulator of the live game has been available, and existing AI
work either advises human players or studies simplified versions of the game
(
Section
2
).
We present
AutoTavern
, a self-improving research system in which a team of specialised LLM
research agents iterates a model autonomously (
Figure
2
). Its principle is
reality-anchored self-improvement. Agents for the environment, training, opponent modelling,
evaluation and deployment communicate only through a typed, versioned research memory; five
verification gates stand between every claim and that memory; and live games on the real ladder
close the loop, turning discrepancies between simulation and reality into fixes of rules, input
encodings and opponent models. The same feedback improves the agents’ research process: errors
they catch become lessons in the memory, loaded by every later session, or new gates, so each
iteration starts from a better world and a better method. Because the loop does not pay for the
same mistake twice, it took the agent from its first version to the level of the server’s best
players in 20 days. The human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. Over 20 days the
framework produced:
•
AutoTavern
, a self-improving research system in which LLM research agents
improve a model, its training world and their own research process from the feedback of a real
environment. In 20 days it ran about 10,000 experiments and delivered 23 agent versions with 418
human messages in all, and the errors it caught became lessons and gates that changed how it
works (
Sections
4
and
8
).
•
TavernGym
, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the
live game: all 978 game objects of patch 36.6.3, deterministic, 190–280 complete
eight-player games per second on a single core, and aligned rule by rule with real games
(
Section
5
). We will open-source it.
•
TavernAgent
, the first Battlegrounds AI to play complete games
on the live ladder, and the strongest. Its 23 successive versions, each passing an evaluation gate, raised the
first-place rate against reality-calibrated opponents from 1.9% to 41.5% (random legal play
and a scripted bot: 0%), and on the live ladder the deployed agent climbed by itself from a rating of
6,000 to about 15,000; on the public leaderboard’s measure its recent results are better than
the server’s ten highest-rated players’ on every statistic (
Section
6
and
Appendix
D
).
•
TavernBench
, the first decision benchmark for Battlegrounds: 960 tasks in
40 scenarios across eight categories, labelled by the simulator
(
Section
7
). We will open-source it.
The benchmark bears out our title (
Figure
1
): asked to make the decisions
themselves, the LLMs that built a ladder-level agent fall well short of the system they built, and
decide far too slowly for a live turn (
Section
7
). LLMs build far better than they play.
Figure 2:
Overview of
AutoTavern
, a self-improving research system.
Six LLM research
agents share one research memory and run three loops: training (minutes), research (hours) and the live ladder (days). The human sets
goals, rules on ambiguous mechanics and presses the keys the AI names. Chart: first-place rate of
the 23 delivered
TavernAgent
versions on one simulator build and three unseen seeds (24,576 games
per point).
2
Related Work
AI for Hearthstone and Battlegrounds.
Research on Hearthstone has focused on the two-player constructed mode
(
Dockhorn and Mostaghim, 2019
)
. For Battlegrounds,
Zolboot et al. (2022)
built a
Monte Carlo tree search assistant on a simplified simulator, evaluated on the first turns of
recorded games; an open-source simulator for reinforcement learning omits heroes
(
Elimelech, 2019
)
; community tools such as Firestone and Bob’s Buddy simulate
only the combat phase to show win odds
(
Zero-to-Heroes, 2017
;
HSReplay.net, 2020
)
; and DeepBattler uses an
LLM to give players advice during live games without an environment or an agent of its own
(
William-Dic, 2025
)
. None reproduces the full live game or trains an agent that plays it
(
Table
2
).
Large-scale game RL.
Superhuman systems for Go, StarCraft II, Dota 2, Honor of Kings, poker, Mahjong, DouDizhu and
Stratego
(
Silver et al., 2016
;
Vinyals et al., 2019
;
Berner et al., 2019
;
Ye et al., 2020
;
Brown and Sandholm, 2019
;
Li et al., 2020
;
Zha et al., 2021
;
Perolat et al., 2022
)
combine self-play or human data with large-scale training and start from an existing
environment. We use a standard learner, PPO
(
Schulman et al., 2017
)
with a transformer
(
Vaswani et al., 2017
)
, and focus on building and correcting the training world itself,
which here is done by agents.
LLM research agents.
The AI Scientist automates idea generation, experiments and paper writing
(
Lu et al., 2024
;
Yamada et al., 2025
;
Yamada et al., 2026
)
; Eureka and AlphaEvolve use
LLMs to propose reward functions and programs that an automatic evaluator scores
(
Ma et al., 2024
;
Novikov et al., 2025
)
; MLAgentBench, MLE-bench, RE-Bench and PaperBench
measure agents on machine-learning tasks
(
Huang et al., 2024
;
Chan et al., 2025
;
Wijk et al., 2025
;
Starace et al., 2025
)
; and recent
systems orchestrate coding agents or improve their own scaffolds
(
Lange et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Srikanth et al., 2026
)
;
Kirgis et al. (2026)
find that
agents complete the engineering of open-ended projects but struggle with the research questions.
AutoTavern
differs in what improves and in how the improvement is judged. Its agents improve
their research process through a memory of lessons and new verification gates rather than by
rewriting their own code. Progress is measured on a live ladder against people, a reality loop
re-anchors simulator and opponents to live games against proxy drift, and verification gates stand
between every claim and the shared memory against false findings.
LLMs as game players.
Benchmarks evaluate LLMs on text, puzzle, video and strategic games
(
Wu et al., 2024
;
Duan et al., 2024
;
Costarelli et al., 2024
;
Paglieri et al., 2025
;
Guertler et al., 2025
;
Hu et al., 2025
)
and on poker decisions
(
Zhuang et al., 2025
)
.
TavernBench
adds a stochastic multiplayer
game of economy and combat with answers verified by a simulator, a strong specialised agent as reference
and a real-time view: the decisions a model gets right within a live turn’s time.
3
Hearthstone Battlegrounds
A game has eight players, each with a hero, 30–40 health and a Hero Power. Every turn consists of
a
recruit
phase and a
combat
phase. In the recruit phase the player spends gold
(3 on turn 1, rising to 10) to buy minions from a tavern of random offers drawn from a pool
shared by all players, sell minions, refresh or freeze the offers, upgrade the tavern tier
(1–7, unlocking stronger minions), play cards from the hand, use the Hero Power and arrange
the warband of up to seven minions. Three copies of a minion merge into a golden version that
offers a discovery from the next tier. Battlecries, deathrattles, auras, magnetic attachments,
tavern spells, trinkets and other mechanics interact across turns. In combat, the warband fights
one opponent automatically, with random targets; the loser takes damage, and players are
eliminated until one remains. The outcome is the placement, 1 to 8.
We model a game as a partially observable stochastic game with a terminal utility of the
placement. A player observes its own state and, for each opponent, only the public leaderboard
and the warband last seen in combat. The current patch (36.6.3) contains 978 game objects: minions, heroes, trinkets, spells and
other cards. A game lasts about 15 turns and about 450 atomic actions per player.
4
The
AutoTavern
System
AutoTavern
is a self-improving research system: LLM research agents improve a model against an
environment they cannot simulate exactly and, from the same feedback, their own research process.
Its central idea is
reality-anchored self-improvement
: every proxy the agents optimise (the
simulator, the opponent model, the exams) is re-anchored to the real game at a fixed cadence, every
claim must survive a check designed to refute it before it changes the shared state, and the
errors these checks catch change the process that made them.

False

later work.
AutoTavern

Self-improvement closes the loop: an iteration updates the artifacts and, when it catches an error,

, so that later iterations do not repeat it.
Role agents.
Long-running LLM research agents own the research roles (
Figure
2
,
Table
5
). A
research lead
chooses the next problem and dispatches work. An
environment agent
implements and verifies rules and repairs discrepancies found in live
games, and an
opponent agent
builds human-like opponents from human statistics and live
games. A
training agent
designs recipes and curricula, an
evaluation agent
measures, re-checks and audits, and a
deployment agent
maintains the client controller and
the models’ input formats. Short-lived workers run probes and implement features.
Typed research memory.
Agents never talk directly; they read and write versioned,
typed stores: a ledger of numbered findings in which a correction is a new entry pointing back, a
registry of rule decisions and open questions, a hand-over note, an experiment registry, and a
store of lessons loaded at the start of every session. A finding is never edited away, so the
memory records how conclusions changed as well as what they are.
Verification gates.
Five gates stand between an idea and the shared state:
•
G1
build: a code change passes the full test suite before it reaches the shared build;
•
G2
contract: every model is tied to the simulator build it was trained on, and the
controller refuses a model trained for another;
•
G3
comparison: models are compared only within one build, over several seeds;
•
G4
delivery: a candidate is delivered only after a re-check on seeds it was not selected on;
•
G5
reality: delivered models play the live ladder, and their games are replayed in the simulator.
The gates acted throughout: candidates were held back after re-checks, findings were revised by
later ones, and live games led to 184 fixes of rules, input encodings, the client controller and
the opponents, counted in
Appendix
A
.
Reality loop.
The controller logs every live game; game records are linked to the
agent’s decisions; the evaluation agent replays real combats and real recruit steps in
TavernGym
and
reports where simulation and reality part; the responsible agent fixes rules, input encodings or
opponents, and the next iteration trains on the corrected world (
Section
8
).
Self-improvement.
The loop improves the research process as well as its products. A
finding that overturns an earlier one is recorded as a correction pointing back. A mistake the
agents trace to their own method becomes a lesson that every later session loads at its start, or
a new gate. Of the six errors in
Section
8
, two became gates (the re-check on unseen
seeds,
G4
, and the comparison of the two input encoders in
G2
) and two became
standing rules (reseed copied games, and calibrate opponents on those the learner meets). Because a
caught error changes the process and not only the current result, the loop does not pay for the
same mistake twice: over the 20 days the 23 delivered versions raised the first-place rate from
1.9% to 41.5% (
Figure
2
).
4.1
The iteration cycle
Algorithm
1
shows one iteration. The cycle runs at three time scales: policy updates every
few seconds to minutes (the training loop), experiments and findings within hours (the research
loop), and live games feeding back into the environment within days (the ladder loop). A
scheduler runs the registered experiments within a resource budget and keeps their successors
queued, so the loop runs for days without a human present. The human researcher enters at two
points only: setting goals, and ruling on mechanics that the game data leave ambiguous.

4.2

versions passed the delivery gate. The human typed 418 messages over the whole project, 0.6% of

for progress or a report, 24% set or change a goal, 11% concern resources, 8% approve a proposal,
6% correct an agent, 5% rule on a game mechanic and 5% report live games.

5
TavernGym
: Reproducing the Real Game
Design.
TavernGym
is a Rust engine with thin Python bindings. One effect context
serves the recruit and the combat phase, so every card is a table of event hooks that work the
same in both; the state is an arena of entities, cheap to copy and serialisable; all randomness
comes from one seeded generator, so a seed and an action sequence reproduce a game bit for bit.
Card data are generated from the game’s own files, later patches are overlays, and a rule hash
identifies every build.
Fidelity to the live game.
All 978 objects of patch 36.6.3 are implemented. 375
verification records and 220 confirmed rule decisions document how each mechanic was checked, and
unit tests, fuzzing with invariant checks after every action and an exact legal-action mask guard
the implementation. Live games led to 46 fixes of rules and card data and 73 of input encodings,
found by replaying live turns, combats and offers in the engine (
Sections
8
and
A
).
Speed and interface.
A complete eight-player game with scripted bots takes 3.6–5.3 ms
on one core (190–280 games per second), and a late-game combat 13–19 µs (52–76
thousand per second). The RL interface exposes 245 discrete actions with an exact legal mask, a
player-view observation with only the information visible in the real client, batched
environments and exact save and restore of running games for lookahead and replays.

TavernAgent
: Learning to Play the Live Game
Model and training.
TavernAgent
is an entity transformer: each own minion, hand card,
tavern offer, pending choice and opponent is a token (up to 56), a card is represented by an
identity embedding, static features and an embedding of its rule text, and a pointer head
produces the 245 masked action logits next to value and placement heads (d=384, 8 layers, 8
heads, 18M parameters, the best of three sizes in an early comparison,
Table
8
).
It is trained with PPO
(
Schulman et al., 2017
)
on about one million
decisions per iteration with a terminal placement utility; each
training stage of 300 iterations covers about 310 million decisions (570 thousand games) and
starts from the previous stage under a KL anchor.
Reality-calibrated opponents.
Rather than self-play, the learner faces seven
library seats
: each turn, a seat takes a board (with hand and hidden counters) from a library
built from statistics of top human players and recalibrated, turn by turn, to the opponents the
agent actually met in live games; exam libraries are never used for training. This was the largest
single gain: from the same checkpoint and with the same budget, training against the
calibrated libraries raises the first-place rate from 20.9% to 27.2% on the main exam and from
10.3% to 13.5% on the harder one (
Table
3
).

the first-place rate rises from 1.9% to 41.5% and the average placement from 3.40 to 2.33
(

Live ladder.
The deployed agent plays the live ranked ladder by itself: the
controller feeds the live game’s state to the policy in the environment’s own encoding, the policy
decides every operation, and a human presses the shortcut key the AI names, a feature of the game’s
official plug-in (
Appendix
D
). Most delivered versions entered this loop, so the agent’s
iterations are also its climb on the ladder (
Figures
3
and
10
): over 392 games on
days 5–18 of the project the rating rose from 6,000 to 14,007. Games in which the client failed (96, flagged by
the controller’s logs, never by the result;
Appendix
D
) measure the client rather than the
agent; without them the average placement is 3.22, with 16.4% first places and 77.1% top-four finishes. The latest versions
(TA-19–23) averaged 2.37 with 32.6% first places and 91.3% top-four. A problem the ladder exposed
paused testing until the loop fixed it (
Figure
3
). By the end of the study the agent was rated about
15,000, in the server’s top 100; on the public leaderboard’s measure its last 20 records average
1.60 against 2.34 for the ten highest-rated players, better on every statistic, with no sign of
a plateau (
Table
11
).

7
TavernBench
: Build, Don’t Play
Design.
TavernBench
asks whether general-purpose LLMs can make the decisions that
TavernAgent
makes: 960 tasks in 40 scenarios and eight categories (
Table
13
). A task
gives the player-visible state as text, the rule text of every card shown, an objective and an
answer format. Labels come from
TavernGym
: rule tasks execute the actions; combat tasks simulate
4,096 combats; short-term decisions are scored by the simulated win rate of the next combat after
the chosen option (correct within three points of the best); strategic decisions are turn
plans cut from natural games (upgrade, buy, refresh or save the Gold), each played out 128 times
by an earlier version (TA-21) and kept when one is better by a quarter place and two standard
errors; hero and trinket choices are scored against
top human players (
Appendix

Results.
Table
4
and
Figure
1
give four findings.
The system the LLM agents built is the strongest player.
TavernAgent
answers 91% of the play tasks;
the best LLM playing directly, GPT-6 Astra, 63%, the Claude models 52–53%, GPT-6.1 Sol 46%,
Gemini 3.8 Flash 44% and the remaining models 22–40%. It is near-perfect on combat, positioning,
ordering and targets, where LLMs must simulate fights in their head; with
TavernGym
as a tool they
recover most of that gap (GPT-6 Astra 62% to 97%,
Table
15
).
Latency rules out live play for the LLMs.
A late recruit turn lasts about two minutes and holds up to about a hundred
operations, so a decision that takes more than a second cannot be played.
TavernAgent
answers a task in 0.03 s
(
Table
4
). Gateway timings are not
comparable across providers, so we time every LLM on one standard footing
(
Artificial Analysis, 2026
)
:
the median time to its first answer token, which includes the model’s typical thinking, plus the
task’s answer at its median output speed. Their median task takes 1.4–26 s, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
without reasoning 0.9 s. Within the one-second budget
TavernAgent
keeps 90%,
DeepSeek its 26% and Jev its 37%, and every other LLM falls to 0%. Speed alone would not suffice: a turn chains dozens of decisions into one plan, so a model that errs on a third of
them does not play a third worse, it loses the plan; per-decision errors compound over a turn
rather than average out.
Reading rules is not playing.
The frontier LLMs execute rules well (GPT-6 Astra 95%, Claude Opus 92%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 90%), yet fall well short on
the play tasks built from the same rules: knowing what each card does is not knowing which play
wins.
Judging a game is not computing a fight.
On the turn plans scored by playing the game
out,
TavernAgent
’s policy answers 75% in 0.03 s; the best LLM reaches 54% with seconds of
reasoning, the others 19–43%.
Its policy also leads on the choices cut from natural games (81%).
8
Lessons from Self-Improvement
The reality loop and the gates caught errors that no simulated metric revealed. We report six,
each found and corrected inside the loop; four of them also changed the research process.
(i) Copied games leak the future.
A search over game copies appeared to add 23.6 points of
first-place rate; the copies carried the random-number state, so the search saw the real future
shop and combat outcomes. Reseeded per sample, the gain vanished (
−
0.65
±
1.14
-0.65\pm 1.14
points).
(ii) Two errors can cancel.
The exam once matched live results only because its late-game
opponents were too strong while the agent’s growth was overstated; once both were fixed, the exam
first-place rate rose to 43–49%.
(iii) Winner’s curse.
The best of many snapshots overstated its gain (+1.2–2.1 points on
selection seeds,
−
-
0.7 on unseen ones); hence gate
G4
.
(iv) Calibrate to the opponents you meet.
Measure a library on the opponents the learner
meets, not on uniform draws.
(v) The ladder catches what simulation praises.
TA-10 nearly doubled its predecessor’s
exam first-place rate (24.2% against 12.8%), yet on the ladder the rating fell
from 8,968 to 7,658 within 32 games, 18 of which also had client failures (
Figure
3
). The
loop paused live testing, traced the fall to client failures and an early- and mid-game
weakness the exam had hidden, and retrained; TA-11 resumed the climb.
(vi) Two encoders drift apart.
Replays of live games showed the agent selling its whole
warband on one turn far more often than in simulation; one input flag was encoded differently by
the controller and the simulator after a trinket choice. The fix added a bit-level comparison of
both encoders to gate
G2
.
9
Conclusion
We presented
AutoTavern
, a self-improving research system: LLM research agents improve a
model, its training world and their own research process from the feedback of a real environment,
in a closed loop of training, research and live games. In 20 days it built
TavernGym
, a faithful,
full-content reproduction of Hearthstone Battlegrounds, and
TavernAgent
, which plays complete games
on the live ladder at the level of the server’s best players. Asked to make the same decisions
directly, frontier LLMs, including the models that built the system, fall well short of it and
decide far too slowly for a live turn: LLM agents build far better than they play. We will
open-source
TavernBench
and
TavernGym
at
https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern
;
limitations and ethics are discussed in
Appendix
D
.

The
AutoTavern
system in detail
Conventions.
Days count from day 1 of the project; all work targets patch 36.6.3.
Agents.
The research ran as several long-lived agent sessions inside our agentic
research framework, each owning one role, plus short-lived sub-agents that a session dispatched
for a probe, a feature with its own test gate, or a check.

priority, dependencies and successors).

Appendix B
TavernGym
details
Figure 4:
TavernGym
.
The Rust engine, its Python bindings and the programs built on them; the client controller feeds the live game to the agent in the same encoding.
Architecture.
TavernGym
is a Rust workspace of two crates: the game engine (about 63
thousand lines, of which 27 thousand are card scripts) and thin Python bindings whose
batched calls release the interpreter lock. Recruit phase and combat share one effect context; every
card is a table of event hooks; the state is an arena of entities with integer identifiers that is
cheap to copy and serialisable to JSON; all randomness comes from one seeded generator.
A source hash identifies every build and a rule hash every rule set, and a checkpoint trained
under another rule hash is not resumed.
Content.
The card table is generated from the game’s data files; later
patches are applied as an overlay. All 978 objects of patch 36.6.3 (minions, heroes and their Hero Powers, spells, trinkets and
other cards) are implemented.
Verification.
Each mechanic was checked against the game data and official and
community sources and the check recorded (375 records); confirmed rulings go to the decision
registry (220) and unresolved ones to a list of open questions. Every mechanic has a unit test, and fuzzing plays random legal actions and checks state
invariants after every action.
RL interface.
245 discrete actions (end turn, refresh, freeze, upgrade, Hero Power,
buy, sell, play or magnetize a hand card to a position, move a minion, choose among offers), each
with an exact legality mask. The observation contains only what the player sees, with opponents’
warbands as last seen in combat. A batched environment runs many eight-player games at once, and
running games can be saved and restored exactly.
Performance.
One core plays 190–280 complete eight-player games per second with scripted
bots and 52–76 thousand late-game combats per second.

Entity tokens, a card representation that includes the card’s rule text, a transformer trunk and three heads.
Architecture.
Each own minion, hand card, tavern offer, pending choice and opponent is a
token (at most 56, plus one global token). A card is the sum of an identity embedding, a projection of
its static features (type, tier, stats, tribe, keywords, mechanics) and a projection of an embedding
of its rule text, which gives rare cards a sensible start. Attachments (magnetic minions, Dark Gifts)
are added to their minion’s token, and the game-wide state (trinkets, persistent effects and
counters) is pooled into the global token. An opponent token holds the public leaderboard
information, the pooled warband last seen in combat and the result of that combat. Inputs are
compressed with a symmetric logarithm. A pointer head scores the 245 masked actions; a value head and
an auxiliary placement head share the trunk (d=384, 8 layers, 8 heads, 18M parameters).

Opponent libraries.
A library entry is one seat’s board at one turn, with its hand and
hidden counters. Libraries were first built from statistics of top
human players (tribe shares, upgrade curves, purchase rates, warband strength by turn) and recorded
games; each turn a library seat takes an entry that matches a target strength curve. They were then
recalibrated to the opponents the agent actually met on the client: strength is measured on the
opponents the learner meets, not on entries drawn uniformly, and a graded set of libraries runs from
aligned ones to harder ones whose late boards carry venomous minions, hands and ceiling builds. Exam
libraries are never used for training; training uses twins built
the same way from other sources.
Training stages.
Learning started from scratch on a simplified rule set, moved to the full
content, then to the player’s view, then to a first-place goal against opponents fitted to human
statistics, and then to library opponents. Later versions are chains of 300-iteration stages (about 310
million decisions and 570 thousand games each), each starting from the previous stage under a KL
anchor for its first 100 iterations. Later stages also used a graded ladder of training libraries; a version is delivered only after
a re-check on unseen seeds.

Appendix D
Live deployment
Setting and ethics.
All games were played in the solo mode of the live game on the
authors’ own account, without commercial purpose, on days 5–18 of the project. The controller

Scenes.
Every static task starts from a real game state that the environment reshapes for its scenario
(turn, tier, gold, health, and warbands drawn from the current card pool by the scenario’s
filter), with heroes whose Hero Powers have no effect in the scene, so that no hidden effect
changes a label. Strategy and natural-choice tasks are instead
cut from games of the main exam lobby (
Table
3
) at decisions of the kind.
Labels and scoring.
Rule tasks execute the stated actions on copies of the scene. A task
whose outcome involves random numbers is kept only when two or three reseeded copies agree.
Combat tasks use 4,096 simulated combats (the damage-distribution scenario 400 single combats), and
arrangement tasks 2,048 combats per arrangement. A probability triple is correct when its most likely
outcome matches and its Brier score is at most 0.1 (graded
1
−
Brier
/
2
1-\text{Brier}/2
).
Decision tasks label every option by 1,024 combats after it. A task is kept when the choice matters:
the best option beats the median one by 5–8 points of win rate, and at most a quarter of the
options are within three points of the best. An answer is correct when its option is within three
points of the best, and its graded score is its win rate over the best one’s.
Strategy tasks are cut at the first decision of a turn in natural games of the main-exam lobby. Four
plans (upgrade the Tavern; buy the minion the labeller prefers; refresh first; end the turn and keep
the Gold), each legal in the state, are each played out 128 times by the labeller (TA-21), which
plays the rest of the turn and the game as it sees fit. A task is kept when the best plan’s mean
placement beats the second-best’s by 0.25 places and two standard errors of the difference, and the
letters A–D rotate so that each is the answer about equally often (chance 25%). Ending the turn is
never the best plan; the contest is among the other three. The labels are outcomes of play, not the
labelling agent’s preferences: answering with its own policy, the labeller (TA-21) reaches 73% on
these tasks, the evaluated TA-23 75%, and the first version TA-1 57%.
Hero and trinket tasks use the average placement of top human players in public statistics and keep
offers whose best option leads by 0.1 (heroes) or 0.15 (trinkets) places.

triples, combat order, keywords, damage), the player-visible state, the rule text of every card

All models were queried through their APIs with the benchmark’s

evaluation

Latency.

•

distribution) and 0–60 for each Attack and Health; legality tasks: legal or illegal for each action.

article.headline: LLM智能体20天自建酒馆战棋AI，超越顶尖玩家
article.lede: 六个LLM研究智能体共享研究记忆，20天自建完整模拟器与PPO智能体，天梯分从6000升至约15000。
article.problem: 现有关于LLM科研智能体的证据多来自基准任务或论文评审，尚不清楚它们能否把一个困难的真实问题从原始数据推进到能与人类对抗的系统。炉石传说酒馆战棋是八人自动战斗游戏，商店与战斗随机、存在隐藏信息、近千张卡牌交互，且此前没有忠实复现线上版本的模拟器，已有AI工作要么只给人类建议，要么研究简化版本。
article.method: 作者提出AutoTavern：环境、训练、对手建模、评估、部署等角色的LLM研究智能体只通过带类型的版本化研究记忆通信，每条结论要先过五道验证闸门，线上天梯对局再把模拟与现实的偏差反馈回规则、输入编码和对手模型。对应地构建了TavernGym（Rust引擎，覆盖36.6.3补丁全部978个游戏对象）与用PPO训练的实体Transformer策略TavernAgent，对手不是自我对弈，而是按人类顶尖玩家统计并在线上对局中逐回合重校准的对手库。
article.results: 20天内系统注册约10,000次实验，交付23个智能体版本，人类只发了418条消息（占全部消息0.6%）。在同一模拟器构建与三个未见种子上，第一名率从TA-1的1.9%升到TA-23的41.5%，平均名次3.40降至2.33（每点24,576局）；天梯上392局内评分从6,000升到14,007，按公开排行榜口径其最近20条记录平均名次1.60、80%第一，而服务器评分最高的十位玩家合计为2.34、59%。TavernBench（960题、40个场景）上，TavernAgent答对91%的对局类任务，最好的直接作答LLM为GPT-6 Astra的63%，Claude两个版本52–53%；每决策耗时0.03秒，而LLM中位1.4–26秒，在一秒实时预算内保持90%，其余LLM最高仅26%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「LLM智能体做研究」的检验从基准任务搬到有真实对手的天梯上，并给出一个可复用范式：让智能体优化代理指标的同时，用现实反馈和验证闸门防止代理漂移与假结论。同时它表明LLM智能体的产出可以远超其自身的直接决策能力——建得比玩得好。
article.limitations: 结论建立在单一游戏、单一补丁（36.6.3）和一次20天运行上，训练对手是校准的对手库而非真人；线上对局由人类按AI指定的键执行，天梯评分也受对局数量影响，与顶尖玩家的比较用的是排行榜根据评分变化估算的名次而非真实对局统计。此外388局有效记录中有96局出现客户端故障，TavernAgent在规则执行类任务上未计分（由TavernGym代答），因此它与前沿LLM在「读懂规则」上的差距并未被这项基准直接衡量。
article.figure_caption_zh: AutoTavern总览：六个LLM研究智能体共享一份研究记忆，运行训练（分钟）、研究（小时）与线上天梯（天）三层循环，图表给出23个交付版本在三个未见种子上的第一名率（每点24,576局）。

figure.caption: {Overview of , a self-improving research system.} Six LLM research agents share one research memory and run three loops: training (minutes), research (hours) and the live ladder (days). The human sets goals, rules on ambiguous mechanics and presses the keys the AI names. Chart: first-place rate of the 23 delivered versions on one simulator build and three unseen seeds (24,576 games per point).

email_papers.title: Novel or Not? PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination
email_papers.abstract: Patent examination is a challenging real-world task that requires agents to discover sparse prior art, iteratively refine queries, inspect technical evidence, and produce novelty assessments documented in Office Actions (OAs) across heterogeneous scientific and technical domains. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on static and limited candidate sets, leaving the full search--reasoning--assessment process underexplored. We present PatEx-Gym, the first framework for developing and evaluating agents for patent examination, which integrates three components. First, PatEx-Bench provides 1K realistic examination tasks, two large-scale retrieval corpora containing over 1M patents and 52K scientific papers, and a harness runtime supporting iterative search, document visits, reasoning, and OA generation. Second, we introduce PASS, an annotation-free Prior-Art Agentic Search Trajectory Synthesis framework. Specifically, it exploits document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors to model intra-turn query behavior, inter-turn search progression, and trajectory-level evidence and outcome quality, yielding PatEx-SynData. Third, we train PatEx-Agent at the 4B scale via supervised fine-tuning on the curated trajectories, establishing a lightweight baseline. Extensive experiments show that final decision accuracy alone does not fully reflect examination quality, while prior-art discovery remains difficult even for strong frontier models. Our PatEx-Agent achieves competitive performance against substantially larger general-purpose agents. These results show that training on PatEx-SynData enables a compact 4B model to serve as a competitive baseline for prior-art search and patent examination. We view patent examination as a demanding testbed for agentic search and deep research agents.

However, existing benchmarks largely focus on static and limited candidate sets, leaving the full search–reasoning–assessment process underexplored.
We present
PatEx-Gym
, the first framework for developing and evaluating agents for patent examination, which integrates three components.
First,
PatEx-Bench
provides 1K realistic examination tasks, two large-scale retrieval corpora containing over 1M patents and 52K scientific papers, and a harness runtime supporting iterative search, document visits, reasoning, and OA generation.
Second, we introduce

, an annotation-free

rior-

rt Agentic

ynthesis framework.
Specifically, it exploits document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors to model intra-turn query behavior, inter-turn search progression, and trajectory-level evidence and outcome quality, yielding

.

1
Introduction
Information retrieval systems have long served as a fundamental gateway to information access, spanning general-purpose Web search
[
Brin and Page, 1998
,
Burges et al., 2005
]
and domain-specific search engines in knowledge-intensive fields such as law
[
Feng et al., 2024
,
Harvey AI, 2026
]
, education
[
Usta et al., 2021
]
, finance
[
Choe et al., 2025
]
, and intellectual property (IP)
[
Roda et al., 2009
]
.
With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), the paradigm of information access is gradually shifting from discriminative relevance estimation
[
Salton and Buckley, 1988
,
Robertson et al., 1994
]
over in-domain corpora toward generative
[
Li et al., 2025
]
and agentic search paradigm
[
Du et al., 2026b
,
Ning et al., 2026
]
. This shift is particularly consequential for patent examination, where reliable novelty assessment fundamentally depends on discovering and reasoning over evidence from large-scale prior-art corpora.
Patent examination is inherently a knowledge-intensive information access task
[
Wang et al., 2026b
]
.
To assess the novelty of an application, examiners must discover relevant evidence from massive collections of prior art rather than relying on pre-identified references.
They then analyze the retrieved prior art against claim limitations to determine whether the invention has been previously disclosed
[
Knappich et al., 2026
]
.
This goes beyond fine-grained relevance matching
[
Risch et al., 2020
,
Ni et al., 2024
]
or reasoning
[
Lim et al., 2025
,
Wang et al., 2026b
]
over given prior-art documents:
novelty assessment in patent examination requires discovering relevant prior art from a large search space and using intermediate findings to guide subsequent search, claim-level comparison, and generate an Office Action (OA)-style report under relevant legal constraints
[
Setchi et al., 2021
]
.
Such a process naturally forms a tight
search–reasoning–assessment
loop, making patent examination a particularly challenging setting for agentic search.
Recent efforts have progressively shifted patent novelty assessment toward more realistic examination settings.
HUPD
[
Suzgun et al., 2023
]
formulated patent examination as application-level acceptance prediction, while IPBench
[
Wang et al., 2026a
]
evaluated the patent examination and classification capabilities of LLMs.
PANORAMA
[
Lim et al., 2025
]
, in contrast, decomposed claim-level examination into prior-art retrieval, relevant-paragraph identification, and novelty or non-obviousness classification.
More recent work further emphasizes fine-grained and process-oriented evaluation: FiNE-Patents
[
Knappich et al., 2026
]
assesses feature-level passage retrieval and novelty reasoning, while PatRe
[
Wang et al., 2026b
]
models the multi-turn lifecycle of
OA
generation and applicant rebuttal.
Existing benchmarks remain static and narrowly scoped relative to realistic examination: they evaluate examination components in isolation, constrain retrieval to small predefined candidate pools, or assume access to relevant prior art. As a result, they cannot capture the adaptive and iterative search, evidence discovery, and reasoning required in realistic patent examination.

Agentic Search and Deep Research
Conventional information retrieval methods estimate the relevance between a user query and documents in a corpus, returning a ranked list through lexical or learned matching functions
[
Robertson et al., 1994
,
Burges et al., 2005
]
.
With the emergence of LLMs, search systems increasingly move beyond scoring for a fixed query toward actively planning and adapting the search process
[

[

and IRCoT

5.2
Main Results on PatEx-Bench
As shown in Table
2
, we report the performance of evaluated models on PatEx-Bench under the Codex harness.
Overall, the agents exhibit substantial performance variation, with Scores ranging from 3.79 to 7.34.
Claude-Opus-5-max achieves the best results in Score, Statute F1, and all three reference-recall metrics.
The Select-R peaks at only 32.4, highlighting substantial room for improvement in statutory reasoning and prior-art search.
Notably, despite its compact 4B scale, PatEx-Agent achieves a Search-R of 38.7, surpassing larger models such as Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, while remaining competitive in OA quality.
We further analyze the differences in terms of prior-art discovery and examination quality as follows.
Strong models still face substantial prior-art discovery challenges.
Claude-Opus-5-max achieves the highest OA quality Score at 7.34, together with the strongest statute identification and reference recall across all three retrieval stages.
Nevertheless, even the strongest Search-R remains below 50% and Select-R below 33%, highlight the difficulty of discovering and retaining examiner-cited references through a progressive search process.
Notably, our PatEx-Agent substantially improves over its Qwen3.5-4B backbone, increasing the OA quality Score from 3.79 to 5.41 (
+42.7%
) and yielding consistent gains across all search and reasoning metrics, ranging from
+17.5%
to
+91.7%
.
These results suggest that effective prior-art discovery is not solely determined by model scale, but can be substantially improved by explicitly training search and reasoning capabilities.

This indicates that PatEx-Agent learns more effective query construction and search behavior from the PatEx-SynData rather than merely relying on a strong tool.
Among the isolated tools, BGE-M3 performs best and allows PatEx-Agent to nearly recover its full-tool performance in Search-R (37.24 vs. 38.70) and

R@100
(35.82 vs. 36.36).
Nevertheless, the full toolset remains stronger in Search-R and Select-R, suggesting that Boolean, lexical, and dense retrieval provide complementary coverage.
5.4.3
Ablation on Semantic Search Tool
We replace the dense retriever while remains the other tools, comparing BGE-M3 with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and PatEmbed-Large.
As shown in Figure
7
(right), stronger retrievers generally improve recalls, but these gains do not always translate into better Select-R.
For Qwen3.5-4B, PatEmbed-Large increases Search-R from 23.20 to 24.60 and R@100 from 24.06 to 24.78, while Select-R slightly decreases from 12.00 to 11.60.
This may indicate that stronger retriever introduces more similar candidates, making evidence selection more difficult.

Case study of two AI-domain patent applications.
The left example retains relevant prior art through search, inspection, and selection,
while the right example retrieves the relevant reference but fails to use it in the final evidence set.
We provide a detailed case study with two contrasting examples in Figure
8
, covering successful prior-art retention and failure to use retrieved evidence in the final decision.
(I)
In the left example, we observe a successful pipeline: the agent decomposes the claim into complementary concepts, reformulates its query across retrieval tools, verifies candidate prior-art, and assigns distinct evidentiary roles before generating the OA.
It preserves the oracle reference throughout the Search–Visit–Select funnel and yields the correct decision and statutory ground.
(II)
In the right example, we observe a different pattern in which the agent retrieves the oracle reference but does not promote it to document inspection or final selection.
Its statutory prediction is incomplete but does not introduce incorrect grounds.
Together, these examples show that effective agentic examination requires both iterative search and disciplined evidence selection:
broad retrieval can expose the necessary prior art, but only verified and correctly selected novelty-aware evidence can support a complete legal conclusion.
6
Conclusion
In this work, we introduced
PatEx-Gym
, a unified framework for developing and evaluating agentic patent examination models, including
PatEx-Bench
, PASS for synthesizing
PatEx-SynData
, and the lightweight baseline
PatEx-Agent
.
Our extensive experiments show that final decision accuracy alone cannot fully capture examination quality, and that prior-art discovery, evidence inspection, and final selection remain challenging even for strong frontier models.
Despite its 4B scale, our PatEx-Agent substantially improves over its base model and achieves prior-art discovery performance comparable to agents with
∼
\sim
30B size.
These findings identify evidence inspection and selection as central challenges for agentic search and deep research.
Moreover, we believe that effective agents must go beyond document search to coordinate adaptive querying, tool-use, evidence integration, and reasoning throughout the search process.
We hope our PatEx-Gym provides a realistic testbed for advancing evidence-grounded agentic search and deep research.

article.headline: PatEx-Gym：专利审查的智能体检索基准
article.lede: 论文构建1K真实专利审查任务与百万级专利检索库，并用PASS合成约3K轨迹训练4B智能体。
article.problem: 现有专利审查基准多依赖静态、小规模候选集，或把检索、段落定位与新颖性判断分开评估，难以覆盖真实审查中的完整搜索—推理—评估闭环。真实审查要求智能体从大规模现有技术中自主发现证据、迭代改写查询、检查全文并生成有法律约束的审查意见。
article.method: 作者提出PatEx-Gym：PatEx-Bench含1,000个USPTO真实审查任务，检索库为1,011,901件专利和52,105篇论文，运行环境提供布尔、BM25、BGE-M3检索及文档访问工具。PASS把文档访问当作隐式相关性与证据获取锚点，对轮内查询、轮间检索进展、轨迹级证据与结果质量分层打分，再用锦标赛排序从10K教师轨迹中筛出约3K条PatEx-SynData。PatEx-Agent以Qwen3.5-4B为底座做监督微调。
article.results: 在PatEx-Bench上，PatEx-Agent-4B的OA质量分为5.41，较底座Qwen3.5-4B的3.79提升42.7%；Search-R从23.2升至38.7，Select-R从12.0升至18.2。最强基线Claude-Opus-5-max的Score为7.34、Search-R为48.7、Select-R为32.4；Qwen3.6-27B决策准确率最高（87.6%），但Score仅5.96、Select-R 19.5，说明最终决策正确不等于检索与审查质量高。NPL检索上，PatEx-Agent的Paper Search-R为69.4，接近Qwen3.8-Max的69.6。
article.why_it_matters: 它把专利审查做成可审计的智能体检索测试床，并显示4B小模型经轨迹筛选与SFT后可在部分检索指标上接近更大模型，对轻量本地部署有吸引力。
article.limitations: 论文未单列局限性分析；从设置看，任务仅覆盖USPTO公开记录与1K条审查任务，OA质量依赖3个LLM评委（评委间Kendall W=0.849），训练轨迹来自教师模型合成，向其他专利局、语言和真实审查流程的泛化仍待验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: PASS的轨迹合成流程：以访问为锚点切分检索轨迹，分层评估查询行为与证据/结果质量，再经锦标赛排序和拒绝采样筛选高质量轨迹。

figure.caption: Overview of Prior-Art Agentic Search Trajectory Synthesis~(PASS) for PatEx-SynData. (A) Visit-guided, relevance-aware rollout segmentation divides trajectories into semantic turns using visits as anchors. $r$ denotes reasoning, $S$ denotes search, $V$ denotes visit, $Z$ denotes the returned tool results, and $W$ denotes workspace tools, e.g. {Write}.~(B) Hierarchical quality modeling evaluates multidimensional quality. (C) Tournament-based ranking with rejection sampling for high-quality trajectories.

email_papers.title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
email_papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally unreasonable actions in preferred trajectories and ignores each action's downstream deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9% and 94.3% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7% and 70.8% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to 2.44times while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS

Abstract
Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental
uniform credit assignment dilemma
that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally unreasonable actions in preferred trajectories and ignores each action’s downstream deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose
Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS)
, a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9% and 94.3% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7% and 70.8% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to
2.44
×
2.44\times
while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes:
https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS
.
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that make sequential decisions through interactions with external environments. Their planning and reasoning capabilities have enabled applications in software engineering (
?
), personal assistance (
?
), and graphical user interface navigation (
?
).
Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for elevating the agentic capacity of LLMs (
??
).
During RL rollouts, agents generate trajectories composed of interleaved environment states and actions, which introduces a fundamental
credit assignment challenge
:
How should trajectory-level rewards and penalties be attributed to individual actions?
Actor-critic algorithms (e.g., PPO (
?
)) address this by learning a separate critic, which introduces substantial computational overhead and optimization instability in long-horizon settings (
??
). Conversely, critic-free algorithms like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (
?
) offer computational efficiency by broadcasting a trajectory-level advantage uniformly to every action (
?
). However, this inherently treats all intra-trajectory actions identically, completely overlooking their critical differences in local validity, task contribution, and downstream influence. As detailed in §
3.2
, we term this structural limitation the
uniform credit assignment dilemma
.
To systematically understand the uniform credit assignment dilemma, we conduct a fine-grained action-intervention analysis (§
4.2
). Our findings reveal a dual suboptimality. First, in preferred trajectories with positive advantages, uniform credit inadvertently reinforces structurally invalid actions (i.e., unreasonable actions) that pollute the context history and impede the agent from reaching success. Second, in unpreferred trajectories with negative advantages, uniform penalization ignores the autoregressive nature of LLMs, where the later deviations may drive from earlier actions. Consequently, they suppress all actions equally but arbitrarily without considering their actual downstream influence.
To resolve this dilemma without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS) in §
4.3
. ProAS leverages an Agentic Reference Graph (ARG, mentioned in §
4.1
), which abstracts task progression into dynamically evolving sub-goals to formally annotate whether an action is
reasonable
(structurally valid) or
progress-advancing
(driving task completion). Using these structural annotations, ProAS asymmetrically reshapes trajectory-level advantages in Eq.
7
:
(1) Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI)
zeros out the local advantages of
unreasonable
actions in preferred trajectories to prevent their inadvertent reinforcement.
(2) Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR)
utilizes Future-Drift (Eq.
6
), the inclusive count of downstream
non-advancing
actions, to assign proportionally heavier penalties to actions triggering severe downstream stagnation.
Extensive experiments in §
6
on ALFWorld (
?
) and WebShop (
?
) using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (
?
) validate ProAS as a versatile, plug-and-play enhancer. It universally elevates mainstream group-based RL baselines (GRPO (
?
), DAPO (
?
), GiGPO (
?
)), boosting success rates by up to 16.7 points (e.g., GRPO on 1.5B ALFWorld) and accelerating training convergence by
1.12
×
1.12\times
to
2.44
×
2.44\times
. On top of that, this orthogonal enhancement propels these standard algorithms to establish new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, consistently eclipsing the strong segment-level baseline, MiGPO (
?
). Notably, GiGPO+ProAS outperforms MiGPO by a massive 13.1 points on WebShop with 1.5B model and secures the highest overall success rate of 94.3% on ALFWorld with 7B model. Furthermore, comprehensive ablations (§
6.2
) show that ProAS’s core mechanisms are both synergistic and superior to alternative advantage shaping variants, and confirm ProAS’s robust efficacy against incomplete or distilled ARGs, underscoring the necessity of ARG’s online evolution mechanism.
In summary, our primary contributions are:
•
Problem Identification:
We expose the uniform credit assignment dilemma in critic-free agentic RL, demonstrating how uniform advantages inadvertently reinforce contextual noise in preferred trajectories and ignore the downstream influence of actions in unpreferred ones.
•
Algorithmic Innovation:
We propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework. Guided by a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG), ProAS achieves fine-grained, critic-free credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR).
•
Empirical Superiority:
ProAS acts as a universal enhancer across multiple model scales and environments. It significantly accelerates training convergence, propels standard group-based algorithms to surpass strong SOTA baselines (e.g., MiGPO), and exhibits high robustness against imperfect and distilled reference guidance.
2
Related Works
Multi-Turn Agentic Tasks.
Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to solve complex real-world tasks (
?
). Given the intricacies of these environments, agents must engage in multi-turn interactions, continuously accumulating contextual knowledge and making sequential decisions to drive task completion. To facilitate the training and evaluation of such agents, the community has introduced various simulated environments. Examples include ALFWorld (
?
) for embodied household tasks, WebShop (
?
) for web navigation, AppWorld (
?
) for application development, and
τ
2
\tau^{2}
-Bench (
?
) for evaluating dynamic conversational abilities in domains like aviation and retail.
Rather than constructing new environments, our work focuses on developing more efficient and effective training paradigms tailored for existing multi-turn agentic tasks.
RL for LLM Agents.
Critic-free RL like GRPO (
?
) is widely adopted for LLM agents (
???
), but suffers from sparse-reward advantage vanishment (
?
) and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment (
?
). While DAPO (
?
) and dense-reward methods (
???
) mitigate this vanishment, their credit assignment remains trajectory-bound. To differentiate intra-trajectory actions, GiGPO (
?
) and MiGPO (
?
) compute relative advantages by matching anchor states or milestones across rollouts.
In this work, we systematically expose the flaws of uniform credit assignment in both preferred and unpreferred trajectories, addressing them through advantage shaping, which serves as a plug-and-play module for existing critic-free RL algorithms.

Experimental Setup
To empirically validate the proposed ProAS framework, we conduct extensive experiments across complex, long-horizon agentic environments. Our experiments are structured to answer the following core research questions:
RQ1: Performance & Efficiency (§
6

Can ProAS consistently elevate task success rates and accelerate training convergence across different model scales under different environments?
RQ2: Algorithm Compatibility (§

Does ProAS seamlessly integrate with mainstream group-based RL baselines (e.g., GRPO, DAPO, GiGPO) as a robust plug-and-play module?
RQ3: Advantage Shaping Design (§

Are MUI and APR each individually necessary and mutually synergistic, and does ProAS’s Future-Drift-based redistribution outperform a simpler masking heuristic?
RQ4: Robustness to ARG (§

Does ProAS remain effective when the reference ARG is randomized, incomplete, static (non-evolving), or distilled from a teacher model?

6.1
Main Results

Baseline Comparisons.
We first contrast ProAS against established learning paradigms. While both SFT and ProAS leverage expert annotations as supervisory signals, ProAS abstracts them into ARGs to structurally guide RL, significantly outperforming SFT’s direct behavior imitation. Specifically, GiGPO+ProAS achieves 91.9% and 94.3% SR on the 1.5B and 7B ALFWorld benchmarks, respectively, surpassing SFT by 12.2 and 14.4 points. Furthermore, ProAS consistently eclipses PPO, a conventional critic-based RL algorithm, across all settings. ProAS variants outpace PPO by 5.5 to 18.7 points in ALFWorld SR, alongside steady improvements of 4.1 to 12.2 points in WebShop TS and 3.4 to 11.5 points in WebShop SR. Ultimately, these results confirm that explicitly integrating ARG-derived progress signals into RL is vastly superior to both passive trajectory imitation and conventional critic-based credit assignment.

State-of-the-Art Performance.
Equipped with ProAS, group-based RL algorithms consistently establish new SOTA records. In ALFWorld, GiGPO+ProAS attains the highest SR of 94.3% on the 7B model. This surpasses the strong segment-level baseline MiGPO and eclipses the proprietary GPT-5.6-Sol by a massive 15.4 points. WebShop presents a notably steeper challenge, evidenced by GPT-5.6-Sol’s severe struggle at 21.9% SR. Despite this difficulty, ProAS variants dominate the leaderboard. On the 1.5B model, both DAPO and GiGPO integrated with ProAS tie for the best SR at 66.7%, outperforming MiGPO by a striking 13.1 points. On the 7B scale, GRPO+ProAS peaks at 70.8%, further extending the lead over MiGPO.
Algorithm Compatibility.
Crucially, ProAS demonstrates remarkable plug-and-play compatibility, universally uplifting baseline RL algorithms across all tested configurations. For ALFWorld, equipping GRPO with ProAS yields the most dramatic improvements, boosting the SR by 16.7 points on the 1.5B model and 8.4 points on the 7B model. Consistent gains are mirrored in WebShop, where DAPO+ProAS generates a 9.4-point uplift at the 1.5B scale, and GRPO+ProAS provides a 3.1-point boost at 7B. This confirms ProAS as a versatile enhancer that elevates both the performance floor and ceiling of diverse group-based RL paradigms.

Incomplete
randomly prunes 40% of the action-state pairs from the clean ARG to simulate severe degradation. Despite this, ProAS still outperforms GRPO by 7.0 points on ALFWorld. This robustness largely comes from ARG evolution (mentioned in Eq.
5

Static

Static

These results confirm the importance of ARG evolution for ProAS, while showing ProAS remains robust to imperfect ARGs.
Distill
tests ProAS with synthetic references, since gold-standard trajectories are often unavailable in practice. We prompt a 7B model to generate successful rollouts across training tasks, building a distilled ARG covering 2,566 tasks. With this synthetic ARG, the 1.5B model reaches 83.6% SR on ALFWorld and 64.8% on WebShop, comparable to GRPO+ProAS and 13.3 and 7.8 points above GRPO, respectively.
This validates ProAS’s applicability even on teacher-distilled trajectories.
7
Conclusion
In this work, we expose the
uniform credit assignment dilemma
in critic-free agentic RL, where uniform advantages reinforce contextual noise in preferred trajectories (
A
i
>
0
A_{i}>0
) and ignore the downstream deviation of actions in unpreferred ones (
A
i
<
0
A_{i}<0
). To address this without critic overhead, we proposed Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), which leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive evaluations across multiple model scales and environments confirm ProAS as a robust, universal enhancer that accelerates convergence and propels mainstream baselines to new state-of-the-art performance. The ablation study further confirms MUI-APR synergy, necessity of ARG evolution and robustness under incomplete or distilled ARGs. Together, these results establish a highly efficient, scalable pathway for elevating autonomous language agents.
