C.1
Time Analysis
We compare the wall-clock training time of vanilla RL and RL + ProAS, measured from TensorBoard logs. As shown in Fig.
2
, ProAS incurs modest overhead on ALFWorld while achieving lower training time on WebShop. article.headline: ProAS：用进度参考图重塑优势，改进多轮智能体R
article.lede: 无critic的GRPO类算法把轨迹级优势平均分给所有动作；ProAS用动态演化的参考图做细粒度信用分配，在ALFWor
article.problem: GRPO等无critic算法为省去critic开销，把轨迹级优势原样广播给轨迹内每个动作。作者指出这造成「统一信用分配困境」：在正优势的成功轨迹里，结构上不合理的动作也被一并强化；在负优势的失败轨迹里，又无视各动作对后续偏差的实际影响。
article.method: ProAS维护一个动态演化的Agentic Reference Graph（ARG），把成功轨迹抽象为按子目标排序的有向无环图，并据此给每个动作打上「合理」与「推进进度」两个二值标签。对正优势轨迹，MUI把不合理动作的局部优势置零；对负优势轨迹，APR按Future-Drift（该步起后续非推进动作的累计数）归一化后重新分配惩罚。整个框架即插即用，不需要critic或额外奖励模型。
article.results: 在Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct和7B-Instruct上，GiGPO+ProAS在ALFWorld取得91.9%和94.3%的成功率；WebShop上DAPO/GiGPO+ProAS（1.5B）与GRPO+ProAS（7B）分别达到66.7%和70.8%。GRPO+ProAS把1.5B模型在ALFWorld上的成功率从70.3%提升到87.0%（+16.7个百分点），训练收敛加速1.12×至2.44×。作者统计，不合理动作占成功GRPO轨迹的41.6%（ALFWorld）和39.6%（WebShop），非推进动作占失败轨迹的93.1%和76.1%；注入四步不合理历史使期望成功率从82%降到58%，而抑制Future-Drift为47、23、11、4的动作后，恢复的期望成功率分别为24%、16%、10%和0%。
article.why_it_matters: 它不引入critic、也不改RL主干，就能普遍抬高GRPO、DAPO、GiGPO的成功率并加快收敛，对算力有限又缺少逐步标注的智能体训练场景有直接吸引力。
article.limitations: ARG质量是关键：换成随机标签会让ALFWorld成功率相对ProAS下降39.3个百分点，关闭在线演化（静态ARG）也使ALFWorld从87.0%降到82.8%，且ALFWorld上实际训练时间略有增加。此外，支撑MUI/APR的干预分析基于单条轨迹、每点50次续采样，作者自己也说明这只能作为诊断趋势的证据，并非普遍因果效应的估计。
article.figure_caption_zh: (a) 多条成功轨迹被统一为有向无环图作为进度参考；(b) 同一状态下注入不合理动作后，50次续采样的期望成功率更低；(c) 抑制不同位置的原动作并重采样50次，恢复的期望成功率随该动作Future-Drift增大而上升。

figure.caption: {(a) The demonstration of ARG.} Diverse successful trajectories are unified into a DAG that serves as a progress reference. {(b) Probing unreasonable actions.} From an identical state, the counterpart injected with unreasonable actions yields a lower Expected Success Rate (ESR) on 50 sampled continuations $\{c_i\}_{i=1}^{50}$. {(c) Suppressing by Future-Drift (FD).} Forcibly suppressing the original action at different trajectory points and resampling 50 continuations shows recovered ESR rises with the suppressed action's FD.

email_papers.title: AgentProofBench: Benchmarking Reusable Verifiers for Web Agents
email_papers.abstract: Reusable Web-agent verification requires a rule to follow changing requirements and support subsequent execution. We introduce AgentProofBench, which connects paired tests of a frozen acceptance rule to execution from identical saved openings. The resource spans 97 tasks, 79 families, and four Web services. Experiments with DeepSeek Flash/Pro establish two linked measurements. Across 48 families, complete-panel and decision-replay tests retain 82/96 Flash and 79/96 Pro source programs; paired reuse-rebuild BA intervals are [-5.47, 1.57] and [-10.16, 0.00] percentage points. Across 22 execution families, deployment-state panel correctness separates program assignments whose two saved openings are both delivered correctly: 32/33 assignments with error-free panels, versus 1/11 with panel errors. All reference-defined program-gate regressions and withheld deliveries occur in the latter group. Neutral continuation attains the highest correct delivery under the tested generic feedback, providing a concrete baseline for measuring the value added by a gate. Released instructions, states, programs, reference rules, and trajectories connect each test failure to its execution consequences. AgentProofBench makes reusable verification assessable at both the requirement and policy levels.

Keywords:
Web agents, reusable verifiers, verifier generation, initial-state generalization, execution-based evaluation
1.
Introduction
Reusable acceptance checks can make Web-agent operation fast and inspectable. A program can encode the conditions for completing a task, inspect the relevant business state, and issue the same explicit checks on subsequent executions. The central challenge is that the public instruction can stay fixed while the required work changes. The current owner of a name, the files belonging to a collection, or the value that must be preserved comes from the initial state of each execution. A verifier that remembers an earlier answer can produce a convincing decision for the wrong requirement.
The decision also becomes part of the agent’s environment. Rejection can trigger further edits, and acceptance can release the resulting state. Evaluating a reusable verifier therefore requires a link between the conditions its tests exercise and the outcomes of the policy that consumes its decisions. Matched continuation histories make that link observable: the same completed work can be preserved, changed, or withheld under different stopping policies.
Existing Web-agent environments establish executable task evaluation
(
Zhou et al., 2023
;
Yao et al., 2024
;
Xie et al., 2024
;
Trivedi et al., 2024
;
Pyskło et al., 2026
)
. Work on automatic assessment and generated verifiers demonstrates the importance of evidence and acceptance of valid alternatives
(
Lù et al., 2025
;
Rosset et al., 2026
;
Yin et al., 2026
)
. Reusable execution policies further show the value of experience across workflow instances
(
Suh et al., 2026
)
. These advances motivate an evaluation that connects three properties of an acceptance rule. It must recognize the permitted terminal outcomes, recover the requirements of a changed initial state, and support effective continuation and delivery decisions.
We introduce AgentProofBench around this connection. An
acceptance program
is executable code that judges task completion through ordinary before/after APIs. A
reuse contract
fixes the public instruction and evidence permissions while initial business data vary. Matched terminal outcomes make the consequences of this variation observable. Shared actor openings then connect the same verifier to the actions taken after its decision. Every measurement is linked to versioned reference predicates, program source, API evidence, and a reconstructable business state.
The benchmark provides three contributions.
•
A paired reuse test that holds the public instruction and generated program fixed while changing its required initial-state bindings. Complete outcome panels and replayed decisions measure complementary obligations.
•
An execution-validity test linking deployment-state panel correctness to matched policy outcomes. The 22-family study preserves 44 program assignments, two openings per assignment, and 352 policy outcomes.
•
An executable resource with 97 tasks across four Web services, including versioned reference rules, legal alternatives, reconstructable states, programs, and action histories.
The central empirical result is the connection between tests and execution. Programs with error-free deployment-state panels correctly deliver both saved openings in 32 of 33 assignments, compared with one of eleven assignments whose panels contain errors. The paired reuse study explains which requirements those panels exercise; replay witnesses expose additional errors in three source programs. Fixed-instance acceptance and cost profiles then describe the operating tradeoffs of the same verification interface. The reported generator, judge, and actor results use DeepSeek Flash/Pro with thinking disabled.

The construction prompt states the reuse contract explicitly. The program must derive state-dependent requirements from its runtime before state. Each assessment runs frozen source in a fresh read-only sandbox with the task actor’s API permissions. Host predicates and terminal controls remain in the scoring harness. One execution allows one CPU, 1 GB memory, 60 seconds, and 80 business operations across both snapshots. Expanded GraphQL root queries count separately.
3.2.
Outcome coverage and reference semantics
Three linked studies address acceptance, reuse, and execution. The acceptance resource contains 97 tasks from 79 families, with 20 family-disjoint development tasks. Its 556-state natural panel includes 452 successes and 104 failures, sampled by reference class with at most six states per task. The reuse study evaluates 576 programs on 558 terminal states from 48 families. The execution study compares policies on 88 saved openings from 22 families. Appendix
A
records the natural-state selection flow and the three post-inspection task exclusions.
Four outcome panels separate common acceptance demands (Figure
7
). Natural outcomes measure ordinary agent endings. Native-prefix pairs use service actions to connect a complete execution to an earlier incomplete state. Typed faults alter a successful anchor through service APIs, allowing the violated requirement to be identified. Legal alternatives change behavior that the public instruction permits. Successful anchors and failed states jointly test valid acceptance and failure rejection.
Reference predicates cover identities, values, collections, and relationships. Versioned selectors recover the required objects from each before state. Native-state and ordinary-API evaluation share the predicates and check restoration and evidence accessibility. Scores measure conformity to this explicit reference contract. Appendix
A
retains the original and explicit-preservation label views.
A separate GPT-6 Astra LLM-as-a-judge audit reviews 195 states across 62 tasks, with reference verdicts withheld during initial judgment. It agrees with 191 of 192 resolved labels (99.5%); three cases are indeterminate. The audit corroborates all 48 requirement changes, rejects all 48 failed replays, and confirms both delivered-regression pairs (Appendix
A
).
The preservation task
linear_52
illustrates the contract. Its instruction assigns Plot B3 to Rashida and requires its initial status to survive. The source state has status
Active
; the related state has
Dormant
. The reference resolves Plot B3 from the current before state, checks the requested assignee, and compares its before/after status identifiers. A correct related outcome therefore keeps
Dormant
. The instruction’s other clauses create a tracker issue and update Plots A7 and C1. They supply additional matched outcomes while the B3 change isolates the state-dependent preservation requirement. The complete instruction and predicates appear in Appendix
A
.
3.3.
Matched initial-state reuse
The matched study, P1, selects one task from each of 48 original families, comprising 18 Linear, 10 Slack, 19 Box, and one Calendar task. Every family contributes one related initial-state transformation. Each public instruction has three initial conditions.
Source
is the construction state.
Background
changes data outside the requested work.
Related
changes a required entity binding, initial value, collection, or preservation condition. An entity binding identifies the object denoted by a public name; a preservation condition requires an initial value to survive execution.
Qualification establishes four properties before prediction. The changed requirement follows the public instruction, service actions construct the states, native and API references agree on matched outcomes, and replaying a source-valid decision becomes invalid under the related condition. This last execution is a
source-decision witness
. It tests the acceptance rule against an earlier valid business decision whose required target or value has changed.
The witness gives initial-state variation a direct semantic test. If the same earlier decision remains valid, a program could succeed by retaining its source answer. A qualified witness requires the verifier to resolve a new condition from the current before state. This separates state-dependent acceptance from incidental differences in a snapshot and makes the changed obligation inspectable in the reference and API trace.
Each initial condition contains a complete result, a distinct legal alternative where available, and two changed failures. Fault recipes and their roles remain matched across conditions; the current before state supplies identifiers and required values. Forty-two tasks have two valid outcomes per condition, and six have one. The 144 initial states support 558 main terminal states, comprising 270 valid and 288 failed entries. Witness pairs add one source-valid and one related-invalid decision per task, with their own scoring support.
DeepSeek Flash and Pro, both with thinking disabled, each generate two source programs and two rebuilt programs at each target condition, producing 576 frozen artifacts. Construction and fresh online API assessment, denoted API12, allow twelve model turns. Programs can read and debug against their construction state. Source programs run on all three conditions, while target rebuilds are compared at their own construction target. Two independent API12 judgments per model and terminal state give 2,232 online observations. The full three-construction by three-assessment matrix additionally measures reverse transfer.
3.4.
Verification during continued execution
The execution study, P2, uses 22 families with a native completion trace containing at least two mutating operations. One Flash and one Pro actor per task generate 44 trajectories from related initial states. Every trajectory supplies a natural ending and a closed
checkpoint
, saved after its first complete tool round containing a mutating request. Each of the 88 openings preserves the original initial state, current business state, and complete interaction history.
Four policies branch from each opening.
Actor stop
delivers on the actor’s final reply. Its non-final checkpoint outcome is a mechanical no-delivery reference.
Fixed continue
allows two neutral continuation phases and delivers on a final reply after phase two.
Program gate
uses a source-built Pro program, assigned by a fixed parity rule per task and actor independently of source quality.
Online gate
uses fresh Pro API12 judgments. Both gates deliver on
Pass
and otherwise permit at most two continuations. The two cohorts retain the same assigned program.
The neutral message asks the actor to finish the original request while preserving completed work. Gate feedback prepends a statement of nonacceptance and carries no program checks or entity identifiers. Thus each branch evaluates a complete feedback-and-stopping policy; Appendix
C
gives the exact messages. An eight-family development study selected this design before formal actor prediction. Each actor phase allows 20 model turns and 100 business operations, with a USD 1 observed-cost stop and a 900-second deadline. Unresolved usage stops further work. Executed writes persist when delivery is withheld.

5.
Using the Benchmark
AgentProofBench supports three concrete evaluation workflows. A verifier generator can be tested on the same natural endings, legal alternatives, and typed failures to establish its acceptance profile. Its frozen outputs can then be evaluated under matched initial-state requirements using both complete-panel and joint witness correctness. Finally, the recorded actor openings support comparison of the policies that consume these decisions, measuring completed work, persistent mutations, and delivered state separately.
The resource connects these workflows through stable task, family, program, and state identities. Each false acceptance links to a violated reference condition; each transfer error links to a source program and target rebuild; each execution outcome links to the gate decision and subsequent requests. A generator improvement can therefore be assessed against the changed requirement it should recover and the policy outcome it should support.
The companion’s Evidence Index provides the acceptance, reuse, and execution entry points. Canonical snapshots and exact row deltas reconstruct the saved states. The
verify(task, before, after)
interface evaluates frozen programs without model calls.
6.
Conclusion
AgentProofBench connects the two requirements of reusable Web-agent verification: recovering the current task obligation and supporting subsequent execution. Paired initial states and replay witnesses test the first; shared actor histories and program-level outcome links test the second. In the DeepSeek Flash/Pro study, deployment-state panel correctness identifies 32/33 assignments whose two openings are delivered correctly, compared with 1/11 assignments containing panel errors. Neutral continuation anchors the measurement of gate value, while acceptance profiles and amortized costs describe operating choices. The released 97-task resource makes this chain reproducible, from a changed requirement to a tested rule and its observed execution consequences.

article.headline: 可复用验证器基准：把测试与执行后果连起来
article.lede: 97个任务、79个族、四个Web服务：新基准把冻结验收程序的配对测试，与其判决之后的执行结果连成一条可复现的链。
article.problem: Web agent 的验收检查往往被写成一段可复用的程序，但公开指令不变时，真正需要满足的条件会随每次执行的初始业务状态改变——名字当前归谁、集合里有哪些文件、哪个值必须保留。记住旧答案的验证器会给出看似可信、实则针对错误需求的判决，而它的判决又会反过来改变后续执行（拒绝触发修改、通过则放行结果状态）。现有 Web agent 环境只做可执行的任务评测，没有把「验证器是否跟得上初始状态变化」与「它的决策导致什么执行后果」放在同一个测量框架里。
article.method: 作者构建 AgentProofBench：每个任务给出公开指令、API 文档与普通认证接口，验证器以 verify(task, before, after) 形式返回 Pass/Fail/Unknown，在只读沙箱中运行冻结源码。研究分三块：97 任务 79 族的验收资源（556 个自然状态，452 成功/104 失败）；48 族的配对复用测试，固定指令与程序、只改初始状态绑定，并用「源决策见证」检验旧判决在新条件下是否应失效；22 族的执行研究，从 88 个保存的开局出发比较四种停止策略（actor 自停、固定续跑、程序门控、在线门控）。所有数字来自 DeepSeek Flash/Pro，关闭 thinking。
article.results: 配对复用研究跨 48 族：源程序在相关状态上的平衡准确率为 Flash 93.23%、Pro 90.36%，复用减重建的区间分别是 [-5.47, 1.57] 和 [-10.16, 0.00] 个百分点，两者都包含零。主面板与见证都正确的联合正确率为 82/96（Flash）与 79/96（Pro），重建程序为 82/96 与 86/96。执行研究里，相关面板无错误的 33 个程序赋值中有 32 个把两个开局都正确交付，而面板含错误的 11 个赋值中只有 1 个，对应正确交付率差 87.9 个百分点，区间 [68.8, 100.0]；全部 17 次程序门控扣留与 3 次参考定义的回归都落在面板出错组。中性续跑在测试的通用反馈中正确交付最高：Flash 20/22、Pro 22/22，而程序门控为 17/22 与 16/22。成本方面，构造费用中位数为 0.0173/0.0765 美元，API 费用盈亏平衡点中位数为 Flash 12 次、Pro 10 次评估。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「验证器生成」的评测从单次固定实例推进到初始状态变化加执行后果两个层面，并给出可直接复用的任务、状态、程序、参考规则与轨迹，使验证器的复用价值第一次能被端到端归因到某次被放行或扣留的交付。中性续跑作为强基线也提醒：门控带来的增益必须超过「什么都不拦」才有意义。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖 DeepSeek Flash/Pro 两个模型且关闭 thinking，结论能否外推到其他模型未知；配对复用的两个预设区间都包含零，即未证明复用优于重建。面板正确性与交付结果的关联被作者明确标为对冻结赋值的探索性分析，支撑单元只有 44 个程序赋值、来自 22 个族，效应量虽大但样本结构受限。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图中对比三类相关工作设置与本文的测量单元：配对的初始状态需求检验冻结的验收程序，匹配的历史则把它的判决与后续执行连起来。

page_papers.title: Multi-Dimensional Featurizers Yield Fine-Grained Steering and Data Shaping in Robot Foundation Models
page_papers.abstract: Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn. We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model's computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than $1.4\%$ of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.

Abstract
Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn.
We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model’s computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than 1.4% of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.
Figure 1:
Block-sparse featurizers (BSFs) recover multi-dimensional robotics concepts.
Examples from vision-language-action models encode end-effector position (top), fruit-and-vegetable semantics (middle), and proprioceptive state (bottom). Each point is a token’s 3D feature code, colored by PCA coordinates, task or semantic labels, and sparse-autoencoder (SAE) assignments across columns. Activations from MolmoAct2 L25, L21, L13 (top to bottom). Left overlays share the PCA colors. SAE features tile distinct regions within each block, showing how BSFs group related variation into a single feature.
1
Introduction
A vision-language-action (VLA) model maps visual observations, language instructions, and robot state to actions in the physical world
(
Black et al., 2025
;
Lee et al., 2026
;
Fang et al., 2026
;
Black et al., 2024
;
Brohan et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2024
;
Deshpande et al., 2026
)
. Although today’s VLAs rarely perform consequential real-world tasks, fully learned robotics models may soon see widespread deployment. Yet little is known about the computations underlying their actions. Understanding these internal representations will be essential for safe deployment.
One way to understand the internal representation of a learned model is through the perspective of
features
, which are recurring internal variables that encode concepts, states, relationships and ultimately underlie the process by which the model converts input to output. A promising line of work, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAEs), leverages the
linear representation hypothesis
(LRH)
(
Park et al., 2023a
;
Huben et al., 2024
;
Gao et al., 2025
;
Elhage et al., 2022
)
and assume that activations are composed of a sparse set of vectors. These methods have been well studied in language and vision modalities
(
Huben et al., 2024
;
Templeton et al., 2026
;
Gao et al., 2025
)
. Examining models in the basis of the features that they express is useful for a plethora of problems, such as to study generalization
(
Gallifant et al., 2025
;
Olson et al., 2025
)
, steer model behavior
(
Templeton et al., 2026
;
Prasad et al., 2026
;
Turner et al., 2023
;
Rimsky et al., 2024
)
, attribute behaviors to training data
(
Kowal et al., 2026
;
Bergen et al., 2026
;
Koh & Liang, 2017
)
, and identify safety-relevant computation
(
Templeton et al., 2026
;
Marks et al., 2025
)
.
However, a featurizer is ultimately a hypothesis about the data-generating process of the activations
(
Fel et al., 2026a
)
. The LRH is particularly questionable for visual domains involving perception, since continuous factors such as viewpoint, illumination, position, and motion naturally generate low-dimensional manifolds that are reflected in learned representations
(
Cohen et al., 2020
;
Kvinge et al., 2024
;
Fel et al., 2026a
;
Engels et al., 2025
;
Michaud et al., 2025
)
. Despite this, the majority of work in VLA interpretability assumes the LRH, with varying degrees of success. Early studies showed that specific MLP directions can offer limited control of variables like speed and height
(
Häon et al., 2025
)
. Complementary studies use linear probes and activation interventions to characterize the contributions of visual, language, and action pathways and identify representations of environmental dynamics and task progress
(
Molinari et al., 2025
;
Grant et al., 2026
;
Bhardwaj et al., 2026
;
Buurmeijer et al., 2026
)
. More recently, SAEs have been applied to recover semantic concepts, motion primitives, task structure, and episode-specific memorization, demonstrating that interventions on individual features can alter policy behavior
(
Swann et al., 2026
;
Khan et al., 2025
;
Jin et al., 2026
;
Grant et al., 2026
)
.Prior work has improved our understanding of VLA policies, but precise behavioral steering remains challenging, with interventions often producing inconsistent, off-target, or weak effects. Much of this work relies on pooled visual activations or small activation corpora, leaving open whether training SAEs on individual token activations at greater scale improves feature discovery and steering.
In this work, we apply recent methods for multi-dimensional feature discovery—block-sparse featurizers (BSFs)
(
Fel et al., 2026a
)
—to frontier open-source VLA models, training BSFs and baseline SAEs on the largest corpora of unpooled VLA token activations to date. BSFs represent features as sparse low-dimensional blocks
(
Yuan & Lin, 2006
;
Eldar & Bölcskei, 2009
;
Jenatton et al., 2010
;
Bach et al., 2012
)
rather than single directions, making them a natural fit for robotic representations. Across models and layers, we recover a broad vocabulary of task-relevant features spanning visual perception, language, proprioceptive state, task variables and episode progress. BSFs outperform matched SAEs on recovering and intervening on task-relevant structure, suggesting that the additional geometry is useful rather than simply excess representational capacity. We then causally validate them through fine-grained steering experiments across multiple layers, inducing targeted changes at several stages of the policy: what is perceived in the observation, which object is selected, where that object is localized. Finally, we perform feature-based attribution to connect interpretable behaviors directly to the episodes in the fine-tuning dataset that shaped them. Related robot data-curation methods select demonstrations with datamodels, influence estimates, or mutual information
(
Dass et al., 2026
;
Agia et al., 2025
;
Hejna et al., 2025
)
. Using a ‘failure-recovery’ feature as as case-study, we isolate fewer than 1.4% of fine-tuning tokens in DROID whose influence is disproportionately associated with this behavior.
Our contributions are:
1.
Comparing block-sparse and linear featurizers for VLAs.
We systematically compare BSFs and SAEs in VLAs. BSFs recover features spanning perception, language, proprioception, task state and episode progress, better capturing computational geometry qualitatively and quantitatively. We also strengthen VLA SAE baselines with substantially larger, unpooled activation corpora to better evaluate multidimensional features.
2.
Causal validation through fine-grained steering.
Across multiple layers, and computational regimes, we causally validate recovered features by steering perception, semantics, target-object selection, geometric localization, and downstream robot behavior.
3.
Feature-based dataset attribution and shaping.
We trace behaviors captured by BSF features to the data that caused them. For failure recovery, masking
∼
1.4
%
\sim 1.4\%
of fine-tuning tokens qualitatively transforms robot behavior, demonstrating precise control over robot datasets and learned policies.
2
From Sparse Directions to Sparse Subspaces
Figure 2:
BSFs better capture low-dimensional manifolds.
(b) One three-coordinate BSF block reconstructs the helix. (c) Many individual SAE features tile the helix.
The goal of a featurizer is to factorize model activations into a set of interpretable concepts

Bussmann et al., 2024
;

Hindupur et al. (2025)

A useful featurizer should enable targeted changes to policy behavior through a small number of feature edits that generalize to new scenes. We evaluate this with a redirection task in which two objects sit at opposite ends of a table, making the first predicted action chunk indicative of the robot’s intended target. We instruct the policy to pick up one object and test the minimum number of feature edits required to redirect its reach toward the other. To scale this evaluation across hundreds of scene–method combinations, we use an automated search to identify compact feature sets that achieve redirection (see Appendix
B.1
for full details) on a ‘train’ set of episodes, and then hold the selected sets fixed and evaluate their effectiveness on held-out episodes.
We apply this procedure at three sites associated with distinct aspects of target grasping (Figure
4
). Editing the early-layer noun token changes
what
the robot is looking for; editing mid-layer image tokens changes
where
it perceives each object; and editing the late-layer action-readout token changes the represented target
position
. At each steering location, replacing the activations with those from the condition targeting the other object flipped the robot’s target action towards the corresponding object. We use this activation-patching effect as a reference, measuring held-out recovery as the fraction of our steering relative to it. Held-out evaluation tests whether the selected feature sets generalize beyond the episodes we found them on, while task completion is evaluated separately in closed loop (Table
1
). Full details are provided in Appendix
B.1
.
Figure
4
reports two metrics averaged over 52 scenes: steerable feature search success, the number of selected features, and held-out recovery. Each feature is one SAE latent or BSF block, and 100% recovery means matching the trajectory shift produced by activation patching (Appendix
B.1

Geometric steering is the most compact: a single BSF block achieves 99.7% recovery, comparable to a single SAE latent. For semantic steering, standard BSFs require fewer features while slightly improving held-out recovery. Perceptual steering reveals a trade-off: the BSF variants require roughly 16–20 blocks, compared with 36 SAE latents, but the SAE transfers more effectively to held-out scenes. Overall, BSFs thus provide more compact semantic and perceptual interventions, although fewer feature edits do not consistently yield better transfer.

Both features illustrate how a block can capture concept variation within a single object category: the marker’s activation geometry varies with the appearance of markers at different stages of manipulation, while the robot feature instead organizes patches from different parts of the arm. In both cases, the block captures recognizable visual content together with structure within that content. Across our models and layers we find plentiful features for a wide range of objects.

Beyond visual and semantic content, we find blocks associated with robot configuration and spatial variables (Figure

A second feature varies with the end-effector’s Cartesian coordinates over a single episode. This association is notable because the policy receives joint angles as proprioceptive input, rather than explicit Cartesian end-effector coordinates. A third example comes from MolmoBot, which is trained on synthetic data. Proprioception, the robot’s state information, enters the VLM backbone as part of the prompt. The two models encode these inputs differently:

The highlighted MolmoACT2 feature notably forms a complex manifold of three looping branches that converge into a common extension. 5
Conclusion
We have shown that BSFs recover interpretable, multidimensional features in vision-language-action models, providing tools for steering robot behavior and tracing it to training data. Targeted interventions establish these features’ behavioral relevance, while feature-guided data masking selectively delays failure recovery and preserves task performance in our evaluation. In terms of limitations, our analysis does not fully explain how these features emerge or participate in policy computation; tracing their geometry to proprioceptive inputs is a promising next step. We demonstrate closed-loop semantic steering, but some interventions are evaluated only open loop. Robust closed-loop visual and geometric steering will require tracking moving image regions and adapting to changing observations and robot state. BSFs are also not uniformly superior: SAEs perform better on some quantitative metrics, and our stronger baselines underscore the importance of unpooled activations and training scale alongside feature geometry.

B.1
Open-Loop Steering Protocol
Our goal is to find a set of features which steers the robot toward a target object on a set discovery inputs and then evaluated, on held-out inputs with fresh noise seeds. Consider a scene with a banana on the left and an apple on the right. We task the robot with “pick up the banana", our goal is to steer it to instead pick up the apple using three different means: steering semantic representations (changing what the model thinks the target object is), steering visual tokens (changing where the model sees the target object) or geometry representations (changing the model’s internal representation of the location of the target object). article.headline: 块稀疏特征器提升 VLA 的精细转向能力
article.lede: 块稀疏特征器用更少特征实现语义、视觉、几何三路 VLA 行为转向，并反查训练数据中承载失败恢复行为的少量 token。
article.problem: 视觉-语言-动作模型（VLA）正被尝试用于真实机器人，但其内部计算几乎无人了解；现有可解释性工作大多默认线性表示假设，用稀疏自编码器（SAE）把激活拆成单个方向。然而视角、位置、光照等连续感知因素天然落在低维流形上，标量特征难以刻画，干预常常效果不一致、偏离目标或过弱。此前 VLA 上的 SAE 研究还普遍使用池化激活或规模很小的语料，难以判断特征发现本身能否做得更好。
article.method: 作者把块稀疏特征器（BSF）用于 MolmoAct2、π0.5 与 MolmoBot：每个特征用低维子空间而非单一方向表示，并保留图像、文本、状态 token 不池化，构建约 5200 万条激活、覆盖 45,344 个 episode 的语料，使 SAE 基线只在块维度上与之不同。他们还加入 Fisher 加权变体，按重建误差对动作似然的影响来加权训练。验证分两部分：在语义、视觉、几何三个位置搜索能改变目标物体的最小特征集并做闭环真机实验；再用特征定位训练数据中与失败恢复有关的片段并掩蔽对应损失。
article.results: 在 52 个留出场景对比中，单个几何 BSF 块即可复现 99.7% 的激活补丁效果；语义转向 BSF 用 2.15 个特征达到 83.8% 恢复率（SAE 为 3.50 个特征、81.9%），视觉转向 BSF 用 20.40 块对 36.25 个 SAE 特征，但 SAE 的留出恢复更高（97.3% 对 84.6%）。闭环语义重定向中，BSF 平均用 2.3 个特征使 93.3% 的试验完成抓取并放置，SAE 用 2.5 个特征为 75.0%。数据侧，作者在 DROID 的 74,604 个 episode 中标出 4,866 个（6.5%）含失败恢复的片段，掩蔽其中约 1.38% 的 token 后，夹爪重开时间由 3.13 秒升至 12.93 秒（表 2），普通抓取放置任务仍为 100% 成功、时长 11.79 秒对 12.13 秒。
article.why_it_matters: 把特征单元从单方向换成低维子空间，能让机器人策略的干预更省特征、更贴合目标，并把可解释特征直接连回训练数据。这为部署前的行为审计和有针对性的数据筛选提供了一条可操作路径，而不只是事后解释。
article.limitations: 作者承认 BSF 并非全面占优：部分量化指标上 SAE 更好，视觉转向时 SAE 的留出恢复也更高（97.3% 对 84.6%），且多数干预只在开环评估，闭环视觉与几何转向仍需跟踪运动图像区域。数据侧结论主要依赖单个失败恢复特征 F1515 与阈值规则；另外，正文称重开时间从 1.89 秒升至 14.25 秒（逾 7 倍），与表 2 的 3.13 秒到 12.93 秒不一致，论文未说明差异来源。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图中展示通过语义、视觉与几何三种表征进行的细粒度转向：在不改变输入图像与指令的情况下，干预把预测动作从被提示的物体改向另一个物体。

page_papers.title: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration
page_papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce DynaFlow, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.

Abstract
Multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse task requirements. We introduce
DynaFlow
, a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the action space of the main agent. The agent decides when collaboration is needed and generates task-specific programs that coordinate sub-agents through sequential or parallel execution, structured information exchange, and verification. Execution results and traces inform subsequent actions, enabling the agent to adapt collaboration as reasoning progresses. We train only the main agent through supervised fine-tuning on distilled trajectories, followed by refinement on examples filtered for unsupported premises, biased verification, and information-flow defects. All sub-agents remain fixed, separating orchestration learning from executor capability improvement. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.90 percentage points with the same Qwen3.5-27B backbone. Workflow analysis finds more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs after training, highlighting cross-stage information flow as a key dimension of multi-agent orchestration.
Figure 1:
Overall accuracy versus collaboration size.
Accuracy versus the mean number of agent roles per question on 688 questions (Qwen3.5-27B). In Forced mode, DynaFlow improves accuracy from Base’s 75.9% to 88.1%. Dynamic achieves 87.9% with 3.44 agent roles per question on average, while answering 47% of questions without workflows.
Figure 2:
Overview of DynaFlow.
(1) Two-stage SFT trains only the Main Agent on first-turn reasoning
r
r
and workflow action
a
1
a_{1}
, using distilled demonstrations followed by a curated subset.
(2) It chooses to answer directly, call a tool, or generate a JavaScript workflow.
(3) Frozen sub-agents collaborate within the workflow according to the Main Agent’s program.
(4) Outputs and execution traces update the history for subsequent decisions.
1
Introduction
The effectiveness of multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) depends on how collaboration is organized. Many systems rely on fixed collaboration structures with pre-designed agent roles, communication patterns, or workflow components
(
Li et al., 2023
;
Wu et al., 2024
;
Hong et al., 2024
;
Dat et al., 2026
)
. Yet coordination requirements vary across tasks: simple queries may need only one agent, independent subtasks can benefit from parallel execution, and dependent stages require reliable access to upstream results. Applying a fixed collaboration structure across these settings can introduce unnecessary communication, latency, and computation
(
Wang et al., 2026
;
Li and Wang, 2026
;
Yin et al., 2026
)
. We argue that scalable MAS require a stronger capability, which we refer to as
Free Orchestration
: the ability to decide when collaboration is useful and construct task-specific workflows during problem solving.
Automated workflow design has begun to address this rigidity. Existing approaches search for effective workflows using execution feedback
(
Zhang et al., 2025c
)
, or generate and adapt query-specific agent systems during inference
(
Ye et al., 2025
;
Gao et al., 2025
;
Tieu et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2025b
;
Ke et al., 2025
;
Ke et al., 2026
)
. However, these advances retain constraints on workflow construction and adaptation. DyFlow revises plans using execution feedback but constructs them from a finite set of operator templates
(
Wang et al., 2025b
)
. MAS-Orchestra formulates orchestration through function calls, yet generates the complete coordination structure in a single decision without observing intermediate execution results
(
Ke et al., 2026
)
. These limitations motivate combining free-form workflow synthesis with repeated orchestration decisions informed by execution feedback. We therefore investigate executable workflow synthesis as a native action of the task-solving agent, alongside ordinary tool use. The same agent decides (i) when to collaborate, (ii) constructs task-specific programs, and (iii) uses their returned outputs and traces to determine how to proceed.
To this end, we introduce
DynaFlow
(Figure
2
), a framework that integrates free-form executable workflow synthesis into the task-solving agent’s action space. We refer to this agent as the
main agent
, which coordinates
sub-agents
responsible for executing delegated subtasks. The Main Agent can answer directly, use ordinary tools, or generate a task-specific workflow program. Through a minimal execution interface, it defines sub-agent responsibilities, sequential or parallel dependencies, and how intermediate outputs are passed, aggregated, and verified directly in code. A budget-constrained runtime executes the program and returns its outputs and execution trace. The Main Agent then uses this feedback to guide subsequent actions, including synthesizing follow-up workflows that adapt collaboration to the observed results.
We decouple orchestration learning from sub-agent training by updating only the Main Agent on distilled workflow demonstrations while keeping all sub-agents fixed. This focuses learning on coordinating existing capabilities and allows pretrained models to be reused as executors without retraining. The training process begins with distilled workflow demonstrations. Since answer correctness alone does not guarantee reliable coordination, we then refine the policy on a curated subset that excludes demonstrations flagged for unsupported premises, biased verification, or incomplete information transfer. This training process makes orchestration quality an explicit criterion for selecting demonstrations, guiding the Main Agent toward more reliable task coordination and information use.
Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, scientific question answering, and multi-hop retrieval, DynaFlow achieves 88.08% overall accuracy in Forced mode, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline using the same backbone by 10.90 percentage points. In Dynamic mode, it maintains accuracy close to Forced execution while answering 47.1% of questions without invoking a workflow. Further analysis finds that training leads to more explicit use, verification, and refinement of upstream outputs. Together, these results support learning both how to organize collaboration and when to invoke it, and identify cross-stage information use as a key dimension of effective orchestration.

Related Work
Agentic Workflows and Orchestration.
A workflow specifies model and tool calls through instructions, control flow, and information dependencies. Control flow determines execution order and branching, while data flow specifies which intermediate outputs later calls receive. Orchestration organizes these calls to solve a task. AutoGen provides programmable agent interactions, while Magentic-One and Apodex 1.1 support runtime coordination and replanning
(
Wu et al., 2024
;
Fourney et al., 2024
;
Apodex Team, 2026a
)
. Graph- and code-based representations support automated workflow design
(
Zhuge et al., 2024
;
Zhang et al., 2025c
)
, and executable code can express tool-use actions and orchestration logic
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
O’Connor, 2026
)
. These advances provide expressive mechanisms for collaboration, while verification-centered systems emphasize checking intermediate decisions and their supporting evidence
(
Apodex Team, 2026b
;
MiroMind Team, 2026
)
. We therefore focus on learning when to invoke collaboration and how to construct task-specific workflows that preserve, check, and reuse intermediate results. We further examine how training changes workflow patterns, focusing on stage dependencies and the use, verification, and refinement of intermediate results. Comparing these changes alongside design quality and task accuracy helps characterize the properties of effective orchestration and their relationship to improved performance (Figures
5
and
4
; §
5.3
).
Learning Task-Specific Orchestration.
Task-specific orchestration raises two related questions: how to learn workflow generation and how to adapt designs using execution feedback, a mechanism also studied in agent–environment interaction and strategy-guided exploration
(
MiroMind Team, 2025
;
Li et al., 2026c
)
. MAS-GPT learns query-specific system generation through supervised training, while FlowReasoner and Mas-Orchestra use reinforcement learning
(
Ye et al., 2025
;
Gao et al., 2025
;
Ke et al., 2026
)
. MAS-Zero revises system designs using intermediate results, and DyFlow plans successive subgraphs using feedback
(
Ke et al., 2025
;
Wang et al., 2025b
)
. FlowSteer learns graph-editing policies from canvas feedback
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
)
. MetaAgent-X further jointly trains designers and executors
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
. DynaFlow integrates free-form executable workflow actions into the task-solving policy, coupling collaboration decisions with workflow construction and subsequent decisions based on execution feedback. Its learning framework explicitly selects demonstrations for orchestration quality and trains only the Main Agent, emphasizing reliable information transfer and independent verification with fixed sub-agents.

Experimental Setup
Our experiments examine whether training the Main Agent improves workflow-based problem solving, how high-quality data selection affects orchestration, and whether adaptive workflow invocation preserves performance while reducing workflow use. Throughout the DynaFlow comparisons, sub-agents remain fixed, allowing us to study changes in the Main Agent under a shared workflow interface and tool configuration.
Benchmarks and models.
We evaluate on 688 questions across six benchmark sets: AIME 2024, 2025, and 2026, PolyMATH
(
Wang et al., 2025c
)
(200), GPQA-Diamond
(
Rein et al., 2024
)
(198), and HotpotQA
(
Yang et al., 2018
)
(200). The PolyMATH and HotpotQA subsets are sampled with random seed 42. These benchmarks cover competition mathematics, multilingual mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, and multi-hop question answering. HotpotQA uses web search for retrieval. The Main Agent uses Qwen3.5-27B
(
Qwen Team, 2026
)
as its backbone. Across all DynaFlow evaluation settings, workflow sub-agents uniformly use the Base Qwen3.5-27B checkpoint without orchestration training and remain fixed. Both the Main Agent and sub-agents operate with thinking enabled; only the Main Agent receives orchestration training.
Training and evaluation settings.
We compare three Main Agent checkpoints:
Base
, the backbone without orchestration training;
Stage 1
, trained by trajectory distillation; and
DynaFlow
, obtained after Stage 2 training on selected high-quality demonstrations. We use GLM-5.3 Max as the teacher model for trajectory distillation. Stage 1 uses QLoRA
(
Dettmers et al., 2023
)
to fine-tune the Main Agent on 2,031 teacher-distilled first-turn examples; Stage 2 continues on 712 selected examples under Eq. (
2
).
The evaluation includes three execution modes:
Direct
answers without tools or workflows;
Dynamic
chooses between direct answering and workflow execution; and
Forced
requires workflow execution before any substantive problem solving. In both workflow-based paths, the Main Agent is restricted to designing and coordinating workflows, assessing returned results, and synthesizing the final answer; substantive solving and verification are delegated to sub-agents. Incomplete results trigger workflow revision or further calls (§
3.1
).
Baselines and metrics.
We compare against CoT, CoT-SC
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
, Self-Refine
(
Madaan et al., 2023
)
, and AFlow
(
Zhang et al., 2025c
)
, all using Qwen3.5-27B. CoT-SC aggregates five sampled answers, while Self-Refine iteratively critiques and revises an answer. For AFlow, we transfer the released MATH workflow to AIME and PolyMATH, and the released HotpotQA workflow to HotpotQA and GPQA-Diamond, without searching for new workflows on our evaluation tasks. We also include
Base + Web search
to contextualize gains on retrieval-dependent questions. The tool-free baselines do not have the same retrieval access as the workflow settings; we therefore interpret their HotpotQA results separately from comparisons with search-enabled systems.
We report final-answer accuracy, counting runs without a valid final answer as incorrect. To examine orchestration behavior, we analyze Forced-mode workflows using structural indicators and four design criteria: task consistency, decomposition appropriateness, logical continuity, and information-flow correctness. Design scores range from 0 (major defect) through 1 (minor weakness) to 2 (no defect).

Results and Analysis
5.1
Overall Performance
DynaFlow achieves the highest overall accuracy, reaching 88.08% in Forced mode and 87.94% in Dynamic mode (Table
1
). Both exceed the strongest baseline by over 10 percentage points and outperform their Base counterparts, with only the Main Agent trained and all sub-agents fixed.
Mathematical reasoning.
DynaFlow achieves the strongest results across competition and multilingual mathematics. Forced execution solves all 90 AIME questions, achieving 100% across the 2024, 2025, and 2026 sets, while both modes exceed the strongest baseline on PolyMATH by 3–4 percentage points. We analyze the generated workflows and find that they organize mathematical solving around complementary derivation, computation, and verification stages. For example, PolyMATH workflows pair symbolic derivations with small-instance numerical checks to identify errors in intermediate expressions. This integration offers a concrete explanation for the strong mathematical performance: intermediate results are exposed to checks that can guide subsequent correction.
Scientific knowledge and reasoning.
DynaFlow improves performance on GPQA-Diamond, which covers graduate-level questions in biology, chemistry, and physics. Forced execution reaches 84.85%, improving over Base, Forced by 7.07 points and exceeding Base, Direct; Dynamic execution also improves over its Base counterpart. With the sub-agents fixed, we obtain stronger scientific question answering through Main Agent training, although Self-Refine and AFlow remain ahead on this benchmark. We examine failed cases and find that incorrect intermediate conclusions from sub-agents can misguide subsequent verification, while the Main Agent can fail to prioritize correct evidence when synthesizing the final answer. These failures highlight the importance of independent verification within workflows and reliable final-answer selection by the Main Agent.
Multi-hop question answering with web search.
DynaFlow achieves the best HotpotQA performance, reaching 84.50% in Dynamic mode and 83.50% in Forced mode. Both exceed Base + Web search by 6–7 points, and Forced execution also improves over Base, Forced under the same workflow requirement. We analyze the retrieval workflows and find that they organize search around intermediate entities and verify the connections between successive hops. For example, a workflow first identifies the city associated with a venue, then retrieves the city’s nickname and checks that both hops refer to the same entity. Such evidence-chain construction and verification provide a plausible account of the gains over a search-enabled baseline and illustrate how DynaFlow organizes retrieval into a coherent solving process.

Workflow Quality and Task-Specific Organization
Connected stages and improved information use.
Figure

Hybrid workflows increase from 3.4% for Base to 83.2% after Stage 1 and 85.6% after Stage 2. Higher-quality information flow and verification.
Our analysis of Stage 1 errors identifies three recurring patterns: unsupported premises introduced by the Main Agent, verification guided toward an expected conclusion, and incomplete or incorrect transfer of intermediate information. These observations motivate selecting Stage 2 demonstrations that avoid premise injection, verification defects, and information-flow defects (§
3.2
). After training on the selected data, we find higher proportions of defect-free workflows across all four design criteria. Major information-flow defects decline from 1.9% in Stage 1 to 0.9% in Stage 2 (Figure
4
), while workflows that specify correction or refinement of intermediate results increase from 28.1% to 35.9% (Figure
5
(e)). These results indicate better workflow design for transferring, integrating, and checking intermediate results through explicit dependencies and structured information exchange, with fewer sub-agents on average (4.16 versus 4.35 in Stage 1). We interpret Base’s relatively high logical-continuity scores in light of its simpler, often single-agent workflows, which involve fewer dependencies between stages.
Task-specific roles and instructions.
Figure
6
shows distinct role configurations across tasks. Solvers and verifiers account for over 90% of nodes on AIME and PolyMATH, while researchers account for 59.6% on HotpotQA. GPQA-Diamond combines a substantial solver component with more research than the mathematics benchmarks. Verification remains common across tasks, accounting for 33.2–43.9% of nodes. This task-specific organization extends to the instructions themselves: the Main Agent generates a prompt for each sub-agent that specifies its objective, relevant inputs, and use of upstream results for the current question (§
3.1
). DynaFlow thus adapts both the division of labor and the instructions that guide execution, connecting task decomposition with information use. Relative to the transferred AFlow workflows used in our evaluation (§
4
), this flexibility supports question-specific mathematical derivation, evidence gathering, and independent checking (§
5.1
).
5.4
Adaptive Workflow Invocation
The Dynamic–Forced accuracy gap narrows from 10.75 percentage points for Base to 1.02 after Stage 1 and 0.14 for DynaFlow (Table
2
). With sub-agents fixed, this trend highlights the contribution of Main Agent training to selective collaboration. In Dynamic mode, DynaFlow answers 47.1% of questions directly while achieving 87.94% accuracy, close to 88.08% under Forced execution. Averaged over all questions, including those answered directly, it uses 2.44 sub-agents per question versus approximately 4.16 under Forced execution, a reduction of about 41% (Figure
1
). These results suggest that a unified Main Agent policy can adapt its solution strategy to task requirements while maintaining performance with fewer sub-agents. We regard the choice between direct answering and workflow execution as an integral part of orchestration: additional agents do not necessarily improve performance, and collaboration should be invoked according to the needs of each question.
6
Discussion
We view reliable information use alongside task decomposition as central to orchestration; gains with fixed sub-agents support learning to coordinate existing capabilities (§
5.2
). Stage 2 gains accompany better information transfer and more frequent refinement of intermediate results, consistent with screening for unsupported premises, constrained verification, and information-flow defects (§
5.3
). Our analysis of GPQA-Diamond failures illustrates how correct intermediate results can be lost or overridden during verification and final synthesis. DynaFlow workflows incorporate complementary evidence gathering, independent checks, and refinement of intermediate results. Future work could train sub-agents for reliable information transfer and independent verification, and extend first-turn supervision to multi-turn trajectories containing disagreements and erroneous results. Such supervision could strengthen the Main Agent’s ability to independently assess conflicting outputs, identify errors, and select actions for error recovery, workflow revision, and final-answer selection.
7
Conclusion
DynaFlow combines free-form executable workflow actions with two-stage Main Agent training through trajectory distillation and demonstration selection based on orchestration quality, keeping sub-agents fixed. Across six benchmarks, it achieves the highest overall accuracy among evaluated methods; Dynamic execution answers nearly half the questions directly with accuracy close to Forced execution. Workflow analysis characterizes how training changes structure and the use of intermediate results.

Appendix A
Experimental Setup Details
Benchmarks.
The evaluation contains 688 questions: 30 from each of AIME 2024, 2025, and 2026; 200 from PolyMATH; 198 from GPQA-Diamond; and 200 from HotpotQA. PolyMATH and HotpotQA are sampled with seed 42. AIME requires integer answers, PolyMATH includes multilingual mathematical questions with free-form answers, GPQA-Diamond uses multiple-choice scientific questions, and HotpotQA requires connecting evidence across retrieval steps.
Models and baselines.
The Agent uses Qwen3.5-27B, and all workflow sub-agents use its Base checkpoint without orchestration training. Both operate with thinking enabled; only the Agent receives orchestration training. CoT, five-sample CoT-SC, Self-Refine, and AFlow use the same backbone. AFlow uses the released MATH workflow on AIME and PolyMATH and the released HotpotQA workflow on HotpotQA and GPQA-Diamond. These workflows are transferred without an additional workflow search on the evaluation tasks. Base + Web search provides a comparison with direct retrieval access.
Appendix B
Workflow Runtime
The Main Agent passes a JavaScript program to the Workflow tool. Programs define sub-agent instructions and pass intermediate outputs through ordinary code. The interface provides
agent
for sub-agent calls,
parallel
for concurrent calls,
pipeline
for dependent stages over multiple items, and
phase
for stage labels. A sub-agent receives the instruction and inputs specified by the program; the Main Agent’s interaction history is not automatically inherited. Calls may request structured outputs through a JSON schema. Workflow completion returns the program result together with execution information, which the Main Agent can use to revise the workflow or produce a final answer. During evaluation, Direct answers without tools, Dynamic selects between direct answering and workflow execution, and Forced requires workflow invocation before substantive problem solving. The corresponding prompts are provided in Appendix
F
.
Appendix C
Training Details
GLM-5.3 Max provides the teacher trajectories. The Stage 1 training set contains 2,257 first-turn demonstrations from HotpotQA and BrowseComp. Supervision covers the first-turn reasoning and action; instructions, questions, and tool definitions are masked from the loss. Only the Main Agent is fine-tuned, while all sub-agents remain fixed.
Stage 2 continues from the Stage 1 checkpoint on 712 complete workflow demonstrations selected from the Stage 1 training set: 449 from HotpotQA and 263 from BrowseComp. Both stages train for two epochs using the objective in Eq. (
2
), with a smaller learning rate in Stage 2 and no separate validation split. Table
3
summarizes the training configuration, and Appendix
E
describes data selection.
We use
ms-swift
4.6.0.dev0 for training with 4-bit NF4 QLoRA, double quantization, BF16 computation, and gradient checkpointing. The Qwen3.5-27B backbone has approximately 27 billion parameters, with 116,727,808 trainable parameters in our configuration. LoRA targets eligible linear layers through
all-linear
, while the visual encoder and alignment module remain frozen. Each stage runs on two NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs, with a single training process sharding the model across both devices. Based on full job wall-clock time, Stage 1 and Stage 2 consume about 52 and 17 GPU-hours, respectively, totaling about 69 GPU-hours. This budget covers fine-tuning only, excluding teacher trajectory generation, evaluation, and LLM-based judging.

Answer scoring.
For DynaFlow, the prediction is extracted from the Main Agent’s final
FINAL ANSWER
line; intermediate reasoning and sub-agent outputs are not substituted for an absent final answer. Runs without a valid final answer are counted as incorrect. AIME answers are matched as integers after normalizing leading zeros, and GPQA-Diamond answers are matched to the question’s option labels. PolyMATH permits exact mathematical equivalence, while HotpotQA accepts answers that identify the reference entity or relation, including equivalent names and aliases. Approximate decimals are not accepted as exact answers when the task specifies no numerical precision.
Workflow quality and structure.
Workflow programs generated in Forced mode are evaluated by
deepseek-flash
(
DeepSeek-AI, 2026
)
with thinking enabled, high reasoning effort, and temperature 0, using the question and program without execution results. Task consistency, decomposition appropriateness, logical continuity, and information-flow correctness are scored as 0 (major defect), 1 (minor weakness), or 2 (no defect). Structurally inapplicable logical-continuity and information-flow ratings are mapped to 2 when no relevant dependencies are required; insufficient-evidence ratings are excluded. : one downstream agent combines multiple upstream results;
Multi-stage
: multiple dependency forms or sequential stages are combined.
Output reuse
None
: no upstream output is passed downstream;
Passed
: an upstream output is supplied, but its meaningful use is not explicitly required;
Consumed
: the actual upstream output is supplied and the downstream instruction explicitly requires using, analyzing, comparing, refining, critiquing, or transforming it.
Aggregation strategy
None
: no result aggregation;
Concatenation
: results are collected without substantive comparison or synthesis;
Selection
: one result or candidate is selected;
Voting
: results are combined by voting or majority agreement;
Comparison
: outputs are explicitly compared;
Synthesis
: outputs are integrated into a new answer or representation;
Correction/refinement
: an upstream result is reviewed and may be revised;
Mixed
: multiple substantive aggregation mechanisms are used.
Agent count
Number of distinct agent reasoning nodes explicitly instantiated in the program, excluding deterministic code, formatting, and simple tool calls. Counts are displayed as 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5+ in Figure
5
.

Workflow structure definitions.
Six structural dimensions used to characterize the workflow programs

P
generated by the Main Agent.
Role assignment.
Figure
6
summarizes the roles of sub-agents executed in each DynaFlow, Forced run, excluding the Main Agent. Based on commonly occurring roles in the generated workflows, we define five broad categories: Verifier, Aggregator, Interpreter, Researcher, and Solver. Categories are assigned using keywords in node labels, with phase names as a fallback. When multiple categories match, the order above determines priority; unmatched nodes are labeled Other. The Aggregator category covers synthesis, merging, and adjudication. Role proportions are computed over executed sub-agent nodes, with results pooled across the AIME benchmarks.
Appendix E
Orchestration Quality Selection
The selection judge is
deepseek-flash
, with thinking enabled, high reasoning effort, and temperature 0. It receives the question, the workflow program generated in the first turn, and any launch arguments, without the Main Agent’s reasoning, final answer, reference answer, or execution results. The rubric checks three defects:
premise injection
, where unsupported answer-relevant claims are supplied as established facts;
verification defects
, where instructions or output constraints favor an expected conclusion or prevent independent correction; and
information-flow defects
, where missing context, incorrect references, or substituted values prevent required information from reaching downstream agents.
The judge cites excerpts from the workflow program or launch arguments to support each reported defect. We verify these excerpts against the supplied text as part of the quality screening. From the 2,254 workflow-containing demonstrations, we retain 712 complete first-turn examples for Stage 2.
Appendix F
Evaluation Prompts and Workflow Interface
Figure
7
presents concise versions of the Direct, Dynamic, and Forced evaluation prompts, the shared answer format, and the Workflow tool interface. These prompts specify the conditions for workflow invocation, task delegation, and use of returned results. The Main Agent determines sub-agent roles, instructions, and workflow structure for each question. Repeated formatting instructions are omitted for brevity.
Direct: task prompt
You are a professional AI assistant. Solve the task using only the supplied information, your existing knowledge, and reasoning, without any task-solving tool calls.
This boundary applies from the beginning of the task and throughout execution, including search, web reading, and code execution. For attachments, use the file contents supplied with the task; report the limitation if required contents are unavailable.
Dynamic: task prompt
Before substantive problem solving, select one execution path:
DIRECT:
Answer using the task information, existing knowledge, and reasoning, without task-solving tools.
WORKFLOW:
Organize the solution through Workflow. Substantive research, calculations, code execution, and verification must occur within the Workflow.
Do not solve the task before selecting the path. If retrieval or another task-solving tool is needed, select WORKFLOW before the first such call. If DIRECT is initially selected but tools are later needed, switch to WORKFLOW first.
Forced: task prompt
Invoke Workflow before substantive problem solving, even when the task could be answered from existing knowledge. Research, calculations, code execution, reasoning, and verification must occur within the Workflow.
The Main Agent may only plan, launch, monitor, revise, assess returned results, and summarize the final answer. This includes the first reasoning turn: understand the task and design its execution, without independently deriving the answer or supplying sub-agents with a pre-solved answer.
A completion status alone is insufficient when required subtasks have not returned results. Treat the run as incomplete and revise or rerun the Workflow.
Shared task and answer format
The task supplies a question and task identifier, with optional attachment names or paths.
Before the final answer, output a record:
{"task_id": "<task_id>",
"Final answer": "<final_answer>"}
If no task identifier is supplied, use an empty string. Finish the response with:
FINAL ANSWER: [YOUR FINAL ANSWER]
Follow the answer format requested by the task and do not include explanations after this final line.
Workflow: delegation and tool interface
Task delegation.
Provide the original task, relevant context, attachment paths, and output requirements. Design the Workflow for the current task, using sub-agents, parallelism, verification, and additional stages as appropriate. Read and follow the tool description and input schema before invocation.
Invocation.
Supply a JavaScript program through
script
, or a stored program through
scriptPath
, with optional
args
. Each script begins with a literal
meta
object containing
name
and
description
; optional
phases
describe its stages. The tool starts execution in the background and returns a task identifier; a completion notification provides the program’s returned result.
Execution primitives.
agent(prompt, options)
launches a sub-agent and returns final text or a validated object when a JSON schema is supplied.
parallel(thunks)
runs calls concurrently and waits for their results.
pipeline(items, stages...)
processes each item through dependent stages without waiting for unrelated items.
phase(title)
labels a stage, and
args
exposes invocation inputs. Ordinary JavaScript passes and transforms intermediate outputs in an asynchronous context.
Result handling.
Do not independently duplicate the Workflow’s problem solving in the Main Agent. If results are incomplete, uncertain, or contradicted by evidence, revise or rerun the Workflow. Answer only when the returned results are sufficient, and base the final answer on them. Report a failure if Workflow is unavailable or cannot complete.

Appendix H
Case Studies of Workflow Changes
We compare selected Base and DynaFlow workflows under Forced execution with fixed sub-agents, complementing the analysis of information use and task-specific organization in §
5.3
. Each diagram is reconstructed from the workflow program and execution record; captions specify the displayed invocation and distinguish executed calls from conditional branches.
Complementary computation and explicit verification.
For the palindrome-counting problem from AIME 2026 (Figure
8
), Base delegates to one solver, which returns 59 after an arithmetic error. DynaFlow assigns enumeration, dynamic programming, and inclusion–exclusion to parallel solvers, then passes their outputs to a verifier for comparison and independent recomputation. All three solvers and the verifier obtain 62. This case illustrates how complementary methods and explicit use of intermediate results support mathematical verification.
Figure 8:
AIME 2026: palindrome counting.
Base uses one solver; DynaFlow connects three complementary computations to a common verifier. The dashed retry branch was not triggered. Repeated input and result packaging is omitted.
Preserving research evidence for scientific adjudication.
For the reaction-product question from GPQA-Diamond (Figure
9
), Base runs two analyses sequentially without passing results between them. DynaFlow assigns four research calls to distinct chemical constraints and checks the candidate products for each reaction. Both checks challenge their initial candidates, and the decision agent receives the research evidence alongside the verification results. Preserving these complementary inputs enables final synthesis to account for both the proposed answers and the objections raised during verification.
Figure 9:
GPQA-Diamond: reaction-product identification.
The dotted Base edge denotes call order without a data dependency; the displayed Base program contains no explicit
return
statement. DynaFlow shows its second invocation, integrating research evidence and verification results before answer selection.
Connecting entity identification to subsequent retrieval.
For the HotpotQA question requiring person identification and year retrieval (Figure
10
), the displayed Base call searches for investment firms and their founding years. DynaFlow instead uses three search routes to identify candidate entities, deduplicates and ranks them, and passes their names, quotations, and sources to candidate-specific resolution agents. Subsequent checks assess the selected proposal. This organization connects retrieval steps through explicit intermediate entities and supporting evidence, as discussed in §
5.1
.
Figure 10:
HotpotQA: person identification and year retrieval.
Base shows the first of three invocations. DynaFlow resolves two candidates under a top-three cap; starred calls lack valid structured outputs and are filtered out. For person candidates, resolution prompts prioritize birth-year retrieval.
Linking solution stages to audits and conditional repair.
For the geometric optimization problem from AIME 2025 (Figure
11
), the displayed Base invocation checks a supplied derivation and returns fixed numeric fields. DynaFlow connects geometric construction, parallel optimization, expression fitting, and independent audits. Optimizer outputs inform the fitted candidate, while audit findings determine whether to invoke a repair step. Together, these cases illustrate the observation in §
5.3
: task-specific orchestration connects stages by specifying what agents receive, how they use it, and how their outputs guide subsequent work.
Figure 11:
AIME 2025: geometric optimization.
Base shows its second invocation; DynaFlow shows its first. The starred optimizer was excluded before fitting because it returned no valid output. Both audits confirmed the candidate, so the dashed conditional repair call was not executed.
Appendix I
Extended Related Work
Multi-Agent Collaboration and Orchestration.
LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have progressed from predefined role-based collaboration toward adaptive, task-specific orchestration. Early approaches establish structured interactions through specialized agents, communication protocols, and iterative reasoning
(
Chen et al., 2024
;
Qian et al., 2024
;
Du et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2025a
)
. Recent methods further explore dynamic agent selection, communication topology optimization, and automatic workflow construction
(
Liu et al., 2024
;
Zhang et al., 2025b
;
Li et al., 2026b
)
.
Similar principles of specialization and selective information integration have been explored in multimodal learning, including cross-spectral augmentation
(
Tan et al., 2024b
)
, modality-decoupled representations
(
Feng et al., 2025a
)
, sparse mixture-of-experts
(
Feng et al., 2025b
)
, attention-guided alignment
(
Tan et al., 2026
)
, and dynamic cross-modal coordination
(
Lin et al., 2026
)
.
Unlike approaches relying on predetermined collaboration structures, DynaFlow learns to synthesize executable workflows according to individual task requirements and adapt subsequent decisions using execution feedback.
Efficiency and Reliable Information Flow.
Effective collaboration requires balancing reasoning quality, computational efficiency, and reliable information exchange. AgentPrune reduces redundant communication
(
Zhang et al., 2025a
)
, while broader MAS efficiency studies investigate topology optimization and resource allocation
(
Li et al., 2026a
)
. Meanwhile, analyses of multi-agent failures highlight challenges involving task decomposition, information propagation, and verification
(
Cemri et al., 2025
)
.
Related research has explored robust information selection through saliency-guided transfer
(
Tan et al., 2024a
)
, semantic label verification
(
Zhang et al., 2025d
)
, uncertainty-guided expert selection
(
Zhang et al., 2025e
)
, and generalization-preserving or collaborative continual learning
(
Zhang et al., 2025f
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. Reliable evidence integration and structured information dependencies also arise in multimodal hallucination mitigation
(
Shu et al., 2026
)
, dense video correspondence
(
Wu et al., 2026
)
, and constrained visual generation
(
Wu et al., 2025
)
.
These studies highlight complementary aspects of information selection, coordination, and reliability. DynaFlow addresses these challenges at the agent-workflow level by selectively invoking collaboration, explicitly organizing dependencies, and training the Main Agent on demonstrations filtered for orchestration quality.
Positioning of DynaFlow.
DynaFlow unifies task-specific workflow synthesis, adaptive collaboration decisions, and feedback-driven orchestration within a single policy. Unlike methods that optimize fixed workflows or separately train multiple agents, DynaFlow updates only the Main Agent while keeping sub-agents fixed. Its emphasis on explicit information transfer and independent verification enables flexible collaboration tailored to individual tasks.

article.headline: DynaFlow：主智能体现场生成多智能体工作流
article.lede: 只训练主智能体生成 JavaScript 工作流调度固定子智能体，六基准总体 88.08%，超最强基线 10.90 点。
article.problem: 现有多智能体系统大多依赖预先设计好的角色、通信模式或工作流组件，把同一套协作结构套到所有任务上，会带来不必要的通信、延迟和算力开销。已有的自动工作流方法仍受限制：DyFlow 只能从有限的算子模板里拼计划，MAS-Orchestra 则在一次决策中生成完整协作结构，看不到中间执行结果。作者因此提出「自由编排」：智能体应自行判断何时需要协作，并在解题过程中构造任务专属工作流。
article.method: DynaFlow 把「生成可执行工作流」直接加进主智能体的动作空间：每一步可以给出最终答案、调用普通工具，或写一段 JavaScript 程序，用 agent、parallel、pipeline、phase 等原语定义子智能体职责、串并行依赖与中间结果如何传递、聚合和校验。运行时在资源约束下执行程序，把输出与执行轨迹回灌到历史，主智能体据此决定是继续写新工作流还是作答。训练只更新主智能体、子智能体全部冻结：先用教师模型蒸馏出的首轮（推理+工作流动作）做 SFT，再用 LLM 判官筛掉「前提注入」「验证偏置」「信息流缺陷」的样本做第二阶段微调，正文称 Stage 1 用 2,031 条、Stage 2 用 712 条示例。
article.results: 在 688 道题、六个基准上，用同一 Qwen3.5-27B 主干，DynaFlow 在 Forced 模式取得 88.08% 总体准确率，比最强评测基线高 10.90 个百分点，Dynamic 模式为 87.94%。AIME 2024/2025/2026 在 Forced 下均为 100%，PolyMATH 90.50%，GPQA-Diamond 84.85%，HotpotQA 83.50%（Dynamic 为 84.50%）。Dynamic 模式有 47.1% 的题直接作答，平均每题只调用 2.44 个子智能体，比 Forced 的约 4.16 个减少约 41%。工作流分析显示，混合串并行结构占比从 Base 的 3.4% 升到 Stage 2 的 85.6%，显式要求下游使用上游输出的比例从 12.6% 升到 97.7%，重大信息流缺陷从 Stage 1 的 1.9% 降到 0.9%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「何时协作」和「怎么协作」放进同一个策略里学习，并证明在主智能体训练、子智能体完全冻结的前提下也能大幅涨点，说明编排能力本身可以单独学习、与执行者能力解耦。跨阶段信息传递被单独拎出来作为有效编排的关键维度，对后续多智能体系统的设计有直接参考价值。
article.limitations: 实验只训练主智能体、子智能体固定为 Qwen3.5-27B，主干单一，尚未验证更换执行者或联合训练子智能体的效果；GPQA-Diamond 上仍落后于 Self-Refine 与 AFlow，说明科学问答不是稳赢。此外 Stage 1 训练样本数在正文（2,031）与附录（2,257）中不一致，工作流质量与缺陷判定依赖 LLM 判官（deepseek-flash）自动打分，所给材料未报告与人工标注的具体一致率，训练也没有单独验证集。
article.figure_caption_zh: DynaFlow 总览：两阶段 SFT 只训练主智能体，使其在首轮选择直接作答、调用工具或生成 JavaScript 工作流，冻结的子智能体按程序协作，执行结果与轨迹再回灌历史用于后续决策。

figure.caption: {Overview of DynaFlow.} (1) Two-stage SFT trains only the Main Agent on first-turn reasoning $r$ and workflow action $a_1$, using distilled demonstrations followed by a curated subset. (2) It chooses to answer directly, call a tool, or generate a JavaScript workflow. (3) Frozen sub-agents collaborate within the workflow according to the Main Agent's program. (4) Outputs and execution traces update the history for subsequent decisions.

page_papers.title: Work Agents: Systems, Capabilities, and Optimization
page_papers.abstract: As foundation models evolve from information generation to digital work execution, agents are increasingly capable of completing complex tasks across tools, applications, and workflows. However, existing research lacks a unified perspective on how agents reliably accomplish delegated work. To address this gap, we present a work-centric, system-level perspective that views work agents as systems combining foundation models and runtime harnesses to execute tasks in stateful workspaces and deliver verifiable outcomes. We introduce two complementary dimensions, work persistence and work openness, to characterize working conditions, and classify digital work into five forms according to task scope and organization. Building on this framework, we identify five core capability families required for reliable work execution and examine approaches to model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization. We further analyze existing evaluation methods and metrics from the perspective of work outcomes. Finally, we discuss future research directions, including sustained work delegation, adaptation to open environments, and the interaction between work execution and capability improvement. This paper provides a unified framework for understanding, optimizing, and evaluating work agents, supporting the development of systems capable of delivering reliable, verifiable, and practically valuable work outcomes.

Building on this framework, we identify five core capability families required for reliable work execution and examine approaches to model optimization, harness optimization, and their joint optimization.
