Finally, we discuss future research directions, including sustained work delegation, adaptation to open environments, and the interaction between work execution and capability improvement. This paper provides a unified framework for understanding, optimizing, and evaluating work agents, supporting the development of systems capable of delivering reliable, verifiable, and practically valuable work outcomes.

article.headline: 把智能体当「工作系统」：一个统一框架
article.lede: 论文以「工作」为中心给出系统级视角，用工作持续性与工作开放性两个维度刻画智能体的工作条件。
article.problem: 基础模型正从生成信息转向执行数字工作，智能体已能在多种工具、应用与工作流中完成复杂任务。但现有研究缺少统一视角，来回答智能体究竟如何可靠地完成被委派的工作。论文试图补上这一概念空白，把「工作」本身作为分析单位。
article.method: 作者把工作智能体定义为「基础模型 + 运行时 harness」的组合：模型负责决策，harness 负责提供上下文、在有状态工作区中执行动作并接收观测。在此之上提出工作持续性与工作开放性两个互补维度来刻画工作条件，并按任务范围与组织方式把数字工作分为五类形态。论文进一步归纳可靠执行所需的五类核心能力，并分别讨论模型优化、harness 优化及两者的联合优化，最后从工作产出的角度梳理评测方法与指标。
article.results: 这是一篇框架性论文，未报告实验或基准分数，论文未给出具体数字。可计数的结构性产出包括：两个刻画工作条件的维度（工作持续性与工作开放性）、五种数字工作形态，以及五类核心能力家族。论文还给出一个系统视图，把任务规格（目标、约束、资源、权限、完成条件）、harness、模型、产出与验证串成闭环，并指出验证可由程序、人工或模型评判者按任务特定标准执行，既可在线反馈也可事后评估。
article.why_it_matters: 它把讨论焦点从「模型能力」移到「模型加运行时」的整机系统，为比较不同智能体系统、定位失败环节提供了共同语言。对做 agent 工程的团队来说，这个框架把 harness 设计、验证机制与持续运行责任放到了与模型同等的位置。
article.limitations: 论文是概念与综述性质的工作，没有实证实验或量化对比来支撑五类形态与五类能力的划分，维度和类别的边界是否互斥、可操作仍待检验。此外，验证环节依赖任务特定标准，在开放环境与长周期责任场景下如何落地，论文只作为未来方向提出。
article.figure_caption_zh: 工作智能体的系统视图：模型与 harness 构成虚线框内的工作智能体，任务规定目标、约束、资源、权限与完成条件，产出经程序、人工或模型评判者按任务标准验证并可反馈至后续决策。

figure.caption: A system view of work agents. The model and harness form the work agent within the dashed boundary. The task specifies the objective, constraints, resources, permissions, and completion conditions. The harness supplies context to the model, carries out proposed actions in the stateful workspace, and receives observations. Outcomes include answers, artifacts, state changes, and process outcomes. For ongoing responsibilities, they also include maintained conditions and event responses over an agreed interval. Verification assesses evidence from these outcomes, workspace states, and execution records against task requirements. Programs, humans, or model-based judges apply task-specific criteria. Verification may occur during execution, with feedback informing subsequent decisions, or afterwards to assess the work.

page_papers.title: Δτ-Bench: Pushing Agents Toward a Moving Capability
page_papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce Δτ-Bench, an executable agent benchmark that models the structural evolution of large tool ecosystems. In Δτ-Bench, independently evolving services continually reshape how tasks can be accomplished: familiar tools may disappear or be replaced, while more efficient alternatives emerge amid overlapping functionality and noisy documentation. Against this moving capability frontier, we evaluate whether agents can proactively discover efficient tool-use paths and promptly revise their accumulated procedural knowledge, bringing together demands that existing benchmarks fail to examine. Δτ-Bench comprises 1,588 validated multi-turn tasks across 42 domains and six successive ecosystem states generated through capability-preserving transformations. Our evaluation shows that even the strongest evaluated model or harness achieves only 42.3% task success, while initial gains from existing skill-learning methods can not consistently translate into better adaptation as the ecosystem evolves. These findings motivate Steward, an ecosystem manager that jointly manages tools and procedural knowledge through incremental skill maintenance and dynamic provisioning during task execution. Experiments show that Steward sustains higher task success across ecosystem changes with lower skill-maintenance overhead, while improving both recovery from disrupted workflows and adoption of more efficient alternatives.

article.headline: 新基准考察智能体对工具生态演化的适应
article.lede: Δτ-Bench 用 1,588 个多轮任务和六个生态状态，测试智能体能否跟上工具能力的变化。
article.problem: 在大工具生态中，服务会独立演化：常用工具可能消失或被替换，更高效的替代方案会在功能重叠和文档噪声中出现。现有基准未能同时考察智能体主动发现高效工具使用路径，以及及时修正已积累的程序性知识这两类需求。
article.method: 论文提出可执行智能体基准 Δτ-Bench，用于建模大型工具生态的结构性演化。它包含 1,588 个经验证的多轮任务，覆盖 42 个领域，并通过保持能力的变换生成六个连续生态状态。作者进一步提出生态管理者 Steward，通过增量式技能维护和任务执行中的动态供给，联合管理工具与程序性知识。
article.results: Δτ-Bench 包含 1,588 个多轮任务、覆盖 42 个领域和六个连续生态状态；最强评估模型或执行框架仅达到 42.3% 的任务成功率。现有技能学习方法带来的初始收益，也不能随生态演化稳定转化为更好的适应能力。Steward 在生态变化中维持了更高的任务成功率，并降低了技能维护开销，同时改善了工作流中断后的恢复和对更高效替代方案的采用。
article.why_it_matters: 它把评估焦点从静态工具调用转向生态演化下的工具发现与程序性知识更新，为构建能持续适应环境变化的智能体系统提供了测试床。
article.limitations: 生态变化由保持能力的变换生成，可能与真实工具生态中不规则的下线、文档噪声和竞争关系存在差距；Steward 的提升幅度与跨模型泛化效果论文未给出具体数字。

page_papers.title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
page_papers.abstract: Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improvement through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows. CLE comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. Across 17 harness-model configurations using frontier LLMs, feedback and revision yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points. Yet the best-performing system clears only 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels in just 23.3% of tasks, highlighting the difficulty of sustained learning from experience for existing frontier LLMs. As such, the dataset can also be used to post-train LLMs to strengthen their continual learning capabilities.
page_papers.content:
Continual Learning Exam
Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
CLE Team
Abstract
Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improvement through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows.
CLE
comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a
five-level ladder
, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. Across 17 harness–model configurations using frontier LLMs, feedback and revision yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points. Yet the best-performing system clears only 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels in just 23.3% of tasks, highlighting the difficulty of sustained learning from experience for existing frontier LLMs. As such, the dataset can also be used to post-train LLMs to strengthen their continual learning capabilities.

1
Introduction
For large language model (LLM) agents,
continual learning
unfolds over a long time horizon, as agents acquire, refine, and apply knowledge across successive tasks and interactions while retaining useful prior knowledge
[
56
,
49
,
31
]
. This ability is essential for sustained deployment, enabling agents to adapt to changing environments and task demands while building on past experience and avoiding repeated mistakes. Typically, this accumulated experience can improve agents through updates to model parameters, using supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning
[
78
,
79
]
, or through adaptations to their harness while keeping model parameters fixed. Harness-based learning includes retaining information in long-term memory
[
47
,
81
,
12
]
, extracting lessons through reflection
[
58
,
89
,
94
]
, and developing reusable skills
[
70
,
73
,
64
,
95
]
. For example, an agent may learn from a failed tool call, refine its tool-use procedure, and reuse the improved procedure in subsequent tasks. Evaluating continual learning therefore requires tracking performance across a sustained sequence of tasks to determine whether accumulated experience leads to lasting improvements while preserving previously acquired capabilities.
However, most existing agent benchmarks assess individual task performance without directly measuring such improvement. This limitation arises from how they are constructed. General capability benchmarks such as GAIA evaluate whether agents solve individual problems
[
40
,
28
,
50
]
. Tasks are presented and scored independently; their scores therefore characterise task-solving performance, rather than how that performance improves through continued learning. Memory benchmarks such as LoCoMo test retrieval and reasoning over interaction histories through question answering
[
36
,
76
,
75
]
, without evaluating how retained knowledge improves subsequent task execution. Benchmarks for Claw-based automation assistants, such as WildClawBench, evaluate agents in executable environments with persistent state, long tool-use trajectories, and cross-application workflows
[
17
,
38
,
83
]
. Persistent state supports continuity in workflow execution, but does not by itself establish that an agent becomes more capable through experience. Evaluating cumulative improvement requires a sequence of task attempts that supports experience reuse under controlled feedback conditions.
To address this evaluation gap, we introduce the Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark for evaluating continual learning in realistic human–AI cowork settings. Created by 50+ industry experts, CLE comprises 120 human-authored and human-verified tasks spanning 89 professional roles across twelve professional domains, each organised as a five-level ladder, for a total of 600 levels. These tasks are supported by 23,981 real-world input files, 19 simulated applications, and 16,125 human-authored evaluation criteria. In the main evaluation setting, agents must pass each level to unlock the next. CLE also supports custom evaluation through blocks, defined as contiguous segments of a task ladder that can begin at any level, with the required support files provided. Later levels introduce new assignments that build on knowledge and experience accumulated through earlier work. We design the task ladders around five forms of knowledge that agents can acquire, retain, and reuse across levels. These five forms reflect common scenarios encountered by LLM agents in real-world workflows. Tools and Skills capture reusable knowledge of how to use tools and carry out tasks, while Data Dependency connects later assignments to earlier information and artefacts. Strategy guides the choice of effective approaches and the avoidance of recurring pitfalls. User Context and Domain Knowledge help align task execution with users’ preferences and professional rules and conventions.
CLE provides a realistic environment for large-scale continual learning evaluation, supported by extensive working materials, stateful software applications, and detailed outcome verification. It includes 23,981 real-world input files spanning 77 distinct file extensions. To simulate the software environments used in these assignments, CLE provides 19 stateful mock applications exposing 1,024 APIs. Together, these resources support collaborative workflows such as integrating collaborators’ changes in Git repositories, coordinating meeting times around participants’ availability and preferences, and synchronising project updates across applications. By carrying the effects of earlier actions into later levels of each task, these stateful applications preserve the sequential nature of real-world workflows. Submissions are assessed against human-authored and human-verified rubrics containing 16,125 criteria across the benchmark. For each criterion, task authors specify a single, unambiguous expected outcome and the evidence required to verify it. A multi-turn evaluation agent acts as a verifier, using tools to extract evidence from submitted artefacts and final environment state and check it against these predefined outcomes.
We evaluate eleven frontier backbone model variants in 17 configurations across four agent harnesses. All systems execute the same fixed sequence of task ladders with model parameters frozen, retaining reusable harness state across tasks. Trial 1 (
K
=
1
K{=}1
) permits one submission per level without diagnostic feedback. In Trial 2 (
K
=
2
K{=}2
), a failed first submission returns diagnostic feedback based on the rubric, after which the agent can revise and submit once more. Even with diagnostic feedback and an opportunity to revise failed submissions, the best-performing system, Claude Code with Opus 5, completes only 47.67% of levels. GPT-5.6-Sol and GPT-5.6-Terra each reach 33.17% under Codex. These results highlight continual learning as a key challenge for
current agent harnesses
.
Our main contributions are:
•
We introduce
CLE
, a large-scale continual learning benchmark comprising 120 five-level task ladders spanning 89 professional roles across twelve domains, created by 50+ industry experts. The ladders connect distinct assignments through five forms of transferable knowledge, allowing agents to acquire, retain, and reuse experience in realistic human–AI cowork settings.
•
We develop an executable environment with 23,981 real-world input files, 19 stateful mock applications exposing 1,024 APIs, and an evaluation agent that grades submissions against 16,125 human-authored rubric criteria.
•
We evaluate 17 configurations spanning 4 agent harnesses and 11 backbone model variants. Diagnostic feedback and an additional submission yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points, yet even the best-performing system completes only 47.67% of levels.
2
Background and Preliminaries
This section connects the definitions of continual learning with a hierarchy of learning capabilities and a discussion of related concepts and mechanisms. We first introduce a common formulation that encompasses both updates to model parameters and changes to persistent state, trace the development of continual learning in neural networks and LLM agents, and illustrate how this formulation applies to CLE’s task structure (
Section
2.1
). Next, we organise continual learning capabilities into five cumulative tiers according to the autonomy and scope of the learning process (
Section
2.2
). We then discuss concepts related to continual learning in the context of LLM agents (
Section
2.3
).

Continual Learning in Neural Networks.
In 1989, research on sequential neural-network training showed that successive updates to shared weights could overwrite previously learned knowledge, leading to catastrophic interference
[
37
]
. Subsequent work on continual and lifelong learning in the 1990s articulated the broader goal of accumulating knowledge and transferring it so that earlier learning facilitates later learning
[
52
,
67
]
. To pursue this goal in deep neural networks, representative studies in 2016–2017 explored complementary approaches to preserving earlier capabilities while learning new tasks, including distillation, regularisation, replay, and architectural expansion
[

,

Representative approaches keep the backbone fixed and learn compact sets of additional parameters that capture new task knowledge, allowing the system to build on pretrained representations while mitigating forgetting across successive tasks

]

2.2
Capability Hierarchy
We organise continual learning capabilities into five cumulative
tiers
(T1–T5), based on autonomy in learning decisions, adaptation across domains, and autonomy in research design and problem selection (
Figure
3
). Each tier requires the capabilities of all preceding tiers.
At
T1
, predefined rules determine which experience the agent learns from, when and how it updates, and how it retains and reuses knowledge. At
T2
, the agent makes these learning decisions during execution under externally supplied task goals within a given task family, using experience and feedback to check and revise what it has learned. At
T3
, it adapts this learning process to unfamiliar domains without a new human-designed procedure for each domain, while preserving and transferring useful prior knowledge. At
T4
, the agent extends these learning capabilities to research by designing investigations to generate and validate new knowledge for an externally supplied research problem, without a supplied investigation or validation plan. It formulates testable subquestions, chooses and carries out experiments, analyses, or proofs, and determines how to check the resulting findings. It retains and reuses verified findings in later investigations. At
T5
, the agent also sets its own research goals and formulates, selects, and prioritises research problems to pursue, revising its research agenda as verified findings accumulate.
CLE provides a foundation for evaluating agents’ continual learning capabilities across T1–T5. In current LLM agent systems such as Claude Cowork and Codex, predefined memory and skill workflows provide the rule-governed foundation described at T1. Later levels introduce new objectives and expected deliverables, with requirements that can draw on information, constraints, and procedures established in preceding levels. This structure supports evaluating whether agents acquire and retain knowledge from earlier assignments and use it to improve their performance on later ones. Across the benchmark, we organise these connections around five forms of transferable knowledge.
Tools and Skills
require agents to apply or adapt tool-use knowledge and procedures acquired during earlier assignments to later work.
Data Dependency
makes earlier information and artefacts inputs to subsequent deliverables, requiring agents to retrieve and integrate them with current task inputs.
Strategy
connects earlier experience to later decisions through the reuse of effective approaches and lessons for avoiding recurring pitfalls.
User Context
requires preferences learned through earlier interactions to inform subsequent decisions and outputs.
Domain Knowledge
requires professional rules and conventions established or inferred earlier to be applied under new task requirements. These connections extend beyond adjacent levels, requiring agents to identify and use relevant experience from different points in the ladder. Human-authored rubrics specify the outcomes and constraints that submissions must satisfy, allowing the evaluator to assess the resulting deliverables and environment state.
Diagnostic feedback.
Feedback is derived from human-authored rubrics that group detailed checklist items into broader assessment categories. When the submission budget permits, a failed submission receives feedback identifying the relevant rubric category, while individual checklist items and reference answers remain hidden. This feedback provides an explicit learning signal that the actor can use to investigate the problem, revise its approach, and test the revision through another submission. Lessons from this process can be retained in the harness and reused in later levels or tasks to avoid repeating the same mistakes. The grading procedure is described in
Section
3.2
.
Stateful mock service.
We use stateful mock services to provide agents with a realistic environment for carrying out professional assignments. In everyday work, people rely on applications to access information, update records, and collaborate with others. Our mock services simulate these interactions, allowing agents to perform the corresponding operations through tool calls. Real applications also retain the effects of users’ actions as work continues across assignments. We reproduce this continuity by using the same application database throughout a task ladder, so records created or modified in one level remain available in later levels.

provides
19

1,024

These applications support collaborative workflows such as integrating collaborators’ changes in shared repositories and coordinating meetings around participants’ availability and preferences. Each task supplies real-world input files and specifies the workspace and application state required for its assignments. Each application maintains its own database, initialised separately for each run.

3.2
Agentic Evaluation
CLE
evaluates each submission against a human-authored and human-verified rubric. For each level, the task file describes the assignment, while a separate evaluation file contains the rubric. The evaluation file and its reference materials remain hidden from the agent under test. For each checklist item, task authors specify a concrete target, an expected outcome, and the evidence required for verification. Each item is designed to admit a single, unambiguous pass/fail judgement for a given submission. A multi-turn evaluation agent uses tools to extract evidence from submitted artefacts and authoritative application state and check it against these predefined targets. The evaluator verifies the submitted work against human-verified reference materials rather than independently solving the task to generate its own reference answer. A submission passes only when every checklist item is satisfied. With a per-level submission budget of
K
=
1
K{=}1
, the actor can submit once and receives no diagnostic feedback. With
K
=
2
K{=}2
, a failed first submission returns diagnostic feedback based on the rubric, after which the actor may revise its work and submit once more.
The evaluation agent runs in an isolated grading environment, separate from the agent under test. A unique API credential identifies each run; a unified interface provides task inputs, file transfer, task services, and grading requests, allowing actor execution and grading on separate machines. The actor cannot access the evaluator’s private grading materials or workspace. Each grading request starts a fresh Docker container isolated from the actor and other grading executions. Requests are logged to support reproduction, re-grading, and auditing.

Data Construction
The task environments and grading specifications are authored by domain professionals. We recruited
50+
industry experts across a broad range of knowledge-intensive occupations. They include PhD researchers across disciplines, software and hardware engineers, accountants, and financial and operations analysts, among others. Each expert authors benchmark tasks around work from their own role that would benefit from agent assistance and grounds those tasks in authentic input files rather than AI-generated artefacts. A domain expert drafts each task from a workflow in their own professional practice. The draft is audited by the review agent and cross-reviewed by two randomly assigned human reviewers, and it enters
CLE
only after clearing both gates. A rejection at either gate returns the task to its author for revision.
For each level, the task designer defines the occupational role and working context, provides the input artefacts, specifies the expected deliverable, and writes a checklist of criteria that a passing submission must satisfy. A task-review agent then audits the draft using a review skill authored and refined by human experts over multiple iterations. Following the skill’s predefined review criteria, the agent checks whether each task meets the benchmark’s design requirements. The review includes checks on format compliance, the authenticity of input files, answer leakage, rubric verifiability, and continual-learning design. The review agent also switches to an actor role and runs the task end to end through the same interface available to an evaluated agent. This real execution verifies that the task functions as intended, poses a realistic and non-trivial challenge, and exhibits a clear progression in difficulty across levels. These checks help keep the benchmark challenging for current agents, leaving room to measure gains from continued learning. Each review returns one of five conference-style verdicts, Strong Accept, Accept, Borderline, Major Revision, or Reject, together with itemised findings and concrete revision suggestions. Task designers revise and resubmit their drafts until they meet the acceptance standard. We provide further details in Appendix
C
.
Tasks receiving Accept or higher proceed to final human review. Each task is assigned two randomly selected reviewers, who independently conduct a full manual review. A task is admitted only if both reviewers accept it; otherwise, it returns to the task designer for revision. The 120 tasks that clear both the automated and human review stages constitute the released benchmark.

Every system is run over the full benchmark as a single serial stream of all 120 ladders in one fixed order. The agent under test uses the benchmark API provided by

Overall performance.
Even the best-performing configuration, Claude Code with Opus 5, completes only 42.17% of levels in Trial 1 and 47.67% in Trial 2 (
Figure
9
A). In Trial 2, it completes all five levels in 28 of the 120 tasks. Across the 17 configurations, the median cumulative pass rate in Trial 2 is 62.50% at L1 but only 8.33% at L5 (
Table
1
). These results indicate that
CLE
remains far from saturated for the evaluated models and agent harnesses.
Feedback and revision.
Higher completion in Trial 1 does not necessarily imply larger absolute gains in Trial 2. Of the 17 configurations, 16 achieve higher overall completion in Trial 2, with a median increase of 5.33 percentage points (pp). Although Claude Code with Opus 5 leads in Trial 1 completion, Sonnet 5 shows a larger increase, at 13.17 pp compared with 5.50 pp (
Figure
9
A–B). These results motivate evaluating gains from the additional feedback and revision opportunity alongside performance under a single submission.
Improvements in overall completion do not always extend to later levels of the task ladder. With Sonnet 5, the number of fully completed tasks increases from 8 in Trial 1 to 23 in Trial 2. By contrast, both Qwen3.8-Max configurations show higher cumulative pass rates at L1–L3 but unchanged rates at L4–L5 (
Table
1
). These results motivate examining both how agents improve with feedback and revision and whether those gains extend to later assignments that build on earlier experience.
Figure 9:
Completion Rates and Feedback Gains.
Harness comparison.
CLE evaluates the continual learning capability of the complete agent, including how its harness retains and reuses experience and how its model reflects on feedback. To examine differences across harnesses, we compare Hermes-Agent and OpenClaw on their six shared backbones. Hermes-Agent achieves higher completion for every backbone under both submission budgets (
Figure

A). Its mean advantage increases from 9.56 pp in Trial 1 to 11.42 pp in Trial 2, where their mean completion rates are 28.17% and 16.75%, respectively. The differences extend to gains from feedback and revision. With DeepSeek V4 Pro, Hermes-Agent improves by 5.50 pp, whereas OpenClaw declines by 1.33 pp (
Figure
9
B). Appendix
F
provides the detailed comparisons.

A–B show all 17 Trial 2 configurations; colours identify harnesses. Upper left is better. Bold labels and larger markers identify the observed Pareto frontier, traced by the step. Resource totals cover full evaluation runs.
Resource costs.
Resource comparisons depend on both the completion metric and the resource considered. In Trial 2, Codex with Terra and Sol both achieve 33.17% overall completion, but Terra costs $83.16 and takes 20.20 hours, compared with $210.83 and 28.20 hours for Sol. However, Sol completes 21 full tasks compared with Terra’s 15 (
Table
1
). Equal overall completion thus masks differences in full-task completion, which matter when interpreting total resource use.
Monetary cost and runtime also yield different trade-offs. Hermes-Agent with Hy3 lies on the observed cost–completion frontier but not the runtime–completion frontier, achieving 27.33% completion for $16.18 while requiring 80.30 hours (
Figure
10
A–B). These totals cover complete evaluation runs, whose workloads vary with the levels reached and revisions performed. Together, these results motivate assessing resource use alongside both overall and full-task completion, while treating monetary cost and runtime as separate constraints.

Related Work
5.1
General Agent Capability Benchmarks
General agent benchmarks evaluate capabilities such as reasoning, information gathering and synthesis, planning, and tool use. These capabilities are assessed through tasks ranging from question answering and software engineering to everyday workflows, with performance measured by answer correctness or successful task completion
[
40
,
96
,
80
,
28
,
90
]
.
Professional workflows bring additional demands on task duration, environment continuity, and outcome verification. Agents’ Last Exam covers expert-developed, long-horizon tasks with verifiable outcomes across multiple industries
[
61
]
. ClawMark models multi-day workflows in which stateful services change between turns and checks the resulting service state with deterministic verifiers
[
38
]
. WildClawBench runs tasks inside deployed command-line agent harnesses using real tools, combining rule-based checks, environment-state auditing, and model-based judgement to verify outcomes
[
17
]
. These benchmarks characterise task-solving performance across diverse domains and workflow lengths. CLE evaluates task completion across connected professional assignments that allow experience to accumulate and inform later work.
5.2
Memory and Context Learning Benchmarks
Memory benchmarks assess the retention and use of information from interaction histories. LoCoMo evaluates long-term conversational memory through question answering, event summarisation, and multimodal dialogue generation
[
36
]
. LongMemEval studies reasoning across sessions, tracking changing knowledge, and abstaining when historical evidence is insufficient
[
76
]
. LongMemEval-V2 evaluates memory of environment-specific experience through questions about web-agent state changes, workflows, and recurring failure modes, using evidence gathered from stored interaction trajectories
[
75
]
. CL-bench evaluates the acquisition and application of knowledge supplied in context through expert-authored tasks requiring new domain knowledge, rules, procedures, and patterns inferred from empirical data
[
18
]
. These evaluations address both access to prior information and the application of newly acquired knowledge. CLE evaluates knowledge reuse through professional task outcomes, while allowing each harness to determine what to retain and how to use it.
5.3
Experience Accumulation and Reuse Benchmarks
Recent work has introduced benchmarks that evaluate knowledge transfer, memory use, skill evolution, and adaptation over sequences of tasks. LifelongAgentBench constructs skill-grounded, interdependent tasks in database, operating-system, and knowledge-graph environments, with verifiable outcomes and sequential evaluation of knowledge transfer
[
92
]
. MemoryArena couples memory formation with later action through human-crafted, interdependent subtasks across web navigation, preference-constrained planning, information search, and formal reasoning
[
23
]
. SkillFlow organises tasks into families with shared workflows: agents begin without stored skills, derive skill updates from execution trajectories and rubric feedback, and reuse the updated skills on subsequent tasks
[
88
]
. StuLife studies experience accumulation across stages of simulated university life, spanning enrolment, academic work, and personal development
[
10
]
. SEA-Eval tracks success rates and token consumption over sequential task streams to characterise adaptation and efficiency
[
27
]
. CLE organises expert-authored professional assignments into five-level task ladders linked through tools and skills, data dependencies, strategies, user context, and domain knowledge. The evaluated harness determines how experience is retained and reused, while a common protocol controls opportunities for rubric-based diagnostic feedback and revision.

Task design.
Human-authored / verified
: every task is human-authored or individually human-verified;
marks mixed provenance such as generated tasks with only sampled human review.
Stateful env.
: the agent interacts with a mutable web, app, API, OS, database, or service environment, rather than only local static files or final-answer strings;
marks environments available for only part of the tasks.
Multi-Modal
: at least one task includes a non-text input the agent must process, such as images, screenshots, audio, video, or visually grounded documents.
Learning protocol.
Tiered tasks
: tasks unlock in an ordered curriculum;
marks a fixed order without gating, or gating present only in a subset of tasks.
Cross-level reuse
: later levels require artefacts, facts, or strategies produced in earlier levels;
marks settings where earlier work only helps, or where the dependence appears only in a subset of tasks.
Config. attempts
: the protocol grants a configurable per-level submission budget in which a failed attempt returns feedback the agent can act on before resubmitting.
Feedback and grading.
Milestone feedback
reports progress through task stages without disclosing failures on individual evaluation criteria.
Agentic judge
denotes grading by an evaluation agent with tools;
indicates LLM-based grading without tool use.
Audit trail
provides access to judgements on individual criteria, supporting evidence, or evaluator logs;
indicates task-level pass/fail results with execution logs only.
6
Conclusion
We introduced the Continual Learning Exam (
CLE
), a benchmark for evaluating continual learning in realistic human–AI cowork settings.
CLE
comprises 120 human-authored and human-verified tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder that connects successive assignments through reusable information and artefacts. Stateful environments and human-defined rubrics support task execution and verification throughout each ladder. Across 17 agent configurations with fixed model parameters, the best-performing system completes only 47.67% of levels, even with diagnostic feedback and an opportunity for revision. Feedback and revision improve most configurations, but these gains do not consistently extend to completing entire task ladders.
CLE
remains challenging for current models and agent harnesses, providing a setting for developing and evaluating methods that acquire, retain, and reuse experience to improve performance across successive assignments.

Appendix C
Agent Auto Review with Feedback
We use a task-review agent to conduct the initial review of each task draft and provide feedback to its author for revision before final review by two human reviewers.
Human expertise as a review skill.
The auto-review process follows criteria derived from human expertise in task design. We consolidate review criteria developed and iteratively refined by the benchmark development team into a reusable review skill. The skill specifies what the review agent should inspect, how to apply the review criteria, and how to organise its findings into actionable feedback for the task contributor.
Feedback-driven human–agent iteration.
As illustrated in
Figures
7
and
11
, an author submits a draft and the review agent applies the skill to the full ladder, including its instructions, artefacts, environment state, and evaluation rubric. It returns evidence-grounded findings that identify the affected component, explain why it violates a design criterion, and suggest a concrete direction for revision. Task authors use the feedback to revise their drafts and submit them for another round of review. This cycle can repeat throughout task construction.
Figure 11:
Review-Agent Interface Used during Task Construction.
A task contributor uploads a complete five-level task together with its supporting files and receives a conference-style verdict, review comments, and revision suggestions after the review agent completes its execution and design checks.
Final human review.
Tasks receiving an automated verdict of Accept or Strong Accept proceed to independent review by two human reviewers. A task is admitted to the benchmark only if both reviewers accept it; otherwise, it returns to the author for revision. This separation of roles combines the coverage and consistency of agent-assisted review with the contextual judgement and accountability of human experts. The development team can refine the review skill based on recurring issues identified during task construction, allowing lessons from earlier review rounds to improve feedback for later task authors.

Hermes-Agent achieves higher full-task completion than OpenClaw for every shared backbone under both submission budgets (
Figure
16
). The margin is only one task in four of the twelve backbone–budget comparisons. Its mean advantage in full-task completion across the six backbones grows from 2.36 pp in Trial 1 to 5.56 pp in Trial 2. Its Trial 2 advantage in overall completion ranges from 6.83 pp for Qwen3.8-Max to 17.33 pp for DeepSeek V4 Pro. In Trial 2, its mean actor-token usage and cost are 1.90 and 1.71 times those of OpenClaw, respectively (
Table
1
). These totals cover runs that reach different levels and perform different amounts of revision, so they do not establish efficiency on matched workloads.
F.4
Effect of Model Generation
To examine whether newer model generations improve performance on
CLE
, we compare Gemini 3.6, 3.7, and 3.8 Flash with Hermes-Agent under both submission budgets (
Table
7
). Across generations, we hold the harness configuration, task set and order, tools, and state retention fixed.
Gemini 3.7 Flash achieves the highest overall completion and full-task completion in both trials. In Trial 1, its overall completion reaches 25.33%, compared with 21.00% for Gemini 3.6 and 21.17% for Gemini 3.8. Gemini 3.8 also consumes more actor tokens than Gemini 3.7 (795.78M versus 486.25M), while completing fewer levels and full tasks.
All three models improve in Trial 2. Gemini 3.8 shows the largest increase in overall completion, gaining 9.50 percentage points, but still trails Gemini 3.7 in both overall completion (30.67% versus 33.67%) and fully completed tasks (14 versus 19). Across these three generations, performance therefore does not improve consistently with model updates, even when diagnostic feedback and revision are available.

article.headline: 持续学习基准CLE：最强系统仅通过47.7%关卡
article.lede: 50余位专家做出120个五级任务阶梯，17套前沿智能体配置中最好的一套也只通过47.67%的关卡。
article.problem: 现有智能体基准大多把任务彼此独立地出题和打分，衡量的是单题解题能力，而不是智能体能否靠积累的经验变得更强。记忆类基准（如 LoCoMo、LongMemEval）考察历史信息的检索与问答，不检验记住的东西是否改善了后续任务执行。带持久状态的工作流基准能模拟跨应用连续操作，但状态延续本身并不等于能力随经验增长，要测「越做越好」就需要一条受控反馈下的任务序列。
article.method: 作者提出 Continual Learning Exam（CLE）：120 个人工撰写并人工审核的任务，每个任务是一个五级阶梯，共 600 关，覆盖 12 个职业领域的 89 种岗位；关卡之间通过工具与技能、数据依赖、策略、用户偏好、领域知识五类可迁移知识相连，后一关建立在前一关的产物与经验之上。环境包含 23,981 个真实输入文件（77 种扩展名）、19 个有状态模拟应用共 1,024 个 API，评分依据 16,125 条人工撰写的细则，由一个多轮评估智能体在隔离容器中取证核验。实验对比两种协议：K=1 每关只能提交一次且无反馈；K=2 首次失败后返回基于细则类别的诊断反馈，并允许修改后重交一次。
article.results: 在 17 套 harness–模型配置上，最好的 Claude Code + Opus 5 在 K=1 下通过 42.17% 的关卡，K=2 下升至 47.67%，完整通关五级的任务仅占 23.33%（28/120）。17 套配置中 16 套在加入诊断反馈与重交后提升，中位增益 5.33 个百分点；Claude Sonnet 5 提升最大，为 13.17 个百分点（完整通关任务从 8 个增至 23 个）。整体上半程与后半程落差明显：K=2 下各配置的关卡通过率中位数在 L1 为 62.50%，到 L5 仅 8.33%；在六个共用基座模型上，Hermes-Agent 相对 OpenClaw 的平均优势从 K=1 的 9.56 个百分点扩大到 K=2 的 11.42 个百分点。评估智能体与人工标注在细则条目级别的一致率为 96.86%，重复三次评分的一致率为 99.46%（553/556）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「经验复用」从抽象口号变成了可打分的任务阶梯，为后训练和 harness 设计提供了明确的靶子：目前前沿智能体在单关尚可，跨关卡累积经验几乎失效。数据集也可直接用于后训练，以强化模型的持续学习能力。
article.limitations: 实验中模型参数全程冻结，测的只是 harness 层面的非参数学习，标题里的「RSI」对应的是论文自设能力分级中的 T4/T5，本次评测并未覆盖。K=1 与 K=2 的对比把诊断反馈和额外重交混在一起，论文自己也指出，仍缺少一个把 harness 重置到初始状态、其余条件固定的对照来分离跨任务知识保留的贡献；此外后期关卡的统计样本很小（K=2 下 L4→L5 的中位分母仅 14 个任务，17 套配置中有 7 套不足 10 个），成本也不低（Opus 5 在 K=2 下单次评测耗资 720.56 美元、58.90 小时）。
article.figure_caption_zh: CLE 概览：每个任务由五个前后衔接、靠可迁移知识串联的关卡组成，智能体通过 API 操作有状态应用，评估智能体依据人工撰写的评分细则核验提交结果；K=1 时每关仅一次提交且无诊断反馈，K=2 时首次失败后给出反馈并允许再提交一次。

figure.caption: {Overview of .} Each human-authored task comprises five sequential levels linked by transferable knowledge. Agents interact with stateful applications through APIs, and an evaluation agent verifies submissions against human-authored rubrics. A per-level submission budget of $K{=}1$ allows one submission without diagnostic feedback; $K{=}2$ provides diagnostic feedback after a failed first submission and permits {one resubmission}.

page_papers.title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model
page_papers.abstract: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.
page_papers.content: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.

article.headline: 用坑点预判世界模型引导黑盒智能体
article.lede: PAWM在有限多步未来内预判失败，仅在可能踩坑时介入，以引导黑盒LLM智能体。
article.problem: 黑盒大语言模型智能体擅长长程推理与精确动作生成，但对特定任务环境如何演化缺乏内化知识。已有世界模型通常逐步预测下一观测，成本高且信息有限，因为单步观测提供的任务指导有限，而且并非每一步都需要预见。论文因此追问：面向智能体任务，世界模型应当预测什么、又该在何时被调用。
article.method: 作者提出坑点预判世界模型PAWM，在有限多步未来内预判潜在坑点，并选择性地在坑点出现时介入，预测即将发生的失败以引导智能体避开。PAWM分两阶段训练：先在带智能体坑点标签的合成数据上做监督微调，再与黑盒LLM进行GRPO协同训练，以在目标环境中进一步优化。
article.results: 以Claude Sonnet 4.5为黑盒智能体时，PAWM在ScienceWorld上提升24.3%，在WebArena-Lite上提升7.7%，并优于多种基线；论文未给出其他基准或绝对分数。
article.why_it_matters: 它把世界模型的用途从逐步预测观测转向选择性预判失败，为黑盒LLM智能体提供了一种更聚焦的环境特定引导方式。若能在更多环境复现，这类介入机制可能降低长程任务中的试错成本。
article.limitations: 论文仅在ScienceWorld和WebArena-Lite两个基准上报告结果，跨模型、跨环境的泛化能力仍待验证。选择性介入若漏判坑点可能失效，原文未给出漏判率或额外调用成本。

page_papers.title: Build, Don't Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players
page_papers.abstract: Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback, their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days AutoTavern built TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of TavernAgent, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games. TavernAgent plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard's measure, its last 20 records average a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server's ten highest-rated players on every statistic (2.34, 59%). TavernBench, 960 tasks in 40 scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player: TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern.
page_papers.content:
Build, Don’t Play:
Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a
Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players
Changlian Ma
Affiliation:
Nanjing University
Affiliation:
Shanghai AI Laboratory
Email:
changlianma@smail.nju.edu.cn
Limin Wang
Affiliation:
Nanjing University
Affiliation:
Shanghai AI Laboratory
Email:
lmwang@nju.edu.cn
Abstract
Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own
against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and
battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present
AutoTavern
, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed
research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback,
their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days
AutoTavern
built
TavernGym
, the
first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of
TavernAgent
, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games.
TavernAgent
plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard’s measure, its last 20 records average a
placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server’s ten highest-rated players on
every statistic (2.34, 59%).
TavernBench
, 960 tasks in 40
scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player:
TavernAgent
answers
91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in
0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no
LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source
TavernBench
and
TavernGym
at
https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern
.
1
Introduction
Figure 1:
TavernBench
at a glance.
(a) Accuracy (%) per capability, with the play score
counting only answers within the second a live turn allows per decision; numbers:
TavernAgent
. (b) Play score against seconds per
decision; shaded: too slow for a live turn. All systems are in
Table
4
.
Games have long served as milestones for artificial intelligence, from Go and chess
(
Silver et al., 2016
;
Silver et al., 2018
)
to StarCraft II, Dota 2, poker, Mahjong and
Stratego
(
Vinyals et al., 2019
;
Berner et al., 2019
;
Brown and Sandholm, 2019
;
Li et al., 2020
;
Perolat et al., 2022
)
.
Each of these systems was the product of a large team of human experts who built the
environment, designed the learning algorithm and debugged the countless ways in which a
simulated training world differs from the real game. Today, LLM agents write and run much of
the code behind such systems, and a growing line of work asks whether they can automate the
research itself
(
Lu et al., 2024
;
Yamada et al., 2026
;
Wijk et al., 2025
;
Srikanth et al., 2026
)
.
Existing evidence, however, comes from benchmark tasks or paper reviews; it remains open whether
agents can carry a hard, real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against
people, where performance is ultimately measured in the real game.
We study this question in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, Blizzard’s eight-player auto-battler, played by millions. Each
turn a player spends gold in a randomly stocked tavern to buy, sell and position minions, then
fights an automatic battle against one opponent; players are eliminated in turn until one
remains. The game combines stochastic shops and battles, hidden information about seven
opponents, a shared card pool, a horizon of hundreds of decisions with a reward only at the end,
and a content base of nearly one thousand interacting cards, heroes and trinkets that changes
with every patch. No faithful simulator of the live game has been available, and existing AI
work either advises human players or studies simplified versions of the game
(
Section
2
).
We present
AutoTavern
, a self-improving research system in which a team of specialised LLM
research agents iterates a model autonomously (
Figure
2
). Its principle is
reality-anchored self-improvement. Agents for the environment, training, opponent modelling,
evaluation and deployment communicate only through a typed, versioned research memory; five
verification gates stand between every claim and that memory; and live games on the real ladder
close the loop, turning discrepancies between simulation and reality into fixes of rules, input
encodings and opponent models. The same feedback improves the agents’ research process: errors
they catch become lessons in the memory, loaded by every later session, or new gates, so each
iteration starts from a better world and a better method. Because the loop does not pay for the
same mistake twice, it took the agent from its first version to the level of the server’s best
players in 20 days. The human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. Over 20 days the
framework produced:
•
AutoTavern
, a self-improving research system in which LLM research agents
improve a model, its training world and their own research process from the feedback of a real
environment. In 20 days it ran about 10,000 experiments and delivered 23 agent versions with 418
human messages in all, and the errors it caught became lessons and gates that changed how it
works (
Sections
4
and
8
).
•
TavernGym
, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the
live game: all 978 game objects of patch 36.6.3, deterministic, 190–280 complete
eight-player games per second on a single core, and aligned rule by rule with real games
(
Section
5
). We will open-source it.
•
TavernAgent
, the first Battlegrounds AI to play complete games
on the live ladder, and the strongest. Its 23 successive versions, each passing an evaluation gate, raised the
first-place rate against reality-calibrated opponents from 1.9% to 41.5% (random legal play
and a scripted bot: 0%), and on the live ladder the deployed agent climbed by itself from a rating of
6,000 to about 15,000; on the public leaderboard’s measure its recent results are better than
the server’s ten highest-rated players’ on every statistic (
Section
6
and
Appendix
D
).
•
TavernBench
, the first decision benchmark for Battlegrounds: 960 tasks in
40 scenarios across eight categories, labelled by the simulator
(
Section
7
). We will open-source it.
The benchmark bears out our title (
Figure
1
): asked to make the decisions
themselves, the LLMs that built a ladder-level agent fall well short of the system they built, and
decide far too slowly for a live turn (
Section
7
). LLMs build far better than they play.
Figure 2:
Overview of
AutoTavern
, a self-improving research system.
Six LLM research
agents share one research memory and run three loops: training (minutes), research (hours) and the live ladder (days). The human sets
goals, rules on ambiguous mechanics and presses the keys the AI names. Chart: first-place rate of
the 23 delivered
TavernAgent
versions on one simulator build and three unseen seeds (24,576 games
per point).
2
Related Work
AI for Hearthstone and Battlegrounds.
Research on Hearthstone has focused on the two-player constructed mode
(
Dockhorn and Mostaghim, 2019
)
. For Battlegrounds,
Zolboot et al. (2022)
built a
Monte Carlo tree search assistant on a simplified simulator, evaluated on the first turns of
recorded games; an open-source simulator for reinforcement learning omits heroes
(
Elimelech, 2019
)
; community tools such as Firestone and Bob’s Buddy simulate
only the combat phase to show win odds
(
Zero-to-Heroes, 2017
;
HSReplay.net, 2020
)
; and DeepBattler uses an
LLM to give players advice during live games without an environment or an agent of its own
(
William-Dic, 2025
)
. None reproduces the full live game or trains an agent that plays it
(
Table
2
).
Large-scale game RL.
Superhuman systems for Go, StarCraft II, Dota 2, Honor of Kings, poker, Mahjong, DouDizhu and
Stratego
(
Silver et al., 2016
;
Vinyals et al., 2019
;
Berner et al., 2019
;
Ye et al., 2020
;
Brown and Sandholm, 2019
;
Li et al., 2020
;
Zha et al., 2021
;
Perolat et al., 2022
)
combine self-play or human data with large-scale training and start from an existing
environment. We use a standard learner, PPO
(
Schulman et al., 2017
)
with a transformer
(
Vaswani et al., 2017
)
, and focus on building and correcting the training world itself,
which here is done by agents.
LLM research agents.
The AI Scientist automates idea generation, experiments and paper writing
(
Lu et al., 2024
;
Yamada et al., 2025
;
Yamada et al., 2026
)
; Eureka and AlphaEvolve use
LLMs to propose reward functions and programs that an automatic evaluator scores
(
Ma et al., 2024
;
Novikov et al., 2025
)
; MLAgentBench, MLE-bench, RE-Bench and PaperBench
measure agents on machine-learning tasks
(
Huang et al., 2024
;
Chan et al., 2025
;
Wijk et al., 2025
;
Starace et al., 2025
)
; and recent
systems orchestrate coding agents or improve their own scaffolds
(
Lange et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Srikanth et al., 2026
)
;
Kirgis et al. (2026)
find that
agents complete the engineering of open-ended projects but struggle with the research questions.
AutoTavern
differs in what improves and in how the improvement is judged. Its agents improve
their research process through a memory of lessons and new verification gates rather than by
rewriting their own code. Progress is measured on a live ladder against people, a reality loop
re-anchors simulator and opponents to live games against proxy drift, and verification gates stand
between every claim and the shared memory against false findings.
LLMs as game players.
Benchmarks evaluate LLMs on text, puzzle, video and strategic games
(
Wu et al., 2024
;
Duan et al., 2024
;
Costarelli et al., 2024
;
Paglieri et al., 2025
;
Guertler et al., 2025
;
Hu et al., 2025
)
and on poker decisions
(
Zhuang et al., 2025
)
.
TavernBench
adds a stochastic multiplayer
game of economy and combat with answers verified by a simulator, a strong specialised agent as reference
and a real-time view: the decisions a model gets right within a live turn’s time.
3
Hearthstone Battlegrounds
A game has eight players, each with a hero, 30–40 health and a Hero Power. Every turn consists of
a
recruit
phase and a
combat
phase. In the recruit phase the player spends gold
(3 on turn 1, rising to 10) to buy minions from a tavern of random offers drawn from a pool
shared by all players, sell minions, refresh or freeze the offers, upgrade the tavern tier
(1–7, unlocking stronger minions), play cards from the hand, use the Hero Power and arrange
the warband of up to seven minions. Three copies of a minion merge into a golden version that
offers a discovery from the next tier. Battlecries, deathrattles, auras, magnetic attachments,
tavern spells, trinkets and other mechanics interact across turns. In combat, the warband fights
one opponent automatically, with random targets; the loser takes damage, and players are
eliminated until one remains. The outcome is the placement, 1 to 8.
We model a game as a partially observable stochastic game with a terminal utility of the
placement. A player observes its own state and, for each opponent, only the public leaderboard
and the warband last seen in combat. The current patch (36.6.3) contains 978 game objects: minions, heroes, trinkets, spells and
other cards. A game lasts about 15 turns and about 450 atomic actions per player.
4
The
AutoTavern
System
AutoTavern
is a self-improving research system: LLM research agents improve a model against an
environment they cannot simulate exactly and, from the same feedback, their own research process.
Its central idea is
reality-anchored self-improvement
: every proxy the agents optimise (the
simulator, the opponent model, the exams) is re-anchored to the real game at a fixed cadence, every
claim must survive a check designed to refute it before it changes the shared state, and the
errors these checks catch change the process that made them.

Role agents.
Long-running LLM research agents own the research roles (
Figure
2
,
Table
5
). A
research lead
chooses the next problem and dispatches work. An
environment agent
implements and verifies rules and repairs discrepancies found in live
games, and an
opponent agent
builds human-like opponents from human statistics and live
games. A
training agent
designs recipes and curricula, an
evaluation agent
measures, re-checks and audits, and a
deployment agent
maintains the client controller and
the models’ input formats. Short-lived workers run probes and implement features.
Typed research memory.
Agents never talk directly; they read and write versioned,
typed stores: a ledger of numbered findings in which a correction is a new entry pointing back, a
registry of rule decisions and open questions, a hand-over note, an experiment registry, and a
store of lessons loaded at the start of every session. A finding is never edited away, so the
memory records how conclusions changed as well as what they are.
Verification gates.
Five gates stand between an idea and the shared state:
•
G1
build: a code change passes the full test suite before it reaches the shared build;
•
G2
contract: every model is tied to the simulator build it was trained on, and the
controller refuses a model trained for another;
•
G3
comparison: models are compared only within one build, over several seeds;
•
G4
delivery: a candidate is delivered only after a re-check on seeds it was not selected on;
•
G5
reality: delivered models play the live ladder, and their games are replayed in the simulator.
The gates acted throughout: candidates were held back after re-checks, findings were revised by
later ones, and live games led to 184 fixes of rules, input encodings, the client controller and
the opponents, counted in
Appendix
A
.
Reality loop.
The controller logs every live game; game records are linked to the
agent’s decisions; the evaluation agent replays real combats and real recruit steps in
TavernGym
and
reports where simulation and reality part; the responsible agent fixes rules, input encodings or
opponents, and the next iteration trains on the corrected world (
Section
8
).
Self-improvement.
The loop improves the research process as well as its products. A
finding that overturns an earlier one is recorded as a correction pointing back. A mistake the
agents trace to their own method becomes a lesson that every later session loads at its start, or
a new gate. Of the six errors in
Section
8
, two became gates (the re-check on unseen
seeds,
G4
, and the comparison of the two input encoders in
G2
) and two became
standing rules (reseed copied games, and calibrate opponents on those the learner meets). Because a
caught error changes the process and not only the current result, the loop does not pay for the
same mistake twice: over the 20 days the 23 delivered versions raised the first-place rate from
1.9% to 41.5% (
Figure
2
).
4.1
The iteration cycle
Algorithm
1
shows one iteration. The cycle runs at three time scales: policy updates every
few seconds to minutes (the training loop), experiments and findings within hours (the research
loop), and live games feeding back into the environment within days (the ladder loop). A
scheduler runs the registered experiments within a resource budget and keeps their successors
queued, so the loop runs for days without a human present. The human researcher enters at two
points only: setting goals, and ruling on mechanics that the game data leave ambiguous.

TavernGym
: Reproducing the Real Game
Design.
TavernGym
is a Rust engine with thin Python bindings. One effect context
serves the recruit and the combat phase, so every card is a table of event hooks that work the
same in both; the state is an arena of entities, cheap to copy and serialisable; all randomness
comes from one seeded generator, so a seed and an action sequence reproduce a game bit for bit.
Card data are generated from the game’s own files, later patches are overlays, and a rule hash
identifies every build.
Fidelity to the live game.
All 978 objects of patch 36.6.3 are implemented. 375
verification records and 220 confirmed rule decisions document how each mechanic was checked, and
unit tests, fuzzing with invariant checks after every action and an exact legal-action mask guard
the implementation. Live games led to 46 fixes of rules and card data and 73 of input encodings,
found by replaying live turns, combats and offers in the engine (
Sections
8
and
A
).
Speed and interface.
A complete eight-player game with scripted bots takes 3.6–5.3 ms
on one core (190–280 games per second), and a late-game combat 13–19 µs (52–76
thousand per second). The RL interface exposes 245 discrete actions with an exact legal mask, a
player-view observation with only the information visible in the real client, batched
environments and exact save and restore of running games for lookahead and replays.

TavernAgent
: Learning to Play the Live Game
Model and training.
TavernAgent
is an entity transformer: each own minion, hand card,
tavern offer, pending choice and opponent is a token (up to 56), a card is represented by an
identity embedding, static features and an embedding of its rule text, and a pointer head
produces the 245 masked action logits next to value and placement heads (d=384, 8 layers, 8
heads, 18M parameters, the best of three sizes in an early comparison,
Table
8
).
It is trained with PPO
(
Schulman et al., 2017
)
on about one million
decisions per iteration with a terminal placement utility; each
training stage of 300 iterations covers about 310 million decisions (570 thousand games) and
starts from the previous stage under a KL anchor.
Reality-calibrated opponents.
Rather than self-play, the learner faces seven
library seats
: each turn, a seat takes a board (with hand and hidden counters) from a library
built from statistics of top human players and recalibrated, turn by turn, to the opponents the
agent actually met in live games; exam libraries are never used for training. This was the largest
single gain: from the same checkpoint and with the same budget, training against the
calibrated libraries raises the first-place rate from 20.9% to 27.2% on the main exam and from
10.3% to 13.5% on the harder one (
Table
3
).

Live ladder.
The deployed agent plays the live ranked ladder by itself: the
controller feeds the live game’s state to the policy in the environment’s own encoding, the policy
decides every operation, and a human presses the shortcut key the AI names, a feature of the game’s
official plug-in (
Appendix
D
). Most delivered versions entered this loop, so the agent’s
iterations are also its climb on the ladder (
Figures
3
and
10
): over 392 games on
days 5–18 of the project the rating rose from 6,000 to 14,007. Games in which the client failed (96, flagged by
the controller’s logs, never by the result;
Appendix
D
) measure the client rather than the
agent; without them the average placement is 3.22, with 16.4% first places and 77.1% top-four finishes. The latest versions
(TA-19–23) averaged 2.37 with 32.6% first places and 91.3% top-four. A problem the ladder exposed
paused testing until the loop fixed it (
Figure
3
). By the end of the study the agent was rated about
15,000, in the server’s top 100; on the public leaderboard’s measure its last 20 records average
1.60 against 2.34 for the ten highest-rated players, better on every statistic, with no sign of
a plateau (
Table
11
).

TavernBench
: Build, Don’t Play
Design.
TavernBench
asks whether general-purpose LLMs can make the decisions that
TavernAgent
makes: 960 tasks in 40 scenarios and eight categories (
Table
13
). A task
gives the player-visible state as text, the rule text of every card shown, an objective and an
answer format. Labels come from
TavernGym
: rule tasks execute the actions; combat tasks simulate
4,096 combats; short-term decisions are scored by the simulated win rate of the next combat after
the chosen option (correct within three points of the best); strategic decisions are turn
plans cut from natural games (upgrade, buy, refresh or save the Gold), each played out 128 times
by an earlier version (TA-21) and kept when one is better by a quarter place and two standard
errors; hero and trinket choices are scored against
top human players (
Appendix
E
).
TavernAgent
’s interface.
TavernAgent
does not read the text: it receives the task’s
engine state as in a game. Its policy answers the choices judged by playing the game out, its value
head the hero offers. Combat questions and short-term decisions use
TavernGym
as the agent’s
model of the game: it applies each option and simulates 256 combats after it (one-step
lookahead). Rule tasks ask what the environment does, which
TavernGym
answers by construction;
TavernAgent
is not scored on them, and its row shows a dash.
Protocol.
LLMs answer with one JSON object within a fixed output budget, reasoning
included (more is scored as wrong), in the fastest mode that answered a pilot of one task from each
scenario (
Appendix
E
).
All systems answer the same 368 tasks (eight per scenario, all play-out tasks). Jev
(
TypeSafe AI, 2026
)
, a decision model that picks among typed options without generating text, gets
the same text with each task posed as a choice over its candidates (
Appendix
E
).

Results.
Table
4
and
Figure
1
give four findings.
The system the LLM agents built is the strongest player.
TavernAgent
answers 91% of the play tasks;
the best LLM playing directly, GPT-6 Astra, 63%, the Claude models 52–53%, GPT-6.1 Sol 46%,
Gemini 3.8 Flash 44% and the remaining models 22–40%. It is near-perfect on combat, positioning,
ordering and targets, where LLMs must simulate fights in their head; with
TavernGym
as a tool they
recover most of that gap (GPT-6 Astra 62% to 97%,
Table
15
).
Latency rules out live play for the LLMs.
A late recruit turn lasts about two minutes and holds up to about a hundred
operations, so a decision that takes more than a second cannot be played.
TavernAgent
answers a task in 0.03 s
(
Table
4
). Gateway timings are not
comparable across providers, so we time every LLM on one standard footing
(
Artificial Analysis, 2026
)
:
the median time to its first answer token, which includes the model’s typical thinking, plus the
task’s answer at its median output speed. Their median task takes 1.4–26 s, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
without reasoning 0.9 s. Within the one-second budget
TavernAgent
keeps 90%,
DeepSeek its 26% and Jev its 37%, and every other LLM falls to 0%. Speed alone would not suffice: a turn chains dozens of decisions into one plan, so a model that errs on a third of
them does not play a third worse, it loses the plan; per-decision errors compound over a turn
rather than average out.
Reading rules is not playing.
The frontier LLMs execute rules well (GPT-6 Astra 95%, Claude Opus 92%, Gemini 3.8 Flash 90%), yet fall well short on
the play tasks built from the same rules: knowing what each card does is not knowing which play
wins.
Judging a game is not computing a fight.
On the turn plans scored by playing the game
out,
TavernAgent
’s policy answers 75% in 0.03 s; the best LLM reaches 54% with seconds of
reasoning, the others 19–43%.
Its policy also leads on the choices cut from natural games (81%).
8
Lessons from Self-Improvement
The reality loop and the gates caught errors that no simulated metric revealed. We report six,
each found and corrected inside the loop; four of them also changed the research process.
(i) Copied games leak the future.
A search over game copies appeared to add 23.6 points of
first-place rate; the copies carried the random-number state, so the search saw the real future
shop and combat outcomes. Reseeded per sample, the gain vanished (
−
0.65
±
1.14
-0.65\pm 1.14
points).
(ii) Two errors can cancel.
The exam once matched live results only because its late-game
opponents were too strong while the agent’s growth was overstated; once both were fixed, the exam
first-place rate rose to 43–49%.
(iii) Winner’s curse.
The best of many snapshots overstated its gain (+1.2–2.1 points on
selection seeds,
−
-
0.7 on unseen ones); hence gate
G4
.
(iv) Calibrate to the opponents you meet.
Measure a library on the opponents the learner
meets, not on uniform draws.
(v) The ladder catches what simulation praises.
TA-10 nearly doubled its predecessor’s
exam first-place rate (24.2% against 12.8%), yet on the ladder the rating fell
from 8,968 to 7,658 within 32 games, 18 of which also had client failures (
Figure
3
). The
loop paused live testing, traced the fall to client failures and an early- and mid-game
weakness the exam had hidden, and retrained; TA-11 resumed the climb.
(vi) Two encoders drift apart.
Replays of live games showed the agent selling its whole
warband on one turn far more often than in simulation; one input flag was encoded differently by
the controller and the simulator after a trinket choice. The fix added a bit-level comparison of
both encoders to gate
G2
.
9
Conclusion
We presented
AutoTavern
, a self-improving research system: LLM research agents improve a
model, its training world and their own research process from the feedback of a real environment,
in a closed loop of training, research and live games. In 20 days it built
TavernGym
, a faithful,
full-content reproduction of Hearthstone Battlegrounds, and
TavernAgent
, which plays complete games
on the live ladder at the level of the server’s best players. Asked to make the same decisions
directly, frontier LLMs, including the models that built the system, fall well short of it and
decide far too slowly for a live turn: LLM agents build far better than they play. We will
open-source
TavernBench
and
TavernGym
at
https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern
;
limitations and ethics are discussed in
Appendix
D
.

Appendix B
TavernGym
details
Figure 4:
TavernGym
.
The Rust engine, its Python bindings and the programs built on them; the client controller feeds the live game to the agent in the same encoding.
Architecture.
TavernGym
is a Rust workspace of two crates: the game engine (about 63
thousand lines, of which 27 thousand are card scripts) and thin Python bindings whose
batched calls release the interpreter lock. Recruit phase and combat share one effect context; every
card is a table of event hooks; the state is an arena of entities with integer identifiers that is
cheap to copy and serialisable to JSON; all randomness comes from one seeded generator.
A source hash identifies every build and a rule hash every rule set, and a checkpoint trained
under another rule hash is not resumed.
Content.
The card table is generated from the game’s data files; later
patches are applied as an overlay. All 978 objects of patch 36.6.3 (minions, heroes and their Hero Powers, spells, trinkets and
other cards) are implemented.
Verification.
Each mechanic was checked against the game data and official and
community sources and the check recorded (375 records); confirmed rulings go to the decision
registry (220) and unresolved ones to a list of open questions. Every mechanic has a unit test, and fuzzing plays random legal actions and checks state
invariants after every action.
RL interface.
245 discrete actions (end turn, refresh, freeze, upgrade, Hero Power,
buy, sell, play or magnetize a hand card to a position, move a minion, choose among offers), each
with an exact legality mask. The observation contains only what the player sees, with opponents’
warbands as last seen in combat. A batched environment runs many eight-player games at once, and
running games can be saved and restored exactly.
Performance.
One core plays 190–280 complete eight-player games per second with scripted
bots and 52–76 thousand late-game combats per second.

Entity tokens, a card representation that includes the card’s rule text, a transformer trunk and three heads.
Architecture.
Each own minion, hand card, tavern offer, pending choice and opponent is a
token (at most 56, plus one global token). A card is the sum of an identity embedding, a projection of
its static features (type, tier, stats, tribe, keywords, mechanics) and a projection of an embedding
of its rule text, which gives rare cards a sensible start. Attachments (magnetic minions, Dark Gifts)
are added to their minion’s token, and the game-wide state (trinkets, persistent effects and
counters) is pooled into the global token. An opponent token holds the public leaderboard
information, the pooled warband last seen in combat and the result of that combat. Inputs are
compressed with a symmetric logarithm. A pointer head scores the 245 masked actions; a value head and
an auxiliary placement head share the trunk (d=384, 8 layers, 8 heads, 18M parameters).

Opponent libraries.
A library entry is one seat’s board at one turn, with its hand and
hidden counters. Libraries were first built from statistics of top
human players (tribe shares, upgrade curves, purchase rates, warband strength by turn) and recorded
games; each turn a library seat takes an entry that matches a target strength curve. They were then
recalibrated to the opponents the agent actually met on the client: strength is measured on the
opponents the learner meets, not on entries drawn uniformly, and a graded set of libraries runs from
aligned ones to harder ones whose late boards carry venomous minions, hands and ceiling builds. Exam
libraries are never used for training; training uses twins built
the same way from other sources.
Training stages.
Learning started from scratch on a simplified rule set, moved to the full
content, then to the player’s view, then to a first-place goal against opponents fitted to human
statistics, and then to library opponents. Later versions are chains of 300-iteration stages (about 310
million decisions and 570 thousand games each), each starting from the previous stage under a KL
anchor for its first 100 iterations. Later stages also used a graded ladder of training libraries; a version is delivered only after
a re-check on unseen seeds.

matches the top 1% of human players up to turn 9 and builds two to eight times their totals from

Appendix D
Live deployment
Setting and ethics.
All games were played in the solo mode of the live game on the
authors’ own account, without commercial purpose, on days 5–18 of the project. The controller
feeds the live game’s state to the current
TavernAgent
version in the environment’s own encoding;
the AI decides every operation and names it, and a human presses the shortcut key that performs
that purchase, sale, play, choice or target, exactly as named, making no decision of their own.
Shortcut keys and state-based hints are both features of the game’s official plug-in. When a
proposal was illegal in the client (an encoding or controller error), the game was abandoned and
the error fixed before play resumed, so no human judgement enters the games counted. The study
covers one game and one patch, with calibrated library opponents in training.
Records.
Each ladder result (392 games, read from the game’s history screens) is
linked to the controller’s decision logs, which name the model in play. The rating chain is
continuous from 6,000 to 14,007; four results without a recorded placement count in it but not in
the placement statistics (388 valid placements).

Every static task starts from a real game state that the environment reshapes for its scenario
