the best option beats the median one by 5–8 points of win rate, and at most a quarter of the
options are within three points of the best. An answer is correct when its option is within three
points of the best, and its graded score is its win rate over the best one’s.
Strategy tasks are cut at the first decision of a turn in natural games of the main-exam lobby. Four
plans (upgrade the Tavern; buy the minion the labeller prefers; refresh first; end the turn and keep
the Gold), each legal in the state, are each played out 128 times by the labeller (TA-21), which
plays the rest of the turn and the game as it sees fit. A task is kept when the best plan’s mean
placement beats the second-best’s by 0.25 places and two standard errors of the difference, and the
letters A–D rotate so that each is the answer about equally often (chance 25%). Ending the turn is
never the best plan; the contest is among the other three. The labels are outcomes of play, not the
labelling agent’s preferences: answering with its own policy, the labeller (TA-21) reaches 73% on
these tasks, the evaluated TA-23 75%, and the first version TA-1 57%.
Hero and trinket tasks use the average placement of top human players in public statistics and keep
offers whose best option leads by 0.1 (heroes) or 0.15 (trinkets) places.

One system prompt for all tasks; the user prompt has a rules summary (economy,

evaluation

article.headline: LLM智能体20天自建酒馆战棋AI，超越顶尖玩家
article.lede: 六个LLM研究智能体共享研究记忆，20天自建完整模拟器与PPO智能体，天梯分从6000升至约15000。
article.problem: 现有关于LLM科研智能体的证据多来自基准任务或论文评审，尚不清楚它们能否把一个困难的真实问题从原始数据推进到能与人类对抗的系统。炉石传说酒馆战棋是八人自动战斗游戏，商店与战斗随机、存在隐藏信息、近千张卡牌交互，且此前没有忠实复现线上版本的模拟器，已有AI工作要么只给人类建议，要么研究简化版本。
article.method: 作者提出AutoTavern：环境、训练、对手建模、评估、部署等角色的LLM研究智能体只通过带类型的版本化研究记忆通信，每条结论要先过五道验证闸门，线上天梯对局再把模拟与现实的偏差反馈回规则、输入编码和对手模型。对应地构建了TavernGym（Rust引擎，覆盖36.6.3补丁全部978个游戏对象）与用PPO训练的实体Transformer策略TavernAgent，对手不是自我对弈，而是按人类顶尖玩家统计并在线上对局中逐回合重校准的对手库。
article.results: 20天内系统注册约10,000次实验，交付23个智能体版本，人类只发了418条消息（占全部消息0.6%）。在同一模拟器构建与三个未见种子上，第一名率从TA-1的1.9%升到TA-23的41.5%，平均名次3.40降至2.33（每点24,576局）；天梯上392局内评分从6,000升到14,007，按公开排行榜口径其最近20条记录平均名次1.60、80%第一，而服务器评分最高的十位玩家合计为2.34、59%。TavernBench（960题、40个场景）上，TavernAgent答对91%的对局类任务，最好的直接作答LLM为GPT-6 Astra的63%，Claude两个版本52–53%；每决策耗时0.03秒，而LLM中位1.4–26秒，在一秒实时预算内保持90%，其余LLM最高仅26%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「LLM智能体做研究」的检验从基准任务搬到有真实对手的天梯上，并给出一个可复用范式：让智能体优化代理指标的同时，用现实反馈和验证闸门防止代理漂移与假结论。同时它表明LLM智能体的产出可以远超其自身的直接决策能力——建得比玩得好。
article.limitations: 结论建立在单一游戏、单一补丁（36.6.3）和一次20天运行上，训练对手是校准的对手库而非真人；线上对局由人类按AI指定的键执行，天梯评分也受对局数量影响，与顶尖玩家的比较用的是排行榜根据评分变化估算的名次而非真实对局统计。此外388局有效记录中有96局出现客户端故障，TavernAgent在规则执行类任务上未计分（由TavernGym代答），因此它与前沿LLM在「读懂规则」上的差距并未被这项基准直接衡量。
article.figure_caption_zh: AutoTavern总览：六个LLM研究智能体共享一份研究记忆，运行训练（分钟）、研究（小时）与线上天梯（天）三层循环，图表给出23个交付版本在三个未见种子上的第一名率（每点24,576局）。

figure.caption: {Overview of , a self-improving research system.} Six LLM research agents share one research memory and run three loops: training (minutes), research (hours) and the live ladder (days). The human sets goals, rules on ambiguous mechanics and presses the keys the AI names. Chart: first-place rate of the 23 delivered versions on one simulator build and three unseen seeds (24,576 games per point).

page_papers.title: Novel or Not? PatEx-Gym: Agentic Prior-Art Search for Novelty Assessment in Patent Examination
page_papers.abstract: Patent examination is a challenging real-world task that requires agents to discover sparse prior art, iteratively refine queries, inspect technical evidence, and produce novelty assessments documented in Office Actions (OAs) across heterogeneous scientific and technical domains. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on static and limited candidate sets, leaving the full search--reasoning--assessment process underexplored. We present PatEx-Gym, the first framework for developing and evaluating agents for patent examination, which integrates three components. First, PatEx-Bench provides 1K realistic examination tasks, two large-scale retrieval corpora containing over 1M patents and 52K scientific papers, and a harness runtime supporting iterative search, document visits, reasoning, and OA generation. Second, we introduce PASS, an annotation-free Prior-Art Agentic Search Trajectory Synthesis framework. Specifically, it exploits document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors to model intra-turn query behavior, inter-turn search progression, and trajectory-level evidence and outcome quality, yielding PatEx-SynData. Third, we train PatEx-Agent at the 4B scale via supervised fine-tuning on the curated trajectories, establishing a lightweight baseline. Extensive experiments show that final decision accuracy alone does not fully reflect examination quality, while prior-art discovery remains difficult even for strong frontier models. Our PatEx-Agent achieves competitive performance against substantially larger general-purpose agents. These results show that training on PatEx-SynData enables a compact 4B model to serve as a competitive baseline for prior-art search and patent examination. We view patent examination as a demanding testbed for agentic search and deep research agents.

Abstract
Patent examination is a challenging real-world task that requires agents to discover sparse prior art, iteratively refine queries, inspect technical evidence, and produce novelty assessments documented in Office Actions (OAs) across heterogeneous scientific and technical domains.
However, existing benchmarks largely focus on static and limited candidate sets, leaving the full search–reasoning–assessment process underexplored.
We present
PatEx-Gym
, the first framework for developing and evaluating agents for patent examination, which integrates three components.
First,
PatEx-Bench
provides 1K realistic examination tasks, two large-scale retrieval corpora containing over 1M patents and 52K scientific papers, and a harness runtime supporting iterative search, document visits, reasoning, and OA generation.
Second, we introduce
PASS
, an annotation-free
P
rior-
A
rt Agentic
S
earch Trajectory
S
ynthesis framework.
Specifically, it exploits document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors to model intra-turn query behavior, inter-turn search progression, and trajectory-level evidence and outcome quality, yielding
PatEx-SynData
.
Third, we train
PatEx-Agent
at the 4B scale via supervised fine-tuning on the curated trajectories, establishing a lightweight baseline.
Extensive experiments show that final decision accuracy alone does not fully reflect examination quality, while prior-art discovery remains difficult even for strong frontier models.
Our PatEx-Agent achieves competitive performance against substantially larger general-purpose agents.
These results show that training on PatEx-SynData enables a compact 4B model to serve as a competitive baseline for prior-art search and patent examination.
We view patent examination as a demanding testbed for agentic search and deep research agents.
1
Introduction
Information retrieval systems have long served as a fundamental gateway to information access, spanning general-purpose Web search
[
Brin and Page, 1998
,
Burges et al., 2005
]
and domain-specific search engines in knowledge-intensive fields such as law
[
Feng et al., 2024
,
Harvey AI, 2026
]
, education
[
Usta et al., 2021
]
, finance
[
Choe et al., 2025
]
, and intellectual property (IP)
[
Roda et al., 2009
]
.
With the rapid development of large language models (LLMs), the paradigm of information access is gradually shifting from discriminative relevance estimation
[
Salton and Buckley, 1988
,
Robertson et al., 1994
]
over in-domain corpora toward generative
[
Li et al., 2025
]
and agentic search paradigm
[
Du et al., 2026b
,
Ning et al., 2026
]
. This shift is particularly consequential for patent examination, where reliable novelty assessment fundamentally depends on discovering and reasoning over evidence from large-scale prior-art corpora.
Patent examination is inherently a knowledge-intensive information access task
[
Wang et al., 2026b
]
.
To assess the novelty of an application, examiners must discover relevant evidence from massive collections of prior art rather than relying on pre-identified references.
They then analyze the retrieved prior art against claim limitations to determine whether the invention has been previously disclosed
[
Knappich et al., 2026
]
.
This goes beyond fine-grained relevance matching
[
Risch et al., 2020
,
Ni et al., 2024
]
or reasoning
[
Lim et al., 2025
,
Wang et al., 2026b
]
over given prior-art documents:
novelty assessment in patent examination requires discovering relevant prior art from a large search space and using intermediate findings to guide subsequent search, claim-level comparison, and generate an Office Action (OA)-style report under relevant legal constraints
[
Setchi et al., 2021
]
.
Such a process naturally forms a tight
search–reasoning–assessment
loop, making patent examination a particularly challenging setting for agentic search.
Recent efforts have progressively shifted patent novelty assessment toward more realistic examination settings.
HUPD
[
Suzgun et al., 2023
]
formulated patent examination as application-level acceptance prediction, while IPBench
[
Wang et al., 2026a
]
evaluated the patent examination and classification capabilities of LLMs.
PANORAMA
[
Lim et al., 2025
]
, in contrast, decomposed claim-level examination into prior-art retrieval, relevant-paragraph identification, and novelty or non-obviousness classification.
More recent work further emphasizes fine-grained and process-oriented evaluation: FiNE-Patents
[
Knappich et al., 2026
]
assesses feature-level passage retrieval and novelty reasoning, while PatRe
[
Wang et al., 2026b
]
models the multi-turn lifecycle of
OA
generation and applicant rebuttal.
Existing benchmarks remain static and narrowly scoped relative to realistic examination: they evaluate examination components in isolation, constrain retrieval to small predefined candidate pools, or assume access to relevant prior art. As a result, they cannot capture the adaptive and iterative search, evidence discovery, and reasoning required in realistic patent examination.

To address these gaps, we present
PatEx-Gym
, to the best of our knowledge, the first framework for developing and evaluating agents for novelty-oriented prior-art search and reasoning, with generated OAs serving as a downstream signal of novelty assessment.
Specifically, it integrates three core components that unify benchmarking, scalable trajectory synthesis, and supervised agent training within a single framework, as illustrated in Figure
1
.
Beyond evaluating final OA alone, our PatEx-Gym exposes the complete
search–reasoning–assessment
process, enabling both fine-grained search behavior analysis and the construction of high-quality trajectory for training stronger patent examination agents.
More importantly, PatEx-Gym also serves as a challenging testbed for general search agents, since its broad coverage across IPC sections naturally spans heterogeneous scientific and technical domains, requiring agents to perform cross-domain
query adaptation
,
tool use
,
evidence integration

technical reasoning

report generation
.
Our main contributions are as follows:
•
We introduce
PatEx-Bench
, the first benchmark for agentic prior-art search and novelty assessment in patent examination scenario, comprising 1K realistic tasks.
It’s supported by large-scale
Patent-1M
,
Paper-52K
, and a diverse search toolset for prior-art search, reasoning, and OA generation.
•
We propose

,
i.e.

ynthesis, a annotation-free framework that synthesizes high-quality prior-art search trajectories.
By treating document visits as implicit relevance signals and evidence-acquisition anchors, PASS models intra- and inter-turn search behavior and progression, together with rollout-level evidence and outcome quality, yielding
PatEx-SynData
, which contains 3K filtered trajectories for agent training.
•
Building on PatEx-SynData, we develop
PatEx-Agent
at
4B
scale via SFT for prior-art search and novelty assessment in patent examination.
Despite its compact scale, our PatEx-Agent exhibits strong performance and establishes a lightweight baseline: the 4B variant performs comparably to models with
∼
\sim
30B parameters and achieves Searched Recall (Search-R) on par with Qwen3.7-Max.
This also demonstrates the potential of lightweight agents for efficient local deployment in practical patent examination settings.
2
Related Work
2.1
Agentic Search and Deep Research
Conventional information retrieval methods estimate the relevance between a user query and documents in a corpus, returning a ranked list through lexical or learned matching functions
[
Robertson et al., 1994
,
Burges et al., 2005
]
.
With the emergence of LLMs, search systems increasingly move beyond scoring for a fixed query toward actively planning and adapting the search process
[
Li et al., 2025
]
.
ReAct
[
Yao et al., 2023
]
and IRCoT
[
Trivedi et al., 2023
]
provide foundations for interleaving reasoning with environment actions or retrieval.
Recent work further focuses on training search agents.
Search-R1
[
Jin et al., 2025
]
learns multi-turn reasoning and search through reinforcement learning and TIPS
[
Xie et al., 2026
]
leverage turn-level reward to optimize search-augmented LLMs.
FORT-Searcher
[
Deng et al., 2026
]
constructs shortcut-resistant search tasks and trajectories.
And SearchArt
[
Mei et al., 2026
]
combines verified task synthesis with multi-stage post-training.
These methods formulate search as a sequential decision process in which retrieved evidence informs subsequent queries and reasoning.

Agentic search has further expanded to long-horizon Web research

and specialized document retrieval.
Deep Research (DR)
[
Shi et al., 2025

represents a prominent form of agentic search, in which agents conduct multi-step retrieval, synthesize evidence across sources, and produce citation-grounded answers or reports.
Recent DR benchmarks and methods evaluate and train agents in terms of answer quality, citation correctness, and search behavior
[
Li et al., 2026
,

.
In specialized settings, PaperScout
[
Pan et al., 2026
]
dynamically combines direct search with citation expansion for academic literature retrieval.
Patent examination requires search to support a formal, claim-level decision under strict evidentiary and legal constraints.
Our
PatEx-Gym
adapts the agentic search paradigm to patent examination, where agents search a large-scale prior-art corpus and connect iterative evidence discovery with claim-level reasoning to produce traceable examination.
2.2
Patent Retrieval and Examination
Prior-art retrieval is fundamental to patent examination, as reliable novelty assessments depend on identifying relevant earlier disclosures from massive patent collections.
NTCIR Patent Retrieval
[
Fujii et al., 2004
]
and CLEF-IP
[
Piroi et al., 2011
]
establish benchmarks for prior-art search, catalyzing advances in lexical retrieval, query expansion, cross-lingual matching, and patent-specific ranking.
Within the broader examination process, retrieval is interleaved with query refinement, inspection of full disclosures, and reasoning that connects prior-art evidence to legally grounded decisions.
Beyond ranking-based evaluation of prior-art retrievers
[
Fujii et al., 2004
,
Suzgun et al., 2023
]
, recent benchmarks incorporate finer-grained evidence and reasoning into patent examination using LLMs
[
Wang et al., 2026a
]
.
PANORAMA
[
Lim et al., 2025

3
PatEx-Bench
In this section, we introduce
PatEx-Bench
, the first benchmark for evaluating agentic prior-art search and novelty assessment in patent examination scenario.
Unlike settings in fixed candidate documents, PatEx-Bench requires an agent to autonomously discover temporally eligible patents and non-patent literature (NPL) and inspect their underlying disclosures.
The agent must then reason over claims and produce an evidence-grounded novelty assessment in the form of a traceable Office Action (OA).
Each task runs in an isolated Codex harness that provides the workspace and toolsets over our large-scale Patent-1M and Paper-52K corpora.
This design makes it possible to evaluate not only the final OA, but also the complete
search–reasoning–assessment
trajectory.

4
PatEx-SynData and PatEx-Agent
Building upon the workspace environment of PatEx-Gym, we further investigate whether strong prior-art search capabilities can be acquired through agentic training.
We propose
PASS
, a scalable trajectory synthesis framework that generates prior-art search trajectories with a teacher model and leverages document visits as implicit relevance signals to segment trajectories, model fine-grained trajectory quality, and curate high-quality search behaviors.
We further use PASS to construct
PatEx-SynData
, a curated training set of approximately 3K high-quality prior-art search trajectories selected from 10K teacher-generated rollouts.
Based on PatEx-SynData, we train
PatEx-Agent
to acquire effective agentic search behaviors for prior-art discovery in realistic patent examination scenario.

5.2
Main Results on PatEx-Bench
As shown in Table
2
, we report the performance of evaluated models on PatEx-Bench under the Codex harness.
Overall, the agents exhibit substantial performance variation, with Scores ranging from 3.79 to 7.34.
Claude-Opus-5-max achieves the best results in Score, Statute F1, and all three reference-recall metrics.
The Select-R peaks at only 32.4, highlighting substantial room for improvement in statutory reasoning and prior-art search.
Notably, despite its compact 4B scale, PatEx-Agent achieves a Search-R of 38.7, surpassing larger models such as Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, while remaining competitive in OA quality.
We further analyze the differences in terms of prior-art discovery and examination quality as follows.
Strong models still face substantial prior-art discovery challenges.
Claude-Opus-5-max achieves the highest OA quality Score at 7.34, together with the strongest statute identification and reference recall across all three retrieval stages.
Nevertheless, even the strongest Search-R remains below 50% and Select-R below 33%, highlight the difficulty of discovering and retaining examiner-cited references through a progressive search process.
Notably, our PatEx-Agent substantially improves over its Qwen3.5-4B backbone, increasing the OA quality Score from 3.79 to 5.41 (
+42.7%
) and yielding consistent gains across all search and reasoning metrics, ranging from
+17.5%
to
+91.7%
.
These results suggest that effective prior-art discovery is not solely determined by model scale, but can be substantially improved by explicitly training search and reasoning capabilities.

Case study of two AI-domain patent applications.
The left example retains relevant prior art through search, inspection, and selection,
while the right example retrieves the relevant reference but fails to use it in the final evidence set.
We provide a detailed case study with two contrasting examples in Figure
8
, covering successful prior-art retention and failure to use retrieved evidence in the final decision.
(I)
In the left example, we observe a successful pipeline: the agent decomposes the claim into complementary concepts, reformulates its query across retrieval tools, verifies candidate prior-art, and assigns distinct evidentiary roles before generating the OA.
It preserves the oracle reference throughout the Search–Visit–Select funnel and yields the correct decision and statutory ground.
(II)
In the right example, we observe a different pattern in which the agent retrieves the oracle reference but does not promote it to document inspection or final selection.
Its statutory prediction is incomplete but does not introduce incorrect grounds.
Together, these examples show that effective agentic examination requires both iterative search and disciplined evidence selection:
broad retrieval can expose the necessary prior art, but only verified and correctly selected novelty-aware evidence can support a complete legal conclusion.
6
Conclusion
In this work, we introduced
PatEx-Gym
, a unified framework for developing and evaluating agentic patent examination models, including
PatEx-Bench
, PASS for synthesizing
PatEx-SynData
, and the lightweight baseline
PatEx-Agent
.
Our extensive experiments show that final decision accuracy alone cannot fully capture examination quality, and that prior-art discovery, evidence inspection, and final selection remain challenging even for strong frontier models.
Despite its 4B scale, our PatEx-Agent substantially improves over its base model and achieves prior-art discovery performance comparable to agents with
∼
\sim
30B size.
These findings identify evidence inspection and selection as central challenges for agentic search and deep research.
Moreover, we believe that effective agents must go beyond document search to coordinate adaptive querying, tool-use, evidence integration, and reasoning throughout the search process.
We hope our PatEx-Gym provides a realistic testbed for advancing evidence-grounded agentic search and deep research.

article.headline: PatEx-Gym：专利审查的智能体检索基准
article.lede: 论文构建1K真实专利审查任务与百万级专利检索库，并用PASS合成约3K轨迹训练4B智能体。
article.problem: 现有专利审查基准多依赖静态、小规模候选集，或把检索、段落定位与新颖性判断分开评估，难以覆盖真实审查中的完整搜索—推理—评估闭环。真实审查要求智能体从大规模现有技术中自主发现证据、迭代改写查询、检查全文并生成有法律约束的审查意见。
article.method: 作者提出PatEx-Gym：PatEx-Bench含1,000个USPTO真实审查任务，检索库为1,011,901件专利和52,105篇论文，运行环境提供布尔、BM25、BGE-M3检索及文档访问工具。PASS把文档访问当作隐式相关性与证据获取锚点，对轮内查询、轮间检索进展、轨迹级证据与结果质量分层打分，再用锦标赛排序从10K教师轨迹中筛出约3K条PatEx-SynData。PatEx-Agent以Qwen3.5-4B为底座做监督微调。
article.results: 在PatEx-Bench上，PatEx-Agent-4B的OA质量分为5.41，较底座Qwen3.5-4B的3.79提升42.7%；Search-R从23.2升至38.7，Select-R从12.0升至18.2。最强基线Claude-Opus-5-max的Score为7.34、Search-R为48.7、Select-R为32.4；Qwen3.6-27B决策准确率最高（87.6%），但Score仅5.96、Select-R 19.5，说明最终决策正确不等于检索与审查质量高。NPL检索上，PatEx-Agent的Paper Search-R为69.4，接近Qwen3.8-Max的69.6。
article.why_it_matters: 它把专利审查做成可审计的智能体检索测试床，并显示4B小模型经轨迹筛选与SFT后可在部分检索指标上接近更大模型，对轻量本地部署有吸引力。
article.limitations: 论文未单列局限性分析；从设置看，任务仅覆盖USPTO公开记录与1K条审查任务，OA质量依赖3个LLM评委（评委间Kendall W=0.849），训练轨迹来自教师模型合成，向其他专利局、语言和真实审查流程的泛化仍待验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: PASS的轨迹合成流程：以访问为锚点切分检索轨迹，分层评估查询行为与证据/结果质量，再经锦标赛排序和拒绝采样筛选高质量轨迹。

figure.caption: Overview of Prior-Art Agentic Search Trajectory Synthesis~(PASS) for PatEx-SynData. (A) Visit-guided, relevance-aware rollout segmentation divides trajectories into semantic turns using visits as anchors. $r$ denotes reasoning, $S$ denotes search, $V$ denotes visit, $Z$ denotes the returned tool results, and $W$ denotes workspace tools, e.g. {Write}.~(B) Hierarchical quality modeling evaluates multidimensional quality. (C) Tournament-based ranking with rejection sampling for high-quality trajectories.

page_papers.title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
page_papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally unreasonable actions in preferred trajectories and ignores each action's downstream deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9% and 94.3% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7% and 70.8% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to 2.44times while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS

Abstract
Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental
uniform credit assignment dilemma
that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally unreasonable actions in preferred trajectories and ignores each action’s downstream deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose
Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS)
, a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9% and 94.3% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7% and 70.8% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to
2.44
×
2.44\times
while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes:
https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS
.
1
Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that make sequential decisions through interactions with external environments. Their planning and reasoning capabilities have enabled applications in software engineering (
?
), personal assistance (
?
), and graphical user interface navigation (
?
).
Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for elevating the agentic capacity of LLMs (
??
).
During RL rollouts, agents generate trajectories composed of interleaved environment states and actions, which introduces a fundamental
credit assignment challenge
:
How should trajectory-level rewards and penalties be attributed to individual actions?
Actor-critic algorithms (e.g., PPO (
?
)) address this by learning a separate critic, which introduces substantial computational overhead and optimization instability in long-horizon settings (
??
). Conversely, critic-free algorithms like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (
?
) offer computational efficiency by broadcasting a trajectory-level advantage uniformly to every action (
?
). However, this inherently treats all intra-trajectory actions identically, completely overlooking their critical differences in local validity, task contribution, and downstream influence. As detailed in §
3.2
, we term this structural limitation the
uniform credit assignment dilemma
.
To systematically understand the uniform credit assignment dilemma, we conduct a fine-grained action-intervention analysis (§
4.2
). Our findings reveal a dual suboptimality. First, in preferred trajectories with positive advantages, uniform credit inadvertently reinforces structurally invalid actions (i.e., unreasonable actions) that pollute the context history and impede the agent from reaching success. Second, in unpreferred trajectories with negative advantages, uniform penalization ignores the autoregressive nature of LLMs, where the later deviations may drive from earlier actions. Consequently, they suppress all actions equally but arbitrarily without considering their actual downstream influence.
To resolve this dilemma without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS) in §
4.3
. ProAS leverages an Agentic Reference Graph (ARG, mentioned in §
4.1
), which abstracts task progression into dynamically evolving sub-goals to formally annotate whether an action is
reasonable
(structurally valid) or
progress-advancing
(driving task completion). Using these structural annotations, ProAS asymmetrically reshapes trajectory-level advantages in Eq.
7
:
(1) Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI)
zeros out the local advantages of
unreasonable
actions in preferred trajectories to prevent their inadvertent reinforcement.
(2) Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR)
utilizes Future-Drift (Eq.
6
), the inclusive count of downstream
non-advancing
actions, to assign proportionally heavier penalties to actions triggering severe downstream stagnation.
Extensive experiments in §
6
on ALFWorld (
?
) and WebShop (
?
) using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (
?
) validate ProAS as a versatile, plug-and-play enhancer. It universally elevates mainstream group-based RL baselines (GRPO (
?
), DAPO (
?
), GiGPO (
?
)), boosting success rates by up to 16.7 points (e.g., GRPO on 1.5B ALFWorld) and accelerating training convergence by
1.12
×
1.12\times
to
2.44
×
2.44\times
. On top of that, this orthogonal enhancement propels these standard algorithms to establish new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, consistently eclipsing the strong segment-level baseline, MiGPO (
?
). Notably, GiGPO+ProAS outperforms MiGPO by a massive 13.1 points on WebShop with 1.5B model and secures the highest overall success rate of 94.3% on ALFWorld with 7B model. Furthermore, comprehensive ablations (§
6.2
) show that ProAS’s core mechanisms are both synergistic and superior to alternative advantage shaping variants, and confirm ProAS’s robust efficacy against incomplete or distilled ARGs, underscoring the necessity of ARG’s online evolution mechanism.
In summary, our primary contributions are:
•
Problem Identification:
We expose the uniform credit assignment dilemma in critic-free agentic RL, demonstrating how uniform advantages inadvertently reinforce contextual noise in preferred trajectories and ignore the downstream influence of actions in unpreferred ones.
•
Algorithmic Innovation:
We propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework. Guided by a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG), ProAS achieves fine-grained, critic-free credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR).
•
Empirical Superiority:
ProAS acts as a universal enhancer across multiple model scales and environments. It significantly accelerates training convergence, propels standard group-based algorithms to surpass strong SOTA baselines (e.g., MiGPO), and exhibits high robustness against imperfect and distilled reference guidance.
2
Related Works
Multi-Turn Agentic Tasks.
Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to solve complex real-world tasks (
?
). Given the intricacies of these environments, agents must engage in multi-turn interactions, continuously accumulating contextual knowledge and making sequential decisions to drive task completion. To facilitate the training and evaluation of such agents, the community has introduced various simulated environments. Examples include ALFWorld (
?
) for embodied household tasks, WebShop (
?
) for web navigation, AppWorld (
?
) for application development, and
τ
2
\tau^{2}
-Bench (
?
) for evaluating dynamic conversational abilities in domains like aviation and retail.
Rather than constructing new environments, our work focuses on developing more efficient and effective training paradigms tailored for existing multi-turn agentic tasks.
RL for LLM Agents.
Critic-free RL like GRPO (
?
) is widely adopted for LLM agents (
???
), but suffers from sparse-reward advantage vanishment (
?
) and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment (
?
). While DAPO (
?
) and dense-reward methods (
???
) mitigate this vanishment, their credit assignment remains trajectory-bound. To differentiate intra-trajectory actions, GiGPO (
?
) and MiGPO (
?
) compute relative advantages by matching anchor states or milestones across rollouts.
In this work, we systematically expose the flaws of uniform credit assignment in both preferred and unpreferred trajectories, addressing them through advantage shaping, which serves as a plug-and-play module for existing critic-free RL algorithms.

Since RL fundamentally optimizes policies by incentivizing or suppressing action likelihoods, tailored credit assignment requires understanding both the intrinsic properties of each step (e.g., reasonableness and progress advancement) and how modulating them dictates the final outcome. To quantify these step-level properties, §

constructs an Agentic Reference Graph (ARG). Guided by an intervention study probing these modulation effects (§
4.2
), §
4.3
introduces Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a lightweight framework designed to resolve the uniform credit dilemma via asymmetric advantage shaping.

6.1
Main Results
Table

Baseline Comparisons.
We first contrast ProAS against established learning paradigms. While both SFT and ProAS leverage expert annotations as supervisory signals, ProAS abstracts them into ARGs to structurally guide RL, significantly outperforming SFT’s direct behavior imitation. Specifically, GiGPO+ProAS achieves 91.9% and 94.3% SR on the 1.5B and 7B ALFWorld benchmarks, respectively, surpassing SFT by 12.2 and 14.4 points. Furthermore, ProAS consistently eclipses PPO, a conventional critic-based RL algorithm, across all settings. ProAS variants outpace PPO by 5.5 to 18.7 points in ALFWorld SR, alongside steady improvements of 4.1 to 12.2 points in WebShop TS and 3.4 to 11.5 points in WebShop SR. Ultimately, these results confirm that explicitly integrating ARG-derived progress signals into RL is vastly superior to both passive trajectory imitation and conventional critic-based credit assignment.

State-of-the-Art Performance.
Equipped with ProAS, group-based RL algorithms consistently establish new SOTA records. In ALFWorld, GiGPO+ProAS attains the highest SR of 94.3% on the 7B model. This surpasses the strong segment-level baseline MiGPO and eclipses the proprietary GPT-5.6-Sol by a massive 15.4 points. WebShop presents a notably steeper challenge, evidenced by GPT-5.6-Sol’s severe struggle at 21.9% SR. Despite this difficulty, ProAS variants dominate the leaderboard. On the 1.5B model, both DAPO and GiGPO integrated with ProAS tie for the best SR at 66.7%, outperforming MiGPO by a striking 13.1 points. On the 7B scale, GRPO+ProAS peaks at 70.8%, further extending the lead over MiGPO.
Algorithm Compatibility.
Crucially, ProAS demonstrates remarkable plug-and-play compatibility, universally uplifting baseline RL algorithms across all tested configurations. For ALFWorld, equipping GRPO with ProAS yields the most dramatic improvements, boosting the SR by 16.7 points on the 1.5B model and 8.4 points on the 7B model. Consistent gains are mirrored in WebShop, where DAPO+ProAS generates a 9.4-point uplift at the 1.5B scale, and GRPO+ProAS provides a 3.1-point boost at 7B. This confirms ProAS as a versatile enhancer that elevates both the performance floor and ceiling of diverse group-based RL paradigms.

These results confirm the importance of ARG evolution for ProAS, while showing ProAS remains robust to imperfect ARGs.
Distill
tests ProAS with synthetic references, since gold-standard trajectories are often unavailable in practice. We prompt a 7B model to generate successful rollouts across training tasks, building a distilled ARG covering 2,566 tasks. With this synthetic ARG, the 1.5B model reaches 83.6% SR on ALFWorld and 64.8% on WebShop, comparable to GRPO+ProAS and 13.3 and 7.8 points above GRPO, respectively.
This validates ProAS’s applicability even on teacher-distilled trajectories.
7
Conclusion
In this work, we expose the
uniform credit assignment dilemma
in critic-free agentic RL, where uniform advantages reinforce contextual noise in preferred trajectories (
A
i
>
0
A_{i}>0
) and ignore the downstream deviation of actions in unpreferred ones (
A
i
<
0
A_{i}<0
). To address this without critic overhead, we proposed Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), which leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive evaluations across multiple model scales and environments confirm ProAS as a robust, universal enhancer that accelerates convergence and propels mainstream baselines to new state-of-the-art performance. The ablation study further confirms MUI-APR synergy, necessity of ARG evolution and robustness under incomplete or distilled ARGs. Together, these results establish a highly efficient, scalable pathway for elevating autonomous language agents.

Time Analysis
We compare the wall-clock training time of vanilla RL and RL + ProAS, measured from TensorBoard logs. As shown in Fig.

article.headline: ProAS：用进度参考图重塑优势，改进多轮智能体R
article.lede: 无critic的GRPO类算法把轨迹级优势平均分给所有动作；ProAS用动态演化的参考图做细粒度信用分配，在ALFWor
article.problem: GRPO等无critic算法为省去critic开销，把轨迹级优势原样广播给轨迹内每个动作。作者指出这造成「统一信用分配困境」：在正优势的成功轨迹里，结构上不合理的动作也被一并强化；在负优势的失败轨迹里，又无视各动作对后续偏差的实际影响。
article.method: ProAS维护一个动态演化的Agentic Reference Graph（ARG），把成功轨迹抽象为按子目标排序的有向无环图，并据此给每个动作打上「合理」与「推进进度」两个二值标签。对正优势轨迹，MUI把不合理动作的局部优势置零；对负优势轨迹，APR按Future-Drift（该步起后续非推进动作的累计数）归一化后重新分配惩罚。整个框架即插即用，不需要critic或额外奖励模型。
article.results: 在Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct和7B-Instruct上，GiGPO+ProAS在ALFWorld取得91.9%和94.3%的成功率；WebShop上DAPO/GiGPO+ProAS（1.5B）与GRPO+ProAS（7B）分别达到66.7%和70.8%。GRPO+ProAS把1.5B模型在ALFWorld上的成功率从70.3%提升到87.0%（+16.7个百分点），训练收敛加速1.12×至2.44×。作者统计，不合理动作占成功GRPO轨迹的41.6%（ALFWorld）和39.6%（WebShop），非推进动作占失败轨迹的93.1%和76.1%；注入四步不合理历史使期望成功率从82%降到58%，而抑制Future-Drift为47、23、11、4的动作后，恢复的期望成功率分别为24%、16%、10%和0%。
article.why_it_matters: 它不引入critic、也不改RL主干，就能普遍抬高GRPO、DAPO、GiGPO的成功率并加快收敛，对算力有限又缺少逐步标注的智能体训练场景有直接吸引力。
article.limitations: ARG质量是关键：换成随机标签会让ALFWorld成功率相对ProAS下降39.3个百分点，关闭在线演化（静态ARG）也使ALFWorld从87.0%降到82.8%，且ALFWorld上实际训练时间略有增加。此外，支撑MUI/APR的干预分析基于单条轨迹、每点50次续采样，作者自己也说明这只能作为诊断趋势的证据，并非普遍因果效应的估计。
article.figure_caption_zh: (a) 多条成功轨迹被统一为有向无环图作为进度参考；(b) 同一状态下注入不合理动作后，50次续采样的期望成功率更低；(c) 抑制不同位置的原动作并重采样50次，恢复的期望成功率随该动作Future-Drift增大而上升。

figure.caption: {(a) The demonstration of ARG.} Diverse successful trajectories are unified into a DAG that serves as a progress reference. {(b) Probing unreasonable actions.} From an identical state, the counterpart injected with unreasonable actions yields a lower Expected Success Rate (ESR) on 50 sampled continuations $\{c_i\}_{i=1}^{50}$. {(c) Suppressing by Future-Drift (FD).} Forcibly suppressing the original action at different trajectory points and resampling 50 continuations shows recovered ESR rises with the suppressed action's FD.

page_papers.title: AgentProofBench: Benchmarking Reusable Verifiers for Web Agents
page_papers.abstract: Reusable Web-agent verification requires a rule to follow changing requirements and support subsequent execution. We introduce AgentProofBench, which connects paired tests of a frozen acceptance rule to execution from identical saved openings. The resource spans 97 tasks, 79 families, and four Web services. Experiments with DeepSeek Flash/Pro establish two linked measurements. Across 48 families, complete-panel and decision-replay tests retain 82/96 Flash and 79/96 Pro source programs; paired reuse-rebuild BA intervals are [-5.47, 1.57] and [-10.16, 0.00] percentage points. Across 22 execution families, deployment-state panel correctness separates program assignments whose two saved openings are both delivered correctly: 32/33 assignments with error-free panels, versus 1/11 with panel errors. All reference-defined program-gate regressions and withheld deliveries occur in the latter group. Neutral continuation attains the highest correct delivery under the tested generic feedback, providing a concrete baseline for measuring the value added by a gate. Released instructions, states, programs, reference rules, and trajectories connect each test failure to its execution consequences. AgentProofBench makes reusable verification assessable at both the requirement and policy levels.

1.
Introduction
Reusable acceptance checks can make Web-agent operation fast and inspectable. A program can encode the conditions for completing a task, inspect the relevant business state, and issue the same explicit checks on subsequent executions. The central challenge is that the public instruction can stay fixed while the required work changes. The current owner of a name, the files belonging to a collection, or the value that must be preserved comes from the initial state of each execution. A verifier that remembers an earlier answer can produce a convincing decision for the wrong requirement.
The decision also becomes part of the agent’s environment. Rejection can trigger further edits, and acceptance can release the resulting state. Evaluating a reusable verifier therefore requires a link between the conditions its tests exercise and the outcomes of the policy that consumes its decisions. Matched continuation histories make that link observable: the same completed work can be preserved, changed, or withheld under different stopping policies.

We introduce AgentProofBench around this connection. An
acceptance program
is executable code that judges task completion through ordinary before/after APIs. A
reuse contract
fixes the public instruction and evidence permissions while initial business data vary. Matched terminal outcomes make the consequences of this variation observable. Shared actor openings then connect the same verifier to the actions taken after its decision. Every measurement is linked to versioned reference predicates, program source, API evidence, and a reconstructable business state.
The benchmark provides three contributions.
•
A paired reuse test that holds the public instruction and generated program fixed while changing its required initial-state bindings. Complete outcome panels and replayed decisions measure complementary obligations.
•
An execution-validity test linking deployment-state panel correctness to matched policy outcomes. The 22-family study preserves 44 program assignments, two openings per assignment, and 352 policy outcomes.
•
An executable resource with 97 tasks across four Web services, including versioned reference rules, legal alternatives, reconstructable states, programs, and action histories.
The central empirical result is the connection between tests and execution. Programs with error-free deployment-state panels correctly deliver both saved openings in 32 of 33 assignments, compared with one of eleven assignments whose panels contain errors. The paired reuse study explains which requirements those panels exercise; replay witnesses expose additional errors in three source programs. Fixed-instance acceptance and cost profiles then describe the operating tradeoffs of the same verification interface. The reported generator, judge, and actor results use DeepSeek Flash/Pro with thinking disabled.

3.2.
Outcome coverage and reference semantics
Three linked studies address acceptance, reuse, and execution. The acceptance resource contains 97 tasks from 79 families, with 20 family-disjoint development tasks. Its 556-state natural panel includes 452 successes and 104 failures, sampled by reference class with at most six states per task. The reuse study evaluates 576 programs on 558 terminal states from 48 families. The execution study compares policies on 88 saved openings from 22 families. Appendix
A
records the natural-state selection flow and the three post-inspection task exclusions.
Four outcome panels separate common acceptance demands (Figure
7
). Natural outcomes measure ordinary agent endings. Native-prefix pairs use service actions to connect a complete execution to an earlier incomplete state. Typed faults alter a successful anchor through service APIs, allowing the violated requirement to be identified. Legal alternatives change behavior that the public instruction permits. Successful anchors and failed states jointly test valid acceptance and failure rejection.
Reference predicates cover identities, values, collections, and relationships. Versioned selectors recover the required objects from each before state. Native-state and ordinary-API evaluation share the predicates and check restoration and evidence accessibility. Scores measure conformity to this explicit reference contract. Appendix
A
retains the original and explicit-preservation label views.
A separate GPT-6 Astra LLM-as-a-judge audit reviews 195 states across 62 tasks, with reference verdicts withheld during initial judgment. It agrees with 191 of 192 resolved labels (99.5%); three cases are indeterminate. The audit corroborates all 48 requirement changes, rejects all 48 failed replays, and confirms both delivered-regression pairs (Appendix
A
).

3.3.
Matched initial-state reuse
The matched study, P1, selects one task from each of 48 original families, comprising 18 Linear, 10 Slack, 19 Box, and one Calendar task. Every family contributes one related initial-state transformation. Each public instruction has three initial conditions.
Source
is the construction state.
Background
changes data outside the requested work.
Related
changes a required entity binding, initial value, collection, or preservation condition. An entity binding identifies the object denoted by a public name; a preservation condition requires an initial value to survive execution.
Qualification establishes four properties before prediction. The changed requirement follows the public instruction, service actions construct the states, native and API references agree on matched outcomes, and replaying a source-valid decision becomes invalid under the related condition. This last execution is a
source-decision witness
. It tests the acceptance rule against an earlier valid business decision whose required target or value has changed.
The witness gives initial-state variation a direct semantic test. If the same earlier decision remains valid, a program could succeed by retaining its source answer. A qualified witness requires the verifier to resolve a new condition from the current before state. This separates state-dependent acceptance from incidental differences in a snapshot and makes the changed obligation inspectable in the reference and API trace.
Each initial condition contains a complete result, a distinct legal alternative where available, and two changed failures. Fault recipes and their roles remain matched across conditions; the current before state supplies identifiers and required values. Forty-two tasks have two valid outcomes per condition, and six have one. The 144 initial states support 558 main terminal states, comprising 270 valid and 288 failed entries. Witness pairs add one source-valid and one related-invalid decision per task, with their own scoring support.
DeepSeek Flash and Pro, both with thinking disabled, each generate two source programs and two rebuilt programs at each target condition, producing 576 frozen artifacts. Construction and fresh online API assessment, denoted API12, allow twelve model turns. Programs can read and debug against their construction state. Source programs run on all three conditions, while target rebuilds are compared at their own construction target. Two independent API12 judgments per model and terminal state give 2,232 online observations. The full three-construction by three-assessment matrix additionally measures reverse transfer.
3.4.
Verification during continued execution
The execution study, P2, uses 22 families with a native completion trace containing at least two mutating operations. One Flash and one Pro actor per task generate 44 trajectories from related initial states. Every trajectory supplies a natural ending and a closed
checkpoint
, saved after its first complete tool round containing a mutating request. Each of the 88 openings preserves the original initial state, current business state, and complete interaction history.
Four policies branch from each opening.
Actor stop
delivers on the actor’s final reply. Its non-final checkpoint outcome is a mechanical no-delivery reference.
Fixed continue
allows two neutral continuation phases and delivers on a final reply after phase two.
Program gate
uses a source-built Pro program, assigned by a fixed parity rule per task and actor independently of source quality.
Online gate
uses fresh Pro API12 judgments. Both gates deliver on
Pass
and otherwise permit at most two continuations. The two cohorts retain the same assigned program.
The neutral message asks the actor to finish the original request while preserving completed work. Gate feedback prepends a statement of nonacceptance and carries no program checks or entity identifiers. Thus each branch evaluates a complete feedback-and-stopping policy; Appendix
C
gives the exact messages. An eight-family development study selected this design before formal actor prediction. Each actor phase allows 20 model turns and 100 business operations, with a USD 1 observed-cost stop and a 900-second deadline. Unresolved usage stops further work. Executed writes persist when delivery is withheld.

5.
Using the Benchmark
AgentProofBench supports three concrete evaluation workflows. A verifier generator can be tested on the same natural endings, legal alternatives, and typed failures to establish its acceptance profile. Its frozen outputs can then be evaluated under matched initial-state requirements using both complete-panel and joint witness correctness. Finally, the recorded actor openings support comparison of the policies that consume these decisions, measuring completed work, persistent mutations, and delivered state separately.
The resource connects these workflows through stable task, family, program, and state identities. Each false acceptance links to a violated reference condition; each transfer error links to a source program and target rebuild; each execution outcome links to the gate decision and subsequent requests. A generator improvement can therefore be assessed against the changed requirement it should recover and the policy outcome it should support.
The companion’s Evidence Index provides the acceptance, reuse, and execution entry points. Canonical snapshots and exact row deltas reconstruct the saved states. The
verify(task, before, after)
interface evaluates frozen programs without model calls.
6.
Conclusion
AgentProofBench connects the two requirements of reusable Web-agent verification: recovering the current task obligation and supporting subsequent execution. Paired initial states and replay witnesses test the first; shared actor histories and program-level outcome links test the second. In the DeepSeek Flash/Pro study, deployment-state panel correctness identifies 32/33 assignments whose two openings are delivered correctly, compared with 1/11 assignments containing panel errors. Neutral continuation anchors the measurement of gate value, while acceptance profiles and amortized costs describe operating choices. The released 97-task resource makes this chain reproducible, from a changed requirement to a tested rule and its observed execution consequences.

article.headline: 可复用验证器基准：把测试与执行后果连起来
article.lede: 97个任务、79个族、四个Web服务：新基准把冻结验收程序的配对测试，与其判决之后的执行结果连成一条可复现的链。
article.problem: Web agent 的验收检查往往被写成一段可复用的程序，但公开指令不变时，真正需要满足的条件会随每次执行的初始业务状态改变——名字当前归谁、集合里有哪些文件、哪个值必须保留。记住旧答案的验证器会给出看似可信、实则针对错误需求的判决，而它的判决又会反过来改变后续执行（拒绝触发修改、通过则放行结果状态）。现有 Web agent 环境只做可执行的任务评测，没有把「验证器是否跟得上初始状态变化」与「它的决策导致什么执行后果」放在同一个测量框架里。
article.method: 作者构建 AgentProofBench：每个任务给出公开指令、API 文档与普通认证接口，验证器以 verify(task, before, after) 形式返回 Pass/Fail/Unknown，在只读沙箱中运行冻结源码。研究分三块：97 任务 79 族的验收资源（556 个自然状态，452 成功/104 失败）；48 族的配对复用测试，固定指令与程序、只改初始状态绑定，并用「源决策见证」检验旧判决在新条件下是否应失效；22 族的执行研究，从 88 个保存的开局出发比较四种停止策略（actor 自停、固定续跑、程序门控、在线门控）。所有数字来自 DeepSeek Flash/Pro，关闭 thinking。
article.results: 配对复用研究跨 48 族：源程序在相关状态上的平衡准确率为 Flash 93.23%、Pro 90.36%，复用减重建的区间分别是 [-5.47, 1.57] 和 [-10.16, 0.00] 个百分点，两者都包含零。主面板与见证都正确的联合正确率为 82/96（Flash）与 79/96（Pro），重建程序为 82/96 与 86/96。执行研究里，相关面板无错误的 33 个程序赋值中有 32 个把两个开局都正确交付，而面板含错误的 11 个赋值中只有 1 个，对应正确交付率差 87.9 个百分点，区间 [68.8, 100.0]；全部 17 次程序门控扣留与 3 次参考定义的回归都落在面板出错组。中性续跑在测试的通用反馈中正确交付最高：Flash 20/22、Pro 22/22，而程序门控为 17/22 与 16/22。成本方面，构造费用中位数为 0.0173/0.0765 美元，API 费用盈亏平衡点中位数为 Flash 12 次、Pro 10 次评估。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「验证器生成」的评测从单次固定实例推进到初始状态变化加执行后果两个层面，并给出可直接复用的任务、状态、程序、参考规则与轨迹，使验证器的复用价值第一次能被端到端归因到某次被放行或扣留的交付。中性续跑作为强基线也提醒：门控带来的增益必须超过「什么都不拦」才有意义。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖 DeepSeek Flash/Pro 两个模型且关闭 thinking，结论能否外推到其他模型未知；配对复用的两个预设区间都包含零，即未证明复用优于重建。面板正确性与交付结果的关联被作者明确标为对冻结赋值的探索性分析，支撑单元只有 44 个程序赋值、来自 22 个族，效应量虽大但样本结构受限。

page_papers.title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges
page_papers.abstract: AI systems built around large models increasingly use experience and feedback to make persistent changes to models, prompts, memories, tools, and workflows. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) extends this process to inductive biases and to the mechanisms that govern future updates, which can themselves be revised and reused across improvement cycles. Yet self-modification alone does not guarantee trustworthy improvement. Reported gains may reflect flawed evaluations, previously acquired capabilities may deteriorate, and compliance with behavioral constraints may weaken. Compromised artifacts or sensitive information may also persist in successor systems. Changes to improvement mechanisms may invalidate earlier verification results and make human oversight less effective. This survey presents an operational definition and process framework for RSI and organizes the requirements for trustworthy RSI into four interconnected themes: genuine and sustained improvement; behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness; system security and privacy; and transparency and controllability. We examine these themes from three perspectives: Improvement Validity, Constraint Preservation, and Effective Oversight. This analysis covers improvement diagnosis, proposal generation, proposal evaluation, and update implementation (S1--S4), including the recursive application of these stages to improvement mechanisms (RI). We review risks, safeguards, and evaluation evidence for individual updates, effects inherited by successor systems, and revisions to improvement mechanisms, while distinguishing direct RSI findings from evidence in related systems. Finally, we examine evaluation settings, identify requirements for independent and longitudinal assessment, and discuss applications and open research problems.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
AI systems built around large models increasingly use experience and feedback to make persistent changes to models, prompts, memories, tools, and workflows. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) extends this process to inductive biases and to the mechanisms that govern future updates, which can themselves be revised and reused across improvement cycles. Yet self-modification alone does not guarantee trustworthy improvement. Reported gains may reflect flawed evaluations, previously acquired capabilities may deteriorate, and compliance with behavioral constraints may weaken. Compromised artifacts or sensitive information may also persist in successor systems. Changes to improvement mechanisms may invalidate earlier verification results and make human oversight less effective. This survey presents an operational definition and process framework for RSI and organizes the requirements for trustworthy RSI into four interconnected themes: genuine and sustained improvement; behavioral constraints, alignment, and fairness; system security and privacy; and transparency and controllability. We examine these themes from three perspectives: Improvement Validity, Constraint Preservation, and Effective Oversight. This analysis covers improvement diagnosis, proposal generation, proposal evaluation, and update implementation (S1–S4), including the recursive application of these stages to improvement mechanisms (RI). We review risks, safeguards, and evaluation evidence for individual updates, effects inherited by successor systems, and revisions to improvement mechanisms, while distinguishing direct RSI findings from evidence in related systems. Finally, we examine evaluation settings, identify requirements for independent and longitudinal assessment, and discuss applications and open research problems.

Conclusions
Trustworthy RSI requires evidence that improvements are genuine and sustained, applicable constraints remain satisfied, and authorized oversight remains effective as systems change. These requirements connect the consequences of an individual update to inherited behavior and to the mechanisms producing later updates. Evidence at one level supports a different claim from evidence at another: successful successors alone do not establish that a revised updater improves the process that generates them. The central evaluation challenge is to align capability, constraint, and intervention measurements across versions under independent, comparable, and reproducible conditions. Versioned evidence and controlled continuations can make these claims testable while keeping unassessed requirements explicit.

article.headline: 递归自我改进的可信性：框架与评估难题
article.lede: 一篇综述为递归自我改进给出可操作定义，把可信性拆成四类要求与三个分析视角，并主张用跨版本纵向证据来检验。
article.problem: 围绕大模型构建的系统正越来越多地用经验与反馈对模型、提示、记忆、工具和工作流做持久修改，递归自我改进（RSI）则把这种修改扩展到归纳偏置乃至「负责后续更新的机制」本身。但自我修改并不等于可信的改进：报告中的收益可能来自有缺陷的评估，已有能力可能退化，行为约束的遵从性可能减弱，被污染的数据或敏感信息也可能残留在后继系统中。更麻烦的是，对改进机制的改动会让此前的验证结果失效，并削弱人类监督的有效性。
article.method: 作者先给出 RSI 的操作性定义与过程框架：把一次完整改进周期拆成诊断、提案生成、提案评估、更新实施四个阶段（S1–S4），并把这一循环递归地施加到改进机制本身（RI）。在此之上，他们把可信 RSI 的要求整理为四类相互关联的主题——真实且可持续的改进、行为约束与对齐公平、系统安全与隐私、透明性与可控性——并通过改进有效性、约束保持、有效监督三个分析视角来审视。文章分别讨论单次更新的风险、后继系统继承的效应、以及改进机制被修订这三类情形，并明确区分「RSI 的直接发现」与「来自相关系统的证据」。
article.results: 作为综述，论文未给出具体实验数字，其贡献是结构与评估规范：四阶段改进循环（S1–S4）加递归修订（RI）、四个可信性主题、三个分析视角，并在表 8 中列出覆盖八个要求组的纵向检查清单。作者对评估协议提出可操作要求：把单项要求的满足与「同一轨迹上的联合满足」分开报告，联合判据要求每个强制要求在声明时间范围内的每次计划评估中都成立；若中间版本出现一次未授权披露，即便首尾版本都通过，整条轨迹也判为失败。论文还要求报告满足联合判据的独立运行比例及其不确定性，未完成的联合评估须标注为「未评估」。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「系统能改自己」和「改得可信」明确拆开，并给出可执行的报告口径：单次更新的成功、后继系统的表现、改进机制本身的修订，分别只能支撑不同强度的结论。对做自改进、持续学习与智能体工程的团队来说，这套分层的证据要求可以直接当作评估设计的检查表。
article.limitations: 论文是综述性质，未给出具体实验数字，框架本身尚缺实证校准；作者也承认，把 RSI 的直接发现与相关系统中的间接证据区分开来本身就有难度，公平性跨版本、纠正或删除后的隐私保持等要求仍被列为后续评估重点。此外，「联合判据在整条轨迹上始终成立」这类要求在现有公开实验中往往只能标注为未评估。
article.figure_caption_zh: 纵向评估设计示意：RI 将 S1–S4 作用于更新函数 U，因此必须评估后续各版本；报告结果不进入搜索反馈，且不同对照回答的是不同问题，仅做产物访问消融并不能隔离更新器本身的效应。

page_papers.title: Qwen-Image-PE: Learning Visual Design for Text-to-Image Prompt Enhancement
page_papers.abstract: Learning visual design is essential for prompt enhancement (PE) to turn underspecified user requests into coherent visual specifications for text-to-image (T2I) generation. Existing methods preserve user intent and improve overall visual appeal, with less explicit emphasis on fine-grained design dimensions. To address this gap, we introduce Qwen-Image-PE, which learns visual design through two-stage training. Supervised fine-tuning with Caption-Based Reverse Distillation (CRD) uses dense captions of well-designed images as design supervision. Reinforcement learning with Groupwise Design Reward (GDR) jointly compares all candidate images for the same request to refine lighting, composition, layout, and detail. On Qwen-Image-Bench with Qwen-Image-2.1, Qwen-Image-PE-397B improves over original requests by 7.81 points, while Qwen-Image-PE-9B outperforms all evaluated PE baselines. Further evaluations show gains in visual design, aesthetics, image quality, and human preference. We find that PE scales along three axes: training data, model size, and information density, with sufficient information density as a prerequisite for effective enhancement. Moreover, we demonstrate that Qwen-Image-PE generalizes to four additional T2I backbones, even surpassing native prompt enhancers on HunyuanImage-2.1 and FLUX 3 Image Klein. We release Qwen-Image-PE-9B at https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-PE-T2I.

Qwen-Image-PE: Learning Visual Design for
Text-to-Image Prompt Enhancement

Corresponding author.

Abstract
Learning visual design is essential for prompt enhancement (PE) to turn underspecified user requests into coherent visual specifications for text-to-image (T2I) generation. Existing methods preserve user intent and improve overall visual appeal, with less explicit emphasis on fine-grained design dimensions. To address this gap, we introduce Qwen-Image-PE, which learns visual design through two-stage training. Supervised fine-tuning with Caption-Based Reverse Distillation (CRD) uses dense captions of well-designed images as design supervision. Reinforcement learning with Groupwise Design Reward (GDR) jointly compares all candidate images for the same request to refine lighting, composition, layout, and detail. On Qwen-Image-Bench with Qwen-Image-2.1, Qwen-Image-PE-397B improves over original requests by 7.81 points, while Qwen-Image-PE-9B outperforms all evaluated PE baselines. Further evaluations show gains in visual design, aesthetics, image quality, and human preference. We find that PE scales along three axes: training data, model size, and information density, with sufficient information density as a prerequisite for effective enhancement. Moreover, we demonstrate that Qwen-Image-PE generalizes to four additional T2I backbones, even surpassing native prompt enhancers on HunyuanImage-2.1 and FLUX 3 Image Klein. We release Qwen-Image-PE-9B at
https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-PE-T2I
.
Figure 1:
Qwen-Image-PE improves visual design.
Within each pair, Qwen-Image-2.1 outputs from enhanced prompts (right) show more expressive lighting, more cohesive compositions, clearer layouts, and richer details than those from original requests (left).
1
Introduction
Modern text-to-image (T2I) models can follow increasingly detailed visual specifications, offering control over lighting, composition, layout, and fine-grained detail
(
Wu et al., 2025b
;
Zhao et al., 2026
;
Black Forest Labs, 2026
)
. However, user requests are often brief and leave many of these choices unspecified
(
Zhang et al., 2026
)
. Prompt enhancement (PE) bridges this gap by expanding user requests into detailed prompts. The visual choices introduced during enhancement shape how the requested content is presented, making visual design an important capability for prompt enhancers.
Existing prompt enhancement methods pursue semantic alignment by preserving and clarifying user intent
(
Wang et al., 2025
;
Boogu Team, 2026
;
ERNIE Team, Baidu, 2026
;
Black Forest Labs, 2026
)
. Beyond semantic correctness, other approaches improve visual appeal through aesthetic or preference optimization
(
Hao et al., 2022
;
Cao et al., 2023
;
Tang et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025
)
. However, these approaches primarily optimize overall visual appeal, with less explicit emphasis on individual design dimensions. We therefore study how PE can explicitly learn and refine fine-grained design dimensions, including lighting, composition, layout, and detail. The challenge is how to translate fine-grained visual design into effective supervision targets and optimization feedback.
Our key insight is that: (1) Well-designed images demonstrate how design choices work together. Dense captions make these choices explicit, providing concrete supervision for PE to learn visual design. (2) Jointly comparing all candidate images for the same request provides a common basis for calibrating design scores. This groupwise comparison helps distinguish their relative quality, providing more informative feedback.
Guided by these insights, we introduce Qwen-Image-PE, which learns visual design through a two-stage training paradigm. First, supervised fine-tuning via
Caption-Based Reverse Distillation (CRD)
enables PE to imitate the design choices in well-designed images. We construct request–image pairs, select images for design quality and request consistency, and densely caption their visual content and design choices to obtain enhanced-prompt targets. These captions, together with synthesized design rationales, provide supervision for learning visual design. Second, reinforcement learning with
Groupwise Design Reward (GDR)
refines the enhancer through visual comparison. For each request, we generate images from a group of sampled enhanced prompts and arrange the images into a grid. A multimodal judge jointly scores the candidates under explicit design rubrics, conditioning each candidate’s scores on the full group. We combine these design scores with an alignment reward to optimize the enhancer while keeping the T2I backbone frozen.
We evaluate Qwen-Image-PE on Qwen-Image-Bench
(
Li et al., 2026
)
for overall generation performance, complemented by assessments of visual design, aesthetics, image quality, and human preference. On Qwen-Image-Bench with a common Qwen-Image-2.1 backbone, Qwen-Image-PE-397B improves the Overall score over original requests by 7.81 points, while Qwen-Image-PE-9B outperforms all evaluated prompt enhancement baselines in Overall. Complementary evaluations show gains in visual design, aesthetics, image quality, and human preference.
We further study the scaling properties and generalization behavior of PE, with four main findings. (1) PE scales with training data, model size, and information density. (2) Sufficient information density is a prerequisite for effective enhancement. (3) Both PE variants outperform original requests on four additional T2I backbones without access to their training captions. (4) On HunyuanImage-2.1 and FLUX 3 Image Klein, both variants outperform native prompt enhancers, suggesting that PE learns transferable visual design principles rather than generator-specific caption patterns.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
•
Training paradigm of PE.
We propose a two-stage training paradigm for learning visual design. First, supervised fine-tuning via Caption-Based Reverse Distillation (CRD) enables PE to imitate the design choices in well-designed images. Second, reinforcement learning with Groupwise Design Reward (GDR) refines fine-grained design dimensions, including lighting, composition, layout, and detail, through groupwise visual comparison.
•
Scaling properties of PE.
We discover that PE performance scales along three axes: training data, model size, and information density. Our experiments suggest that sufficient information density is a prerequisite for effective prompt enhancement in the evaluated setting.
•
Generalization behavior of PE.
We demonstrate transfer across four T2I backbones without access to their training captions, with higher Overall scores than native prompt enhancers on HunyuanImage-2.1 and FLUX 3 Image Klein. This suggests that PE learns transferable visual design principles rather than generator-specific caption patterns.
2
Method
Qwen-Image-PE learns visual design through a two-stage training paradigm (
Figure
2
). After formulating prompt enhancement (
Section
2.1
), we describe supervised fine-tuning with Caption-Based Reverse Distillation (CRD) to learn design choices from well-designed images (
Section
2.2
) and reinforcement learning with Groupwise Design Reward (GDR) to refine these choices through groupwise visual comparison (
Section
2.3
).

(1)
User requests often leave visual design choices unspecified. Our objective is to learn a prompt enhancer that specifies these choices coherently while preserving the user’s explicit requirements. We focus on four fine-grained visual design dimensions.
Lighting
concerns physically coherent illumination: consistent light direction, shadows, highlights, and reflections, with natural color temperature, light falloff, and material sheen.
Composition
concerns subject placement and scale, focal hierarchy, balance, and depth layering.
Layout
concerns the alignment, spacing, whitespace, and typographic hierarchy of text, graphics, and content modules.
Detail
concerns the richness of material textures, local structures, environmental details, and meaningful informational content.
2.2
Supervised Fine-Tuning with Caption-Based Reverse Distillation
To ground design supervision in visual examples, we introduce
Caption-Based Reverse Distillation (CRD)
. Unlike forward-based prompt enhancement, which directly expands user requests into detailed prompts using a zero-shot or trained language model, CRD derives enhanced-prompt targets by densely captioning well-designed images. CRD constructs supervision in the image-to-text direction, reversing the direction of T2I generation. We then train the enhancer to predict these targets from user requests.
Motivation.
(1) Transfer visual design through captions.
Dense captions describe how visual content is organized and presented in an image. As shown in
Figure
3
a, captions of well-designed images guide Qwen-Image-2.1 to regenerate key aspects of lighting, composition, layout, and detail. These examples suggest that dense captions encode visual design choices in a form that guides T2I generation. This motivates training the enhancer to predict such captions from user requests, thereby learning to imitate the design choices embodied in the source images.
(2) Bridge the prompt–caption distribution gap.
T2I generators are trained with caption-image pairs, while forward-based prompt enhancement can produce text that differs from their training caption distributions. We obtain enhanced prompts from Qwen-Image-PE-397B and Qwen-3.8-Max for the same 1,000 requests from Qwen-Image-Bench. Using Qwen-Image-2.1 text-encoder embeddings, we jointly visualize these prompts and 1,000 sampled T2I training captions with t-SNE (
Figure
3
b). Our prompt embeddings exhibit greater overlap with the training-caption embeddings than forward-enhanced prompt embeddings do. This suggests that CRD helps narrow the prompt–caption distribution gap by training the enhancer on dense image captions. Further quantitative results in
Section
3.3.1
support this closer alignment.

2.3
Reinforcement Learning with Groupwise Design Reward
To further refine visual design, we introduce
Groupwise Design Reward (GDR)
. Existing reward models, such as PickScore
(
Kirstain et al., 2023
)
and HPSv3
(
Ma et al., 2025
)
, provide overall preference scores without explicit feedback on our four fine-grained design dimensions. Given the strong visual understanding and reasoning capabilities of MLLMs, we use an MLLM-based judge to assess these dimensions under explicit rubrics. While pointwise judging can assess individual images, it lacks shared visual references for distinguishing subtle design differences. Pairwise judging provides relative comparisons, but lacks a holistic view of the rollout group and incurs substantial evaluation overhead when all candidate pairs are compared. GDR combines full rollout-group context with efficient joint scoring. By evaluating all candidates together, it provides shared visual references while avoiding separate judge calls for individual images or candidate pairs.

Evaluation.
We assess overall generation performance, visual design, aesthetics, image quality, and human preference. The requests used for model evaluation do not overlap with those used for SFT or RL. The evaluation metrics described below are distinct from the training reward functions and are not used to optimize the enhancer.
Qwen-Image-Bench
(
Li et al., 2026
)
covers real-world creation scenarios using criteria developed with professional artists. Its hierarchy comprises five L1 dimensions (Quality, Aesthetics, Alignment, Real-world Fidelity, and Creative Generation) and finer L2 capabilities, including design-related dimensions like Lighting, Composition, Layout, and Detail. On images generated from Qwen-Image-Bench requests,
UniPercept
(
Cao et al., 2025
)
provides Image Aesthetics Assessment (IAA), Image Quality Assessment (IQA), and Image Structure and Texture Assessment (ISTA), measuring aesthetic appeal, visual quality, and structural and textural richness. We further assess aesthetics-related human preference using
HPSv3
and
PickScore
(
Kirstain et al., 2023
)
on images generated from GenEval prompts
(
Ghosh et al., 2023
)
, whose shorter length accommodates these metrics’ text-input limits. Finally,
Good/Same/Bad (GSB)
human evaluation assesses request fulfillment and visual appeal, recording whether annotators prefer our output, consider the outputs comparable, or prefer the baseline.

3.3.2
Effectiveness of Groupwise Design Reward
Refining visual design through groupwise feedback.
Starting from the 397B model trained with Caption-Based Reverse Distillation, we compare reinforcement learning with Pointwise Design Reward and Groupwise Design Reward. Both use the same design rubric: Pointwise Design Reward evaluates each image independently, while Groupwise Design Reward jointly scores candidate images for the same request. We do not include exhaustive pairwise judging, as its quadratic number of MLLM calls per rollout group makes it impractical for online RL at our training scale. We evaluate both models on Qwen-Image-Bench using Qwen-Image-2.1 as the T2I backbone. As shown in
Table
3
(b), Groupwise Design Reward achieves 62.17 Overall, exceeding Pointwise Design Reward by 0.81 points and the initialization by 0.65 points. It improves four of the five dimensions over pointwise scoring, with the largest gain in Aesthetics (+1.70). These results support groupwise visual comparison as effective feedback for refining visual design.
Agreement with human design preferences.
To evaluate the ranking signal used during training, we compare reward orderings with blinded human judgments on rollout image pairs across Lighting, Composition, Layout, and Detail. Agreement measures how often the higher-scoring image matches the annotator’s preference. Groupwise Design Reward achieves 59.1% agreement, compared with 50.9% for Pointwise Design Reward (+8.2 percentage points). These results suggest that groupwise scoring provides a ranking signal that better reflects human judgments of visual design.
Benchmark performance during RL training.
We evaluate Qwen-Image-PE-397B on Qwen-Image-Bench during RL training, using Qwen-Image-2.1 as the T2I backbone (
Figure
6
). Lighting exhibits the most consistent improvement, rising from 72.14 to 77.64. Composition and Detail show positive but noisier trends, while Layout improves only slightly with substantial fluctuations. While GDR provides MLLM-based groupwise training rewards, benchmark evaluation uses pointwise scoring by Q-Judger, a separate evaluator trained on expert annotations. This consistency between GDR’s design objectives and independently measured improvements further supports its effectiveness in refining visual design.

Figure
7
a, Overall increases from 55.87 to 56.68, 57.31, and 57.61 as the training set grows, for a total gain of 1.74 points. Each doubling improves performance, but the incremental gains decrease from 0.81 to 0.63 and then 0.30 points. These results show that additional training data consistently benefits the enhancer, although the smaller gain from 50K to 100K indicates diminishing returns over the evaluated range.
Scaling Model Size.
We fix the training set to the same 50K examples, retain their original caption supervision, and train five PE models following the same SFT recipe:
Qwen3.5-2B
,
Qwen3.5-4B
,
Qwen3.5-9B
,
Qwen3.5-35B-A3B
, and
Qwen3.5-397B-A17B
. The sweep includes both dense and MoE models. Overall increases monotonically from 49.56 for the smallest model to 59.86 for the largest (
Figure
7
b), a gain of 10.30 points. Comparing the smallest and largest models, all five benchmark dimensions improve, with the largest gains in Creative Generation (+19.66) and Alignment (+14.80). With the training data fixed, larger enhancers improve both creative generation and adherence to the user’s requirements over the evaluated range.
Scaling Information Density.
We fix the PE model at
Qwen3.5-9B
and the training-data size at 50K examples, providing captions at four information-density levels (L1–L4) as supervision. We measure the information content of each trained model’s sampled enhanced prompts using
Grounded Perplexity Gain (GPG)
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
. GPG measures how much observing a paired image increases the text’s likelihood under a frozen vision-language model. For each model’s outputs on Qwen-Image-Bench, we use frozen Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct to sum token log-likelihood gains from observing the corresponding generated images and average over prompts. Mean total GPG for L1–L4 is 14.42, 41.16, 87.25, and 170.36.
As shown in
Figure
7
c, Overall rises from 44.65 to 51.36, 55.39, and 57.31 across the four levels, a total improvement of 12.66 points. Information density yields the largest Overall gain among the three scaling axes over the evaluated ranges, highlighting its central role in PE performance. Interestingly, L1 and L2 underperform Original Request (54.36), whereas L3 and L4 exceed this baseline by 1.03 and 2.95 points. This transition from degradation to improvement suggests that sufficient information density is a prerequisite for effective prompt enhancement in this setting.
