Generalization behavior of PE.
Both PE variants outperform original request on four T2I backbones, surpassing native enhancers on HunyuanImage-2.1 and FLUX 3 Image Klein.
5
Generalization Behavior of Qwen-Image-PE
To assess transfer beyond the training backbone, Qwen-Image-2.1, we apply
Qwen-Image-PE-9B
and
Qwen-Image-PE-397B
to four frozen T2I backbones: FLUX.2-dev, Krea 2 Turbo, HunyuanImage-2.1, and FLUX 3 Image Klein. We evaluate on Qwen-Image-Bench against original requests and the available native prompt enhancers.
Consistent improvements across backbones.
As shown in
Table
5
, both variants outperform original requests on all four backbones, with improvements across all five benchmark dimensions. Overall improves by 2.53–6.74 points with
Qwen-Image-PE-9B
and by 3.86–8.03 points with
Qwen-Image-PE-397B
. These consistent improvements show that the learned prompt enhancement capability generalizes beyond the generator used during training.
Transfer beyond native prompt enhancement.
Interestingly, both variants surpass the native prompt enhancers in Overall on HunyuanImage-2.1 and FLUX 3 Image Klein.
Qwen-Image-PE-397B
exceeds HunyuanImage-2.1-PE-32B and FLUX 3 Image Klein PE by 3.07 and 2.74 points, respectively. Achieving these gains without access to the target generators’ training captions suggests that Qwen-Image-PE learns visual design principles that transfer across generators.
6
Related Work
Text-to-Image Generation.
Text-to-image (T2I) generation aims to synthesize images that correspond to textual descriptions. Earlier work advanced image fidelity and text–image alignment, enabling models to generate visually plausible subjects and scenes from text
(
Rombach et al., 2022
;
Podell et al., 2023
)
. More recent systems support increasingly precise control over visual presentation, allowing detailed prompts to guide lighting, composition, layout, and fine-grained detail
(
Wu et al., 2025a
;
Zhao et al., 2026
;
ByteDance Seed, 2026
;
Black Forest Labs, 2025
;
OpenAI, 2026b
;
Google DeepMind, 2026
)
. Although these models support detailed visual control, user requests often leave design choices unspecified. Our work studies how prompt enhancement can specify and coordinate these choices through detailed prompts to form coherent visual designs.
Prompt Enhancement for Text-to-Image Generation.
Prompt enhancement (PE) transforms user requests into detailed prompts while preserving user intent. A central objective is semantic alignment, which involves clarifying user intent and expanding generation conditions while preserving explicit content and spatial constraints
(
Boogu Team, 2026
;
Black Forest Labs, 2026
;
Chen et al., 2026
)
. HunyuanImage-2.1-PE further employs chain-of-thought reasoning to produce detailed prompts that faithfully express user requirements
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
. Beyond semantic correctness, existing approaches optimize visual appeal through aesthetic and preference rewards
(
Hao et al., 2022
;
Cao et al., 2023
;
Tang et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025
)
. ERNIE-Image-PE also enriches requests with structured descriptions of layout, composition, textual content, and scene structure
(
ERNIE Team, Baidu, 2026
)
.
Our work optimizes fine-grained visual design dimensions, including lighting, composition, layout, and detail. Supervised fine-tuning with Caption-Based Reverse Distillation trains the enhancer to imitate design choices captured in dense captions of well-designed images, while reinforcement learning with Groupwise Design Reward refines these choices through groupwise visual comparison. Concurrent work WanPE
(
Zhu et al., 2026
)
also constructs supervision from captions for text-to-video prompt enhancement. It targets coherent cinematic planning across shots and over time, whereas our work focuses on fine-grained visual design within individual images. In addition, we study the scaling properties of PE and its generalization behavior across T2I backbones.
7
Conclusion
We present Qwen-Image-PE, which learns fine-grained visual design through imitation and comparative refinement. Supervised fine-tuning via Caption-Based Reverse Distillation provides concrete design supervision, while reinforcement learning with Groupwise Design Reward refines design choices through groupwise visual comparison. Experiments show improvements in overall generation performance, visual design, and human preference. Our scaling experiments suggest that sufficient information density is a prerequisite for effective enhancement. Both PE variants also improve Overall over original requests on four additional T2I backbones without access to their training captions, supporting the transfer of learned visual design principles. We hope this work encourages future research to make visual design a central objective of prompt enhancement.

article.headline: Qwen-Image-PE：让提示词学会视觉设计
article.lede: 两阶段训练把「设计」变成提示增强的学习目标：397B版本在Qwen-Image-Bench上比原始请求高7.81分。
article.problem: 用户给文生图模型的请求往往很简短，光照、构图、版式、细节这些视觉设计选择大量留空，而提示增强（PE）在补全这些选择时几乎决定了画面如何呈现。现有提示增强方法主要保证语义对齐，或用美学/偏好奖励优化整体观感，对单个设计维度的显式建模不足。论文因此追问：如何把细粒度视觉设计转化为可用的监督信号与优化反馈。
article.method: 作者提出Qwen-Image-PE，采用两阶段训练。第一阶段是「基于描述的反向蒸馏」（CRD）：先用强文生图系统生成或筛选高质量图像，再用多模态模型为图像写稠密描述，把描述（连同LLM合成的设计思路CoT与长宽比）作为增强提示的监督目标，让增强器学习模仿优秀图像中的设计选择。第二阶段用「组内设计奖励」（GDR）做强化学习：对同一请求采样多条增强提示并渲染成图，把整组候选图拼成网格，由多模态裁判按光照、构图、版式、细节四项评分标准一次性联合打分，多次打乱顺序取平均，再与对齐奖励加权，用GRPO优化增强器，同时冻结文生图主干。
article.results: 在Qwen-Image-Bench、以Qwen-Image-2.1为冻结主干时，Qwen-Image-PE-397B的Overall为62.17，比原始请求54.36提升7.81分；Qwen-Image-PE-9B为60.28，超过所有对比的提示增强基线（GPT-5.5为60.10，FLUX 3 Image Klein PE为59.90）。人类GSB评测（500例）中397B对原始请求的净胜率为35.48%，对GPT-5.5为17.09%。消融显示CRD相比前向式监督把Overall从59.86提升到61.52（+1.66），GDR相比逐点奖励从61.36提升到62.17（+0.81），与人判断的一致率为59.1%对50.9%。缩放实验中，训练数据从12.5K增到100K使Overall从55.87升到57.61（+1.74）；模型从2B到397B-A17B从49.56升到59.86（+10.30）；信息密度L1到L4从44.65升到57.31（+12.66）。在另外四个主干上，9B与397B分别带来2.53–6.74和3.86–8.03的Overall提升，并在HunyuanImage-2.1与FLUX 3 Image Klein上分别超过原生增强器3.07和2.74分。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「视觉设计」从模糊的审美偏好拆成可监督、可奖励的四个维度，并给出了一条从图像描述反向蒸馏加组内比较的可复制训练路线；信息密度是有效增强前提这一发现，也直接提示了提示增强的数据构造比堆量更关键。
article.limitations: 评测主要依赖自动基准与MLLM裁判，而GDR奖励与人类判断的一致率仅59.1%，说明奖励信号本身并不可靠；人类评测只覆盖397B且仅500例，开源的只有9B。信息密度实验还显示L1、L2两档（Overall 44.65、51.36）反而低于不增强的54.36，数据缩放从50K到100K增益也已降到0.30分，说明方法的收益高度依赖高质量描述数据且存在递减。
article.figure_caption_zh: 同一请求下，使用增强后提示（右）生成的图像相比原始请求（左）在光照、构图、版式与细节上更具表现力。

page_papers.title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
page_papers.abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

Abstract
Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion-
and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy based on
Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL.
To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density,
we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the
negative MaxEnt objective.
Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same
actor, using action regression for value improvement and
distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy.
The actor updates require neither direct samples from
the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density
or score estimation.
Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove
convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step
limit followed by the long-time limit.
On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
achieves the highest aggregate
normalized return among all evaluated methods,
while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based
baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

Generative policies offer expressive action distributions
for online reinforcement learning (RL).
Diffusion- and flow-based policies can capture multimodal
distributions that are difficult to represent with a single
Gaussian
(
Dong et al., 2025
;
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
However, many of these approaches generate actions through
iterative sampling, requiring repeated network evaluations
during training and inference.
Recent MeanFlow-based methods reduce this cost through
few-step or one-step action generation
(
Dong et al., 2026
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting offers a different way to train one-step
generators
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
At each training iteration, it uses target data to
move generated samples toward the desired distribution,
then trains the generator to reproduce the moved
samples from the same inputs.
Through these repeated updates, the generator learns
to produce samples from the target distribution in
a single forward pass at inference.
This approach has shown better performance than
MeanFlow variants in one-step image generation on
ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
These results motivate exploring Drifting for online
RL, where its use remains less studied.
We consider the maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL objective,
which balances expected return with policy entropy
to encourage exploration
(
Haarnoja et al., 2018
)
.
The critic defines a Boltzmann target distribution
for policy improvement, but does not directly provide
samples from it
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
We therefore adopt an energy-based view of Drifting
(
Gretton et al., 2026
;
Han et al., 2026
)
,
using the negative MaxEnt policy-improvement objective
as the energy.
This energy guides updates to actions generated by
the current policy.
For the value term, critic gradients tell us how to
move actions toward higher values.
The entropy term is harder to use: an implicit actor
generates actions but does not provide a tractable
density for computing their distribution’s entropy.
We therefore need training targets that capture
the effect of entropy without explicitly computing it.
We propose
DriftSpread
, a one-step generative policy in the
Drifting model family for online MaxEnt RL.
Our key idea is to derive two updates from this energy
and fit them sequentially to the same actor through
repeated Drift–Spread cycles.
In each cycle, Drift uses critic gradients to move
generated actions toward higher values.
The actor then learns to reproduce these updated
actions from the same inputs through regression.
Spread captures the entropy contribution through
diffusion of the action distribution.
We approximate this diffusion by adding appropriately
scaled independent noise to actions from the updated
actor, then train the actor to match the resulting
distribution.
This allows the actor to learn the effect of entropy
without explicitly computing it.
For a fixed critic, we prove
that the learned policy converges to the Boltzmann
target distribution in the small-step, long-time limit.
Our main contributions are:
(1) We introduce
DriftSpread
, a Drifting model for online
MaxEnt RL with expressive policies and one-step action
generation.
(2) We develop sequential Drift–Spread training through
critic-guided regression and entropy regularization to
address the challenge of entropy computation for implicit
policies.
(3) On MuJoCo,
DriftSpread
outperforms 13 baselines
in aggregate normalized return, with lower training
costs than the diffusion, flow, and MeanFlow baselines
(Figure
1
).

Related Work
Generative policies for online RL.
Diffusion and flow models provide expressive action
distributions for online RL.
One line of work optimizes policies by backpropagating
critic gradients through diffusion or flow sampling
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Lyu et al., 2025
)
.
DIME also differentiates through diffusion sampling
while optimizing a variational lower bound on the
MaxEnt objective
(
Celik et al., 2025
)
.
Another line of work constructs training targets
for learning critic-defined Boltzmann distributions.
DQS uses weighted averages of critic gradients
to construct score targets
(
Jain et al., 2025
)
.
SDAC and MaxEntDP instead use critic values to weight
denoising supervision and noise estimates, respectively
(
Ma et al., 2025
;
Dong et al., 2025
)
.
Reverse flow matching unifies these gradient-expectation
and noise-expectation formulations through posterior-mean
estimation
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
These approaches use iterative action sampling,
motivating few-step and one-step policies for online RL.
MeanFlow was introduced for one-step generative modeling
and learns average velocities
(
Geng et al., 2025
)
.
Recent online RL methods use this formulation
to learn policies with fewer generation steps.
FPMD trains rectified-flow and MeanFlow policies
through policy mirror descent, with both variants
supporting one-step inference
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
.
MFPO trains few-step MeanFlow policies using velocity
estimates for critic-defined Boltzmann targets
(
Dong et al., 2026
)
, while SOM constructs velocity
targets from critic-based score estimates to train
one-step MeanFlow policies
(
Kim et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting models and policy learning.
Drifting learns one-step generators by repeatedly
moving generated samples and training the generator
to reproduce their updated positions.
This approach has achieved state-of-the-art performance
in one-step image generation on ImageNet
(
Deng et al., 2026
)
.
Subsequent work relates specific Drifting fields
to Wasserstein gradient flows
(
Gretton et al., 2026
)
and uses
optimal-transport couplings to construct sample
updates
(
He et al., 2026
)
.
W-Flow derives sample movements from an objective
over distributions and trains a one-step generator
on the resulting samples
(
Han et al., 2026
)
.
Drifting has also been applied to policy learning.
For offline RL, DriftQL combines critic-guided
policy improvement with a Drifting regularizer
based on the behavior distribution
(
Houssaini et al., 2026
)
.
For offline-to-online RL, Drifting Field Policy
derives a KL-regularized policy update through
Wasserstein gradient flow and constructs training
targets from actions ranked by the critic
(
Koo et al., 2026
)
.
Our work focuses on online MaxEnt RL from scratch.

Conclusion and Limitations
We introduced
DriftSpread
, a Drifting-based approach to
learning expressive one-step policies for online RL.
Building on an energy-based view of Drifting, we derive
critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from
the MaxEnt objective.
The two updates are learned sequentially by the same
actor: Drift moves actions toward higher values,
while Spread matches a broader distribution constructed
from the updated actor.
This design incorporates the effect of entropy without
estimating policy densities or scores, while allowing
each action sample to be generated in one forward pass.
Under exact fitting, our analysis establishes convergence
to the fixed-critic Boltzmann target in the small-step,
long-time limit.
MuJoCo experiments show that
DriftSpread
combines strong
control performance with efficient training and inference,
supporting Drifting as a practical approach to
generative policy learning.
Our work leaves two directions for future research.
First, our evaluation is limited to simulation
environments.
Testing on real-world control tasks would help
assess robustness to observation noise and changes
in system dynamics.
Second, we use a fixed spreading-noise distribution
and scale during training.
Adapting the spreading strength as learning progresses
may better balance exploration and value improvement.

article.headline: 先漂移后扩散的一步生成策略
article.lede: DriftSpread 用 critic 梯度做 Drift、用噪声分布匹配做 Spread，在 MuJoCo 上以一步
article.problem: 扩散和流策略能表达多峰动作分布，但推理常需多次网络评估，训练和部署成本高。在线最大熵 RL 还需处理熵项，而隐式生成策略没有可处理的密度，难以直接计算熵或策略 score。
article.method: 作者提出 DriftSpread：从负 MaxEnt 目标推导出 critic 引导的 Drift 和熵诱导的 Spread，并在同一个一步 actor 上顺序执行。Drift 用动作回归把样本沿 critic 梯度移动，Spread 用 MMD/特征函数匹配带噪分布来近似熵扩散，因此不需要从 Boltzmann 目标直接采样，也不需要密度或 score 估计。
article.results: 在五个 MuJoCo-v3 任务、每个任务 100 万环境交互、5 个随机种子下，DriftSpread 在 13 个基线中取得最高聚合归一化回报；平均推理为 0.15 ms/动作，低于 DIME 的 1.24 ms 和两步 MeanFlow 策略 MFPO 的 0.36 ms。作者还报告其训练成本低于扩散、流和 MeanFlow 基线。
article.why_it_matters: 这为在线 MaxEnt RL 提供了一条兼顾表达性与一步推理的生成策略路线，尤其适合对动作生成延迟敏感的控制场景。
article.limitations: 局限是只在 MuJoCo 仿真中评估，未验证真实控制任务；理论收敛依赖固定 critic、精确拟合和小步长/长时间极限，Spread 噪声分布与尺度在训练中也固定。
article.figure_caption_zh: DriftSpread 概览：(a) 训练在 critic 学习与顺序 Drift–Spread actor 更新间交替；(b) 示意负 MaxEnt 目标下 Drift 提升 critic 值、Spread 扩展分布以体现熵。

The maps $f_ $ represent the same actor at different training stages, each generating an action sample from reference noise in one forward pass. (b) The surface schematically represents the negative MaxEnt objective over policy distributions. The samples below illustrate how Drift moves actions toward higher critic values and Spread then broadens the post-Drift distribution to capture the effect of entropy.

page_papers.title: RynnVLA-Latent: Scaling Robotic Manipulation Foundation Models with 3D-Grounded Latent Actions
page_papers.abstract: Scaling vision-language-action (VLA) models is constrained by scarce action-labeled demonstrations and incompatible control spaces across robot embodiments. We present RynnVLA-Latent, a framework that turns heterogeneous interaction videos into scalable supervision for robot policy pretraining. At its core, RynnLAM learns continuous, 3D-grounded latent actions from visual transitions without requiring native robot controls. By combining residual future-feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling, RynnLAM encourages representations that capture control-relevant motion rather than appearance changes alone. We apply RynnLAM to 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, producing 745.52M latent-action descriptors. RynnVLA-Latent then learns to predict latent-action chunks from visual observations and language through flow matching, before adapting its pretrained backbone and action expert to embodiment-specific robot actions. The resulting 4B policy achieves 98.8% success on LIBERO, 84.7% on LIBERO-Plus without benchmark-specific adaptation, 51.9% average success across five VLABench tracks, and 88.6% average success on the RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual benchmark. It also achieves the highest observed success rates among the compared methods on six real-world manipulation tasks across dexterous-hand and mobile-gripper platforms. Together with representation ablations and data-scaling results, these findings demonstrate the potential of latent-action supervision for scaling robot policy learning beyond native action-labeled data.

Abstract
Scaling vision-language-action (VLA) models is constrained by scarce action-labeled demonstrations and incompatible control spaces across robot embodiments. We present
RynnVLA-Latent
, a framework that turns heterogeneous interaction videos into scalable supervision for robot policy pretraining. At its core,
RynnLAM
learns continuous, 3D-grounded latent actions from visual transitions without requiring native robot controls. By combining residual future-feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling, RynnLAM encourages representations that capture control-relevant motion rather than appearance changes alone. We apply RynnLAM to 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, producing 745.52M latent-action descriptors. RynnVLA-Latent then learns to predict latent-action chunks from visual observations and language through flow matching, before adapting its pretrained backbone and action expert to embodiment-specific robot actions. The resulting 4B policy achieves 98.8% success on LIBERO, 84.7% on LIBERO-Plus without benchmark-specific adaptation, 51.9% average success across five VLABench tracks, and 88.6% average success on the RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual benchmark.
It also achieves the highest observed success rates among the compared methods on six real-world manipulation tasks across dexterous-hand and mobile-gripper platforms. Together with representation ablations and data-scaling results, these findings demonstrate the potential of latent-action supervision for scaling robot policy learning beyond native action-labeled data.

(

;

;

. Scaling policy learning, however, requires supervision that connects visual observations and task instructions to actions across diverse embodiments

;

Robot demonstrations are expensive to collect, and their native controls differ in dimensions, coordinate frames, and semantics
(
Zhao et al., 2026b
;
Zhao et al., 2026c
)
. Human and web videos provide much broader interaction coverage but lack corresponding robot commands. These sources cannot simply be pooled under one native-action prediction objective. A shared supervision interface is needed to exploit their visual transitions before adapting a policy to a particular robot.
Latent actions provide such an interface by encoding changes between observations without native control labels
(
Ye et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2025c
;
Bu et al., 2025b
;
Gao et al., 2026
;
Gao et al., 2025
;
Schmidt and Jiang, 2024
;
Chen et al., 2024
)
. Existing approaches demonstrate the value of transition reconstruction and feature-space prediction, but visual change can include camera motion, static appearance, and effects unrelated to the agent’s control. A representation that reconstructs images well therefore need not be equally useful for predicting low-level manipulation actions.
We address this through geometric supervision and explicit camera-motion separation. We introduce
RynnLAM
, which encodes a frame pair into motion tokens, a global action latent, and a camera latent. Residual future-feature prediction preserves transition information through the bottleneck, while camera-compensated 3D-flow pseudo-labels and contrastive feature warping encourage motion-sensitive representations. Camera-pose prediction and gradient reversal further encourage separation of ego-motion from manipulation-related cues. These objectives provide geometric grounding without requiring manually annotated robot actions; they encourage camera decoupling rather than guaranteeing exact viewpoint invariance or physical identifiability.
Using RynnLAM as an offline labeler, we construct shared latent-action supervision for 25 video sources spanning human interaction, real robots, and simulation. The corpus contains approximately 30.1K hours and 3.057B frames and yields 745.52M latent-action descriptors. We then pretrain
RynnVLA-Latent
, a Mixture-of-Transformers policy that couples a pretrained vision-language backbone with a narrow action expert. The policy predicts latent-action chunks from multi-view observations and language via flow matching, without native-action or proprioceptive supervision. In robot post-training, we reuse both the backbone and action-expert trunk, introduce proprioception, and retarget the output projection to native robot commands. This separates video-based motion supervision from embodiment-specific action alignment.
Our evaluation follows the same path from representation learning to robot deployment. On LARY, frozen-representation probes test whether the descriptors predict low-level control targets, with the full descriptor achieving average relative-action MSE

Six real-world tasks on stationary dexterous and mobile gripper platforms test the interface after adaptation to different controls. Data-scaling and component studies further characterize where the approach helps and where performance remains limited.
Our contributions are as follows:
•
3D-grounded latent-action supervision.
We introduce RynnLAM, which combines residual feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling to construct continuous transition representations without native robot-action labels.
•
Scalable VLA pretraining from heterogeneous video.
We develop RynnVLA-Latent, which learns shared latent-action targets from 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, and transfers the pretrained policy to native robot controls through embodiment-specific post-training.
•
Representation and policy-level validation.
We demonstrate control predictability through frozen-representation probes, competitive manipulation performance across simulation and real-world platforms, and improvements with increasing latent-action pretraining data.

RynnVLA-Latent
A central obstacle to scaling robotic manipulation is that the most abundant sources of manipulation knowledge—human videos, web videos, simulation, and heterogeneous robot datasets—do not share a common action representation. We address this problem by learning a shared latent-action space supervised by visual transitions and geometric pseudo-labels, without requiring identical native control spaces. This latent space serves both as an automatic annotation for large-scale unlabeled video and as an intermediate control representation that can later be aligned with concrete robot actions. Our framework consists of three components. We first assemble and preprocess the multi-embodiment video corpus (Sec.
3.1
). We then train RynnLAM (Sec.
3.2
) with future-feature prediction, dynamic 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling, and use its encoder to label the corpus offline. Finally, we train RynnVLA-Latent (Sec.
3.3
), a vision-language-action policy that learns to generate these latent actions from visual observations and language via flow matching. In post-training, the same flow-matching objective is retargeted from latent actions to the target robot’s action space, so that costly action-labeled demonstrations are required only for the final embodiment alignment.

3.3
RynnVLA-Latent
The latent actions produced by RynnLAM provide an embodiment-agnostic interface between video understanding and control; Fig.
4
summarizes the resulting training pipeline. Because the same encoder maps heterogeneous videos into a common descriptor layout, human, robot, and simulation videos can contribute to one policy objective without reconciling their native action conventions. Building on this interface, RynnVLA-Latent separates the learning of generalizable manipulation dynamics from embodiment-specific action alignment. During pre-training, the policy learns to generate latent actions from raw observations and language; during post-training, the same flow-matching objective is retargeted from latent actions to the target robot’s action space. This decoupling allows the model to scale on unlabeled multi-embodiment videos, while requiring costly action-labeled demonstrations only for the final embodiment alignment.
Architecture.
RynnVLA-Latent adopts a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture
(
Liang et al., 2024
)
that couples a pretrained vision-language model with a narrow action expert. The VLM backbone, RynnBrain
(
Li et al., 2026a
)
, jointly encodes multi-view images and the language instruction into a causal prefix. The action expert is a randomly initialized transformer stream with the same depth as the VLM but a smaller hidden width. At each layer, tokens from the two streams are jointly attended, while their output projections and feed-forward pathways remain separate. The VLM prefix remains causal and cannot attend to the action suffix, whereas the action suffix is bidirectional and attends to the full VLM prefix. This design allows the action expert to exploit rich visual-language context without duplicating the full VLM capacity, and permits action-prediction gradients to refine the VLM representation. We instantiate RynnVLA-Latent with 2B and 4B VLM backbones while keeping the action expert narrow. The 2B and 4B names refer to the backbone variants; total policy parameter counts, including the action expert, are reported in Tab.
2
.

Multi-view conditioning.
Embodiments differ not only in action spaces but also in camera configurations. To avoid hard-coding a fixed set of views, RynnVLA-Latent organizes latent-action generation using canonical camera slots. For each present view, its VLM patch embeddings are pooled into a slot token and prepended to the action expert. Empty slots are masked in attention and in the loss. This slot-based interface accommodates samples with different available views without supervising absent outputs. Camera configurations are mapped to the canonical slots; the interface alone does not guarantee invariance to an unseen viewpoint.

Post-training: embodiment-specific action alignment.
Pre-training yields a model that generates embodiment-agnostic latent actions but does not yet produce executable robot commands. In post-training, we retarget the same flow-matching objective from RynnLAM latents to the target robot’s action space and fine-tune the full model on demonstrations from that embodiment. Proprioceptive state is introduced only at this stage. No separate action decoder is added: the readout trunk pretrained during pre-training is retained and terminated by a thin newly initialized projection to the target action dimension, so the expert’s pretrained capacity is reused rather than duplicated. We use a unified action layout and mask dimensions not used by the target embodiment, allowing one interface to support different robots.

The VLM prefix is computed once and reused across integration steps. The resulting action chunk is executed in full before replanning. Post-training updates the policy parameters and changes the prediction target to native actions while retaining this sampling procedure; execution requires no separate latent-to-action decoder.
4
Experiments
We evaluate the proposed framework from three complementary perspectives.
First, we assess the quality of the latent action representation itself, asking whether RynnLAM learns a representation that is predictive of low-level control signals rather than merely encoding visual semantics or appearance change.
Second, we report completed downstream policy evaluations on simulation benchmarks covering manipulation success, robustness to perturbations, and language grounding. We additionally evaluate bimanual manipulation on RoboTwin 2.0 under the Native protocol.
Third, we evaluate post-trained policies on real-world dual-arm platforms with different end-effectors and mobility, testing applicability across these deployment settings after embodiment-specific adaptation.

Real-World Robot Tasks
We evaluate post-trained policies on six tasks spanning bimanual coordination, tool use, and mobile manipulation. The tasks are distributed across two dual-arm platforms:
Marvin-WUJI
, a stationary dual-arm robot equipped with dexterous hands, and
Astribot-S1
, a wheeled mobile dual-arm robot equipped with parallel grippers. The demonstrations are collected through the teleoperation setup described in Appendix
B
, with per-task episode counts reported in Tab.
11
. The six tasks are defined as follows:
Tasks performed on Marvin-WUJI (Dual-Arm Dexterous Hands):
•
(1) Plate-Placement:
The robot reaches toward a shelf, uses its dexterous hands to securely grasp a plate, and places it on the tabletop to the left of the oven, requiring precise spatial alignment and stable grasping of thin, fragile objects.
•
(2) Steak-Cooking:
The robot uses a spatula to flip a steak in a pan, requiring coordinated tool manipulation.
•
(3) Plate-Wiping:
A highly dexterous bimanual coordination task in which one hand grasps and stabilizes a plate while the other hand holds a cloth to wipe the plate’s surface before returning the plate to the shelf, requiring coordinated manipulation.
Tasks performed on Astribot-S1 (Wheeled Mobile Dual-Arm Grippers):
•
(4) Table-Cleaning:
The mobile robot collects scattered items on the table into a box and then places the box on a shelf, combining object collection with mobile manipulation.
•
(5) Steak-Serving:
The robot approaches the dining area, uses its dual grippers to stably lift a plate containing a cooked steak, and accurately serves it onto the designated spot on the dining table, integrating mobile navigation with precise placement.
•
(6) Plate-Retrieval:
Following the meal, the robot identifies and grasps used, dirty plates left on the dining table, collects the associated cutlery, and returns the items to their designated positions.

Latent Actions as Cross-Embodiment Action Alignment.
We compare RynnLAM-based supervision against two strategies for aligning heterogeneous action spaces: a shared canonical action vector with masking
(
Yuan et al., 2026a
;
Intelligence et al., 2025
)
and embodiment-specific input and output projections
(
Agarwal et al., 2026
;
Zheng et al., 2026
)
. For human videos without native action labels, both explicit alignment baselines use motion-capture-derived wrist poses and fingertip positions as pseudo-action supervision, with implementation details provided in Appendix
C
. As shown in Tab.
9
, under the same approximately 1,000-hour pretraining subset, RynnLAM-based pretraining achieves higher LIBERO-Plus success than both alternatives: 82.3% versus 80.5%/82.1% for 2B, and 84.2% versus 83.5%/83.6% for 4B. In contrast, the explicit action-alignment variants achieve higher LIBERO success. These results suggest that latent-action supervision can favor robustness to distribution shifts, while explicit native-action alignment remains competitive for in-distribution task execution.
Backbone, camera slots, and latent-action targets.
Under the shared training subset, the RynnBrain-based models outperform their Qwen-VL counterparts on LIBERO-Plus by 3.5 and 4.5 percentage points for 2B and 4B, respectively. Removing canonical camera slots reduces LIBERO-Plus success by 0.4 and 1.3 percentage points, while replacing RynnLAM descriptors with LAPA targets reduces it by 2.1 and 2.9 percentage points. These results support the combined design of the vision-language backbone, multi-view conditioning interface, and continuous latent-action supervision, with the most consistent differences appearing under perturbation-based evaluation.
Scaling Behavior.
We investigate the impact of latent-action pretraining data scale by training RynnVLA-Latent with 10%, 30%, 50%, 70%, and 100% of the video corpus and evaluating the resulting policies on LIBERO-Plus under the same downstream protocol. As shown in Fig.
8
, both 2B and 4B models achieve their highest success rates with the full pretraining corpus, demonstrating an overall benefit from scaling up heterogeneous video supervision. While the 2B model improves monotonically across the evaluated data fractions, the 4B model exhibits a slight decrease from 10% to 30% before improving with larger data scales. These results suggest that increasing latent-action pretraining data generally improves downstream robustness within the evaluated range, although the relationship is not strictly monotonic for every model size.
5
Conclusion
We presented a framework for latent-action pretraining of vision-language-action policies from heterogeneous interaction video. RynnLAM combines residual feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow pseudo-labels, contrastive warping, and camera-pose decoupling to produce continuous transition descriptors without native robot-action labels. RynnVLA-Latent learns to predict these descriptors through flow matching, then reuses its pretrained backbone and action expert while retargeting the output space to robot commands.
The evaluation supports this interface at two levels. Frozen probes show that the descriptor is predictive of low-level controls, with average relative-action MSE
0.38
0.38
on LARY. After native-action post-training, the 4B policy achieves
98.8
%
98.8\%
on LIBERO,
84.7
%
84.7\%
on LIBERO-Plus,
51.9
%
51.9\%
average success on the five reported VLABench tracks, and
88.3
%
88.3\%
under the RoboTwin 2.0 Native protocol. It also attains the best success rate among the compared baselines on all six real-world tasks across stationary dexterous and mobile gripper platforms. Performance remains task-dependent, and RoboTwin scores remain below the strongest listed baselines. Together with the data-scaling trend, these findings support shared transition supervision as a practical route to policy pretraining across incompatible control spaces.
Limitations.
Depth, camera poses, and flow are estimated pseudo-labels, so geometric supervision does not guarantee calibrated metric motion or complete separation of camera and manipulation information. Low-level control probes measure predictability, and decoded flow provides qualitative interpretation, rather than proof of causal action identifiability. Policy performance varies across tasks and perturbations, and deployment still requires embodiment-specific action-labeled demonstrations. The current results also do not establish a general scaling law or isolate pretraining-data volume from all differences in optimization exposure. Future work will improve geometric consistency, viewpoint robustness, and transfer with less target-robot supervision.

A.1
Latent Action Representation Quality
We first evaluate the latent action representation itself. Rather than judging latent
actions by downstream manipulation success, which entangles representation quality with
the rest of the VLA stack, the LARY benchmark
(
Nie et al., 2026
)
probes the frozen
representation directly. We adopt its
low-level control regression
track, which
decodes end-effector trajectories from a frozen representation through a lightweight
MLP action expert, scored by MSE across CALVIN
(
Mees et al., 2022
)
and
VLABench
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
(7-DoF Franka), RoboCOIN
(
Wu et al., 2025
)
(12-DoF bimanual) and AgiBotWorld-Beta
(
Bu et al., 2025a
)
(16-DoF AgiBot G1); we leave
aside its semantic classification track, which scores category separability rather than
physical grounding. The official targets are
absolute
end-effector states in a
fixed base frame. At the short stride (
s
=
5
s{=}5
) used to form each image pair, the currently
visible pose can help predict these targets. Absolute-target performance may
therefore reflect static pose information as well as transition information. We therefore also report a
relative
setting that re-expresses the same targets as displacements from the
end-effector state at the first frame, leaving the probe, splits, stride and metric
untouched, so that the probe emphasizes displacement prediction rather than absolute pose reconstruction. We compare
against three of the paradigms of
(
Nie et al., 2026
)

Assran et al., 2025

)

LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus.
LIBERO
(
Liu et al., 2023
)
is a language-conditioned tabletop benchmark on a Franka Emika
Panda. Its four suites—
Spatial
,
Object
,
Goal
,
Long
, 10
tasks each with 50 human-teleoperated demonstrations—isolate spatial grounding, target
disambiguation, goal following, and long-horizon chaining. We fine-tune a single policy
jointly across all 40 tasks and evaluate each suite over 500 rollouts (50 per task).

perturbing seven factors—layout, viewpoint,
robot initial state, language, lighting, background, and sensor noise—over 10,030
curated episodes. We evaluate the LIBERO-finetuned checkpoint without additional LIBERO-Plus adaptation to measure robustness under these perturbations.
VLABench.
VLABench
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
returns to a fixed Franka Panda but shifts the
difficulty from control to grounding: task categories spanning primitive and
composite interactions, built in MuJoCo over 2,164 objects in 163 categories, with instructions
written to convey intent implicitly rather than by template. We fine-tune on
the benchmark’s official primitive-task split and evaluate on the fixed
episode sets of the benchmark’s public tracks, which hold the tasks constant while
varying what the policy must resolve to locate the target:
in-distribution
,
cross-category
,
common-sense
,
semantic-instruction
, and
unseen-texture
. We omit the benchmark’s cross-task
track, whose train/test partition is left to the user and whose numbers are therefore not
comparable across papers.
RoboTwin 2.0.
RoboTwin 2.0
(
Chen et al., 2025a
)
contains 50 bimanual manipulation tasks, including handovers, cooperative lifting, and stabilization followed by manipulation. The benchmark provides 731 object instances in 147 categories and supports multiple dual-arm embodiments. We use ALOHA-AgileX and the Native protocol, with 50 clean and 500 randomized demonstrations per task (27,500 in total). A single policy is trained jointly across all 50 tasks and evaluated in clean and randomized scenes. Randomization covers clutter, lighting, background, tabletop height, and language. Because randomized demonstrations are included during training, the two evaluation domains measure performance within this training protocol rather than zero-shot transfer from clean training to randomized scenes. Results for this protocol are reported in Tab.
6
.
Appendix B
Teleoperation Setup
For Marvin-WUJI, we collect demonstrations through the teleoperation system shown in Fig.
10
. The hardware setup consists of dual Tianji 7-DOF robotic arms and dual Wuji 20-DOF dexterous hands, yielding a total of 54 degrees of freedom.
For arm control, the human operator wears five HTC Vive trackers (mounted on the chest, both wrists, and both upper arms). The system computes wrist-to-chest relative transforms at 100-120 Hz and feeds them into a Pinocchio-based inverse kinematics solver running in a separate process. The resulting joint commands are further smoothed by a Ruckig trajectory generator with velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints before being sent to the robot arms at 200 Hz.
For hand control, the operator wears Manus data gloves. The raw glove signals are converted to a 21-point MediaPipe hand skeleton format and retargeted to the 20-DOF Wuji hand joint space via a dedicated retargeting module, with an exponential moving average filter applied for motion smoothing.

Motion trackers control the dual robot arms, and data gloves control the dexterous hands.
Appendix C
Details of Action-Alignment Baselines
To compare our latent-action-based cross-embodiment alignment with conventional action-alignment strategies, we implement two baselines commonly used in VLA pretraining.
C.1
Shared Vector Representation
Following prior VLA research
(
Yuan et al., 2026a
;
Intelligence et al., 2025
)
, we map heterogeneous state and action spaces from different data sources and embodiments into a unified
85

1.

dual-arm joint positions, with
7
7

2.

Cartesian end-effector position (
3

6

3.

one gripper-position dimension for each arm.
4.

20

dimensions reserved for each dexterous hand.
5.

4
4

6.

3

dimensions for head and neck motion.
7.

4

Different embodiments populate different subsets of this unified vector according to their available degrees of freedom. Unused dimensions are excluded from the training loss through a per-dimension binary mask, preventing spurious supervision on structurally absent action dimensions.
C.2
Domain-specific Projection
Following prior work
(
Agarwal et al., 2026
;
Zheng et al., 2026
)
, this variant retains a shared action expert but replaces the common input and output projections with a bank of domain-specific projections. Each physical robot embodiment is assigned a domain identifier, which selects the corresponding projection parameters for that sample. In this design, the main policy remains shared across embodiments, while the lightweight boundary projections capture embodiment-specific differences in action parameterization and distribution.
C.3
Human Egocentric Datasets
For human egocentric datasets, we treat human motion as a separate embodiment type when using domain-specific projections. These videos carry no native control labels; wrist poses and the positions of five fingertips are mapped to the corresponding slots of the unified vector.
C.4
Delta Actions and Normalization
During training, all action slots use a delta-action representation: each action in an action chunk is expressed relative to the robot’s current state. For normalization, the
6
6

and

Appendix D
RynnVLA-Latent Dataset
Video captioning.
We use Qwen3-VL
(
Bai et al., 2025
)
to generate captions for the video data. Specifically, we leverage the model’s strong video-language understanding capabilities to produce detailed, structured descriptions of each video clip. The videos are first sampled at a frame rate of 1 FPS and split into segments of 5 seconds. For each segment, we provide the following prompt to the model:
Please describe this video in detail. Include the following aspects:
1. The main subject and action in the video.
2. The environment and background.
3. Any objects and their interactions.
4. The overall scene context and atmosphere.
Provide a concise but comprehensive caption in one paragraph.
The generation is performed with a maximum output length of 512 tokens and a temperature of 0.7 to balance creativity and coherence. The generated captions are then collected and stored in JSON format for downstream tasks.
Optical flow annotation.
We employ DPFlow
(
Morimitsu et al., 2025
)
, a state-of-the-art optical flow estimation model. For each video, frame pairs are processed sequentially at native resolution, and the estimated flow fields are visualized via color encoding and saved as MP4 videos at 25 FPS.
Depth annotation.
We employ Depth Anything 3
(
Lin et al., 2025
)
, specifically the
DA3NESTED-GIANT-LARGE-1.1
checkpoint, which provides dense per-frame depth predictions along with camera pose estimation. Each video is sampled at 30 FPS and processed at a working resolution of 392 pixels (short side, upper-bound resize).

article.headline: 3D 接地潜在动作统一异构视频预训练
article.lede: RynnVLA-Latent 从 30.1K 小时人类、机器人与仿真视频中提取 745.52M 潜在动作描述子，用流匹配
article.problem: 扩展视觉-语言-动作模型受限于两点：带动作标注的机器人演示稀缺，且不同本体的控制空间在维度、坐标系和语义上互不兼容。人类与网络视频提供了更广的交互覆盖，却没有对应的机器人指令，因此无法与机器人数据简单合并在同一个原生机动作预测目标下训练。作者认为需要一个与本体无关的共享监督接口，先在视频上学到运动表示，再适配到具体机器人。
article.method: RynnLAM 把相邻帧对编码为 8 个运动 token、64 维全局动作潜在和 32 维相机潜在，合成 608 维描述子；训练目标包括残差未来特征预测、相机补偿的 3D 场景流伪标签、对比式特征 warp、相机位姿解码，以及用梯度反转把自运动从动作潜在中分离。RynnVLA-Latent 采用 Mixture-of-Transformers 结构，把 RynnBrain 视觉语言主干与较窄的动作专家耦合，用流匹配从多视角观测和语言预测长度为 6 的潜在动作块。机器人后训练复用预训练主干与动作专家躯干，只把输出投影重定向到目标机器人的动作维度并引入本体感知，不额外添加潜在到动作的解码器。
article.results: 作者用 RynnLAM 离线标注 25 个视频源、约 30.1K 小时、3.057B 帧，得到 745.52M 个潜在动作，策略训练索引含 121.06M 样本。在 LARY 低层控制回归探针上，完整描述子的平均 MSE 为 0.27（绝对）和 0.38（相对），优于 DreamDojo（0.55）、Moto（0.77）和 LAPA（0.93）的相对结果，但 DreamDojo 在相对 CALVIN 上更好（0.35 对 0.40）。4B 策略在 LIBERO 上达到 98.8%、LIBERO-Plus 上 84.7%（未做基准特定适配）、VLABench 五个 track 平均成功率 51.9%、RoboTwin 2.0 Native 协议平均 88.6%（Clean 88.7%、Randomized 88.4%）。真实世界六个任务每个 35 次试验，4B 变体在全部六项上为所比方法中最高，例如 Table-Cleaning 从 π0.5 的 25.71% 提升到 40.00%，Steak-Serving 从 40.00% 提升到 57.14%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“无动作标签视频”变成可直接用于策略预训练的连续监督信号，并让预训练目标与具体本体解耦，只在最后的后训练阶段引入原生机动作和本体感知。这为在动作标注昂贵、本体异构的条件下扩展机器人基础模型提供了一条可操作的路径。
article.limitations: 深度、相机位姿与光流都是估计出的伪标签，因此几何监督并不保证度量准确，也不保证相机运动与操作信息被完全分离；LARY 探针只衡量可预测性，解码出的 3D 流也只是定性解释，不能证明动作可辨识。性能仍随任务和扰动类型波动（例如相机与机器人初始状态扰动下不如 π0.5），部署仍需目标本体的动作标注演示；此外论文对 RoboTwin 结果的表述不一致，正文与表格给出 88.6%，结论段写 88.3% 并称仍低于最强基线，与表 6 中 88.6% 为最高值相矛盾。

The policy predicts these descriptors from observations and language. {(b) Robot post-training.} Both the pretrained RynnBrain backbone and action-expert trunk are reused. The output projection is retargeted to native robot actions, and proprioceptive state is introduced. page_papers.title: Spatial Audio Generation and Editing with Executable Plans and Self-Distilling Transfusion
page_papers.abstract: Spatial audio authoring coordinates source decisions with soundfield synthesis. For editing, plans specify what to change and retain, while reference audio supplies further acoustic detail. We present AMBIT, a unified framework for native First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) generation and editing with three connected contributions. First, a shared Transfusion backbone couples autoregressive planning with rectified-flow rendering through executable ScenePlans that specify source content, activity, and 3D trajectories. For editing, the plan describes the full target scene, including retained sources; contrastive features ground the requested change, while full reference latents supply residual acoustic detail for preservation. Second, an FOA-aware continuous VAE combines shared-decoder omnidirectional recovery, asymmetric grouped KL, and spatial covariance matching to preserve content and inter-channel structure. Third, joint Transfusion on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) refines planning on student-generated prefixes and rendering at sampling states reached under student plans, with target-conditioned teachers supervising both modes of the shared student. Evaluations across speech, music, and sound show improved generation content and spatial quality, acoustic fidelity during instruction-guided editing, and unedited-source preservation over the compared baselines. Project page: https://wjm-george.github.io/AMBIT/

Abstract
Spatial audio authoring coordinates source decisions with soundfield
synthesis. For editing, plans specify what to change and retain, while
reference audio supplies further acoustic detail.

Introduction
Spatial audio authoring supports immersive media, virtual acoustics, and
interactive environments
(
Zhu et al., 2025
)
through text-driven generation and
instruction-guided editing. Both tasks require decisions about what
each source produces, when it is active, and how it moves to be realized
in a coherent soundfield
(
Guo et al., 2025a
)
. Editing adds a further requirement: changing selected attributes while
retaining the surrounding sources.
An executable plan can state both the requested change and the sources
to keep at the semantic and structural level; reference audio then
supplies residual acoustic detail beyond these symbolic fields.
This motivates learning source decisions and multichannel synthesis
together, with plans governing what changes or stays and reference
latents supporting the acoustic preservation of retained sources.

article.headline: 可执行计划加自蒸馏：空间音频生成与编辑
article.lede: 把声源内容、时序与轨迹写成可执行计划，再合成空间声场；编辑时计划指明改什么、留什么，参考音频补齐细节。
article.problem: 空间音频创作要同时决定每个声源发出什么、何时活跃、如何移动，并把这些决定落实为一个连贯的多声道声场。编辑则在此之上再加一条约束：改变选中声源的属性时，必须保留周围声源及其空间结构。论文认为，声源层面的决策与多声道合成不应分开学习，而应由一份可执行计划统一约束。
article.method: 系统把「可执行计划」作为生成与编辑的共同接口：自回归规划器预测声源级字段（内容、时序、轨迹），解码端在一阶 Ambisonics（FOA）潜空间合成声场，VAE 编码器/解码器负责波形与潜变量的往返。编辑时，计划在语义与结构层面同时声明要改的与要留的，参考音频经编码后提供符号字段之外的残余声学细节，用于保住未改动声源。论文标题中的「self-distilling transfusion」是合成骨干，但材料只描述了规划器与 VAE 层面的设计，具体的自蒸馏机制未展开。
article.results: 训练数据为 160 万条合成与录制的 FOA 样本、外加 100 万对编辑数据，覆盖语音、音乐与环境声；评测使用 8k 生成基准与 5k 编辑基准，VAE 单独在 2000 条 FOA 片段上评估。内容质量方面，Ambit 的词错率/字错率（WER/CER）低于 Qwen3-TTS，但 UTMOS 也更低，作者将其解释为源描述与逐字转写提升了语义与词汇保真，而感知与分布排序各有胜负。轨迹控制基准中，初始距离落在 [2.2, 3.25) 米，线性接近或远离使距离增减 [0.75, 1) 米，自由径向运动则保持距离不变。
article.why_it_matters: 把编辑意图显式写成可执行计划，使「只改一个声源、其余原样保留」成为可检查、可度量的操作，对沉浸式媒体、虚拟声学与交互式声场制作是实用的中间表示；计划本身也可当作评估空间音频可控性的接口。
article.limitations: 材料给出的结论段落中没有明确的局限讨论，无法引用作者自述的不足。从数据看，语义指标（WER/CER）改善伴随感知质量（UTMOS）落后于 Qwen3-TTS，保真与自然度之间存在权衡；轨迹评测又限定在 2.2–3.25 米等规则化区间内，真实场景与复杂运动的泛化仍未验证。

page_papers.title: Principia: Test-Time Hypotheses to Principle Construction for Scientific Discovery
page_papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires identifying the scientific principles underlying observed phenomena to guide further investigation. As these empirical principles are often unknown in complex discovery processes, they are constructed via a hypotheses-to-principle pipeline to obtain recurring causalities from progressively accumulated observations during test-time discovery. However, constructing this knowledge requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, making this translation stage a bottleneck for scientific discovery. To address this limitation, we propose Principia, an LLM-based framework that constructs and continually refines scientific principles at test time. Drawing on how human researchers develop principles, Principia forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and their observed outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships across these hypotheses into inductive principles. By applying the constructed hypotheses and inductive principles to the task, it obtains new observations, revises the hypotheses used based on these new observations, and reconstructs principles from the updated hypotheses, allowing scientific knowledge to continuously evolve throughout test-time discovery. Across benchmarks spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction, Principia outperforms baselines relying on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, while generating principles that are plausible and consistent with the scientific literature, demonstrating its effectiveness in constructing and refining task-specific hypotheses and principles at test time for scientific discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongkiKim95/Principia.

Abstract
Scientific discovery requires identifying the scientific principles underlying observed phenomena to guide further investigation. As these empirical principles are often unknown in complex discovery processes, they are constructed via a hypotheses-to-principle pipeline to obtain recurring causalities from progressively accumulated observations during test-time discovery. However, constructing this knowledge requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, making this translation stage a bottleneck for scientific discovery. To address this limitation, we propose

Introduction
Scientific discovery has long driven human progress, enabling advances across chemistry, biology, and medicine. Central to this process is identifying scientific principles that govern the systems of interest. In complex scientific discovery processes such as drug discovery, the scientific principles are usually unknown due to the complexity of the underlying systems. Therefore, empirical principles are usually constructed from progressively accumulated experimental observations during test-time discovery to explain causality between input characteristics and experimental outcomes
(
Scheiner and Willig, 2008
;
Hone et al., 2015
;
Pearlstein et al., 2021
)
. Specifically, hypotheses that explain a specific scope of individual observations are formed and then generalized into principles that cover a broader scope of observations, being formulated as a hypotheses-to-principle construction pipeline
(
Lamma et al., 2000
;
Kakas and Michael, 2020
;
Engelschalt et al., 2023
)
.
However, constructing such principles by human researchers requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, creating a bottleneck in scientific discovery. As illustrated in Fig.
1
, human researchers also follow the hypotheses-to-principle construction pipeline, while leveraging an extensive body of prior knowledge. They interpret the experimental observations, hypothesize the plausible causal relationships, generalize them by analyzing the recurring patterns, and revise hypotheses when new observations contradict prior explanations. This continued reliance on expert interpretation limits the pace of scientific discovery by slowing the translation of accumulated observations into scientific principles. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs)
(
Anthropic, 2026
;
OpenAI, 2026b
;
OpenAI, 2026a
;
Xu et al., 2026
)
have motivated growing efforts to automate scientific research
(
AI4Science and Quantum, 2023
)
, including idea generation
(
Wang et al., 2024
;
Li et al., 2025
;
Baek et al., 2025
)
, experimental design
(
Gottweis et al., 2026
;
Schmidgall et al., 2026
)
, and candidate optimization
(
Wang et al., 2025a
;
Wang et al., 2025b
;
Roohani et al., 2025
;
Ran et al., 2025
)
. Despite these advances, constructing and continually refining principles for scientific discovery from progressively accumulated experimental observations remains underexplored.
Figure 1:
Scientific principle construction as a bottleneck in scientific discovery.
As experimental observations accumulate, researchers formulate tentative explanations of individual outcomes, generalize recurring relationships across observations into scientific principles, and reassess these explanations in light of new observations. The resulting principles guide further investigation, forming an iterative discovery cycle. However, this process requires substantial domain expertise, time, labor, and financial resources, limiting the pace of scientific discovery.
In this work, we explore the test-time construction of empirical principles that explain how input characteristics contribute to observed outcomes using LLMs. However, operationalizing this process presents two challenges. First, an individual input and its observed outcome provide limited guidance for an LLM to distinguish among possible explanations. Multiple input characteristics can account for the same outcome, making it difficult to identify which factors to emphasize when generating a hypothesis. Hypothesis generation therefore requires evidence that helps narrow the range of possible explanations. Second, the observations accumulated during discovery cover only a small fraction of the vast space of scientific inputs. LLM-generated hypotheses based on this limited coverage can provide incomplete or incorrect explanations for other inputs, and these limitations can carry over into the principles constructed from them. As new observations accumulate, they can expose these limitations, making it necessary to reassess and revise earlier hypotheses.
To address these challenges, we propose

Principia
compares related inputs and their experimental outcomes rather than a single observation to formulate causal hypotheses, narrowing the factors considered to their shared and differing characteristics. For principle construction, it groups related inputs and inductively combines recurring relationships across their hypotheses into principles. These hypotheses and principles guide subsequent prediction or optimization through retrieval, getting new observations. Finally, new observations are used to revise the used hypotheses and reconstruct the resulting principles, allowing the knowledge to evolve during test-time discovery.

Principia
achieves comparable optimization performance with a 55% reduction in experimental budget compared with an experience-summary baseline, demonstrating its cost-effectiveness in scientific optimization. Qualitative analyses show that the constructed hypotheses capture relationships between inputs and experimental outcomes, while the induced principles are consistent with scientific literature. These results show that constructing empirical principles at test time can improve both the effectiveness and efficiency of scientific discovery.

article.headline: 让大模型在发现过程中自建科学原理
article.lede: Principia 让大模型在测试时从累积观测中构造假设与原理，论文称在优化任务上以少 55% 的实验预算达到相当性能。
article.problem: 在药物发现等复杂场景中，支配系统的科学原理往往未知，研究者只能从逐步积累的实验观测中归纳出经验原理，再用这些原理指导后续实验。但这一「假设到原理」的翻译过程高度依赖领域专家，耗时耗力，成为科学发现流程中的瓶颈。现有 LLM 自动化研究多集中在想法生成、实验设计与候选优化，如何从不断累积的观测中构建并持续修正原理仍缺乏探索。
article.method: Principia 不再依赖单条输入与其结果，而是把相关输入及其实验结果放在一起比较，利用它们的共性与差异缩小候选解释范围，从而生成因果假设。在原理构建阶段，它把相关输入分组，并将各组假设中反复出现的关系归纳为原理；这些假设与原理通过检索用于后续预测或优化，产生新的观测。新观测再被用来修正已有假设并重建原理，使知识在测试时的发现过程中持续演化。
article.results: 论文称，与「经验总结」（experience-summary）基线相比，Principia 在达到相当优化性能的同时将实验预算减少 55%。分子优化任务从 ZINC 池中预采样 200 个分子出发，每代最多生成 100 个后代，总预算为 1,000 次不同的 oracle 评估；蛋白序列任务从 48 条序列（含野生型）出发，预算为 200 次评估；基因任务中 Scharenberg22 与 IFNG 的 oracle 预算分别为 192 和 768 个不同基因。评价指标包括 AUC@10 与 Avg@100（序列任务为 Avg@50），定性分析称构建的假设能捕捉输入与实验结果之间的关系，归纳出的原理与已有文献一致。
article.why_it_matters: 如果把「从观测到原理」这一步也交给模型，并在测试时随新数据不断修正，自动化科学发现就有望从单点候选优化扩展到可累积、可修订的知识构建，而不必每一步都等待专家解读。
article.limitations: 所提供的材料在方法定义处即被截断，完整算法、基线设置与统计显著性均未给出，55% 的预算节省也仅针对单一经验总结基线，缺少与其他知识增强方法的系统对比。评测集中在分子、蛋白序列与基因等计算基准上，未涉及真实湿实验，「原理与文献一致」也只是定性陈述，论文未给出具体数字。
article.figure_caption_zh: 原文未提供图注；图 1 示意人类研究者从单条观测提出假设、把反复出现的关系归纳为原理，并在新观测下重新评估的迭代发现循环，该环节正是论文所指的瓶颈。

page_papers.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
page_papers.abstract: Scaling embedding capacity alongside Transformer computation is an emerging trend in language models. This trend makes high compression rates increasingly useful. Hence, we study extreme compression of Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which follow this trend and account for 35.2% of the parameters of Gemma 4 E4B. At such rates, conventional quantizers give each token-layer vector its own code of only a few bytes. We instead develop OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes), which stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at every layer with a layer-specific affine decoder. Codes and decoders are fitted to the PLE output path rather than to the stored vectors. At about 100times PLE compression of bfloat16 (BF16) E4B, OPTIC retains an aggregate 97.8% of the uncompressed model's performance across seven benchmarks, whereas product quantization, the strongest of six conventional baselines, retains 66.3%. At 594times and 1,002times PLE compression of BF16 E4B, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. On the official E4B release with 4-bit linear weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about 100times PLE compression. During inference at about 100times PLE compression, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory than with uncompressed PLE at the same key-value cache size, while running at most 0.40% slower.

We study Gemma 4 E2B and E4B for their strong performance and potential

two checkpoints, respectively, making it a substantial target for
storage reduction as models expand their embedding capacity.
An ordinary input embedding maps a token to one vector at the model’s
input. PLE provides a separate vector at each decoder layer: E4B stores
11 million token–layer vectors of width 256, and near
100
×
100\times
compression leaves about five bytes for each. Conventional quantizers spend
these bytes on a separate code for every vector.
OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes) builds on two
observations. First, PLE stores one vector for every pair of token and
layer, so a compact representation can share storage along either index.
OPTIC shares along both. All tokens of a layer use one layer-specific
affine decoder, whose storage does not grow with the vocabulary size. All
layers of a token use one code tuple, so a token’s bytes form one larger
code instead of many small per-layer codes, and the layer decoders preserve
the differences between layers.
Second, the model uses PLE vectors through a gate and an output projection.
The fitting objective should therefore account for reconstruction error
after the gate and output projection, rather than only in the stored
coordinates. OPTIC fits its codes and decoders to minimize error at the
projection output.

7
Related Work
Embedding compression.
Multi-codebook representations have been used to compress word embeddings
for NLP.
Shu and Nakayama (2018)
learn compositional discrete codes and
codebooks for an embedding matrix. Our setting has an additional layer axis:
the same vocabulary item has a different embedding at each layer. We exploit
this correspondence by decoding one token representation into multiple
layer-specific rows. CARVQ combines grouped residual codes with a nonlinear
corrective adaptor for ordinary token embeddings
(
Gou et al., 2025
)
;
our representation instead shares a token’s latent codes across layers.
Vector quantization and low-rank representations.
Product quantization divides a vector into subspaces and quantizes each
subspace
(
Jegou et al., 2010
)
; optimized product quantization learns a
transformation before quantization
(
Ge et al., 2013
)
.
Residual and additive quantizers represent vectors through sums of
codewords
(
Chen et al., 2010
;
Babenko and Lempitsky, 2014
)
.
Low-rank factorization instead stores continuous coordinates and a shared
basis; randomized SVD offers a practical fitting
procedure
(
Halko et al., 2011
)
. OPTIC combines a shared
latent representation with discrete token codes and layer-specific
affine decoders. This shares the code storage across layers while keeping a separate
reconstruction map for each layer.
Output-aware model compression.
Weight reconstruction can account for a model’s inputs and activations.
GPTQ uses approximate second-order information for post-training weight
quantization
(
Frantar et al., 2022
)
, while AWQ uses activation statistics
to choose channel scales that protect salient
weights
(
Lin et al., 2024
)
.
AQLM combines input-adaptive additive quantization with joint block
optimization
(
Egiazarian et al., 2024
)
. Our loss follows the gated PLE
output path instead of a linear weight matrix. Compressing this separate
embedding table complements backbone weight quantization, as our BF16
and W4A16 experiments demonstrate.
Our comparisons include the AQLM Euclidean beam encoder and
output-path-fitted additive codes; Appendices
A
and
E
give their PLE adaptations and storage budgets.
8
Conclusion
OPTIC stores one code tuple per token, which every layer decodes through its
own affine decoder, and fits codes and decoders at the PLE projection
output, before normalization. Near
100
×
100\times
PLE compression, it achieves
seven-task retention of 97.8% on BF16 E4B and 96.9% on W4A16 E4B. Independent latent codes
for each vector retain 79.3% on BF16 E4B with nearly equal storage.
At
594
×
594\times
and
1002
×
1002\times
PLE compression, OPTIC retains
90.5% and 84.1% of BF16 E4B performance, respectively.
Served directly from OPTIC codes with a fixed key–value cache size,
BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory with at most 0.40% added wall time.
These results show substantial compression potential in Gemma 4’s expanded
embedding tables. They motivate designing embedding capacity and compressed
representations together, with deployment memory as a constraint.
Our BF16 and W4A16 results show that PLE compression complements backbone
quantization; extending this combination to other embedding structures
is a promising direction.
Limitations
The study evaluates PLE in Gemma 4 E2B and E4B.
The main comparisons and Table
3
use one fixed
fitting seed, so the paired-bootstrap intervals describe benchmark sampling
uncertainty. The three-fit comparisons and controls describe fitting variation under
the common Euclidean initialization.
At a matched byte budget, removing code sharing also changes how bytes are
divided between codes and decoders, so the code-sharing ablation measures this
combined effect with the fitting recipe held fixed. The fixed-code objective ablation applies
to continuous fitting, and the output-path loss holds the gates fixed and
measures error only at each layer’s projection output. The baselines, including the
AQLM Euclidean beam encoder, are adaptations of their original methods to PLE. A single low-count task can strongly affect retention.
Ethical Considerations
Compression reduces the resources needed to study and deploy existing
models. It can broaden access to model research, although the same
resource savings can also lower the cost of harmful applications.
AI assistants were used for language polishing and code assistance.
The authors remain responsible for the results, references,
implementation and writing.

The controlled comparisons use checkpoint-matched uncompressed evaluations

The following descriptions specify the prompts and scoring used for

We score all 1,838 validation items with zero demonstrations.

article.headline: 跨层共享码本，PLE 压缩百倍仍保 97.8%
article.lede: 研究者提出 OPTIC：每个 token 只存一个量化码元组，各层用专属仿射解码器还原 PLE 行，并按输出路径拟合。
article.problem: Per-Layer Embeddings 为词表中每个 token 在每一解码层都存一个向量，Gemma 4 E4B 中 PLE 占模型参数的 35.2%，E4B 共约 1100 万个 token–层向量、宽度 256。在约 100 倍压缩下，每个向量平均只剩约 5 字节，传统量化器要给每个 token–层向量单独分配一份极短的码，难以保真。
article.method: OPTIC 把同一 token 在所有层的 PLE 向量表示为一个跨层共享的量化码元组，每层再用一个专属仿射解码器把它映射回本层的 PLE 行，因此码的存储不再随层数增长，而解码器不随词表增长。码本与解码器不拟合存储向量本身，而是在 PLE 经门控与输出投影之后的路径上最小化误差；训练在连续更新码本、解码器与离散重分配码字之间交替，并用输出路径加权的 PCA 与 OPQ 特征值分配做初始化。
article.results: 在约 100 倍 PLE 压缩下，BF16 E4B 保留七项基准聚合性能的 97.8%，六种常规基线中最强的乘积量化仅保留 66.3%；官方 W4A16 版本上 OPTIC 保留 96.9%，最强基线为 82.8%。在 594 倍和 1002 倍压缩下，BF16 E4B 仍分别保留 90.5% 和 84.1%；同等存储下，逐向量独立隐码只保留 79.3%。E2B 上 BF16 与 W4A16 分别为 89.1% 和 91.5%。在 RTX 4090 上以固定 KV cache 推理时，BF16 E4B 的 GPU 内存降低 29.7%，最慢仅增加 0.40% 的实际耗时。
article.why_it_matters: 嵌入容量正成为独立于计算规模的扩展维度，PLE 这类按层展开的查表会持续推高参数与显存占比；OPTIC 表明可以在几乎不掉点的前提下把这块存储压掉两个数量级，并与骨干权重量化互补。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖 Gemma 4 E2B 与 E4B，主比较和关键消融使用单一拟合种子，配对 bootstrap 区间只反映基准采样不确定性。此外，在匹配字节预算下取消跨层码共享会同时改变码与解码器之间的字节分配，因此该消融测的是组合效应；基线方法均为作者对 PLE 场景的改编，且单个低样本任务可能强烈影响聚合保留率。
article.figure_caption_zh: 每个 token 只存一个共享码元组，各层专属仿射解码器据此还原本层 PLE 行；同色表示对应层，省略号表示略去的层与码本。

Each index $q_{tm}$ selects the highlighted codeword of codebook $C_m$. Concatenating these codewords forms one shared latent $ z_t$, from which each affine decoder reconstructs its layer's PLE row. page_papers.title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning
page_papers.abstract: Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39x and 1.47x the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier.

miniTE
: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning
September, 2026
Abstract
Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39
×
\times
and 1.47

\times
the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier.
1  Introduction
Reinforcement learning is central to large language model (LLM)
post-training, supporting instruction following
(
Ouyang et al., 2022
)
and mathematical reasoning
(
Shao et al., 2024
;
DeepSeek-AI, 2025
)
.
Repeated generation, policy evaluation, and updates
(
Yu et al., 2026
)
span an autoregressive sampler and a learner that optimizes on sampled
sequences. Native low-precision computation must accelerate these engines
while preserving effective learning.
Four-bit weight storage
(
Dettmers et al., 2023
)
and native four-bit
training
(
Castro et al., 2025
;
NVIDIA et al., 2025
)
address different
execution paths. Quantized sampling, matched precision, and
quantization-aware RL address learner–sampler mismatch
(
Huang and others, 2025
;
Xi et al., 2026
;
Zhuge et al., 2026
;
Gu et al., 2026
)
; recent systems
also support per-token NVFP4 and high-precision backward
(
Cursor Research, 2026
;
Li et al., 2026
)
. We focus on native
weight-and-activation four-bit (W4A4) expert computation, connecting
cross-engine diagnosis, a practical numerical path, and complete learner gains.
RL makes cross-engine numerical behavior consequential. Probabilities
computed by the learner and sampler enter importance ratios and clipping
decisions
(
Schulman et al., 2017
;
Zheng et al., 2025
)
; implementation differences
therefore enter optimization even at a shared parameter version.
Training–inference mismatch and execution-aligned references have been
studied in RL pipelines
(
Yao et al., 2025
;
Zhong et al., 2026
)
.
NVFP4 adds choices in scale domains, rounding, accumulation, and operator
composition that a format name does not specify. This raises a concrete
question:
which numerical dependencies must be exposed and controlled
when native low-bit computation spans two execution engines?
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models combine continuous expert computation
with discrete routing. Selective router precision and routing replay
address sensitivity in expert selection
(
Fedus et al., 2022
;
Ma et al., 2025
)
.
We examine what remains after controlling parameter updates and
matching assignments at the observed layer. Frozen-policy scoring
shows that NVFP4 enlarges the cross-engine log-probability tail.
Target-layer routing agreement leaves FC1/FC2 output discrepancies,
and a sampler-only scaling change does not establish agreement
(Figure
1
). These controls identify an execution
specification, extending beyond bit width and expert IDs, as a useful
unit of diagnosis and implementation.
Motivated by these findings, we introduce
miniTE
to connect this diagnosis
with practical native NVFP4 training (Figure
2
). Our framework checks quantized
operands, expert outputs, and policy evaluation across the sampler and
learner. Strict execution provides a cross-engine reference for diagnosis;
the default path combines our per-token quantization and native grouped-GEMM
implementation with BF16 backward. Its purpose is stable, high-throughput
learning under the existing RL objective. Arithmetic throughput is only
one component of this cost: routed expert workloads also require operand
preparation, representation conversion, and dispatch. We therefore
optimize quantization and grouped GEMM as a connected dataflow,
reducing repeated preparation around the numerical core so that FP4
arithmetic gains translate into faster learner updates. Comparisons between
our initial and optimized operator implementations check the numerical
effects of those changes.
Long-horizon Qwen3-30B-A3B runs show sustained learning with
miniTE
and higher mathematical evaluation scores than naive NVFP4.
Same-recipe module comparisons show
2.46
×
2.46\times
expert-forward speedup
over TE U3045. Complete learner updates on fixed text reach
1.39
×
1.39\times
BF16 throughput in the optimized configuration and
1.33
×
1.33\times
in a
repeated core study. The module comparison measures native implementation
gains; complete learner updates measure the numerical path and
implementation together.
Separate colocated RL measurements identify weight conversion and
synchronization as an integration bottleneck.
Our contributions are:
1.
Execution-gap diagnosis.
Frozen-policy, routing-conditioned,
and scaling controls identify numerical differences beyond nominal NVFP4
recipe agreement; strict execution supplies an actionable alignment
reference.
2.
Practical native NVFP4 RL.
An integrated W4A4 expert-forward
path with BF16 backward sustains long-horizon learning and improves
all four mathematics benchmarks over naive NVFP4 without modifying
the RL objective.
3.
A lightweight framework with numerically faithful
acceleration.
miniTE
exposes configurable numerical recipes, replaceable expert
operators, and reusable diagnostics for developing custom low-bit
training settings. Operator-level numerical checks
and complete learner benchmarks substantiate its execution
optimizations. We release Dockerfiles, reference configurations, and
single-command launch scripts to support reproducible experiments
and extensions across the supported low-bit RL paths.

3  Diagnosing the Execution Gap
The frozen-policy study scores identical token sequences under teacher forcing with a frozen
Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base checkpoint
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
. Tails use 32 prompts
and 69,088 matched tokens; localization uses 12 prompts at 11 depths.
Confidence intervals use 2,000 prompt-cluster bootstrap resamples. Within-stack
self-comparisons are bitwise exact. Appendix
C
specifies the collectors and full protocol.

version. The P99 of

An execution specification records scale domains, rounding, logical
layouts, and the placement of casts and router coefficients. Comparisons
fix the weight version, token IDs, and scoring context, then decode
codes and scales to a common layout. Input provenance and expert IDs
identify the comparison boundary: naturally accumulated inputs reveal
cross-engine differences, while common-input comparisons test the
operators applied at that boundary. This distinction follows directly
from the residual differences under matched target-layer routing.

The strict execution reference matches learner kernels, formulas, and
reduction orders to the sampler, including surrounding normalization
and communication paths. It retains native NVFP4 expert forward and

recipe. It tests whether an API or layout transformation preserves
quantized operands and outputs. The practical learner below is evaluated
as a complete learning configuration; its implementation checks use
the latter reference.

The learner applies router probabilities to the SwiGLU activation before
