4.3  Joint Design of Quantization and Grouped GEMM
Routed expert computation requires operand preparation and scheduling
in addition to matrix multiplication. Expert-dependent group sizes,
empty groups, and padding affect the interface between these operations.
We optimize that interface as a connected dataflow.
A shared producer–consumer representation.
The reference quantizer already processes grouped inputs, but returns
expert views or lists from which grouped GEMM reconstructs its arguments.
miniTE
writes packed FP4 codes, block scales, and outer-scale information
directly into contiguous buffers consumed by GEMM. Device-side offsets
describe expert boundaries, and metadata storage and workspaces are reused.
This removes repeated splitting and argument preparation between two
grouped interfaces while retaining expert-dependent offsets and padding,
including support for empty groups.
Statistics travel with their activations.
The FC1 reference permutes tokens, pads them, and scans the padded rows
for maxima.

Layout and native GEMM execution.
Fused scale layout preparation supplies the format consumed by Tensor
Cores. FC1 and FC2 use GEMM configurations adapted to their different
reduction lengths, coupling tile selection and tensor-memory allocation.
The optimized path combines these choices with the dense representation,
permutation fusion, and amax reuse. Sections
5.3
and
5.4
report implementation gains and numerical
checks for these transformations;
Appendix
F

Framework integration.
Users integrate
miniTE
by replacing the expert grouped-linear module
through a common expert-computation interface. Quantization recipes and
backward precision are configurable separately, with BF16 and MXFP8
backward available for the supported NVFP4 paths. Compatible quantizer
and grouped-GEMM implementations provide layout and scheduling options
within the existing RL orchestration. The operand, expert-output, and
policy-evaluation boundaries in Section
4.1
provide reusable
comparison points for checking each recipe or kernel change.
5  Experiments
We evaluate learning behavior, complete learner efficiency, and the

The frozen comparisons in Section

Complete learner updates.

7  Conclusion
Frozen-policy and routing-conditioned measurements expose execution
differences beyond nominal NVFP4 agreement. We introduced
miniTE
,
combining cross-engine diagnostics, native W4A4 forward with
independently selected backward precision, and jointly optimized
quantization and grouped GEMM. On Qwen3-30B-A3B,
miniTE
sustained
learning over a long RL training horizon and outperformed standard
TE NVFP4 on all four mathematics benchmarks, with a five-task
average close to that of BF16. The optimized learner achieves
1.47
×
1.47\times
the throughput of TE NVFP4 and
1.39
×
1.39\times
that of
BF16. Separate expert-forward measurements under the same recipe
show a
2.46
×
2.46\times
speedup over Transformer Engine.
With configurable recipes, replaceable operators, and reproducible
launch environments,
miniTE
provides an extensible foundation
for numerical and systems co-design in native low-bit RL.
8  Limitations and Future Work
Numerical fidelity beyond execution alignment.
Although
miniTE
improves mathematical evaluation over standard
TE NVFP4, its practical path still falls short of BF16 in average
evaluation quality and of strict execution in cross-engine
agreement. Matching execution does not eliminate the quantization
error associated with E2M1 values and E4M3 block scales.
However, the remaining quality gap does not isolate the effects
of quantization error from residual execution differences.
Future work should investigate tighter execution alignment
together with format-aware error compensation, aiming to
improve learning quality while retaining native W4A4 computation.
End-to-end efficiency and hardware-aware fusion.
Our colocated measurements identify weight conversion and
synchronization as a substantial integration cost. These
measurements cover selected stages rather than complete RL
iterations, so component speedups alone do not establish
end-to-end gains. Reducing repeated conversion and packing
at learner–sampler boundaries is therefore a priority.
Online amax–quantization–GEMM fusion offers a complementary
direction for reducing operator-side preparation costs.
Its numerical behavior and performance need joint validation,
particularly when scales evolve during accumulation.
Efficient implementations must coordinate scale updates,
accumulator rescaling, and data movement within SM resource
constraints, motivating further hardware–software co-design.
Our learning evidence covers one MoE model with one run per
configuration, and the implementation gains are evaluated on
Blackwell hardware. Broader validation across models, tasks,
independent training seeds, and hardware platforms remains
future work.

Experimental protocols and implementation identities
TIS and experiment scope.
All non-strict RL runs use truncated importance sampling (TIS),
including the BF16 control, naive NVFP4, and
miniTE
paths.
The strict execution configuration runs without TIS. TIS reweights
policy-gradient contributions using bounded learner-to-rollout
likelihood ratios; it is distinct from policy-update ratio clipping
and from numerical execution alignment. The frozen-policy diagnostics,
isolated modules, and fixed-text learner benchmarks do not apply an
RL importance correction. Their numerical-format labels therefore
remain BF16, NVFP4, or
miniTE
without a TIS suffix.
Model and execution environment.
The learner benchmarks use Qwen3-30B-A3B, with 48 layers, hidden size
2,048, 128 experts, top-8 routing, and expert intermediate size 768.
The node contains eight NVIDIA B300 SXM6 GPUs with 275 GB of memory
per GPU. The software stack uses PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0.88,
NCCL 2.28.9, Megatron Core 0.16.0rc0, and driver 590.48.01.
Megatron-LM uses revision 52153937. The core repeated
learner benchmark uses
miniTE
revision 953f17f9; the
optimized batch uses revision b641179, which includes the
dense grouped path and FC1/FC2-specific GEMM-kind selection.
The initial Transformer Engine
revision, eaca54e9, was updated to 8ea5a92d to support
zero-token experts. Both revisions retain the same three integration
patches, and their nonempty-expert paths were checked for parity.
The upstream per-token reference uses revision 690ffea4 in a
separate container built from the same image, with a CUDA 13 compilation
compatibility patch.

article.headline: miniTE诊断NVFP4强化学习执行差距
article.lede: 同权重、同格式下，学习器与采样器的NVFP4执行差异仍会放大log概率尾部，影响RL策略评估。
article.problem: LLM强化学习在采样器与学习器两个引擎上执行策略评估；即便权重和NVFP4量化格式一致，算子组合、缩放域与归约顺序不同仍会造成跨引擎数值差异，并通过重要性比和裁剪进入优化。现有工作多关注量化格式或路由一致性，未充分暴露完整执行路径。
article.method: miniTE把执行规格显式化：记录缩放域、舍入、布局及cast/router位置，提供严格执行参考和算子参考两类诊断。其默认学习路径采用逐token激活缩放的W4A4专家前向、FP32 epilogue重缩放和保存高精度操作数的BF16反向，并把量化与grouped GEMM作为连续数据流联合优化。框架不修改RL目标，可替换专家算子并复用诊断接口。
article.results: 在Qwen3-30B-A3B上，冻结策略诊断显示NVFP4下|δ_num|的P99从BF16的0.1271 nats升至0.2911，配对增加0.1641（95% CI [0.1311, 0.2005]）；仅数值比值超出裁剪范围的token占1.203%，BF16为0.627%；严格执行参考的跨引擎log概率差约10^-8。长程RL第999步，miniTE五任务均值56.35%，高于naive NVFP4的54.57%，低于BF16的58.84%；AIME24/25分别比naive NVFP4高10.00和3.88个百分点，MATH-500高0.55，GSM8K高0.08，但IFEval低5.59个百分点。八卡B300上完整学习器更新达33,540 tokens/s，为BF16的1.39倍、TE NVFP4的1.47倍；同配方专家前向相对TE U3045几何平均加速2.46倍（1.587–3.065倍）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把低比特RL的瓶颈从“位宽是否匹配”推进到“跨引擎执行是否一致”，并给出可复用的诊断边界与内核实现。对需要同时跑采样与训练的MoE RL系统，这提供了一条在不改RL目标的前提下获得原生FP4吞吐的工程路径。
article.limitations: 实际路径的平均评测仍比BF16低2.49个百分点，且IFEval明显落后naive NVFP4；作者也指出剩余质量差距无法区分量化误差与残余执行差异，实验仅覆盖一个MoE模型、每种配置单次运行和Blackwell硬件。共置RL测量中权重转换/同步从9.94 s升至55.26 s，两阶段合计97.82 s对56.98 s，但未覆盖完整迭代，不能据此判断端到端加速；模块级前向+反向还有7/8个单元慢于BF16。

page_papers.title: Not Just a Subject: Capturing Adaptive Scene-Specific Variance for Visual Storytelling
page_papers.abstract: Recent advancements in diffusion models have significantly improved text-to-image generation, enabling their application to visual storytelling, where coherent image sequences are generated from narrative prompts. However, existing methods primarily focus on identity preservation and often fail to adapt to diverse scene variations, resulting in semantic misalignment and structural inflexibility. We propose EOS-Story, a training-free framework that harmonizes identity consistency with scene-specific adaptation across text and vision spaces. In the text space, we decouple the narrative into identity and scene sub-prompts to prevent information dilution, but this leaves the scene without access to appearance cues. To bridge this gap, we introduce Cross-Contextual Bridging, which softly injects a phrase-level appearance residual into the scene's <EOS> embedding. In the vision space, we find that scale mismatch between identity and scene subjects causes a few identity tokens to be repeatedly transferred, producing structural artifacts. We address this with Adaptive Identity Preservation, which anchors identity features at the scene-specific scale (Identity Anchoring) and integrates them via Identity-Aware Self-Attention. To evaluate performance under varied spatial compositions, we extend the Consistory+ benchmark with diverse framing scenarios (Consistory+_+). Extensive experiments show that EOS-Story achieves competitive or superior performance on both benchmarks.

While these methods effectively maintain identity consistency,

scene-specific variance
in both text and vision spaces—the diverse semantic and visual elements that vary across narrative contexts (

First, at the semantic level, current methods
[
17
,
40
,
30
]
often treat narrative prompts as monolithic inputs, where various semantics (e.g., appearance and scene descriptions) are encoded into a unified embedding.
This can lead to
information dilution

[
14
]
.
As a result, even when a prompt contains rich details (e.g., specific actions or environmental changes), the model often fails to selectively extract scene-specific cues from the prompt.
This directly undermines narrative fidelity, producing scenes that ignore their intended semantics (
Fig.
1
a,b).
Second, at the visual level, existing approaches typically rely on spatially blind feature injection, where identity features are transferred without accounting for the spatial constraints or framing of each scene.
This oversight of structural scene variance (e.g., camera angles or subject scales) can lead to
subject inflexibility
, such as contextually mismatched poses or repetitive structural patterns across scenes (
Fig.
1
b,c).
Consequently, subjects are rendered with rigid structural patterns that ignore each scene’s intended layout, further weakening alignment with scene-specific prompts.
Therefore, achieving coherent storytelling requires scene-specific adaptation, where identity consistency is harmonized with the semantic and structural variance of each scene.
To address this issue, we propose
EOS-Story
, a framework designed to adaptively account for scene-specific variance via two complementary modules,
(1) Cross-Contextual Bridging:
We hypothesize that semantic misalignment arises when long and complex prompts are encoded holistically, causing scene-varying attributes to be diluted
[
16
,
14
]
.
Rather than encoding all information in a single prompt, we decouple the narrative into an identity prompt describing the subject and a scene prompt describing the scenario.
For instance, “a woman with blond hair reading a book.” is split into an identity prompt (“a woman with blond hair.”) and a scene prompt (“a woman reading a book.”).
However, this separation introduces a new challenge: since the scene prompt contains no appearance information, the subject generated within the scene has no way to reflect the actual target identity.
To bridge this semantic gap without reverting to monolithic encoding, we preserve the scene sub-prompt as a semantic anchor and softly inject appearance information at the embedding level.

5
Conclusion
In this work, we propose
EOS-Story
, a training-free framework that adaptively models scene-specific variance in visual storytelling across text and vision spaces. We introduce
Cross-Contextual Bridging
, which decouples the narrative into identity and scene sub-prompts and bridges the resulting semantic gap by injecting phrase-level appearance residuals into the scene’s
⟨
\langle
EOS
⟩
\rangle
embedding. To complement this with structural adaptation, we further propose
Adaptive Identity Preservation
, which anchors subject features at the scene-specific scale and refines integration through Identity-Aware Self-Attention. To evaluate scene adaptability, we extend Consistory+ with diverse framing variations (Consistory+_+).
Extensive experiments show that EOS-Story achieves competitive or superior performance in both prompt fidelity and structural adaptability.

Appendix 0.B
Consistory+_+ & Framing Evaluation Details
The ShotBench
[
15
]
includes a wide range of framing phrases across eight categories (
Tab.
7
).
To ensure a focused and rigorous evaluation of scene-specific structural variance, we intentionally restricted the scope to three primary categories, excluding the remaining five based on the following methodological criteria: (1) Prompt Redundancy: Shot Framing descriptors (e.g., “single”, “2 shot”) primarily specify the number of characters, which is already inherently defined by the subject phrases in the storyboard prompts; (2) Redundancy Mitigation: Lens Size phrases (e.g., “wide lens”) are largely redundant as they are semantically encompassed by the Shot Size category (“wide shot”); (3) Domain Incompatibility: Camera Movement is inherently applicable to temporal video sequences and is thus irrelevant to static image generation; and (4) Task Relevance: Lighting-related categories fall outside the scope of our work, as they primarily focus on stylistic or artistic variations rather than the structural and compositional elements that define scene-specific variance.
Framing Phrase Filtering.
Although SDXL generally produces textually well-aligned images, it sometimes struggles to accurately reflect specific framing phrases.
Before incorporating these phrases into our benchmark extension, we first evaluate how well they are captured by the base SDXL model using the ShotBench evaluation mechanism.
To quantitatively assess phrase reflection, we construct approximately 90 diverse scene prompts and append each framing phrase at the end (e.g., “A photo of a woman baking cookies, close-up shot”).
We generate images for 10 random seeds per phrase and compute the top-1 and top-3 accuracy, along with standard deviations, as shown in
Fig.
16
.
For example, in the “shot size” category with 7 phrase options, this results in a total of 6,300 images (90 scenes × 7 phrases × 10 seeds).
We filter out framing phrases whose top-1 accuracy is zero (e.g., “extreme wide shot”), as these are not reliably reflected in the generated outputs from SDXL.
Consistory+_+
With the remaining framing phrases, we extend the original Consistory+ benchmark using GPT-4o.
Since these phrases are visually meaningful primarily for animate subjects, we first guide GPT-4o to determine whether the subject in each prompt is animate.
Then, the model is instructed to append the most appropriate framing phrase for the given scene, resulting in Consistory+_+.
Framing Accuracy Evaluation.
Following the evaluation protocol in
[
15
]
, we provide the generated image along with the corresponding framing category (e.g., shot size) and prompt the model with a multiple-choice question.
For instance, for shot size evaluation, we prompt the model with a multiple-choice question such as
“What is the shot size of this shot?” and provide predefined options (e.g., wide shot, medium shot, close-up shot).
The predicted category is compared against the framing phrase specified in the text prompt, and accuracy is reported.

Layer Application Variation.
We apply Identity Anchoring (IA) and Identity-Aware Self-Attention (IASA) at different layers of the unet decoder in the diffusion model.
While prior works typically transfer identity-related features within the decoder (up-block) layers, we further investigate the impact of layer selection.

Interestingly, when IA and IASA are applied to configurations that include the up-block layers, the CLIP-I score notably improves (surpassing 0.880).
These results empirically highlight the importance of the decoder layers (up-blocks) in effectively conveying identity features and enhancing the image quality during generation.

article.headline: 免训练EOS-Story：兼顾身份一致与场景适配
article.lede: 研究者提出免训练框架EOS-Story，从文本与视觉两个空间入手，让视觉叙事在保持角色身份的同时贴合每个场景的语义与构图
article.problem: 现有视觉叙事方法主要聚焦角色身份保持，却难以适配多样的场景变化，导致语义错位与结构僵化。具体来说，长提示词被整体编码会使细粒度外观信息被稀释，而身份特征的空间盲目注入又忽视了各场景的构图与主体尺度。
article.method: EOS-Story 在文本空间把叙事拆分为身份子提示与场景子提示，并把身份提示相对共享锚点的短语级外观残差注入场景的⟨EOS⟩嵌入，从而既不稀释场景语义，也不丢失外观线索。视觉空间则用身份锚定将身份特征缩放到与场景主体一致的尺度，再通过身份感知自注意力完成融合。整个框架无需训练，基于 SDXL-base-1.0，去噪步数设为 50。
article.results: 在 Consistory+ 上，EOS-Story 的 CLIP-T 为 0.9042、DreamSim 为 0.2005、ImageReward 为 1.1680，优于 1P1S 的 0.8871/0.2132/0.8289 与 Consistory 的 0.8868/0.2355/0.9814；CLIP-I 为 0.8850，低于 IP-Adapter 的 0.9398。在扩展基准 Consistory+_+ 上，CLIP-T 达 0.8998、ImageReward 为 1.3217。20 名参与者、40 个故事板的用户研究中，该方法在 52.8% 的情况下被选为最佳。
article.why_it_matters: 视觉叙事是数字漫画与角色动画的基础应用，这项工作指出场景适配与身份保持同样关键，而且免训练设计便于直接接入现有 SDXL 生成流程。
article.limitations: 身份掩码依赖交叉注意力图，偶尔会定位到无关区域，作者建议显式引入主体掩码作为附加条件；此外，跨上下文桥接依赖 CLIP 的⟨EOS⟩语义汇总特性，无法直接迁移到 T5 或 LLM 文本编码器的模型。
article.figure_caption_zh: EOS-Story 流程图：跨上下文桥接在文本空间注入外观残差，自适应身份保持负责尺度对齐与特征融合。

page_papers.title: Eat Your Precision: Precision Objective Mitigates Reward Hacking in Rubric-based RL
page_papers.abstract: Rubric-based rewards enable effective reinforcement learning on non-verifiable tasks. However, because these rewards are typically defined as a weighted measure of rubric coverage, models are trained primarily to maximize a recall objective. As a result, RL-trained models produce responses that are more complete but also more verbose and contain more unnecessary or factually incorrect content, leading them to be less preferred than responses from the base model. To address this issue, we present the FORK reward, which jointly optimizes recall and a novel precision objective, which requires each unit of a model response to be both necessary and factually correct, as measured by rubric-driven necessity credits and a factual-correctness grader, respectively. Our experimental results show that FORK outperforms existing rubric-based RL methods and achieves Pareto-optimal performance that balances rubric coverage and overall response quality. Compared to the original recall-based reward, FORK substantially improves precision and reduces response length while achieving similar rubric coverage, which leads to significantly higher win rate compared to the base policy (e.g., from 10.6% to 68.0% on RubricHub-Medical and from 22.1% to 74.1% on HealthBench).
page_papers.content:
Eat Your Precision: Precision Objective
Mitigates Reward Hacking in Rubric-based RL
Hyun Ryu  Jongheon Kim  Yiqing Xie  Seungone Kim  Carolyn Rosé  Eunho Yang
Email:
{ryuhyun1905,jongheon,eunhoy}@kaist.ac.kr
Email:
{hyunr,yiqingxi,seungonk,cprose}@cs.cmu.edu
Affiliation:
KAIST AI   Carnegie Mellon University Language Technologies Institute
Abstract
Rubric-based rewards enable effective reinforcement learning on non-verifiable tasks. However, because these rewards are typically defined as a weighted measure of rubric coverage, models are trained primarily to maximize a
recall
objective. As a result, RL-trained models produce responses that are more complete but also more verbose and contain more unnecessary or factually incorrect content, leading them to be less preferred than responses from the base model.
To address this issue, we present the
Fork
reward, which jointly optimizes recall and a novel precision objective, which requires each unit of a model response to be both necessary and factually correct, as measured by rubric-driven necessity credits and a factual-correctness grader, respectively.
Our experimental results show that
Fork
outperforms existing rubric-based RL methods and achieves Pareto-optimal performance that balances rubric coverage and overall response quality.
Compared to the original recall-based reward,
Fork
substantially improves precision and reduces response length while achieving similar rubric coverage, which leads to significantly higher win rate compared to the base policy (e.g., from 10.6% to 68.0% on RubricHub-Medical and from 22.1% to 74.1% on HealthBench).

1
The source code is available at
https://github.com/JHKim631/FORK
.

Introduction
Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has led to rapid advances in AI for math and coding, where the correctness of the answers can be reliably measured and used as reward signals.
In comparison, for non-verifiable tasks such as open-ended generation, the evaluation criteria for model responses can be diverse and sometimes subjective, which makes it difficult to define rewards in RL.
To resolve this issue,
Gunjal et al. (2026)
and
Viswanathan et al. (2026)
leverage rubric-based RL, which first generates a set of rubrics that model responses should satisfy and then uses the weighted coverage of these pre-defined rubrics as rewards.
However, such rubric-coverage-based reward is easily hacked.
As shown in Figure
1
, when a model is only optimized towards maximizing the coverage of pre-defined rubrics,
we observe that although the model responses become more complete, their factual correctness and necessity decrease, and the responses become more verbose. This makes them less preferred than base policy responses
(
Mahmoud et al., 2026
)
.
This reward hacking behavior is not surprising since rubrics as rewards currently behave like a
recall
objective. The missing part is a
precision
objective: whether the content of a model response is factually correct and necessary.
Figure 1:
Reward hacking in rubric-based RL and our mitigation method.
With the standard coverage reward, recall (i.e., weighted coverage of rubrics) quickly saturates, while precision and win rate against a base model continually decreases and responses become more verbose.
With a precision objective included in the reward (
Fork
), the model reaches similar recall while gradually increasing precision and win rate and generating less verbose responses.
Here, we train Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on RubricHub-Medical and evaluate it on an in-domain test set.
With this motivation,
we propose
Fork
, which converts rubric-based rewards from a recall score into an
F
β
F_{\beta}
score that aggregates recall and precision via their weighted harmonic mean.
Given a set of rubrics,
to measure the precision,
we first divide a model response into a sequence of units and then determine the necessity and factual correctness of each unit by prompting an LLM grader.
To improve the accuracy of necessity judgments, which we observe as a bottleneck
2
2
2
Necessity judgments of all candidate training graders show only moderate correlation with stronger reference graders, whereas factual correctness judgments show stronger correlation (Table
7
).
, we develop a credit-based method in which an LLM grader matches rubrics to units, assigns each unit a necessity credit, and determines unit necessity based on a dynamic threshold value.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of
Fork
on both in-domain datasets (the test splits of RubricHub-Medical and RubricHub-Science,
Li et al. (2026)
) and external benchmarks (HealthBench,
Arora et al. (2025)
and ResearchQA,
Yifei et al. (2026)
).
Compared to the standard coverage reward,
Fork
significantly improves the factual correctness
and necessity of responses (e.g., reducing the response length by a factor of 2.6) while maintaining similar rubric coverage.
These improvements also make responses from rubric-based RL-trained models more preferred than base policy responses.
Further analysis supports the effectiveness of
Fork
.
While rubric-coverage rewards
(
Gunjal et al., 2026
;
Rezaei et al., 2025
;
Viswanathan et al., 2026
)
have a negative effect on satisfaction of absence-based rubrics, our method improves satisfaction of both presence-based and absence-based rubrics, enabling models to add necessary content and suppress irrelevant content at the same time.
We also verify that a model trained with our method remains preferred to the base model under different judge prompts and remains more effective than other rubric-based RL methods when evaluated with different LLM graders.
Our key contributions are:
1.
We propose
Fork
, which mitigates reward hacking in rubric-based RL training by incorporating a precision objective into a standard coverage objective.
2.
We develop a reliable method for using an LLM grader to measure the precision of free-form responses given a set of rubrics to be satisfied.
3.
Experiments show that on multiple public benchmarks, compared to the standard coverage reward,
Fork
significantly improves precision while maintaining similar rubric coverage,
which leads to substantial improvements in the preference score (i.e., win rate compared to the base policy).
Fork
also outperforms other rubric-based RL methods, achieving Pareto-optimal performance that balances rubric coverage and overall response quality.
2
Related Works
Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning.
Rubric-based methods decompose response quality into explicit, prompt-specific criteria, providing structured supervision for tasks without readily verifiable outcomes
(
Gunjal et al., 2026
;
Viswanathan et al., 2026
)
.
Rubrics as Rewards uses expert-guided, instance-specific rubrics as on-policy RL rewards, exploring both explicit aggregation of criterion scores and implicit aggregation by an LLM grader
(
Gunjal et al., 2026
)
.
Reinforcement Learning from Checklist Feedback (RLCF) evaluates instruction-specific requirements using LLM graders and specialized verification programs, and converts aggregated checklist scores into preference pairs for direct preference optimization
(
Viswanathan et al., 2026
)
.
RubricHub scales rubric supervision through coarse-to-fine generation that combines principle-guided synthesis, multi-model aggregation, and difficulty evolution, supporting rubric-based RL
(
Li et al., 2026
)
.
These methods establish rubrics as a practical interface for specifying training objectives.
We build on this paradigm while distinguishing coverage of specified requirements from the quality of all generated content.
Rubric Specification and Reward Hacking.
Rubric-based optimization remains vulnerable to incomplete reward specifications.
Mahmoud et al. (2026)
distinguish verifier failure from rubric-design limitations: even with strong verification, rubric-based judges can prefer RL-trained responses that rubric-free judges rate worse overall, with improved completeness but degraded factual correctness and necessity.
Several approaches address insufficiently specified requirements.
RLCF adds universal criteria against excessive or off-topic content after observing verbose preambles under checklist optimization
(
Viswanathan et al., 2026
)
.
Zhang et al. (2026)
refine rubrics by contrasting high-quality, diverse responses, improving discrimination in the high-reward region and delaying over-optimization.
OnlineRubrics augments existing criteria through comparisons between current-policy and control-policy responses
(
Rezaei et al., 2025
)
.
DR Tulu maintains search-grounded, evolving rubrics that capture both newly discovered useful content and undesirable behaviors observed in rollouts
(
Shao et al., 2025
)
.
AMARIS further uses persistent training diagnostics to revise criteria and weights in response to recurring failures
(
Wu et al., 2026
)
.
These specification-refinement strategies motivate a complementary question: how should generated content be evaluated when coverage requirements remain incomplete?
Our method supplements rubric coverage with unit-level assessments of necessity and factual correctness, rather than relying on criterion expansion alone, and does not require online rubric updates.
Fine-Grained Evaluation and Precision–Recall Rewards.
Content-level evaluation provides a complementary perspective on response quality.
Min et al. (2023)
measure factual precision as the proportion of generated atomic facts supported by a reliable knowledge source.
Song et al. (2024)
combine sentence-level faithfulness assessment with keyfact–sentence alignment to measure completeness and conciseness, distinguishing coverage of target information from the fraction of generated sentences contributing that information.
Related work directly incorporates precision–recall signals into policy optimization.
Jhaveri et al. (2025)
train clinical note generators with a claim-level
F
1
F_{1}
reward combining entailment-based precision against the source dialogue and recall over dialogue-derived claims.
For video captioning,
Gao et al. (2026)
verify atomic claims against video evidence and balance factual precision with reference-claim coverage, assigning attenuated credit to supported but unmatched details and bounding their contribution to recall.
Our work adapts this content-level perspective to rubric-based RL: necessity is derived from a unit’s contribution to prompt-specific coverage requirements, and precision counts units that satisfy both necessity and factual correctness.
Combining this precision with rubric-coverage recall through an
F
β
F_{\beta}
reward couples what a response should cover with whether its generated content is warranted and correct.

Experiments
Our experiments address four research questions:
(RQ1)
Can
Fork
improve response precision and overall quality while maintaining comparable rubric coverage?
(RQ2)
Do these improvements generalize to external benchmarks?
(RQ3)
How do precision estimation and precision–recall aggregation affect performance?
(RQ4)
Are the observed improvements robust to changes in evaluation graders and judge prompts?

Evaluation.
We evaluate in-domain performance on RubricHub test sets and cross-dataset generalization on external benchmarks (i.e., HealthBench

We conduct two types of evaluations:
(1) rubric-based evaluations measuring macro rubric recall, macro precision, and macro F1, and
(2) rubric-free evaluations reporting the overall win rate against the base policy model and average response length (i.e., verbosity).
We use GPT-5.4

To measure precision, a reference grader directly determines unit necessity and factual correctness given a set of coverage rubrics. We compute the F1 score as the harmonic mean of rubric recall and precision.

Conclusion
In this work, we introduce
Fork
, a simple method that mitigates reward hacking in rubric-based RL, by adding a complementary precision objective to the original recall-based reward.
To address the observed reward hacking behavior, we define a precision objective to require each unit of a model response to be necessary and factually correct. We propose rubric-driven necessity credits to faithfully measure necessity and use an LLM grader to measure factual correctness.
Our experimental results show that
Fork
outperforms other rubric-based RL methods and achieves Pareto-optimal performance that balances recall and overall response quality.
AI use statement
In this work, we used generative AI tools for searching related previous works and checking grammar.
We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. Specifically, we manually looked at the previous works that the AI tool suggests and verified their relevance. Also, we reviewed grammar-corrected contents so that there is no distortion in the original semantic meaning.

Prompt
Do allergies cause coughing? I had a bad cough all winter, and it went away for a couple months when the weather got warmer. It just started again since the weather has gotten very hot (90 degrees) and rainy. Is there a cough medicine for coughs due to allergies?

Yes, allergies can indeed cause coughing, and your symptoms align with this possibility.
Allergies can trigger a cough through several mechanisms, including:
1.
Postnasal Drip
: When allergens like pollen, dust mites, or mold irritate the nasal passages, they can cause increased mucus production.
This excess mucus can drip down the back of the throat (postnasal drip), stimulating the cough reflex, especially at night or when lying down.
2.
Inflammation and Irritation
: Allergic reactions can cause inflammation in the airways, which can lead to a dry, hacking cough, especially if the airways are sensitive to the allergens.
3.
Bronchospasm
: In some cases, allergies can cause the airways to narrow, leading to wheezing and coughing, which is more common in individuals with asthma that is triggered by allergies.
The pattern you described—coughing worsening in the winter and returning with hot, rainy weather—suggests that your cough may be related to seasonal allergies, possibly to mold, pollen, or other outdoor allergens that are more prevalent in these conditions, or to indoor allergens that may be more active in warmer, humid weather (like dust mites, mold, or pet dander).
Cough Medicines for Allergy-Induced Cough
There are several types of cough medicines that can help manage allergy-induced cough, but it’s important to note that they should be used under the guidance of a healthcare provider, especially if you have underlying health conditions or are taking other medications.
Here are some options:
1.
Antihistamines
: These can help reduce the symptoms of allergies, including sneezing, itching, and runny nose, which can contribute to coughing.
Common over-the-counter antihistamines include diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and cetirizine (Zyrtec).
However, they can cause drowsiness, so it’s best to use them before bedtime or to avoid activities that require alertness, like driving.
2.
Decongestants
: These can help relieve nasal congestion, which can contribute to postnasal drip and cough, but they do not directly treat the cough itself.
Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is a common decongestant, but it can have side effects like increased heart rate and blood pressure, so it’s not recommended for people with high blood pressure, heart disease, or prostate issues.
3.
Cough Suppressants
: These are used to suppress a cough that is dry and unproductive, and they include dextromethorphan (found in many cough syrups and cold medicines).
However, if your cough is productive (producing phlegm), a cough suppressant may not be the best choice, as it can prevent you from clearing the mucus that your body is trying to expel.
4.
Expectorants
: These help loosen mucus and make it easier to cough up, and they include guaifenesin (found in Mucinex). They can be helpful if your cough is productive, but they do not address the underlying allergy.
5.
Nasal Corticosteroids
: These are often more effective for long-term allergy management and can help reduce inflammation in the nasal passages, which can contribute to coughing.
Examples include fluticasone (Flonase) and mometasone (Nasonex), which are available by prescription.
Recommendations
Given the pattern of your cough, it might be beneficial to use a combination of an antihistamine and a decongestant, or an antihistamine and an expectorant, to manage your symptoms.
However, since you’ve had a persistent cough for an extended period, it’s important to consult a healthcare provider to rule out other potential causes, such as a respiratory infection, asthma, or acid reflux, which can also cause chronic cough.

Identify Triggers
: Keep track of when your cough occurs (e.g., during certain times of the day, after being outside, or when the weather changes) to help identify potential allergens.
2.
Environmental Control
: Use air conditioning to keep indoor humidity low (below 50%), use dehumidifiers, and regularly clean or replace air filters to reduce mold and dust mites.
3.
Allergy Testing
: Consider getting allergy testing to identify specific triggers, which can help in tailoring your treatment plan, whether it’s through environmental control, allergy shots, or targeted medications.
4.
Consult a Healthcare Provider
: Speak with a healthcare provider, such as an allergist or primary care physician, to discuss your symptoms, undergo a physical examination, and possibly undergo allergy testing, and to get a prescription for appropriate medications, which might include a combination of antihistamines, decongestants, and/or nasal corticosteroids, as well as advice on managing your cough, such as using a humidifier, staying hydrated, and avoiding irritants like cigarette smoke and air pollution.

article.headline: 评卷式强化学习：补上精确率即可抑制刷分
article.lede: rubric 覆盖率奖励只相当于召回目标，模型学会堆砌冗长内容；Fork 把精确率并入奖励，RubricHub-Medi
article.problem: 基于评分细则（rubric）的奖励让强化学习可以用于开放式生成这类无法直接验证的任务，但奖励通常定义为加权覆盖率，本质是一个召回目标。模型因此学会把响应写得更全，同时也更啰嗦，混入更多不必要或事实错误的内容，最终反而不如基座模型受偏好。论文把这一现象归因于奖励缺少精确率约束：没有任何项惩罚冗余、无关或错误的句子。
article.method: Fork 先把响应切成句子级单元，再由 LLM 评分器把每条 rubric 匹配到相关单元，并按「每条 rubric 的信用均分给命中单元」的方式累积必要性信用，用动态阈值判定单元是否必要；同时独立判定每个单元的事实正确性。精确率定义为「既必要又事实正确」的单元占全部单元的比例，召回率仍用标准加权覆盖率，两者以加权调和平均（Fβ）合成奖励，用 GRPO 更新策略。
article.results: 在 Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 上训练后，RubricHub-Medical 的 rubric 精确率从标准覆盖率奖励的 25.5 升到 53.2，平均响应长度从 9,195 降到 3,533，召回率基本持平（32.5 对 35.7）。相对基座模型的胜率从 10.6% 升到 68.0%，HealthBench 上从 22.1% 升到 74.1%，ResearchQA 上从 26.6% 升到 67.1%，RubricHub-Science 上从 42.5% 升到 61.5%。消融显示，把调和平均换成简单平均会得到更高精确率（+2.1 个百分点）但更低召回率（-6.3 个百分点）；作者还用 40 条响应、723 个单元验证必要性预测，删掉 40% 的单元之前召回率几乎不下降（其中 51% 的单元被判为不必要）。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「该说什么」和「说的每句是否站得住」拆成两个可分别度量的目标，且不需要在线更新 rubric，为开放式任务的 RL 奖励设计提供了一个可直接套用的修正项。
article.limitations: β 的取值仍未系统搜索，医学域用 β=1、科学域用 β=1.25，作者明确把最优 β 留作未来工作；必要性判断被作者称为瓶颈，候选训练评分器与前沿模型的相关性只有中等（选用的 Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 平均 r=0.714），且实验只覆盖单一基座模型、评测本身依赖 GPT-5.4 作为参考评分器。此外，响应长度压缩倍数在摘要写作 2.6 倍、正文 4.2 节写作 2.1 倍，两处数字不一致，需要读者留意。
article.figure_caption_zh: Fork 的训练流程：策略模型采样响应并切成单元，LLM 评分器把 rubric 匹配到单元并分配必要性信用、确定信用阈值，同时判定各单元事实正确性，精确率（必要且正确的单元占比）与召回率（加权 rubric 覆盖率）的调和平均即为奖励。

figure.caption: {Training with {Fork}.} Given a prompt, a policy model samples a response, which is then divided into units. An LLM grader matches rubrics to units to assign each unit a necessity credit and determines a credit threshold for unit necessity. In parallel, the grader assesses the factual correctness of all units. Precision is defined as the fraction of necessary and factually correct units, and recall follows the standard definition of weighted rubric coverage. We update the policy model using their weighted harmonic mean as a reward.

page_papers.title: World-in-Context: Interactive Video World Modeling with In-Context Conditioning
page_papers.abstract: Interactive video world models require coordinated control over viewing perspectives, character actions, and camera motion. Existing methods typically leave view modes implicit in text captions, conflate action with camera motion, and inject controls through fragmented architectural pathways that capture interdependencies only indirectly. In this work, we present World-in-Context, an interactive world modeling framework powered by In-Context Conditioning (ICC). Rather than relying on specialized conditioning pathways, World-in-Context unifies view, action, and camera controls into explicit tokens contextualized directly within a shared self-attention space. Our formulation reveals that (i) explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting dynamics and unlock emergent view switching from single-view data, while (ii) action and camera inputs play complementary roles in governing local responsiveness and global stability. To preserve temporal continuity across execution intervals, we further introduce Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), parameterizing temporal attention with accumulated control transitions. On WBench, World-in-Context-5B achieves navigation performance on par with 22B EchoWM (81.5 vs. 81.6) and attains a 93.8% perspective-switching success rate, substantially outperforming existing 5B baselines (18.8%). Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages of World-in-Context under richer conditioning mixtures, favorable data efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts.

Interactive video world models require coordinated control over viewing perspectives, character actions, and camera motion.
Existing methods typically leave view modes implicit in text captions, conflate action with camera motion, and inject controls through fragmented architectural pathways that capture interdependencies only indirectly.
In this work, we present
World-in-Context
, an interactive world modeling framework powered by In-Context Conditioning (ICC).
Rather than relying on specialized conditioning pathways,
World-in-Context

To preserve temporal continuity across execution intervals, we further introduce Interaction-Transport RoPE (IT-RoPE), parameterizing temporal attention with accumulated control transitions.

At its core, effectively simulating such an interactive world hinges on two fundamental dimensions

7
Conclusion and Positioning
Conclusion.
In this work, we present
World-in-Context
, a video world modeling framework based on In-Context Conditioning (ICC) that unifies view mode, character action, and camera trajectory as tokens within a shared attention space.
We systematically investigate core interactive dimensions, revealing that explicit view tokens disentangle conflicting motion dynamics while enabling emergent in-video switching, and that action and camera signals complement each other in local responsiveness and global stability.
Augmented with IT-RoPE to encode accumulated control progression in temporal attention,
World-in-Context
achieves competitive navigation on WBench (
81.5
81.5
) matching the 22B EchoWM, while establishing strong perspective-switching capability (
93.8
%
93.8\%
).
Controlled analyses further demonstrate compounding advantages under richer conditioning, favorable sample efficiency, and natural applicability to causal rollouts, highlighting shared context modeling as a scalable interface for interactive world simulation.
Positioning of This Report.
This work focuses primarily on the algorithmic formulation of interactive conditioning, rather than training an all-encompassing system artifact, with
World-in-Context
serving as a concrete instantiation of this design. The overall capacity of an interactive world model naturally depends on data quality, model size, and training scale. We use a modest interaction-training set of
100
100
K navigation clips and
500
500
switching sequences. Since comparable training-data statistics are not consistently disclosed by existing methods, we omit cross-method data-scale comparisons from the main table. Instead, we prioritize controlled comparisons that isolate the architectural advantages of shared context modeling and control-aware temporal attention, including their effectiveness across training-data budgets.
Specifically, this work centers around three foundational control modalities,
i.e.
, view mode, character action, and camera motion, as they directly address the core dimensions governing interactive navigation: how the environment is viewed across perspectives and how user inputs steer character actuation alongside viewport evolution. These algorithmic findings complement concurrent advances in scaling, presenting an extensible interface for coordinating diverse interactive controls.

Navigation Suite.
WBench benchmarks trajectory-following navigation across five core dimensions:
•
Quality

•
Physical

article.headline: 统一 token 条件，5B 世界模型视角切换达
article.lede: 把视角、动作、相机统一编码成 token 送入共享注意力空间，5B 模型在 WBench 导航上追平 22B 基线。
article.problem: 现有交互式视频世界模型通常把视角模式隐含在文本描述里，自由相机漫游与第一人称运动语义常被混同，同一几何轨迹在不同视角下的物理含义因而无法区分。同时，角色动作与相机运动多被合并成单一相机轨迹控制，或送进彼此分离的架构分支（如 AdaLN 调制、加性注入），跨条件依赖只能被间接捕捉。
article.method: 作者提出 In-Context Conditioning（ICC），把视角模式（Free/Fpp/Tpp）、离散角色动作和连续相机位姿分别编码为时间对齐的 token 序列，直接拼接在视觉 latent 之前，进入同一自注意力空间，不再设专用条件分支。在此基础上引入 Interaction-Transport RoPE（IT-RoPE），将动作与相机控制诱导的变换沿执行序列累积，以中心化修正项注入时间注意力分数，使模型能区分端点相同但执行顺序不同的轨迹。模型基于 Wan2.2-TI2V-5B，使用 10 万条导航片段与 500 条视角切换序列训练。
article.results: World-in-Context-5B 在 WBench 导航平均分 81.5，与 22B EchoWM 的 81.6 基本持平，交互分由基线 Zing-0.5 的 84.2 升至 86.0；Fpp↔Tpp 视角切换成功率达 93.8%，而现有 5B 基线最高仅 18.8%。无切换监督时成功率已达 37.5%（纯文本条件基线为 6.25%），加入 500 条切换片段后升至 93.8%。动作与相机的对照实验中，仅动作训练在平移与旋转精度上分别高出仅相机训练 6.5 和 3.9 分，仅相机训练在几何与光度一致性上分别高出 2.1 和 1.9 分，联合训练取得旋转精度 90.6、几何一致性 90.8、平移精度 89.3。IT-RoPE 相比 3D-RoPE 将导航从 80.5 提升至 81.2、交互从 86.2 提升至 86.8。数据效率上，5 万加 250 条片段的 ICC 切换率 75.0%，已超过加性注入用两倍数据（10 万加 500）的 71.9%。因果流式版本 WiC-Causal 导航 81.2、切换 90.6%。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作把多维交互控制重构成上下文建模问题，为交互式世界模型提供了一个随控制信号增多而扩展的统一接口，而不必每增加一种模态就新开一条架构分支。
article.limitations: 作者自述这是算法表述报告而非完整系统，训练集仅 10 万导航片段加 500 条切换序列，且离散动作主要由估计出的相机轨迹反推（action inversion）而非引擎遥测，标注噪声与解耦质量存疑。各方法训练数据规模披露不一致，主表因此未做跨方法数据量对比；导航上也只是与 22B 模型持平而非超越，评测仅限 WBench。

page_papers.title: StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent
page_papers.abstract: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while miss the implicit user intent (e.g., "where should I click next?" while a user navigate a website), meanwhile fail to update the state simultaneously as user requests might update continuously. These limitations make them less suited to intent-aware interaction in practical. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark serving as testbed for user intent interaction, with 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically tailors its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with a fleixble lifecycles via a hierarchical memory to track the latest user intent and environmental state. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over other baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intent and deciding when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation over sustained interaction, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction.

Abstract
Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while miss the implicit user intent (
e.g.,
“where should I click next?” while a user navigate a website), meanwhile fail to update the state simultaneously as user requests might update continuously.
These limitations make them less suited to intent-aware interaction in practical.
To address these challenges, we introduce
StreamVibe-Bench
, a new benchmark serving as testbed for user intent interaction, with 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop
StreamVibe-VL
, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically tailors its interactions as these intents evolve.
We further introduce
StreamVibe-Harness
, which maintains user intents as persistent states with a fleixble lifecycles via a hierarchical memory to track the latest user intent and environmental state.
Our experiments reveal three key findings:
(i)
StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over other baselines;
(ii)
existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intent and deciding when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and
(iii)
StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation over sustained interaction, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction.

Figure 1:
Overview of StreamVibe.
(a) StreamVibe studies sustained proactive interaction under explicit, implicit, and dynamically evolving user intents, where the agent continuously observes the environment and decides when and how to assist. (b) Existing paradigms rely on explicit intents, with limited tracking of interaction state and evolving intents. StreamVibe addresses these limitations through proactive streaming policy learning and persistent interaction state modeling that tracks task progress and updates active intents.
1
Introduction
“Mind is activity, a range of dynamic processes of interaction between organism and world.”
— Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, John Dewey
Vision-language models
(
Lu et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
are advancing from offline content understanding
(
Wang et al., 2025c
;
Zhu et al., 2025
)
toward continuous proactive assistance in real-world streaming scenarios
(
Cui et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2025d
;
Orantqing et al., 2026
;
Ding et al., 2025
)
. However, existing proactive interaction approaches are largely designed for explicit queries (e.g. “Notify me when a goal is scored.”), and isolated, single-turn requests
(
Li et al., 2026a
;
Kundu et al., 2026
)
, as illustrated in Figure
1
(i).
However, these paradigm is less suited to real-world open-ended settings across three challenges, where
(
i
) implicit user intents
(e.g. “Help me finish this task whenever I get stuck.”) must be inferred from ongoing observations and interactions.
Beyond identifying user intent, effective assistance requires
(
ii
) task-relevant state tracking
.
As shown in Figure
1
(ii), prior interactions can change the environment and task progress, making a response that was appropriate earlier unnecessary or incorrect later. Although existing streaming models can retain long interaction histories
(
Yao et al., 2026a
;
Wang et al., 2025a
)
, they still struggle to maintain an up-to-date state, resulting in repeated, outdated, or missed responses.
Lastly, as shown in Figure
1
(iii),
(
iii
) user intents is evolving
as the interaction unfolds
(
Tack et al., 2026
;
Tao et al., 2026
;
Yang et al., 2026d
)
. Later feedback may introduce new goals, revise existing constraints, or shift the current focus, while existing methods often fail to update which intents remain relevant and instead continue to rely on earlier requests. These challenges make proactive interaction more than a problem of real-time long-context modeling: it requires the agent to continuously infer and update user intent while tracking the evolving interaction state. This motivates three key research questions forward “
Intent-aware interaction
”:
How can we construct a testbed for proactive interaction with implicit user intent?
How can such intent-aware interaction be internalized as a native model capability?
How to flexible manage context to track environmental and user intent changes?
In this work, we address these three questions through benchmarking, modeling, and agentic design.
Firstly, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a unified intent-aware benchmark for sustained proactive interaction with 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic user intents.
Building on this benchmark, we further develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents and adapts its interactions as these intents evolve. Streaming supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jointly learns when and how to assist, while localized trajectory reinforcement learning (RL) focuses optimization on interaction-critical moments to improve response timing and quality. Lastly, we further develop StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent, updatable states with flexible lifecycles, while hierarchical memory retrieves relevant history to keep subsequent decisions aligned with the current interaction context and user intent. Our main contributions are as follows:
•
To the best of our knowledge, we are the first work to study user intents in proactive streaming interaction. To this end, we construct StreamVibe-Bench, a unified benchmark with 4.1K evaluation and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents.
•
We introduce StreamVibe-VL, a proactive streaming video model that jointly learns when and how to assist under implicit and evolving user intents.
•
We develop the StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains updatable intent states with flexible lifecycles and hierarchical memory for consistent behavior over sustained interaction.
2
Related Work
Streaming Video Benchmark.
Early video benchmarks focus on offline understanding
(
Fu et al., 2025a
;
Zhao et al., 2025
)
, while online benchmarks evaluate sequential perception and response before video completion
(
Li et al., 2025b
;
Huang et al., 2025
)
. Recent proactive benchmarks further require models to decide when to respond, often using annotated trigger points and extending to egocentric or task-guidance settings
(
Wang et al., 2025e
;
Kundu et al., 2026
;
Ran et al., 2026
)
. However, most focus on a single intent type or environment and evaluate responses independently. StreamVibe-Bench instead unifies explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents across physical and digital tasks, with both pointwise and trajectory evaluation.
Proactive Interaction Models.
Online video-language models support continuous perception and low-latency responses
(
Zeng et al., 2025
;
Cui et al., 2026
)
, while real-time and task-guidance systems further learn when to speak or provide assistance during ongoing interaction
(
Sitong et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
)
. However, most existing approaches center on explicitly specified requests or task objectives, with limited support for tracking interaction state and adapting to evolving user intent over time
(
Tack et al., 2026
;
Tao et al., 2026
)
. StreamVibe-VL targets open-ended proactive interaction, where intents must be inferred from user goals, environment changes, and task progress, and updated throughout the interaction.
Memory and Agent Harness.
Agentic systems increasingly incorporate persistent memory
(
Xu et al., 2025
)
, planning
(
Xiong et al., 2025
)
, reflection
(
Yuan et al., 2025
)
, and reusable skills
(
Zheng et al., 2025
)
to preserve and reuse historical context over long-horizon tasks. Recent memory systems further study how to retrieve, integrate, and abstract historical information into reusable experience for long-term interaction
(
Yu et al., 2026
;
Chhikara et al., 2025
)
. However, these methods mainly organize and access past information without explicitly tracking evolving user intents and task progress, which can cause proactive responses to drift from the current interaction state. StreamVibe-Harness addresses this gap by maintaining user intents and task progress as persistent, updatable interaction states and retrieving relevant history before each decision.

3.2
Hierarchical Difficulty
StreamVibe-Bench characterizes proactive interaction along two dimensions:
intent explicitness
and
intent dynamics
.
Existing benchmarks primarily focus on
(i) Level 1: Explicit Intents
, where the user specifies a condition, event, or state to monitor, and the agent responds when it occurs, e.g. Let me know when the water starts boiling.
We further introduce
(ii) Level 2: Implicit Intents
,
where the user provides only a high-level goal, requiring the agent to infer when and how to assist from ongoing observations and task progress,
e.g. Help me keep an eye on this dish.
Finally,
(iii) Level 3: Dynamic Intents
considers intents that evolve throughout the interaction.
As the task unfolds, the user may provide multiple new inputs, requiring the agent to continually update the currently valid task state.
We consider three common forms:
Revision (RV)
, which modifies an existing intent;
Composition (CP)
, which adds a new intent or constraint while preserving existing ones; and
Interruption (IT)
, which introduces an immediate request while the ongoing task remains active.
These changes may occur repeatedly and in combination within a single interaction.
3.3
Benchmark Construction
Task Collection.
We collect task videos from both physical and digital environments to cover two complementary forms of proactive interaction. In (i)
physical
environments, assistance mainly relies on understanding continuous visual processes, including user activities, task progress, and emerging intents. In contrast, user intent in (ii)
digital
environments is often implicit in interaction trajectories such as navigation, content editing, and tool use, requiring the agent to infer user goals, constraints, and task state from the current interface and interaction history. The two settings thus capture user intent through physical behavior and digital interaction, respectively, covering proactive assistance across different interaction environments. Specifically, physical tasks mainly include egocentric daily activities and task execution, while digital tasks focus on GUI and computer-use scenarios.
Annotation and Verification.
For each video-request pair, we use Gemini-3.8-Flash
(
Google DeepMind, 2026
)
to clean the data and identify candidate help points with response windows, preferred times, and reference answers. For dynamic intents, we further construct timestamped multi-turn interactions in which intents may be revised, extended, or interrupted as the task unfolds. Four reviewers then independently verify the user requests and response timing, correcting or removing samples without sufficient evidence and retaining only those approved by all reviewers. The validated annotations are aligned to 1 FPS streams and converted into causal interaction sequences for training and evaluation. Details are provided in Appendix
B.3
.
3.4
Data Statistics
Categories and Scale.
Building on the three proactive interaction settings in Section
3.2
, we organize StreamVibe-Bench into finer-grained task subtypes, as illustrated in Figure
2
(b). The 600
Explicit Intents
samples span Single Event (I), Transition (P), and Recurring Event (R). For
Implicit Intents
, 2,000 samples cover Guidance (G), Learning (L), Monitoring (M), and Tool (T). The remaining 1,500
Dynamic Intents
samples consist of Revision (RV), Composition (CP), and Interruption (IT). Subtypes are evenly distributed within each category. In total, StreamVibe-Bench contains 4,100 evaluation samples, 20,546 help points, and 183.4 hours of video. Additional statistics and detailed explanations are provided in the Appendix
B
.
Training Data Curations.
We construct the StreamVibe-85K training set, consisting of 70K samples for supervised fine-tuning and 15K tasks for reinforcement learning. During supervised fine-tuning, we further incorporate 768K general streaming-video samples from sources including TimeChat-Online
(
Yao et al., 2025
)
and VideoChat-Flash
(
Li et al., 2025a
)
to improve general streaming-video modeling. Detailed components are provided in Appendix
B.4
.
3.5
Evaluation Protocol
Settings.
As illustrated in Figure
2
(c), two complementary evaluation settings are adopted to distinguish local proactive decision-making from sustained interaction behavior.
(i) Pointwise Evaluation
samples positive and negative timestamps around annotated help points and independently predicts whether the model should respond. Both
Gold History
and
Self History
are considered, where the former isolates local decision ability and the latter measures the effect of model-generated history. Independent evaluation avoids error accumulation across time.
(ii) Trajectory Evaluation
runs the model continuously over the full video stream, with each decision conditioned on prior observations and self-generated interaction history. This setting captures error propagation, requirement tracking, and repeated or missed responses. Together, the two settings evaluate local decisions under a given history and sustained interaction under self-generated history.
Metrics.
We evaluate models along two dimensions: response timing and response quality. Timing is measured by Precision, Recall, F1, and False Positive Rate (FPR), capturing response accuracy, coverage, and false activations. Quality is evaluated using Answer Score for overall correctness and relevance, and Content F1 for key-content alignment with reference answers.

RQ1:
StreamVibe-VL achieves stronger proactive interaction while preserving general video understanding.
Table

Under Pointwise Evaluation, it achieves the highest Content F1 while remaining competitive with proprietary models in response quality. RL further improves over SFT, with larger gains on dynamic intents. This trend persists under Trajectory Evaluation, where RL yields higher Content F1 and response quality, indicating stronger sustained interaction when decisions depend on prior history. The gains also transfer to external benchmarks. Figure

♠
\spadesuit
RQ2:
Current proactive agents struggle to sustain reliable behavior over continuous interaction.
Figure
5
and Figure
6
reveal three main findings.
(i) Intent understanding remains difficult.
Implicit and Dynamic Intents are markedly harder than Explicit Intents, indicating that agents struggle to determine what help is needed when intents are unstated or keep changing.
(ii) Response selectivity is insufficient.
Higher Recall often comes with more false triggers, suggesting that current methods cannot yet balance coverage against unnecessary responses.
(iii) Sustained interaction amplifies these problems.
Timing F1 declines steadily with interaction length; Revision shows a sharper late-stage Recall drop, and Composition exhibits weaker content quality, indicating difficulty in continuously updating intents while maintaining multiple constraints. Correct individual judgments are thus insufficient for stable proactive behavior throughout interaction.
♠
\spadesuit
RQ3:
Policy learning improves proactive decision-making, while state tracking enhances sustained interaction stability.
As shown in Figure
6
(2), SFT makes the model more sensitive to potential assistance opportunities, leading to higher Recall but also more unnecessary triggers. RL further improves decision selectivity, substantially reducing FPR while also improving answer quality. Figure
6
(3) further shows that, with the policy fixed, adding the Harness continues to suppress unnecessary responses and improves content quality in most settings, with the clearest gains on Dynamic Intents. These results suggest that policy learning mainly improves local proactive decisions, whereas state tracking helps preserve valid intents and task progress over long-horizon interactions, thereby reducing outdated, redundant, or state-inconsistent outputs.

Across multiple assistance points within the same task, it grounds responses in the current visual evidence and task state, providing assistance at appropriate moments. 6
Conclusion
We study proactive interaction over streaming video, where user intents may be implicit, evolve over time, and must be tracked alongside a changing environment. We introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a unified benchmark spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents with pointwise and trajectory evaluation; StreamVibe-VL, a proactive streaming policy trained with adaptive streaming SFT and localized trajectory RL; and StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents and task progress as persistent interaction states. Experiments show that our model improves response timing and quality while preserving general video understanding, while explicit state tracking further reduces outdated and redundant responses. More broadly, real-world proactive interaction may involve richer intent evolution and tighter coupling between user needs and environmental changes than captured in our current setting. New observations, task outcomes, and prior assistance may jointly reshape both user needs and the environment, leading to new goals and constraints. Future work could further study such co-evolving interactions, particularly the complex feedback between intents and environmental states over longer horizons.

Dataset Construction and Evaluation Details
This section consolidates the taxonomy, source provenance, training mixture,
evaluation cohorts, and metrics summarized in the main paper.
B.1
Overview of Evaluation Datasets
Our evaluation covers proactive interaction and general video understanding.
The former tests when to intervene and whether the response supports the
ongoing task; the latter checks whether proactive policy learning preserves
video perception and temporal reasoning. We describe the datasets below;
protocols and metrics are detailed in Appendix
B.5
.
StreamVibe-Bench.
Our primary benchmark evaluates sustained proactive interaction under
Explicit, Implicit, and Dynamic Intents. Its 4,100 evaluation samples cover
ten subtypes, ranging from responding to specified events to inferring useful
assistance and tracking revised or interleaved requests. Pointwise evaluation
isolates response decisions at individual timestamps, while Trajectory
evaluation tests continuous interaction with model-generated history.
The following subsections describe its taxonomy, sources, and construction.
General-Timing.
We construct General-Timing as a separate evaluation subset drawn from the
publicly released training data of JoyAI-VL-Interaction
(
Yao et al., 2026b
)
.
The selected samples are held out from our training: they are used for
neither supervised fine-tuning nor reinforcement learning, and are reserved
exclusively for evaluation. This subset tests response timing and
content quality on additional streaming-video interactions beyond
StreamVibe-Bench. We apply our Pointwise and Trajectory protocols and report results in Tables
11
and
11
.
EgoProactive.
EgoProactive
(
Kundu et al., 2026
)
evaluates proactive procedural
assistance from wearable, egocentric videos. Its annotations include
out-of-plan deviations and recovery guidance, requiring an assistant to
recognize task progress, decide when an interruption is useful, and provide
appropriate corrective assistance. We use its official evaluation protocol
to assess proactive assistance in physical task execution.
IPIBench.
IPIBench
(
Li et al., 2026b
)
evaluates interactive proactive intelligence
under continuous video streams. It covers proactive monitoring, proactive
task management, and interleaved reactive–proactive requests, including
multi-turn interactions in which users add, modify, or cancel requests.
It complements StreamVibe-Bench by testing the coordination of response
timing and evolving interaction requirements under an external protocol.
We follow its official evaluation setup; results for IPIBench and
EgoProactive are reported in Table
11
.
MVBench.
MVBench
(
Li et al., 2024
)
evaluates video understanding across diverse
temporal tasks that require reasoning beyond a single frame. We use it to
assess whether proactive policy learning preserves general temporal
perception and reasoning, following its official evaluation protocol.
Video-MME.
Video-MME
(
Fu et al., 2025a
)
assesses video understanding across varied
content domains and video durations. It complements MVBench by testing
broader video comprehension over different temporal scales. We follow its
official evaluation protocol and report the corresponding benchmark score.
OVO-Bench.
OVO-Bench
(
Li et al., 2025b
)
evaluates timestamp-aware online video
understanding through backward tracing, real-time perception, and forward
active responding. These settings test whether a model can recall relevant
past events, interpret the current observation, and respond as a stream
unfolds. We retain its official task definitions and evaluation metrics.
OVBench.
OVBench
(
Huang et al., 2025
)
evaluates online video understanding as
visual observations arrive over time. We use it to assess comprehension of
ongoing video streams alongside the proactive interaction benchmarks,
following its official evaluation protocol and reported metrics.

B.3
Human Review Criteria and Inter-Annotator Agreement
Review unit and acceptance rule.
The review unit is a complete candidate sample: the source video, initial
instruction, timestamped user turns, evidence windows, preferred response
times, and reference answers. Four human reviewers independently assess
the same sample against Table
16
. A reviewer
approves a sample only when all applicable criteria are satisfied; a
required correction counts as non-approval of the current version.
A sample is retained only if all four reviewers approve the same
final version. Thus, three approvals are insufficient. Samples with any
objection must be corrected and reviewed again by all four reviewers, or
discarded; changing an annotation invalidates approval of its earlier
version. Unresolvable ambiguity or insufficient visual evidence requires
exclusion rather than a guessed reference answer.
Table 16:
Human review rubric.
Each reviewer checks every applicable
criterion. Acceptance requires four independent approvals of the same
sample version, with no unresolved issue.
Criterion
Standard for approval
Intent fidelity
The instruction is coherent and compatible with the task.
The assigned Explicit, Implicit, or Dynamic category matches the interaction;
inferred intents are supported by the user’s context, not invented.
Evidence and causality
Every annotated intervention has identifiable visual
or interaction evidence available by its response time. Future frames and
later user turns are not needed to justify the response.
Coverage and non-redundancy
Distinct, necessary intervention opportunities
are covered, without duplicate evidence points or repeated assistance after
the relevant intent has already been satisfied.
Temporal validity
Each response window and preferred timestamp correspond
to a moment when the evidence is sufficient and assistance is still useful;
the preferred time lies within the window and neither anticipates evidence
nor misses the actionable moment.
Reference-answer quality
The reference is correct, relevant, and useful for
the active intent. It avoids unsupported details, contradictory advice, and
unnecessary instructions, while remaining consistent with the visible state.
Dynamic-intent consistency
For Dynamic samples, timestamped revisions,
compositions, and interruptions are coherent. References follow the latest
valid intent and preserve unaffected constraints without acting on superseded
ones; this criterion is not applicable to other categories.
Record integrity
The video, source identifier, user-turn timestamps,
evidence windows, and reference answers are complete and aligned. Each
decision refers to an identifiable sample version.

A deterministic update function applies valid events to the corresponding state fields and ignores duplicate updates. User instructions may introduce, revise, or retire requests; visual observations may establish task-relevant events; and observed progress or explicit user confirmation may update procedural state. A delivery record is created only after a response has been emitted to the user.
We enforce source-specific update constraints so that information retains its semantic role across the interaction. In particular, a request specifies what should be monitored rather than what has already occurred; a reference plan describes possible future steps rather than completed actions; and an assistant suggestion is not treated as evidence of user progress. Fields without sufficient support remain unresolved. Historical evidence may be exposed to the policy as context, but cannot by itself create, revise, or retire an intent.
Procedural memory retains at most eight completed steps and twelve evidence intervals that serve as temporal retrieval anchors. Progress is updated only when supported by observation or explicit confirmation. For event-monitoring requests, the auxiliary model additionally extracts and normalizes evidence from causal frames within a two-second window. This event parser updates evidence and event state only; it does not generate user-facing responses and therefore does not constitute a second action policy.
C.2
Intent Lifecycle
Each active intent is assigned a stable identifier and maintains an independent record of its criterion, associated event, evidence reference, and delivery status. A newly registered criterion begins in an evidence-waiting state. Once sufficient evidence supports a match, the criterion is linked to a concrete event instance. If the policy subsequently responds, the resulting delivery record identifies both the addressed event and the associated intents. This design allows multiple intents to remain active concurrently without treating a response to one intent as completion of the others.
The lifecycle explicitly separates
request validity
from
event coverage
. Answering a one-time question closes that pending question. By contrast, reporting an occurrence under a standing request marks only that event instance as addressed while keeping the request active for future evidence. Closing an event returns the corresponding instance to an evidence-waiting state, whereas explicit user cancellation retires the request itself. These transitions update interaction bookkeeping rather than policy behavior: neither an active intent nor a matched event deterministically triggers a response.
Skill library and selection.
The Harness maintains ten fixed, read-only Skill records covering visual question answering, multiple-choice answering, event detection, explanation, hazard monitoring, milestone reporting, mistake monitoring, narration, next-step guidance, and stage summarization. Each Skill specifies request cues, evidence to inspect, response and waiting conditions, interaction cadence, and answer form. Skills are reusable behavioral specifications rather than neural models. Each active criterion maintains its own execution instance, including phase, evidence reference, event association, and delivery status.
Skill selection first restricts candidates to those compatible with the current interaction type and requires non-empty observed memory, procedural context, or event context. A pending question prioritizes the question-answering Skill, followed by direct matches to active criterion types. If neither applies, lexical overlap between the request and observed context is used as a fallback, with at least two shared terms required. At most one Skill is selected for each context construction, and selecting no Skill is a valid outcome. For example, next-step guidance is conditioned on observed task progress, whereas event detection tracks a requested transition and whether the corresponding occurrence has already been reported. Importantly, selecting a Skill does not imply that its response condition has been satisfied.

Summary facts are indexed using normalized text together with stable identifiers, source intervals, and lexical terms.
