article.headline: 让流式视频模型学会何时主动开口
article.lede: Google等提出StreamVibe，把隐式、演变的用户意图建模为可追踪状态，让流式视频模型自己决定何时开口、说什么。
article.problem: 现有主动式视频助手大多只处理显式、单轮的请求，比如“球进了就提醒我”，无法从持续画面中推断“我卡住了就帮我”这类隐式意图。更麻烦的是任务状态会随交互改变，先前恰当的提醒到后来可能已经过时或重复，而用户意图本身还会被修改、叠加或打断。论文把这三类难点分别对应为显式、隐式、动态意图，要求模型同时决定“何时响应”和“响应什么”。
article.method: 作者构建了StreamVibe-Bench，包含4,100条评测样本、20,546个帮助点和183.4小时视频，覆盖物理任务与GUI操作两类环境，并提供逐点评测与时序轨迹评测两套协议。模型侧提出StreamVibe-VL：先用自适应流式SFT联合学习沉默/响应决策与回答内容，再用局部轨迹强化学习在标注帮助点附近采样因果rollout，结合点级时序、内容奖励与轨迹级一致性奖励优化。外层的StreamVibe-Harness把每个意图维护为带独立生命周期的持久状态，用分层记忆压缩并检索相关历史，再交给策略做决策。
article.results: 在StreamVibe-Bench逐点评测中，StreamVibe-VL（RL）在动态意图上的时序F1为66.34，高于SFT的58.70；轨迹评测下隐式意图F1为26.26，高于SFT的22.43。作者报告其响应时机与回答质量比其它基线提升10.7%，加上Harness后持续交互再提升12.3%。消融显示RL主要压低误触发（轨迹评测显式意图FPR从SFT的6.33%降到2.02%），Harness则在多数设置下进一步减少冗余响应，动态意图上增益最明显。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“主动助手”从实时长上下文问题拆成意图追踪与证据定位两个可分别优化的部分，并给出一个同时含隐式与动态意图的公开评测基准，为后续研究提供了可比较的起点。
article.limitations: 增益主要相对开源基线，在轨迹评测的显式意图上ViSpeak的时序F1为32.37，高于StreamVibe-VL（RL）的26.51（后者误触发率2.02%远低于12.75），说明高选择性仍以覆盖率为代价。评测采用±2秒匹配容差、答案质量由Claude Sonnet 4.6打分，训练数据中的候选帮助点由Gemini-3.8-Flash生成；论文也承认时序F1随交互时长下降的问题并未完全解决。
article.figure_caption_zh: StreamVibe总览：推理时Harness维护持久交互状态与意图生命周期并从分层记忆检索历史；训练时自适应流式SFT平衡等待/发言，局部轨迹RL在帮助点附近采样并联合点级与轨迹级奖励。

figure.caption: {Overview of StreamVibe.} (a) During inference, StreamVibe-Harness maintains persistent interaction state, tracks each intent through an independent lifecycle, and retrieves relevant history from hierarchical memory, providing StreamVibe-VL with a unified context for response decisions. (b) Adaptive streaming SFT balances wait/speak decisions and jointly supervises timing and content. (c) Localized trajectory RL samples causal rollouts around help points, combining point-level timing and content rewards with trajectory-level rewards on coverage, density, order, consistency, and redundancy.

page_papers.title: Trajectory2Gym: Decision-Grounded Compositional Interaction Synthesis for Tool-Use Agents
page_papers.abstract: Successful tool-use trajectories are not necessarily useful supervision. Even successful interactions may underrepresent multi-step dependencies or contain actions that are unjustified by the information visible to the agent at decision time. We identify two coupled requirements for effective trajectory supervision: compositional coverage, so that important observation-action dependencies are represented, and decision grounding, so that each supervised action is supported by the learner-visible interaction history. We introduce Trajectory2Gym, which constructs executable interactions around under-supported compositional structures and derives supervision only from grounded decisions in their realized executions. Structural-support selection allocates the resulting experience, while parent-normalized supervised fine-tuning preserves the semantic interaction as the unit of training weight. This reframes trajectory generation as the deliberate construction of learnable interaction experience, rather than the collection of successful trajectories. Across five Qwen3 scales, Trajectory2Gym improves Tau1, Tau2, and BFCL at every tested scale, increasing the equal-weight three-benchmark mean by 16.9-29.8 percentage points. The gains are strongest in stateful and multi-turn interaction, where later decisions depend on earlier observations and feedback. Our results suggest that scaling tool-use agents depends not only on collecting more successful trajectories, but on constructing interactions whose dependencies are represented and whose decisions are learnable from the agent's visible history.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Successful tool-use trajectories are not necessarily useful supervision.
Even successful interactions may underrepresent multi-step dependencies or
contain actions that are unjustified by the information visible to the agent
at decision time.
We identify two coupled requirements for effective trajectory supervision:
compositional coverage, so that important observation–action dependencies
are represented, and decision grounding, so that each supervised action is
supported by the learner-visible interaction history.
We introduce Trajectory2Gym, which constructs executable interactions around
under-supported compositional structures and derives supervision only from
grounded decisions in their realized executions.
Structural-support selection allocates the resulting experience, while
parent-normalized supervised fine-tuning preserves the semantic interaction
as the unit of training weight.
This reframes trajectory generation as the deliberate construction of
learnable interaction experience, rather than the collection of successful
trajectories.
Across five Qwen3 scales, Trajectory2Gym improves Tau1, Tau2, and BFCL at
every tested scale, increasing the equal-weight three-benchmark mean by
16.9–29.8 percentage points.
The gains are strongest in stateful and multi-turn interaction, where later
decisions depend on earlier observations and feedback.
Our results suggest that scaling tool-use agents depends not only on
collecting more successful trajectories, but on constructing interactions
whose dependencies are represented and whose decisions are learnable from
the agent’s visible history.
1  Introduction
Ask a support agent to cancel two orders and update a third. A competent
agent looks up the account; when the email lookup fails, it asks for a
name and ZIP code and retries; it reads each order to check it is
pending, confirms with the user, and only then cancels and swaps items
using catalog-returned identifiers. Each call is simple; what must be
learned is their composition. We call such workflows
compositional
interactions
: an observation, user update, or state change determines a
later decision. Tool-use agents face this composition constantly

6  Conclusion
Successful trajectories are the default supervision for tool-use agents,
yet success certifies an episode, not what it teaches. This paper has
argued that a trajectory’s value lies in properties an outcome filter
cannot see, compositional coverage and decision grounding, and Trajectory2Gym
builds training data around them: it synthesizes the interactions a pool
lacks, certifies supervision one decision at a time, and allocates
structural support per scale. Across scales from 1.7B to 30B, standard
SFT on the constructed interactions improves tool use, especially on
multi-turn and stateful tasks. Matched 8B controls give directional
evidence for the four design choices, with the clearest isolated gain
from parent normalization. The broader lesson is that success should
gate supervision, not license it;
that authentic errors belong in context, not in targets; and that
support is an allocation, not a quantity to maximize.
The resulting training corpus can be viewed at three levels: which
interaction structures are available, which decisions are eligible for
imitation, and how much optimization mass each complete interaction
receives. These levels can vary even when two datasets contain similar
numbers of trajectories or target tokens. Treating them separately makes
data-construction choices explicit and helps interpret why larger
collections do not automatically provide better supervision. For future
tool-use training pipelines, this suggests tracking structural coverage
and decision eligibility alongside data volume, while keeping the
training weight of an interaction independent of its rendering format.
Extending decision-level certification to on-policy rollouts and to web, software,
and terminal agents is the natural next step. What a trajectory teaches
is decided not by its outcome, but by the dependencies it realizes and
the decisions its visible history can justify.

Experimental Protocol
A.1  Benchmarks and Metrics
We evaluate Trajectory2Gym on Tau1, Tau2, and BFCL.
Tau1 contains 115 Retail and 50 Airline tasks, while Tau2 contains
40 Retail, 20 Airline, and 40 Telecom tasks.
For both Tau benchmarks, we report native task success within each domain
and macro-average equally across domains.
BFCL contains 1,718 examples spanning four Non-live categories, three Live
categories, and Multi-turn Base.
We use the same three-group Overall aggregation as in the main text,
equally averaging the Non-live mean, Live mean, and Multi-turn score.
A.2  Training and Evaluation Populations
Training-side interaction construction follows the released data
partitions of each environment.
Tau1 Retail uses separate training and evaluation populations.
Tau1 Airline uses the public 50-task identity set for training-side
interaction construction and fresh-dialogue evaluation; we therefore
treat it as a seen-task, transductive setting rather than task-disjoint
generalization.
For Tau2 Retail, Airline, and Telecom, training-side construction uses
the official train split and evaluation uses the official test split.
BFCL follows its released training-side and evaluation memberships.
This provides example-level separation, although semantically related tool
behaviors may occur across the two populations.
A.3  Comparison Protocol
Our primary comparison pairs each Trajectory2Gym model with its corresponding
public Qwen3 initialization.
Within each scale, the two models are evaluated on the same benchmark
instances with the same agent interface, tool access, decoding
configuration, user simulator where applicable, and native scorer.
These paired evaluations isolate the effect of the post-training procedure
from differences in evaluation conditions.
We additionally report public agent-training checkpoints as external
references.
These models are evaluated on the same benchmark populations and scoring
rules, while retaining model-native prompting and tool-call interfaces
where necessary.
They therefore provide cross-method context rather than matched
interventions; full results and model-specific settings are given in

agent-training baselines, and the matched 8B component controls.
This appendix complements those results in two ways.
First, it reports the complete public-checkpoint reference set evaluated
under our unified benchmark protocol.
Second, it provides additional analysis of the matched controls and
structural-support allocation.

article.headline: 成功轨迹未必是好监督：按决策接地造数据
article.lede: Trajectory2Gym 不再只筛成功轨迹，而是围绕覆盖不足的交互结构合成可执行对话，并且只对智能体可见历史能够支撑
article.problem: 工具调用智能体的训练通常直接拿成功轨迹做监督，但成功只证明整段对话过关，不能证明每一步动作都合理。这类数据往往缺少多步依赖的覆盖，还包含在决策时刻无法由可见信息支撑的动作，因此成功轨迹不等于可用监督。
article.method: 作者提出两个判据：组合覆盖，即重要的观测-动作依赖要在数据中出现；决策接地，即每个被监督的动作都必须由学习者在当时可见的交互历史支持。Trajectory2Gym 围绕支持不足的组合结构构造可执行交互，只在真实执行中对接地的决策提取监督；结构支持选择负责分配经验，父级归一化监督微调则让权重以完整语义交互为单位，而不随渲染格式变化。
article.results: 在五个 Qwen3 规模（1.7B 至 30B）上，Trajectory2Gym 在每个测试规模都提升了 Tau1、Tau2 和 BFCL，三项等权平均提升 16.9–29.8 个百分点，增益主要集中在有状态、多轮交互任务上。评测集规模为 Tau1 含 115 个 Retail 与 50 个 Airline 任务，Tau2 含 40 个 Retail、20 个 Airline 与 40 个 Telecom 任务，BFCL 含 1,718 个样例。匹配的 8B 对照实验对四项设计选择给出方向性证据，其中单独增益最明显的是父级归一化。
article.why_it_matters: 它把轨迹生成从收集成功样本改为刻意构造可学的交互经验，提示数据管线应同时跟踪结构覆盖与决策可监督性，而不只看轨迹或 token 数量。对多轮、有状态的工具调用任务，这比单纯扩大成功轨迹池更可能带来实质提升。
article.limitations: Tau1 Airline 使用的是公开 50 任务同一集合做训练侧构造与全新对话评测，属于 seen-task 转导设置，不是任务不相交的泛化；作者也承认训练与评测划分只做到样例级分离，语义相近的工具行为仍可能跨集出现。组件消融只在 8B 规模上做，作者自称是方向性证据，且结论仅覆盖 Qwen3 系列与三个基准。

Abstract
We introduce PhysLadder, a hierarchical Sim–Real benchmark for evaluating physical interaction capabilities in contact-rich manipulation. Its 16 household tasks span three cumulative levels: contact selection and geometric alignment (L1), force regulation within sustained contact (L2), and coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation (L3). Each task is instantiated in physically and visually matched simulated and real-world environments, with shared task definitions and success criteria. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra zero-shot with three trials per task in each environment. Real-world success rates decline from 80.0% at L1 to 47.6% at L2 and 0.0% at L3, with corresponding simulation rates of 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%. Ten of the 16 tasks have identical success counts across environments; the remaining six differ by one success out of three trials. Across both environments, recurring difficulties in spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordination often prevent local physical progress from accumulating into task completion. These findings characterize Astra’s observed capability boundary across increasing interaction demands and, for this model, support matched simulation as a repeatable, scalable testbed for studying the sustained, coordinated physical interactions that limit reliable manipulation.
1
Introduction
GPT-6 Astra and other general-purpose foundation models have shown promise for robotic manipulation, while reliable execution remains challenging
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Yang et al., 2026
;
Huang et al., 2026
)
. Recent work explores adaptation from demonstrations and interaction feedback without parameter updates
(
Cheng et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026
)
, as well as iterative program development for long-horizon, contact-rich tasks
(
Shen et al., 2026
)
. Practical use in homes and factories, however, requires reliable contact-rich execution: establishing suitable contacts, regulating forces through them, and coordinating contact changes as a task proceeds
(
Suomalainen et al., 2022
;
Noseworthy et al., 2024
)
. Aggregate success rates alone do not identify which physical interaction requirements constrain performance. We therefore ask: which requirements can Astra satisfy as interactions become more demanding, and to what extent do the observed capabilities and limitations persist across simulation and reality?
To address these questions, we introduce PhysLadder, a hierarchical Sim–Real benchmark that organizes 16 household manipulation tasks by their physical interaction requirements (Figure
2
; Section
3
). The hierarchy is organized around two dimensions: contact configuration and force regulation. L1 emphasizes contact selection and geometric alignment. L2 adds task-specific force regulation within sustained contact, directly or through a tool or container, without requiring contact reconfiguration to continue the operation. L3 additionally requires coordinating contact reconfiguration with force regulation. Levels describe task versions rather than task names: blocks clustered at a dustpan entrance can be swept in one stroke (L2), whereas dispersed blocks require successive contacts (L3). Spatial reasoning and execution precision remain relevant throughout. By relating performance to explicit interaction requirements, the hierarchy supports analysis of capabilities and limitations and provides successive evaluation targets beyond grasping and placement.

PhysLadder provides physically and visually matched real-world and simulated environments for each task (Figure
1
). Real-world trials provide a reference for physical execution, while simulation supports controlled, repeatable evaluation at scale. Using the physical setup as the reference, we match workspace layouts, object geometry and appearance, robot embodiment, and camera views. Physical measurements and observed contact responses guide simulation calibration (Section
4
). This correspondence supports comparisons of task completion, intermediate progress, and recurring interaction difficulties. Corresponding task definitions and documented success criteria guide these comparisons.
We evaluate GPT-6 Astra zero-shot with three trials per task in each environment. The evaluation yields three main findings. First, reported success rates decline across the interaction levels: from 80.0% at L1 to 47.6% at L2 and 0.0% at L3 in the real world, with corresponding simulation rates of 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%. Second, local physical progress does not reliably accumulate into task completion. Astra may turn a cap or move a drawer without completing the required operation. Execution analysis identifies four recurring interaction bottlenecks: spatial reasoning and execution precision, contact configuration selection and establishment, force regulation, and coordination within and across interactions (Section
6.4
). Third, for GPT-6 Astra, the two environments show consistent performance trends and similar interaction difficulties. Ten of the 16 tasks have identical reported success counts, and the remaining six differ by one successful trial. Together, these findings characterize Astra’s observed limitations under increasing interaction demands and support matched simulation as a testbed for studying the sustained, coordinated physical interactions that constrain reliable manipulation.
Our main contributions are:
•
PhysLadder, a hierarchical benchmark for physical interaction.
We define three cumulative levels based on contact configuration and force regulation, and organize 16 household tasks according to the requirements of each task version, providing successive evaluation targets beyond grasping and placement.
•
Physically and visually matched Sim–Real environments.
We construct simulated counterparts of physical tasks through scene reconstruction and calibration against observed contact responses, with corresponding task definitions and documented success criteria for comparison across environments.
•
A systematic zero-shot evaluation of GPT-6 Astra.
We characterize task completion, intermediate progress, and four recurring interaction bottlenecks across levels and environments, identifying the physical interaction requirements that challenge reliable execution.
\FloatBarrier
2
Related Work
2.1
Embodied Evaluation of General-Purpose Foundation Models
Embodied evaluation of general-purpose foundation models
(
OpenAI, 2026
;
Anthropic, 2026
, e.g.,)
examines whether models can act on environmental observations and task instructions and use execution feedback to complete tasks.
Existing work follows two main directions: broad interactive benchmarks and agents for challenging robotic manipulation.
EmbodiedEval
(
Cheng et al., 2025
)
and EmbodiedBench
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
assess visual understanding, spatial reasoning, and sequential decision-making through navigation and manipulation tasks, while RobotWorld extends evaluation across diverse simulated tasks and robot embodiments
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
.
Robotic manipulation requires integrating these capabilities with feedback-driven control
(
Diao et al., 2026
)
.
GPT-6 Astra
(
OpenAI, 2026
)
demonstrates task understanding and local error correction, but struggles with precision manipulation, dynamic control, and bimanual coordination
(
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Galbot Team et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
.
RoboColiseum compares frontier models through shared robot-control interfaces and likewise finds a gap between task understanding and reliable manipulation
(
Huang et al., 2026
)
.
Harness refinements and demonstration-based in-context learning can improve execution
(
Pantograph, 2026
;
Yao et al., 2026
)
; RoboICL combines demonstration context and interaction memory without parameter updates
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
, while EmbodiedSWE studies iterative program development for long-horizon, contact-rich simulation tasks
(
Shen et al., 2026
)
.
To characterize the remaining gap, we evaluate GPT-6 Astra across a hierarchy of contact demands in physically and visually matched real and simulated environments, examining whether task understanding and local corrections translate into sustained physical progress.
2.2
Contact-Rich Manipulation Benchmarks
Contact-rich manipulation benchmarks provide an experimental foundation for studying robotic execution under physical constraints, covering individual operations and compositions of multiple operations.
At the level of individual operations, standardized assembly tests and configurable insertion benchmarks vary part geometry, mating clearances, and assembly constraints to assess alignment, insertion, and part mating
(
Kimble et al., 2020
;
Delgado et al., 2026
)
.
Articulated-object benchmarks further examine manipulation under constrained motion and generalization across objects
(
Bao et al., 2023
)
.
At the level of skill composition, benchmarks connect grasping, reorientation, and insertion into complete manipulation sequences, or use furniture assembly to study skill transitions and execution reliability over longer tasks
(
Luo et al., 2024
;
Heo et al., 2023
)
.
These benchmarks support evaluations of individual skills, skill composition, and task completion, but operation categories and task length do not directly determine contact difficulty.
Different tasks may share similar contact requirements, while the same operation may impose different control demands depending on motion constraints, resistance between mating parts, or changes in contact.
To relate these shared requirements across tasks, we organize a hierarchical task suite around contact selection and geometric alignment, force regulation within sustained contact, and coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation.
This hierarchy supports analysis of which physical interaction demands GPT-6 Astra
(
OpenAI, 2026
)
can handle and how execution difficulties arise as these demands change, linking individual task results to a systematic characterization of its contact-rich manipulation capabilities and limits.
2.3
Physical and Visual Matching for Sim–Real Evaluation
Using simulation to assess contact capabilities requires both corresponding experimental conditions and validation against real-world execution.
To establish this correspondence, existing studies use visual and control matching to reduce the effects of observation and action-execution differences on policy evaluation
(
Li et al., 2024
;
Sedlacek et al., 2025
)
.
Real-scene reconstruction broadens the range of environments available for evaluation and, together with appropriate adaptation methods, improves the correlation between simulated and real-world performance
(
Jain et al., 2025
)
.
For contact-rich manipulation, object motion, deformation, and contact responses also determine task outcomes, making physical correspondence an important aspect of evaluation environment construction.
Soft-body interaction evaluations and controlled comparisons of reconstruction pipelines investigate how interaction dynamics, geometry, and physical properties affect agreement in behavior and outcomes between simulation and reality
(
Zhang et al., 2025
;
Verma et al., 2026
)
.
To validate conclusions drawn from simulation, related studies compare policy rankings, performance correlations, and failure patterns under perturbations
(
Wang et al., 2026a
)
, and assess execution quality beyond binary task success
(
Wang et al., 2026b
)
.
These efforts establish a foundation for paired Sim–Real evaluation and show that the value of environment matching must be assessed through real-world execution.
We apply this perspective to the contact-rich capabilities of general-purpose foundation models, evaluating GPT-6 Astra on corresponding simulated and real-world tasks with physical and visual matching.
By comparing performance across the three interaction levels and examining contact processes, we test whether the model’s strengths and limitations observed in simulation recur in real-world execution and identify discrepancies that depend on specific environmental conditions.
\FloatBarrier
3
Hierarchical Benchmark Design for Contact-Rich Manipulation
Robotic manipulation involves rich interactions with objects, requiring an understanding of how contact transmits forces and constrains motion. To understand GPT-6 Astra’s capabilities in these practical contact-rich settings, we design a hierarchical benchmark that characterizes manipulation performance across increasing contact demands. Specifically, we introduce (i) the principles underlying the three-level contact hierarchy in Section
3.1
, (ii) a suite of 16 household manipulation tasks in Section
3.2
, and (iii) task specifications and observable success criteria in Section
3.3
.
3.1
Principles of Hierarchical Task Design

0pt
\titlespacing
*
0pt0.40.6em
Contact-rich manipulation uses contact to transmit forces and constrain motion. The intended physical effect depends on where and how contacts are established and on how the transmitted forces or torques affect objects. We organize the hierarchy around these two coupled dimensions:
•
Contact configuration. This dimension describes where and how the robot contacts task objects, directly or through a tool or container
(
Mason, 2001
)
. It includes end-effector–object, tool–object, container–contents, and object–support contacts used for grasping, pushing, sliding, or support. The selected contacts must permit the intended operation: a secure grasp is insufficient if it obstructs that operation. Contact reconfiguration is required when the robot must release and re-establish contacts to continue the main operation. Initial grasping, final release, and contact changes arising naturally from sliding, rolling, or the release of contents do not by themselves constitute contact reconfiguration.
•
Force regulation. In this benchmark, force regulation refers to controlling how contact forces or torques change or constrain an object’s motion or deformation, beyond ordinary support, transport, and geometric placement. These requirements include overcoming resistance, maintaining pressure, limiting deformation, and regulating an object’s speed or direction of motion through contact. They may be met directly or through a tool or container, using motion or gripper commands
(
Raibert and Craig, 1981
;
Hogan, 1985
)
. Regulation may involve maintaining suitable forces or adjusting them as needed. Direct force measurements or commands are not required; forces during motion alone do not establish a force-regulation requirement.
Level assignment.
These two dimensions define three cumulative levels (Table
1
). L1 requires contact selection and geometric alignment, without force regulation beyond ordinary support, transport, and geometric placement. L2 adds force regulation as defined above, without requiring contact reconfiguration to continue the main operation. L3 additionally requires coordinating contact reconfiguration with force regulation. Contact changes used only for positioning, reorientation, or recovery from a failed grasp do not by themselves raise a task above L1. The table illustrates observable failures; Section
6.4
examines related interaction bottlenecks.

L1: Contact selection and geometric alignment.
The five L1 tasks place or align a held object, so success depends on where the object is grasped and how it is aligned. In Hat Hanging, the grasp must hold the hat securely without blocking its opening, allowing the opening to be aligned with the designated rack branch. Charger Alignment requires aligning the prongs with the socket holes without insertion. Cup Nesting uses two sequential grasps for geometric placement, without additional force-regulation requirements.
L2: Force regulation within sustained contact.
In the seven L2 tasks, force-regulation requirements arise from resistance in Marker Cap Removal, Book Pulling, and Drawer Pull & Return; from damage limits in Orange Handling and Jelly Handling; from the pressing force needed in Whiteboard Wiping; and, in Marble Pouring, from using cup orientation and motion to regulate the marbles’ movement and release into the receiving cup. In Drawer Pull & Return, for example, one handle grasp is kept while the pulling and pushing forces overcome friction along the guide without moving the cabinet.
L3: Coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation.
In the four L3 tasks, a maintained contact configuration cannot complete the main operation. In Bottle Cap Unscrewing, the rotation needed to disengage the thread exceeds the end effector’s turning range within one grasp; regrasping must restore torque transmission for further turning. Nut Unscrewing additionally requires the other arm to hold the unfixed bolt steady. In Stacked-Book Pushing & Rotation, pushing contacts must change to turn the stack through a full rotation. In Block Sweeping, three separated blocks require successive brush–block contacts. These contact changes must be coordinated with forces that continue the operation while preserving earlier progress.
Scope and interpretation.
Levels describe a
task version
: its initial configuration, goal, and process constraints (Section
3.3
), assessed for the evaluated robot setup. They do not follow from task names, model performance, control interfaces, or contact changes observed in a particular execution. Blocks clustered at a dustpan entrance, for example, can be collected in one sweep and impose only L2 demands (Section
6.3
); a partially unscrewed cap needing only a short turn is likewise L2. External support or an end effector that turns a cap without regrasping can change the requirements relative to our two-finger grippers (Section
4.1
). The hierarchy describes increasing physical interaction demands without imposing an absolute difficulty ordering, as perception, spatial reasoning, and geometric precision also affect performance. Comparisons across levels characterize performance under combined demands without isolating any factor’s causal contribution.
3.2
Task Suite Overview
Our benchmark comprises 16 household manipulation tasks: five at L1, seven at L2, and four at L3. Figure
2
(a) shows simulated and real-world views of the complete suite, expanding the representative overview in Figure
1
(b).
L1 covers placement and alignment in Marker Placement, Charger Alignment, Hat Hanging, Cup Nesting, and Flower Transfer. L2 covers constrained motion and separation in Marker Cap Removal, Drawer Pull & Return, and Book Pulling, deformable-object manipulation in Orange Handling and Jelly Handling, pouring loose marbles in Marble Pouring, and sustained tool–surface contact in Whiteboard Wiping. L3 includes Bottle Cap Unscrewing, Nut Unscrewing, Stacked-Book Pushing & Rotation, and Block Sweeping.
The suite spans rigid objects, deformable food objects, and constrained mechanisms, through direct manipulation and tool or container use. This coverage allows us to examine whether strengths and failures recur across different objects and operations with related interaction demands.
Section
4
explains how the corresponding environments and assets are constructed and physically and visually matched.
Figure
2
(b) shows three initial configurations for each of four representative simulation tasks, illustrating variations in object positions, relative placement, and orientation. Task-specific goals and constraints are defined in Section
3.3
and Appendix
A
, while Section
5
specifies the model interface and evaluation protocol.
3.3
Task Specification and Success Criteria
Each task version is specified by its initial conditions, goal, and process constraints. Initial conditions describe object positions and orientations, any external fixation or support, whether the robot already holds an object, and whether a connection has been partially loosened. The task goal specifies the operation to be completed and its required outcome, such as pulling a drawer outward and returning it to its initial opening. Process constraints define permitted actions and tools, together with requirements such as avoiding damage or maintaining object support during execution. These requirements define the manipulation problem without prescribing a unique action sequence. Complete task specifications are provided in Appendix
A
.
Task success is assessed using the explicit task-specific criteria in Appendix
A
, including the required outcomes and process constraints. Completion is assessed through observable outcomes, such as separation, prescribed displacement, or stable support after release. For Jelly Handling, success requires the prescribed lift, return, and release, with no damage throughout execution. Sim–Real comparisons use corresponding success conditions, verified through observable criteria in each environment.
For diagnostic analysis, we define
effective contact
as contact that transmits the force or torque needed for the main operation, and distinguish it from complete success. In Bottle Cap Unscrewing, local cap rotation relative to the fixed bottle indicates that effective contact has been established, whereas complete success requires full thread disengagement and controlled lifting of the cap to the specified separation. Effective contact may be lost and re-established during execution. It helps interpret local physical progress but does not replace the task-level success criterion.
4
Physically and Visually Matched Sim–Real Environments
Our contact-rich manipulation tasks span the matched simulated and real-world environments illustrated in Figure
1

4.1
Real-World Setup
As shown in Figure
3
(a), the real-world platform comprises two ARX R5 robotic arms, each equipped with an R5-series two-finger gripper. Both arms are secured at the table edge and share a tabletop workspace. This configuration supports single-arm manipulation and dual-arm coordination, including tasks in which one arm stabilizes an object while the other manipulates it. Task objects and supporting fixtures are placed within this workspace; their initial configurations and task-specific constraints are defined in Appendix

3
(b) and (c) show how each wrist camera is mounted relative to its gripper on the left and right arms. These three views provide complementary observations of the scene and local manipulation. The arms and grippers have no dedicated contact-force sensors, so no direct contact-force measurements are supplied to the model. Hardware and sensing details are provided in Appendix

Workspace Layout and Task Initialization.
Workspace geometry and task initialization determine the contacts available at the start of a trial and the remaining motion required to complete the task. Measured table dimensions and spatial layout establish the workspace geometry. Task-specific initial configurations follow Appendix
A

Task Assets and Contact Responses.
We reconstruct asset geometry and appearance from multi-view images of real objects and use measured dimensions to set their physical scale, matching object shape, color, and surface texture across environments (Figure
5

Physical parameters are set through direct measurement and refinement against observed interaction responses. Object masses are set from weighing measurements, as illustrated by the jelly example in Figure
5
(b2). Contact friction parameters are adjusted based on relative sliding observed during manipulation. For deformable assets, material parameters are refined by comparing simulated deformation with that observed in the physical objects. The refinement targets contact responses relevant to the evaluated tasks. Figure
5
(b3) shows recorded jelly states before and during gripper contact. A shared global color adjustment is applied to simulated views; these qualitative frames show observed states without quantifying agreement in deformation or contact force.

Evaluation Setup and Protocol
We evaluate GPT-6 Astra on physically and visually matched real and simulated tasks to characterize its physical interaction capabilities and their correspondence across environments. This section describes the task and model configuration, model inputs and closed-loop execution, and evaluation protocol and metrics.
5.1
Task Setup and Model Configuration
Each evaluation task is specified by its initial conditions, physical goal, and process constraints, with detailed task definitions provided in Appendix
A
. Starting from initial configurations matched to the real-world setup, we construct simulated variants by varying target-object positions and orientations (Figure
2
(b)). These variants reflect the placement variability introduced by manual resets in real-world trials and probe generalization across initial layouts. The task objective and success criteria remain fixed across these variants.
We evaluate GPT-6 Astra with reasoning effort set to
xhigh
. Codex
3
3
3
https://github.com/openai/codex
provides the runtime for invoking the model and connecting it to the environment interfaces.
Zero-shot evaluation is defined with respect to the benchmark tasks: the model is not supplied with prior executions, demonstrations, or task-specific strategies for these tasks. It may use observations, actions, and feedback from the current episode to guide subsequent decisions, without carrying evaluation-task experience into later trials. Section
5.2
describes the fixed basic Skills for real-world embodiment and interface adaptation.
5.2
Model Inputs and Closed-Loop Execution
Inputs.
Each episode provides the model with two fixed inputs (Figure
6
(a),
1
): the natural-language task instruction, which states the objects, objective, arm roles where required, and constraints (Appendix
A
), and a description of the execution interface, covering the action space, coordinate conventions, and execution feedback. In simulation, the policy adapter supplies this description as model instructions; in real-world execution, it is provided by the fixed basic Skills prepared before evaluation. Both inputs remain unchanged throughout the episode, and no further task information, hints, or corrections are provided. Image observations, proprioceptive states, execution feedback, and the interaction history are updated as the episode proceeds.
Basic Skills.
Basic Skills follow the Agent Skills mechanism of Codex

https://developers.openai.com/codex/skills
: each Skill is a directory with a
SKILL.md
instruction file and optional reference documents, which the agent reads when relevant. The real-world basic Skills describe the embodiment and interface, including arm identities, arm–camera correspondences, command frames and units, and gripper semantics, and give general guidance on active observation, grasp and contact verification, dual-arm coordination, and local recovery (Figure

). They were prepared before evaluation through general robot interactions and interface testing, contain no strategies or demonstrations from the evaluation tasks, and remain fixed across trials. Simulation uses no Skills: its conventions are fully specified by the simulator configuration, so the policy adapter provides the corresponding description and guidance, including observation guidance adapted from the Skills, as fixed model instructions. Both environments receive the same categories of task-agnostic information by different mechanisms.
Observation.
At each decision, the model observes RGB images from one external camera, which shows the workspace and arm clearance, and two wrist cameras, which show grasps and local contact, together with proprioceptive states and execution feedback (Figure
6
(a),
2

The interaction history retains earlier observations, actions, and feedback within the episode. Without depth images or contact-force measurements, grasp, alignment, and contact outcomes must be inferred from visual changes, proprioceptive states, and execution feedback, and force regulation (Section

5.3
Evaluation Protocol and Metrics
Trial protocol.
Each trial is one episode that starts from reset object and arm states, and each task is evaluated in three trials per environment. Continuation segments resume unfinished episodes with their interaction history and remain part of the same trial; simulation budgets are not replenished. Trials end differently in the two environments. In simulation, a trial ends when the independent evaluator detects success or a task-defined failure state, or when the model-call or time budget is exhausted; a termination request ends the trial only if the evaluator confirms success. In the real world, no preset task-level wall-clock or model-call limit is imposed. The model may end a trial by reporting completion or judging that it cannot complete the task. Trials also end when an operator stops or takes over execution, or when a commanded motion exceeds the arm’s kinematic limits and triggers a protective stop (Appendix
B.1
). Budgets, time limits, initial configurations, and reset procedures are given in Appendix
C.2
.
Success rates.
A trial is an autonomous success only if it achieves the task goal and satisfies all process constraints (Section
3.3
), including release or final-state stability where specified. Both environments use the same success criteria: the evaluator checks them automatically in simulation, whereas real-world outcomes are judged against them after each trial from execution videos (Appendix
C.3
). All other trials count as failures, including budget exhaustion in simulation, real-world termination for inability to complete, protective stops, and operator takeover. For task

6.1
Zero-Shot Performance Across Interaction Levels
Across the 16-task suite, Astra achieves average success rates of 45.8% in the real world and 41.7% in simulation. The results in Table
2
show how this performance varies across tasks and interaction levels.
Astra demonstrates strong zero-shot performance in basic pick-and-place tasks requiring semantic understanding and object localization, but struggles with tasks requiring more complex spatial reasoning.
Marker Placement, Charger Alignment, Cup Nesting, and Flower Transfer each succeed in all three real-world trials. Simulation also records successful executions across these tasks, with Marker Placement and Flower Transfer each reported as successful in all three trials and Charger Alignment and Cup Nesting in two of three. These results show that Astra can coordinate object localization, grasping, orientation adjustment, and placement across varied household objects without task-specific training.
Hat Hanging illustrates the limitation in spatial reasoning: the robot must reason about the relative orientation of the hat opening and the coat-rack branch, then rotate the hat into alignment. Although Astra can grasp and lift the hat, it fails to leave it independently supported by the branch in either environment. Consistent with Section
3.1
, spatial reasoning and geometric precision contribute to task difficulty alongside the interaction demands of L1–L3.
Performance declines as physical interaction demands increase.
Real-world success falls from 80.0% at L1 to 47.6% at L2 and 0.0% at L3; simulation follows the same progression, from 66.7% to 47.6% and 0.0%. None of the four L3 tasks (Bottle Cap Unscrewing, Nut Unscrewing, Stacked-Book Pushing & Rotation, and Block Sweeping) succeeds in any trial in either environment. Their specifications require coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation over successive actions. The absence of complete successes, despite local progress in several executions, identifies sustained physical interaction as a major limitation of the evaluated system and a priority for extending general-purpose models to practical manipulation.
The L1–L3 hierarchy captures the increasing challenges of physical interaction and provides a structured benchmark for characterizing the capability boundaries of general-purpose models.
Grounded in contact configuration and force regulation requirements, it connects task demands to observed execution limits. The decline in completion across both environments reveals challenges in sustained physical interaction that evaluations centered on basic grasping and placement may overlook. This progression provides concrete evaluation targets for advancing reliable physical interaction in general-purpose models.

6.2
Correspondence Between Real and Simulated Performance
For GPT-6 Astra, real-world and simulated evaluations reveal consistent performance trends across levels and individual tasks.
As shown in Table
2
, 10 of the 16 tasks have identical observed success rates (3/3 in three tasks and 0/3 in seven), while the remaining six differ by one successful trial out of three. Both environments exhibit declining completion from L1 to L3, indicating consistent task-level performance profiles.
Real and simulated executions exhibit similar intermediate capabilities and recurring interaction bottlenecks.
Figure
7
illustrates this correspondence through selected interaction stages. In Hat Hanging (L1-03; panel (a)), the robot can grasp and lift the hat in both environments, but its opening remains misaligned with the rack branch. Completing the task requires complex spatial reasoning about relative orientation beyond locating and lifting the object. Marker Cap Removal (L2-01; panel (b)) exposes a different obstacle: inadequate cap grasps fail to establish the contact configuration needed for separation, leaving the cap attached. In Jelly Handling (L2-06; panel (c)), the gripper closes on the jelly, yet the object remains on its support. Grasp location and applied force must work together to sustain a lifting grasp, exposing coupled difficulties in contact configuration and force regulation. Bottle Cap Unscrewing (L3-01; panel (d)) progresses to cap contact, but subsequent slippage or dropping interrupts the operation, showing difficulty maintaining an effective cap grasp during manipulation. The three paired examples in Block Sweeping (L3-04; panel (e)) bring together difficulties in directing dispersed blocks toward the dustpan, establishing a useful brush grasp, and regulating brush contact. Successful collection requires coordinating these capabilities as successive sweeps change the block distribution, while avoiding actions that scatter blocks away from the target. These cases link shared local progress to interaction difficulties that prevent complete task success.

shows why outcome scores need to be interpreted alongside execution behavior. In Charger Alignment (L1-02; panel (a)), both environments show grasping, transport, and positioning near the socket. Both environments apply the same alignment criterion: real-world trials were judged visually and stopped once alignment appeared adequate, whereas simulation checks it with a fixed geometric tolerance; the unsuccessful simulated trial repeatedly refined alignment until exhausting its model-call budget. The outcome difference therefore reflects assessment granularity and execution limits alongside the difficulty of precise alignment. Cup Nesting (L1-04; panel (b)) distinguishes placement progress from final-state stability: the cups remain nested after release in the real-world example but topple after release in one simulated trial. This failure was not observed in the three real-world trials. In Book Pulling (L2-02; panel (c)), the selected configurations illustrate the shared difficulty of choosing effective locations for left-arm pulling and right-arm support. The supporting arm must restrain the upper book while allowing the target book to be extracted; unsuccessful executions reveal inadequate coordination between support and pulling in both environments. The task thus couples contact configuration with bimanual force regulation. Real-world cables and wrist-mounted cameras further restrict access and gripper orientation, making suitable contacts harder to establish. These constraints point to setup details that could be matched more closely across environments. Drawer Pull & Return (L2-05; panel (d)) provides complementary evidence of shared partial capability: both environments show local pulling and pushing, including opening the drawer and moving it inward. These actions do not reliably complete the pull-and-return sequence, which requires effective contact and force regulation throughout.
For GPT-6 Astra, physically and visually matched simulation captures key capabilities and limitations revealed by real-world evaluation.
In our visually reconstructed environments with calibrated basic physical properties, the agreement in outcomes and execution behavior indicates that simulated tasks probe challenges encountered on the real platform. This supports assessing competence and persistent interaction bottlenecks in simulation.
Our simulation benchmark provides a repeatable and scalable testbed whose outcomes correspond to real-world evaluation for GPT-6 Astra.
Explicit task specifications and controlled initialization support systematic comparisons across models, tasks, and initial configurations. Parallel execution reduces dependence on robot availability and manual resets, enabling broader evaluation.

Spatial reasoning and execution precision remain bottlenecks beyond object localization.
Hat Hanging (L1-03; Figure
7
(a)) exposes the difficulty of reasoning about the orientation of the hat opening relative to the rack branch after the object has been located and lifted. Charger Alignment (L1-02; Figure
8
(a)) illustrates the complementary demand for execution precision: reaching the socket vicinity does not ensure that subsequent position and orientation adjustments achieve the required alignment. Together, these cases distinguish determining the required spatial relationships from realizing them accurately through robot motion. Block Sweeping (L3-04; Figure
7
(e)) extends this challenge to sweep planning as object positions change.
Selecting and establishing appropriate contact configurations remains a recurring challenge.
A useful contact must combine an accessible location with an orientation that supports the intended action. Marker Cap Removal (L2-01; Figure
7
(b)) exposes difficulties in establishing a precise pulling grasp on the cap. Orange Handling (L2-04; Figure
10
(a)) adds material constraints: an upright segment remains unlifted when a suitable grasp cannot be established under the no-damage requirement. Nut Unscrewing (L3-02; Figure
10
(c)) further requires contacts that permit subsequent relative rotation; the execution record reports infeasible turning poses despite bimanual contact. Related contact-selection difficulties arise in book extraction, drawer pulling and pushing, and brush pickup (L2-02, L2-05, and L3-04; Figures
8
(c,d) and
7
(e)). Contact selection must therefore account for geometry, access, material properties, and force direction.
Force regulation remains a key limitation in task execution.
After contact is established, actions must produce the required physical effect while preserving grasp and support. Book Pulling (L2-02; Figure
8
(c)) requires coordinated support and extraction: documented attempts either disturb the upper book or leave the target book blocked, highlighting the need to balance right-arm support with left-arm pulling. Drawer Pull & Return (L2-05; Figure
8
(d)) similarly exposes difficulties in regulating both the outward pull and the inward push through the full sequence. Bottle Cap Unscrewing (L3-01; Figure
7
(d)) illustrates loss of grasp during manipulation. Whiteboard Wiping (L2-07; Figure
10
(b)) provides a complementary example in which repeated wiping leaves visible writing. Together, these cases show difficulty producing the required contact effects but do not isolate force regulation from contact configuration or motion execution.
Astra struggles to coordinate contact configuration and force regulation within and across interactions.
Jelly Handling (L2-06; Figure
7
(c)) exposes coupling within a single grasp: contact location and applied force jointly determine whether the deformable object can be supported. The unsuccessful attempts illustrate this coupling without isolating either component as the sole cause. Across successive actions, this coordination must also adapt to the changing physical state. Stacked-Book Pushing & Rotation (L3-03; Figure
10
(d)) achieves partial translation and rotation without completing the required transfer. In Block Sweeping (L3-04), the examples in Figure
7
(e) expose difficulties in sweep planning, brush contact selection, and force regulation; successive sweeps require these capabilities to work together as the block distribution changes. Effective local actions do not reliably accumulate into sustained progress and task completion.
6.5
Limitations and Scope
The evaluation covers 16 household tasks with three trials per task in each environment. Limited real-robot resources and low parallelization constrain trial counts and statistical precision. The Sim–Real correspondence is therefore descriptive and specific to GPT-6 Astra; whether simulation predicts real-world performance for other models remains to be tested. Coverage is limited to the tested task versions, initial configurations, and robot platform. Our analysis characterizes interaction failures in this system; contributions of model decisions, sensing, and robot execution remain to be isolated.
7
Conclusion
We evaluate GPT-6 Astra’s zero-shot contact-rich manipulation capabilities on the 16 household tasks of PhysLadder in matched real and simulated environments. Astra demonstrates strong performance on basic pick-and-place tasks requiring semantic understanding and object localization, but performance declines as physical interaction demands increase, with no complete successes on the tested L3 tasks. Difficulties in complex spatial reasoning, contact configuration, force regulation, and their coordination limit individual actions and sustained progress across successive interactions. These findings reveal a gap between effective local actions and reliable task completion, identifying sustained physical interaction as a priority for general-purpose embodied models.
For GPT-6 Astra, the observed correspondence in task outcomes and interaction bottlenecks indicates that physically and visually matched simulation can reflect key capabilities and limitations revealed by real-world evaluation. PhysLadder’s L1–L3 hierarchy characterizes capability boundaries across increasing demands on contact configuration, force regulation, and their coordination. Explicit task specifications and controlled initialization support repeatable comparisons, while parallel execution reduces dependence on real-robot resources. This provides a standardized, scalable benchmark for evaluating progress toward reliable physical interaction, a prerequisite for general physical intelligence.

L1 Task Specifications
L1-01: Marker Placement.
Initial conditions.
A capped marker, approximately 150 mm long, stands upright to the right of a fixed, upright ceramic cup. The cup is approximately 85 mm high with a 70.8 mm inner opening; the object centers are approximately 300 mm apart. Both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The left arm grasps the marker and places either end inside the cup without removing its cap, then releases it. The right arm observes.
Task instruction.
“Pick up the thick marker with the left arm and place it in the wide-mouth cup, then release it.”
Complete success.
After release and gripper withdrawal, the marker remains inside the cup and is supported by it. This wide-mouth placement task does not require a close-fitting insertion or a specified insertion depth.
Contact requirements.
A stable grasp and geometric alignment of the marker with the cup opening suffice; no additional force regulation is required, which motivates the L1 assignment.
L1-02: Charger Alignment.
Initial conditions.
The charger stands upright in a freely resting grooved support, with its prongs pointing downward and its upper housing exposed. A power strip is fixed separately to its left, with the socket openings facing upward; their centers are approximately 330 mm apart. Both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The left arm lifts the charger clear of its support and aligns its two prongs with the corresponding holes of the designated socket nearest the left arm. The right arm observes.
Task instruction.
“Pick up the power adapter with the left arm and align its prongs with the socket holes closest to the left arm.”
Complete success.
The charger is held near the designated socket with both prongs aligned with their respective holes. Insertion, release, and electrical operation are not required.
Contact requirements.
Precise alignment of both prongs with the socket holes is the main demand; insertion and additional force regulation are not required, which motivates the L1 assignment.
L1-03: Hat Hanging.
Initial conditions.
A yellow open-top visor rests freely on a raised box beside a fixed, approximately 740 mm-high coat rack. The lowest slanted branch faces the left arm, and the visor rim is accessible for grasping. Both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The left arm picks up the visor, passes its head opening over the rounded end of the lowest branch, and releases it so that the band is supported by that branch. The right arm observes.
Task instruction.
“Use the left arm to hang the hat on the lowest rod through its head opening.”
Complete success.
The released visor is supported through its head opening by the designated branch, independently of the gripper. Perching on the branch tip or using another branch is insufficient. Natural oscillation is permitted; no additional stability dwell is required.
Contact requirements.
The grasp must hold the hat securely while leaving its head opening accessible for alignment with the branch; no additional force regulation is required, which motivates the L1 assignment.
L1-04: Cup Nesting.
Initial conditions.
Two identical empty paper cups stand upright and unfixed, one at the left rear and the other at the right front of the workspace. Each is approximately 80 mm high with a 70 mm outer rim diameter. Both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The left arm places the left cup at the central location and releases it. The right arm then places the right cup inside it and releases it; the arms operate sequentially.
Task instruction.
“Use the left arm to place the left cup at the center and release it, then use the right arm to nest the right cup inside it and release it.”
Complete success.
The upper cup is actually nested in and independently supported by the lower cup after release and withdrawal, with stable nesting. No specified yaw orientation or strict centering is required. An open gripper that still traps the cup does not constitute release.
Contact requirements.
Sequential stable grasps and alignment of the upper cup with the lower cup suffice; no additional force regulation is required, which motivates the L1 assignment.
L1-05: Flower Transfer.
Initial conditions.
A white artificial flower rests in the left paper cup, which also contains a charger. The right paper cup, containing glass balls and pearls, is the receiving container. Both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The left arm retrieves the flower from the left cup, inserts its stem into the right cup, and releases it. The grasp must leave sufficient stem length free for insertion. The right arm observes.
Task instruction.
“Pick up the flower from the left cup, insert its stem into the right cup, and release it.”
Complete success.
The flower and receiving cup remain independently stable after release and gripper withdrawal, with the stem inside the receiving cup.
Contact requirements.
A grasp that leaves enough stem free and alignment of the stem with the receiving cup suffice; no additional force regulation is required, which motivates the L1 assignment.
A.3
L2 Task Specifications
L2-01: Marker Cap Removal.
Initial conditions.
An approximately 150 mm-long capped marker lies horizontally on a raised box between the arms, with the body to the right and cap to the left. It is not fixed, and both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The right arm picks up and stabilizes the marker body. The left arm grasps the cap and pulls it away along the marker axis, maintaining both grasps until separation. The task ends at complete separation; placing down or releasing either component is not required.
Task instruction.
“Pick up the black pen with the right arm, then grasp the cap with the left arm and pull it off along the pen’s axis.”
Complete success.
The cap fully separates from the marker body after the instructed bimanual pull. Continued holding is sufficient; placement, release, and arm return are not required.
Contact requirements.
Both grasps must be maintained while the left arm overcomes the cap’s resistance to separation along the marker axis, which motivates the L2 assignment.
L2-02: Book Pulling.
Initial conditions.
Three approximately 220 by 140 by 20 mm books are stacked on a support box. In the reference camera view, the middle book protrudes 40 mm to the right, with 5 mm clearance above it. The exposed side is accessible to the left gripper, and both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The right arm stabilizes the upper book while the left arm grasps the middle book and pulls it 5 cm outward from its initial position. Complete removal from the stack is not required.
Task instruction.
“Hold the top book steady with the right arm and pull the middle book out 5 cm with the left arm.”
Complete success.
The middle book moves the required 5 cm while the upper book remains stabilized. Motion of the entire stack or accumulated end-effector commands does not establish this displacement.
Contact requirements.
The left grasp must pull the middle book out of the stack while the right arm keeps the upper book stable; regulating the pulling force within sustained contact, without displacing the stack, motivates the L2 assignment.
L2-03: Marble Pouring.
Initial conditions.
Two upright paper cups, approximately 80 mm high with a 70 mm outer rim diameter, are placed approximately 200 mm apart. The left source cup contains twelve freely rolling glass marbles; it is not fixed to the table. The right receiving cup is fixed at its initial position. Both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The left arm grasps the source cup, pours into the fixed receiving cup until the source is empty, then returns the source cup to its original position and releases it. The right arm only assists observation.
Task instruction.
“Pick up the left cup with the left arm, pour its contents into the right cup until empty, then place it back and release it.”
Complete success.
The source cup is empty, at least six of the twelve marbles remain in the receiving cup, and the receiving cup remains at its initial fixed position. The source cup is then returned to its original position and released. Cup tilt alone is insufficient.
Contact requirements.
Cup orientation and motion change how the cup supports and guides the marbles, controlling their motion relative to the cup and their velocity at release. Regulating this motion and release falls within the task-level definition of force regulation (Section
3.1
). The robot can maintain its grasp without re-establishing contacts to continue pouring, motivating the L2 assignment.
L2-04: Orange Handling.
Initial conditions.
A peeled orange segment lies freely on a fixed support box between the arms, with its broad flesh side upward and its long axis along the camera-to-robot direction. Both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The left arm lifts the segment 5–20 cm above its initial position, returns it to the same support, and releases it without damage throughout the operation. The right arm observes.
Task instruction.
“Use the left arm to lift the orange segment 5–20 cm without damaging it, then place it back on the box and release it.”
Complete success.
The specified lift and return are completed, and the segment remains independently supported after release, with the no-damage constraint satisfied: no crushing is visible in the real world, and the simulated segment shows no structural damage.
Contact requirements.
A sustained grasp must hold the deformable segment firmly enough to lift it without damaging it, which motivates the L2 assignment.
L2-05: Drawer Pull & Return.
Initial conditions.
The upper drawer of the storage cabinet is partly open, with its initial opening recorded relative to the cabinet. Both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The left arm establishes a grasp, pulls the drawer approximately 5 cm farther out along its guide, and pushes it back to the recorded initial opening. The right arm observes. Moving the cabinet as a whole does not satisfy the task.
Task instruction.
“Use the left arm to pull the partially open top drawer out another 5 cm, then push it back to its original position.”
Complete success.
The drawer first moves outward by the prescribed amount and then returns to its initial opening. Merely ending at the initial opening without the required outward movement, or remaining open after a pull, is insufficient.
Contact requirements.
A sustained grasp must transmit pulling and pushing force along the drawer guide without moving the cabinet, which motivates the L2 assignment.
L2-06: Jelly Handling.
Initial conditions.
An unpackaged jelly rests freely on the green box. Both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The left arm lifts the jelly 5–20 cm above its initial position, returns it to the same box, and releases it without crushing it throughout the operation. The right arm observes.
Task instruction.
“Pick up the jelly from the green box with the left arm, lift it 5–20 cm, then place it back and release it.”
Complete success.
The specified lift and return are completed, and the jelly remains independently supported on its original box after release, with the no-damage constraint satisfied throughout: no crushing is visible in the real world, and the simulated jelly shows no structural damage.
Contact requirements.
A sustained grasp must hold the deformable jelly firmly enough to lift and return it without damaging it, which motivates the L2 assignment.
L2-07: Whiteboard Wiping.
Initial conditions.
A marked whiteboard and a blue rigid eraser are presented separately. The eraser rests on the table, and both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The left arm acquires the eraser and removes all writing with its working surface. The right arm observes. The goal concerns the board’s visible state, not traversal of a nominal path.
Task instruction.
“Pick up the board eraser with the left arm and erase the writing on the whiteboard.”
Complete success.
All writing on the board has been erased. Performing a contact wiping motion without removing the writing is insufficient.
Contact requirements.
Sustained contact between the eraser surface and the board suffices for the operation. Coordinating pressing force with wiping motion to remove the writing motivates the L2 assignment.
A.4
L3 Task Specifications
L3-01: Bottle Cap Unscrewing.
Initial conditions.
The bottle body is fixed to the tabletop with its cap engaged. Both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The right arm grasps and unscrews the cap, then lifts it 3–5 cm away from the bottle opening. The task instruction assigns cap manipulation to the right arm. In simulation, both arms are enabled for manipulation, so this arm-role constraint is specified by the instruction and is not enforced by the action interface. The fixture holds the bottle body throughout the operation.
Task instruction.
“The bottle body is fixed to the table. Unscrew the cap with the right arm, then lift the cap 3–5 cm away from the bottle opening.”
Complete success.
The cap fully disengages from the thread and is separated by 3–5 cm from the bottle opening while the bottle remains fixed. Grasping the cap, issuing a wrist rotation, or partially loosening the thread is not complete success.
Contact requirements.
Regrasping is required when the remaining screw travel exceeds the turning range of one grasp. Coordinating these grasp changes with effective torque transmission against the fixed bottle motivates the L3 assignment.
L3-02: Nut Unscrewing.
Initial conditions.
An expansion-bolt assembly, with an approximately 120 mm-long rod, lies horizontally on a support box, with the body to the right and nut/threaded end to the left. The assembly is unfixed, the nut is pre-loosened by three turns, and both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
The right arm picks up and stabilizes the body; the left arm grasps the hexagonal nut and unscrews it counterclockwise until it completely separates from the threaded rod.
Task instruction.
“Pick up and hold the threaded rod steady with the right arm, then unscrew the hex nut counterclockwise with the left arm until it comes off.”
Complete success.
The nut completely separates from the threaded rod, and both components remain supported. Partial loosening is not complete success. Continued holding of the separated parts is sufficient; placing them on the table is not required.
Contact requirements.
Regrasping is required when the remaining thread travel exceeds the turning range of one grasp, and the turning gripper must restore effective contact after each repositioning while the right arm keeps the body stable. Coordinating these grasp changes with torque transmission motivates the L3 assignment.
L3-03: Stacked-Book Pushing & Rotation.
Initial conditions.
Two books are stacked on the table inside a black rectangular start region. A second black rectangle defines the target region. Both grippers start empty.
Goal and constraints.
Both grippers push the stack from the start region into the target region, rotating it one full in-plane turn (
360
∘
360^{\circ}
) during the transfer. The books must remain stacked and supported by the table throughout; grasping or lifting is prohibited. No centering or prescribed final orientation is required.
Task instruction.
“Use both grippers to push the two stacked books from one black rectangle fully into the other, rotating the stack one full turn along the way. Keep the books stacked on the table without grasping or lifting them.”
Complete success.
Both books are wholly within the target rectangle, the full turn was completed in transit, and the stacking, tabletop-support, and no-grasp/no-lift constraints were maintained throughout.
Contact requirements.
The full-turn transfer requires coordinating changes in pushing contact with force direction and turning torque while preserving the stack and tabletop support. These coupled requirements, rather than the use of two arms alone, motivate the L3 assignment.
L3-04: Block Sweeping.
Initial conditions.
In the reference camera view, a fixed dustpan sits to the left with its thin entrance lip on the table, its opening toward the lower right, and its handle toward the upper left. A brush leans against a green box to the right, with its handle toward the upper right and its bristles toward the lower left. Three blue blocks lie between the brush and dustpan in a triangular arrangement: two nearer the arms and one nearer the camera. Both grippers start empty. Section
6.3
analyzes a separate two-block configuration.
Goal and constraints.
The left arm autonomously picks up the brush and sweeps all three blocks into the fixed dustpan. The right arm observes. The dustpan must remain fixed, and the grippers must not manipulate the blocks directly. Setting down the brush is not required.
Task instruction.
“Pick up the brush next to the green box with the left arm and use it to sweep all three blue blocks into the fixed dustpan. The right arm observes. All three blocks must be inside the pan and supported by it. Keep the dustpan fixed and do not manipulate blocks directly with the grippers. Setting down the brush is not required.”
Complete success.
All three blocks are inside the dustpan and supported by it, with the dustpan remaining fixed and no direct gripper manipulation of the blocks. The final brush position does not matter.
Contact requirements.
Collecting the three spatially separated blocks requires successive changes in brush–block contact coordinated with force direction and sweeping action, which motivates the L3 assignment. The brush must direct each block toward the dustpan while adjusting to the changing collection configuration. Collection is scored by the physical outcome, without prescribing a particular sequence of strokes.
\FloatBarrier
Appendix B
Sim–Real Implementation Details
B.1
Real-World Configuration
Hardware and sensing.
Each ARX R5 arm has six revolute joints and an R5-series coupled two-finger gripper with a single opening degree of freedom. The wrist cameras (Orbbec Gemini 305) acquire
848
×
480
848\times 480
images at 15 fps, and the external camera (Orbbec Gemini Pro) acquires
640
×
480
640\times 480
images at 30 fps. Although these cameras support depth sensing, the model receives only their RGB images; depth images are neither provided nor available through tool calls. Robot states are read from the arms’ CAN feedback.
Image observations.
The camera interface returns JPEG snapshots at the above resolutions without resizing or cropping. The model requests observations through tools rather than receiving every camera frame. Frame identifiers and host receipt times are used to check freshness; the three cameras are not hardware synchronized. The stated frame rates describe camera acquisition, not model observation or control rates.
Control and protection.
Gripper commands specify a normalized opening, with 0 denoting closed and 1 open, which is mapped through the per-arm profiles to SDK position values; these commands do not specify contact force. A control service runs the robot SDK, limits command transmission, and requests protection when heartbeat or feedback from the frontend is lost. When a commanded motion exceeds the arm’s kinematic limits, the arm controller triggers a protective stop and halts the arm; the trial then ends and counts as a failure (Section
5.3
). Command frames, units, and gripper semantics available to the model are described with the basic Skills (Appendix
C.1
).
B.2
Simulation Implementation

Contact and material models.
Rigid objects retain their collision geometry; fixed objects and supports are anchored in the scene, and passive joints represent constrained motions such as drawer sliding. The orange and jelly use GPU finite-element models: the orange applies explicit contact and rest offsets, and the jelly uses the elastic material of its asset. Whiteboard Wiping approximates erasure by accumulating force-weighted coverage over ink cells: contact force is projected onto the board normal, force and motion deadbands are applied, and a cell disappears once its coverage reaches a threshold, so the rendered board shows the remaining ink. This is a simulation proxy rather than a measured material-removal law. Dimensions and masses follow physical measurements (Section
4.3
); parameters that could not be measured, such as the jelly’s elastic coefficients, are estimates.
Outcome measurement.
The automatic evaluator uses simulator-side quantities that are not part of the model’s observations: filtered contact-force matrices for gripper–object and support contacts, soft-object displacement and gripper proximity, and the ink-cell states of Whiteboard Wiping. Proximity alone is not treated as a contact-force measurement.
