Appendix C
Evaluation Protocol Details
C.1
Basic Skills Description
Basic Skills provide the interface description and general operating guidance for real-world execution (Section
5.2
). They are made available to Codex before each session and remain unchanged across trials. Figure
S1
summarizes their content in condensed form. The guidance is task-agnostic: it specifies how to read the embodiment and interface, observe and verify physical outcomes, coordinate the two arms, and recover locally, but not how to complete any evaluation task.
Basic Skills for Real-World Execution
Task, interface, and embodiment
–
Identify the objects, goal, arm roles, permitted contacts, prohibited actions, and completion criteria
from the task instruction
.
–
Read enable and hold/motion states, faults, feedback freshness, target and measured joint values, tracking error, and gripper opening. Confirm control ownership and live images.
–
Verify arm identities, command frames and units, tool length, gripper geometry, and tabletop position. Image left–right does not determine robot-coordinate directions. Use the deployed limits, not
historical case-specific values
.
Active visual observation
–
Verify the overview and physical left- and right-wrist views from live images. Use the overview for scene and arm clearance, and wrist views for grasping and local contact.
–
Resolve occlusion with complementary views. If needed, hold the working arm and move the empty observation arm along a checked path, accounting for its links, gripper, and cables.
–
Inspect fresh images before selecting the next action. If observations become stale, refresh them and reassess the action. Do not infer physical insertion or contact from image overlap alone.
Gripper control and grasp verification
–
Treat gripper opening as a position target, not a force command. Align height and depth before gradual closure; further closure cannot compensate for fingers that do not surround the object.
–
Verify grasping from the object’s response to subsequent permitted motion. A closing command, completed arm motion, or reached joint target alone does not establish a stable grasp.
Segmented motion and contact verification
–
Raise and reorient in clear space, then approach in bounded segments. Reduce increments near the tabletop, objects, or the other gripper, while preserving the deployed motion limits.
–
Check feedback before each segment; monitor faults, tracking error, and feedback freshness during execution. Afterwards, hold and inspect the views before continuing.
–
Compare the object, its support, and the surrounding scene before and after motion. Check whether the intended displacement or contact occurred and whether support, alignment, and stability were maintained.
Dual-arm coordination
–
Plan from a consistent current state and check clearance throughout the motion, including links, tools, and cables. Single-arm reachability does not establish collision-free dual-arm motion.
–
Concurrent requests do not imply synchronized hardware execution.
Stopping and local recovery
–
Stop advancing if motion is blocked, objects slip or tilt, arms approach each other, or contact becomes unclear. Use the verified stop/hold mechanism for abnormal conditions.
–
Reassess depth, contact location, object support, and viewpoint before retrying. Regrasp or retreat only when support and the path are clear; do not repeatedly close or lift at the same failed grasp.
–
Resume only with new evidence supporting the correction. Replan from the current state rather than replaying a trajectory or blindly returning home. Preserve holding when disabling could cause an arm to sag.
Completion verification
–
Verify the final goal, required constraints, and object stability. Inspect actual boundaries and support from complementary views; an upper-surface projection alone may not establish the object’s footprint.
–
Report completion as unconfirmed when evidence is insufficient. State whether the grippers have withdrawn and whether either arm remains enabled or has an active trajectory.
Execution report
Report the outcome, supporting observations, corrections, remaining uncertainty, and final arm/hold state. Distinguish measured feedback from visual judgments.
Figure S1:
Basic Skills for real-world execution.
The guidance covers embodiment checks, active observation, gripper control, contact verification, dual-arm coordination, recovery, and completion assessment.
C.2
Trial Execution and Model Calls
Initial states and resets.
Simulated initial states are defined by saved scenes and layout configurations. Some layouts are generated from random seeds, checked for geometry and reachability, and then saved; others apply predefined pose transformations or use separate scene files. Each episode loads its configuration, resets and settles the scene, and then obtains the first observation; run records preserve the loaded configuration. In the real world, an operator manually restores object placement, supports or fixtures, and mechanical engagement to the initial conditions in Appendix
A
, using a fixed set of object instances with repeated copies where needed. Real and simulated initial states thus follow the same task specifications, but exact object poses are not matched one-to-one.
Budgets and continuations.
By default, a simulated episode is limited to 150 model calls and 5 hours of wall-clock time. Real-world episodes have no preset time or model-call limit and end when the model reports completion or judges the task infeasible; the latter counts as failure. Trials also terminate on an operator stop or takeover, or a protective stop (Section
5.3
). Continuations resume unfinished episodes with their interaction history and remain within the same trial; simulation budgets are not replenished. Independently reset executions are new trials. An operator may stop the robot after confirming autonomous completion; completion that requires operator assistance does not count as autonomous success.
Model context in simulation.
Each simulated decision is a separate Codex CLI call with tool use and Skill discovery disabled. The fixed model instructions contain the interface description, general operating guidance, arm roles, and a brief initial-state note. Each call carries the full text history of the episode, the current images, and images from the two most recent decisions; history is cleared between episodes.
Model calls.
A model call is one inference request actually issued to the model; tool invocations, robot actions, controller updates, and calls made during Skills preparation are not counted, and calls in continuation segments belong to the original episode. Table
S3
reports mean model calls per task for reference only: the environments differ in execution granularity (one structured action per simulated call versus several tool calls per real-world action), termination limits, and counting methods, so the counts are not directly comparable.

C.3
Bottleneck Criteria and Outcome Qualifications
Table
S4
lists the observable evidence, drawn from execution videos, action records, and robot feedback, used to assign the interaction bottlenecks in Section
6.4
. Assignment is qualitative: a trial may show several bottlenecks, and budget exhaustion or protective stops are termination conditions, not bottlenecks.
Reported outcome qualifications.
Both environments apply the success criteria in Appendix
A
. Simulation checks them automatically with fixed, executable conditions (Appendix
B.2
), whereas real-world outcomes are judged visually by a human observer and therefore involve subjective judgment. This mainly affects Charger Alignment (Section
6.2
), where trials were accepted and manually terminated once alignment appeared adequate, and Whiteboard Wiping, where trials were accepted once the writing appeared erased overall even if faint marks remained. Real-world outcomes of these tasks may thus vary slightly with the observer’s judgment.
Table S4:
Observable evidence for the four interaction bottlenecks.
Bottleneck
Observable evidence
Spatial reasoning and execution precision
Object localization is achieved, but relative orientation, placement, alignment, or motion planning does not realize the spatial relationship required for the task.
Contact configuration selection and establishment
The chosen contact location or orientation does not provide an accessible, stable, and effective interaction under the relevant geometry and material constraints.
Force regulation
Action records and physical responses indicate difficulty controlling the task-required effects of contact forces or torques on motion or deformation, beyond ordinary support, transport, and geometric placement. A missed grasp or final-state instability alone is insufficient.
Coordination within and across interactions
Contact configuration and force regulation fail jointly within an interaction, or successive actions do not adapt to changing physical states and accumulate into task completion.

article.headline: GPT-6 Astra 接触操作在 L3 全部失败
article.lede: 16 项家务任务分三层、模拟与真实各三次试验：GPT-6 Astra 零样本 L1 成功率 80.0%，L3 为零。
article.problem: 通用基础模型在接触密集型操作上的表现越来越受关注，但总体成功率无法说明究竟是哪些物理交互要求卡住了执行。作者要回答两件事：随着接触要求逐级加码，GPT-6 Astra 能完成哪些任务；在仿真中观察到的能力与瓶颈，能否在真实世界中重现。
article.method: 作者构建 PhysLadder：16 项家务任务按累积要求分为三层——L1 只需选择接触并做几何对齐，L2 增加持续接触中的力调节，L3 还要求接触重构与力调节协同。每项任务都在物理与视觉匹配的仿真（Isaac Sim）与真实环境（两台 ARX R5 加双指夹爪、一外置两腕部相机）中各运行 3 次，任务定义与成功判据共享。GPT-6 Astra 以零样本方式闭环执行，只有三路 RGB 视图与本体反馈，没有深度图和接触力传感器，力调节只能通过运动指令和夹爪开合实现。
article.results: 真实世界成功率从 L1 的 80.0% 降至 L2 的 47.6%、L3 的 0.0%；仿真对应为 66.7%、47.6%、0.0%。整体成功率真实 45.8%（22/48）、仿真 41.7%（20/48），16 项任务中有 10 项在两环境成功次数完全相同，其余 6 项相差一次成功（共 3 次试验）。L3 四个任务（拧瓶盖、拧螺母、推转书堆、扫积木）在任一环境都没有完整成功，尽管部分执行出现局部进展。
article.why_it_matters: 这说明现成的前沿模型在语义理解与抓取放置上已经可用，但在需要持续接触、力调节和接触切换的任务上存在明确断层。分层且匹配的仿真基准若对同一模型能复现真实瓶颈，就有希望替代部分真机试验，用于可重复、可扩展的评测。
article.limitations: 作者自己承认，16 项任务、每项每环境仅 3 次试验，真机资源限制了统计精度，且仿真与真实的对应只在 GPT-6 Astra 上做了描述性比较，能否预测其他模型尚未验证。评测也无法分离模型决策、感知与机器人执行各自的贡献，Charger Alignment 与 Whiteboard Wiping 等任务的真机结果还依赖人工目视判定。
article.figure_caption_zh: 真实实验装置：两台 ARX R5 机械臂配双指夹爪共享桌面工作区，由一台外置 Orbbec Gemini Pro 相机和两台腕部 Orbbec Gemini 305 相机提供三路视角，照片拍摄于放置任务物体之前。

The external-camera mount is visible at left; the inset identifies the camera used. (b) Left and (c) right wrist cameras with their two-finger grippers. journals.title: Nerve activity initiates autoimmune hair loss
journals.summary:
Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03258-x

Understanding the triggers of autoimmunity might lead to better therapies, with hair loss among the conditions for which underpinning factors have come to light.
journals.blurb: 《Nature》刊文指出，神经活动可启动自身免疫性脱发，为理解自身免疫触发机制提供了新线索。该发现有望帮助开发更精准的治疗策略，值得关注其后续机制研究与转化进展。

journals.title: Women might have invented language — but not alone
journals.summary:
Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03392-6

An eloquent analysis of the origins of human speech suggests that social cohesion, not conflict, drove our use of words.
journals.blurb: 《Nature》刊出的一篇分析探讨人类言语的起源，作者提出推动我们使用词语的可能是社会凝聚力，而非冲突。文章以富有说服力的论证重新审视语言如何在社会互动中形成，对关注语言与交流的计算研究者亦有启发。
